meaning: Or something, Any... (with question words), No matter (who)
summary: A word used for expressing undetermined possibilities or choices.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About でも
text: でも is one of many adverbial particles in Japanese. These are particles that behave like a regular {助詞|じょし} (in that they appear after the words that they are referencing), but their role is a little bit more specific. でも itself has several uses, and the use that we will examine in this grammar point is called {例示|れいじ}. Basically this means 'presenting examples'.
In English, this results in a translation similar to 'even', or 'or something'. To use this structure, simply attach でも to the end of any noun, or pronoun.

When grouped with a standard noun as above, でも is just showing that the noun is an example/suggestion, and that there are other choices/possibilities available. However, when the noun is a word like {誰|だれ}, どこ, {何|なん}, or いつ, the translation becomes much closer to English words like 'anyone', 'anywhere', 'anything', or 'anytime'.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: When grouped with {何|なに}, the pronunciation will almost always change to なん. This is purely to make なんでも easier to say.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: もしも～なら・もしも～でも (N3, If, Supposing): もしも～なら and もしも～でも emphasize a hypothetical situation, similar to 'supposing that (A)' or 'even if (A)' in English. Separately, でも can attach to question words to mean 'any~', e.g. 誰でも 'anyone' and なんでも 'anything', or follow regular nouns to suggest a casual option, as in お茶でも飲みませんか？ ('Want some tea or something?').

か (N5, Or): The particle か can follow nouns to mean 'or,' clearly specifying alternatives (e.g., 今日か明日休みます = 'I'll take off today or tomorrow'). On the other hand, でも, which also follows nouns, means 'or something,' suggesting an open-ended alternative (e.g., お茶でも飲みましょうか = 'Shall we drink tea or something?').

か何か (N2, Or something, Or something like that): Both か何か and でも can suggest alternatives, like 'or something' in English. か何か places more emphasis on the idea of other specific options, e.g. お茶か何か飲みませんか？ ('How about some tea or something else?'), while でも is vaguer and implies the suggestion is just one of many possibilities, e.g. お茶でも飲みませんか？ ('How about some tea or something?').

誰か・どこか・誰も・どこも (N5, Someone, Somewhere, Not anyone, Not anywhere): The 誰か・どこか・誰も・どこも pattern combines question words like 誰 ('who') and どこ ('where') with particles to express ideas like 'someone' or 'somewhere.' Similarly, でも can also be attached to question words to express the idea of 'anyone' (誰でも), 'anywhere' (どこでも), and so forth.

ても (N4, Even if, Even though): The particle でも can attach to question words to mean 'any~' as in 誰でも 'anyone' or なんでも 'anything', or follow nouns to suggest a casual option, like in お茶でも飲みませんか？ ('Want some tea or something?'). This looks similar to ても, which becomes でも after nouns and な-adjectives, but means 'even if', as in 日本語でも大丈夫です ('It's fine even if it's in Japanese.').

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About やすい
text: {易|やす}い is an い-Adjective that is regularly seen attached to the ます stem of verbs (the form of a verb that can be used as a noun). When attached in this way, it carries the meaning of 'easy to (A)', where (A) is the verb that comes before やすい.
Sometimes, やすい has a translation that is a bit closer to 'prone to (A)', or 'likely to (A)' in English. This nuance is regularly seen when the verb is related to emotions.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: There is another adjective {安|やす}い that has the meaning of 'cheap'. This kanji should never be used with verbs to mean 'easy'. Most of the time, やすい itself will be written in hiragana, and usage of {易|やす}い is quite limited.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: にくい (N4, Difficult to, Hard to): やすい and にくい express opposite ideas: 'easy to do' and 'hard to do.' Both attach to verb stems, e.g. 食べやすい 'easy to eat' and 食べにくい 'hard to eat', and function as い-adjectives, meaning they can be seen with tenses like 食べやすかった 'was easy to eat', and modify nouns like with 食べやすい果物 'an easy-to-eat fruit'.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About にくい
text: Like {易|やす}い, にくい is an い-Adjective that is regularly attached to the ます stem of verbs. However, instead of meaning 'easy to (A)', it means 'difficult to (A)'. (A) will always represent the verb that comes before にくい.

The nuance of にくい is that (A) is a task that is difficult to do, because of the required skill level, or similar factors. This is different from づらい, which focuses more on a task that is difficult due to being unbearable/hard to endure for some reason.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: An easy way to remember the difference in nuance between にくい and づらい, is that にくい comes from the same kanji as {難|むずか}しい, which usually carries the meaning of 'difficulty' (in relation to skill being required).

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: がたい (N3, Hard to, Difficult to): がたい and にくい both attach to verb stems and express the idea of 'difficult to do', but with different nuance and formality levels. にくい is used in everyday speech and reflects the speaker's personal sense of difficulty or discomfort. がたい is more formal/written-style and implies something is nearly impossible or extremely difficult due to factors beyond the speaker's control.

やすい (N4, Easy to, Likely to): やすい and にくい express opposite ideas: 'easy to do' and 'hard to do.' Both attach to verb stems, e.g. 食べやすい 'easy to eat' and 食べにくい 'hard to eat', and function as い-adjectives, meaning they can be seen with tenses like 食べやすかった 'was easy to eat', and modify nouns like with 食べやすい果物 'an easy-to-eat fruit'.

sections.heading: About づらい
text: Like にくい, づらい is an い-Adjective that attaches to the ます stem of verbs to express that something is 'difficult to do'. meaning: Gradually, Little by little, Step by step
summary: A phrase showing that (A) is gradually increasing, step by step.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About だんだん
text: だんだん is an adverb that is used to express the slight, but constant, progression of something. Originally, it comes from the kanji construction {段々|だんだん}, which can be thought of as meaning 'step by step', 'stepwise', or even 'steadily'. だんだん is similar to ほとんど, in that it can modify the meaning of entire phrases, rather than just single words.
To use だんだん, simply put it before the phrase that you want to express as '(A) that is increasing steadily'.
While だんだん can take the particle と, it is not required. In fact, と is very often omitted from adverbs/onomatopoeic words (words that represent a sound or motion) in Japanese.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: どんどん (N4, Progressively, Rapidly increasing, More and more): だんだん and どんどん are similar-sounding adverbs that both describe change over time, but with different nuances. だんだん suggests a slow, step-by-step progression, like 'gradually' or 'bit by bit'. どんどん implies faster, more dynamic change; something happening quickly or in leaps and bounds.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About どんどん
text: どんどん (or ドンドン) is one of the countless words in Japanese that represent a particular sound or sensation. These words are known as onomatopoeia (オノマトペ in Japanese). どんどん represents the sound of banging (like on a drum), or the pounding of feet. In this way, it is regularly translated as 'rapidly', or 'quickly'.
Like だんだん, どんどん may be used before almost any phrase.
While どんどん can take the particle と, it is not required. In fact, と is very often omitted from adverbs/onomatopoeic words in Japanese.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: When the と particle is used with onomatopoeic words, it is very similar to one of と's main usages as a quotation marker in Japanese. This means that と has a similar role to words like 'went', or 'goes' in English. For example, In English, we would say:
The door 'goes' BANG with the wind.
However, the door doesn't actually 'go' anywhere. This is similar to what と is doing here.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: どんどん - Swift change, だんだん - Gradual change

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: 一方だ (N3, More and more, Continue to, Keep on, -er and -er): どんどん is an adverb that implies rapid or dramatic change, often in leaps and bounds, and is common in everyday speech. In contrast, 一方だ is more formal and used to describe ongoing change that continues beyond the speaker's control. Structurally, 一方だ follows the verb, unlike どんどん, which appears before it.

ば〜ほど (N3, The more…the more): どんどん is an adverb that implies rapid or dramatic change, often in leaps and bounds, e.g. どんどん大きくなる 'grow rapidly'. 〜ば〜ほど is a structure that shows proportional change, like 'the more (A), the more (B)' in English. For example, 大きくなればなるほどいい ('The bigger it gets, the better.').

だんだん (N4, Gradually, Little by little, Step by step): だんだん and どんどん are similar-sounding adverbs that both describe change over time, but with different nuances. だんだん suggests a slow, step-by-step progression, like 'gradually' or 'bit by bit'. どんどん implies faster, more dynamic change; something happening quickly or in leaps and bounds.

ますます (N3, Increasingly, More and more, Decreasingly, Less and less, Keep -ing): どんどん and ますます are both adverbs used to describe change over time. どんどん emphasizes rapid progress or sudden development, often in leaps and bounds. ますます focuses on something already in a certain state becoming even more so, and is often used in polite expressions like wishes for continued health or success.

summary: A casual suffix which is used to identify groups of (A), by stating (A) and etc.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ～ら
text: There are many prefixes and suffixes in Japanese that are used depending on what the speaker wants to highlight. ら is a suffix (component used after the main part of a word) that implies that there is 'more than one' of something. Due to this, ら is often called a 'pluralizing suffix'. ら comes from the same kanji as {等|など}, and the literal meaning is closer to '(A) etc'.
This 'etc' is where the implication of 'more than one' originates. To use ら, attach it to the end of any pronoun.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Because ら has a literal meaning that is close to '(A) etc', or '(A) and so on', it may sometimes be considered a bit rude (due to being dismissive). Because of this, it is recommended to not use this suffix in relation to people, unless it is absolutely essential to indicate plural. In most cases, {達|たち} will be a far better choice.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Spoken casual, may be considered rude

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: と (N5, And): ら is often called a pluralizing suffix, and is used after nouns to mean '(A) and others'. と, on the other hand, is a particle that links nouns like 'and' in English. ら can follow a single noun and implies a group with the other members not mentioned, while と connects multiple items and lists all members explicitly.

や (N5, Things like, And the like): ら is a pluralizing suffix that attaches to nouns to mean '(A) and others'. や is a particle that links multiple nouns, similar to 'and' in English. While ら can follow a single noun, や must connect two or more. Both imply the presence of other people or things not explicitly mentioned.

meaning: To ~ and go, To go on, To start
summary: A phrase that is used to describe that an action will be completed before performing the next action.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ていく
text: This grammar construction is a mix of the conjunction particle て, and the verb {行|い}く 'to go'. To use this grammar point, you will need to attach て to any verb, and then follow it with いく.
This nuance is usually that '(A) happened and then went', or 'will happen, and then go'. In other words, it will depend on whether いく is in present, or past tense.

ていく can be used when representing time, or when representing a physical place. When representing a physical place, it is more likely that the kanji structure, {行|い}く will be used. However, this is not a set rule, and depends on the writer.
When used in relation to time, the nuance is usually that something has already started/is about to start, and then will continue to progress in the same way.
This is the opposite of てくる, which indicates that something has finally reached a certain state, after progressing in that way for some time.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: When compared to English, ていく is very similar to the phrase 'to go on to (A)', in relation to time. It focuses on the fact that the speaker is required to make some type of journey to arrive at a specific point. For example, 'She went on to become a doctor after university'.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: てくる (N4, To come to, To become, To continue, To be starting to, Has been ~ing): てくる and ていく combine the て-form of a verb with 来る or 行く to express movement or change over time. てくる suggests movement toward the speaker or a change that started in the past and leads up to now. ていく implies movement away from the speaker or a change that begins now and continues into the future.

へいく (N5, To go to, To head toward): The verb いく expresses movement in a direction, literally or figuratively. へいく is used after nouns to indicate moving toward a place (e.g., 学校へいく = 'go to school'). When used as ていく (Verb + て + いく), it implies a continuing action or change moving forward. Note that いく is written in kanji as 行く when used alone, but typically in hiragana in the ていく form.

Verb + にいく (N5, To go ~, To go in order to ~): Verb + にいく combines the verb stem with にいく to express going somewhere to do something (e.g., 食べに行く = 'go to eat'). In contrast, ていく (Verb + て + いく) expresses sequential actions (e.g., 食べて行く = 'eat, then go') or actions that progress over time (e.g., 上手くなっていく = 'get better over time').

はじめる (N4, To start, To begin to): ていく expresses either literal movement away from the speaker or a change that begins now and continues into the future. In contrast, はじめる attaches to the verb stem to mean 'to start (A)'. The key difference is nuance: ていく highlights ongoing progression and continuation going forward, while はじめる focuses on the starting point and the idea of commencing an action.

meaning: To come to, To become, To continue, To be starting to, Has been ~ing
summary: A phrase used when a specific event is coming, or has come to be a certain way.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About てくる
text: This grammar point is a combination of the conjunction particle て, and the verb {来|く}る 'to come'. To use this grammar point, you will need to attach て to any verb, and then follow it with くる. This nuance is usually that '(A) happened, and then came', or 'will happen, and then come'. In other words, it will depend on whether くる is in present, or past tense.

てくる can be used when representing time, or when representing a physical place. When representing a physical place, it is more likely that the kanji structure, {来|く}る will be used. However, this is not a set rule, and depends on the writer.
When used in relation to time, the nuance is usually that something has already come to pass, or will start to happen from now.
This is the opposite of ていく, which indicates that something will change from the way that it is now, or will continue progressing in a certain way.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: When compared to English, てくる is very similar to the phrase 'to have come to (A)', in relation to time. This means that it focuses on the fact that the speaker will 'become (A)', should things continue in a specific way. In practice though, it is used like 'gotten' in most situations.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: つづける (N4, To continue): Both つづける and てくる can show the progression of an action over time. つづける attaches to the verb stem and focuses on the continuation of the action itself. てくる uses the て-form and emphasizes that the action started in the past and has continued up to the present.

ていく (N4, To ~ and go, To go on, To start): てくる and ていく combine the て-form of a verb with 来る or 行く to express movement or change over time. てくる suggests movement toward the speaker or a change that started in the past and leads up to now. ていく implies movement away from the speaker or a change that begins now and continues into the future.

ばかりだ (N3, (Only) continue to, Keep on -ing, More and more): ばかりだ attaches to the dictionary (non-past) form of a verb and is used to show that an action, often a negative one, keeps happening or is the only thing happening. In contrast, てくる combines the て-form of a verb with くる to describe an action that began in the past and has continued to the present. Unlike ばかりだ, てくる can be used for both positive and negative situations.

くる (N5, To come): The verb くる commonly expresses movement toward the speaker, similar to the English 'come.' When combined with the て form of a verb, it can be used literally (e.g., 持ってくる = 'bring') or figuratively to express progression or change over time, like the English 'come to be' (e.g., 雨が降ってくる = 'it will come to rain').

～になる・～くなる (N5, To become (Adjective)): Both ～になる／～くなる and てくる describe changes in state but differ in usage. ～になる／～くなる are used with nouns and adjectives to show something becoming a certain condition. てくる, used with verbs, suggests a gradual change over time. They can also be combined. For example, 面白くなってきた means 'It gradually became interesting.'

meaning: Way of ~ing, How to ~, Manner of ~ing
summary: A common structure highlighting the way in which (A) is done.
formation: ［する］Verb + の + 仕方（しかた）
Noun + の + Verb［stem］+ 方（かた）
飲（の）みます + 方（かた）
勉強（べんきょう）+ の + 仕方（しかた）

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About かた
text: When {方|かた} is attached to the ます stem of a verb, it carries the nuance of the 'way of doing (A)'. This is identical to {方|かた}'s standard meaning of 'way', or 'direction'.

When used with する verbs, sometimes the construction {仕方|しかた} is seen. This has exactly the same meaning as the form without kanji, and may be thought of as meaning 'way of dealing/attending to (A)', as {仕|し}'s original meaning is 'to attend to (A)'. In these cases, the する verb is followed by の, and then {仕方|しかた}.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: たほうがいい (N5, It'd be better to, Should do): かた and たほうがいい are distinct grammar patterns both containing 方 (which can be read as かた or ほう) but have different meanings and structures. かた attaches to the verb stem and means 'way of doing (A)' or 'how to (A)', e.g. 書き方 'way of writing' or 'how to write'. In contrast, たほうがいい connects to the past tense of a verb and is used to give advice or make suggestions.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About だけで
text: だけで is a combination of the adverbial particle だけ, and the case marking particleで. This expression is regularly thought of as meaning 'just by (A), (B)'. However, the literal translation is a bit closer to 'with only (A), (B)'. This reflects the で particle's standard usage of showing a 'tool' that is being used to achieve a certain result.
To use だけで, simply attach it to the end of any (non ます) form of verb, or noun.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: だけ differs from しか in one very important way. だけ highlights that there is/was more than one option, but that only one thing was chosen/used. However, しか implies that there is only one possible option to begin with.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: だけあって (N2, Is only natural, …Being the case, Because, As might be expected): だけあって and だけで may look similar, but they have distinct meanings. だけあって is used when a result is seen as natural or expected, similar to 'as you'd expect from (A)'. This is close in nuance to a separate expression, だけに. In contrast, だけで expresses that something is 'enough' to accomplish something else, like 'just by (A)' or 'only with (A)' in English.

だけ (N5, Only, Just): だけ conveys the meaning of 'only' or 'just.' だけで is the combination of だけ with the particle で, conveying the idea of the manner or means by which something is done. だけで expresses 'just by' or 'merely with' (literally, 'with/using only A'). It typically follows either nouns or verbs, suggesting that the thing or action was the only thing needed to achieve a certain result.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About だが・ですが
text: While だが (or ですが as a polite equivalent) are classified as their own words, they are actually just combinations of だ, or です, and が. だが is usually used as a formal way of saying 'but', or 'nevertheless'. Due to this, we can see that だ is being used to 'determine' that a statement is true, while が simply shows that there is other important information to follow.
In this way, だが is very similar to the expression 'that may be, but…' in English. だが may be used at the beginning of any phrase, or between sentences.
To make だが sound a little bit softer, sometimes ね is added. However, this is not so common in modern-day Japanese, and is more limited to the older generation.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: Due to だが and ですが using が (the formal equivalent of けど), this phrase can sound quite stiff. Therefore, it is far more common to hear でも at the beginning of a sentence in casual speech.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: それでも (N4, But still, And yet, Even so, Nevertheless): Both それでも and だが・ですが express contrast, similar to 'but' or 'however' in English, but with different nuances. それでも highlights a result or situation that goes against expectations. だが・ですが is more neutral and often used to transition to a contrasting point. Structurally, だが・ですが can appear mid-sentence or at the end of a clause, while それでも typically begins a sentence.

けど・だけど (N5, But, However): Both けど・だけど (and the polite ですけど), as well as だが・ですが, express contrast, similar to 'but,' or sometimes just indicate a transition (like 'and'). The key difference is that だが is more formal and used in written contexts, while けど is more casual. Both can be used at the end of a sentence to imply something is left unsaid.

けれども (N5, But, Although): Both of these are linking phrases used to express contrast in Japanese. だが and ですが sound a bit stiffer than けれども or the more casual けど, and must follow a noun or な-adjective (in contrast, けれども would become だけれども in this case). Besides showing contrast, both が and けれども (or けれど・けど) can also be used to add background information without directly meaning 'but'.

ところが (N3, Even so, However, Even though, But): Both だが・ですが and ところが express contrast, but with different nuances. だが・ですが is a neutral transition similar to 'but' or 'however,' and can appear in various positions within a sentence. ところが usually comes at the start of a sentence and emphasizes an unexpected or surprising result, often appearing in storytelling or narration.

が (N5, But, However): The particle が in both patterns expresses contrast, similar to 'but' in English, or sometimes indicates a transition to additional information (like 'and'). The difference is that が follows directly after an い-Adjective or verb, while it requires だ or です after a な-Adjective or noun. が is somewhat formal and often used in writing or formal speech.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About なくて
text: In Japanese, なくて is a construction that combines ない (in its conjugation form, なく), with the conjunction particle て. This results in the same 'and' meaning as the standard て form, but with the negative meaning of ない. なくて can be translated as 'to not (A), and…', or 'not (A), and…', depending on what type of word it is used with.

As discussed in our initial lesson about ない, there are two forms of this particular word. One form is an auxiliary verb, and is used with verbs. The other form of ない is an い-Adjective ({形容詞|けいようし}), and is used with nouns, な-Adjectives, and い-Adjectives.

The difference between these two, is that the い-Adjective form may have は in between it and the word it is connected to (では in the case of nouns and な-Adjectives). With verbs, due to ない being an auxiliary verb, this is not possible.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: Adjective + て・Noun + で (N5, And... (Conjunctive)): Adjective + て or Noun + で is used to connect adjective or noun phrases with the rest of the sentence, similar to the English 'and.' なくて is similar, but connects phrases that are in the negative (ない) form. For example, 安くてよかった means 'I'm glad it was inexpensive,' while 高くなくてよかった would mean 'I'm glad that it wasn't expensive'.

ないで (N4, Without doing, Not ~ and ~): ないで and なくて are both negative connecting forms, but with different uses. ないで is used in negative requests or to mean 'without doing' something, e.g. 食べないでください ('Please don't eat it.'). and 朝ご飯を食べないで学校に行った ('I went to school without eating breakfast.'). なくて connects clauses to describe reasons or states, similar to 'and', e.g. 高くなくて便利です ('It's not expensive, and it's convenient.').

ではなくて・じゃなくて (N3, Not A but B, Conjunctive): ではなくて (formal) and じゃなくて (casual) are used to connect negative forms of nouns and な-adjectives, while なくて is used with verbs and い-adjectives. For example, 先生ではなくて、学生です ('He's not a teacher, but a student.') and 弟にはあげなくて、妹にあげた ('I didn't give it to my brother, but to my sister.').

meaning: Not ~ and, Not so, Because not (Examples)
summary: A casual, simple negative conjunctive form, indicating (A) as being the reason or cause for (B).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About なくて
text: In Japanese, なくて is a construction that combines ない (in its conjugation form, なく), with the conjunction particle て. This results in the same 'and' meaning as the standard て form, but with the negative meaning of ない.

なくて is often used when the phrase that comes before it is being highlighted as an example/reason for a specific result. In these situations, the translation is usually 'because not (A), (B)', or 'because I didn't (A), (B)'.

When なくて is used in this way, it is often followed by the speaker's feelings (in the form of an adjective), verbs in the potential form, or something that is generally beyond the control of the speaker. It is due to this fact that the result is 'beyond control' that the translation becomes 'because'.

Some examples of words that express things beyond the control of the speaker are {困|こま}る (to be troubled), {嬉|うれ}しい (to be happy), {疲|つか}れている (to feel weary), {心配|しんぱい} (to feel anxiety/worry), {安心|あんしん} (to feel relief).

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: Verb[て] + B (N4, And・and so, Due to, Because of, Since, Conjunctive): Both structures use the て-form to express cause or reason. Verb [て] + B uses the affirmative form to explain a positive reason, e.g. 行けてよかったです ('I'm glad I could go.'). In contrast, なくて is the て-form of the negative ない and expresses a negative reason, e.g. 行けなくて残念でした ('It was unfortunate I couldn't go.').

ないで (N4, Without doing, Not ~ and ~): ないで and なくて are both connecting forms of ない, but with different uses. ないで is used in negative requests or to mean 'without doing' something, e.g. 食べないでください ('Please don't eat it.') and 朝ご飯を食べないで学校に行った ('I went to school without eating breakfast.'). なくて can express a reason or cause, e.g. 行けなくて残念でした ('I couldn't go, which was disappointing.').

ではなくて・じゃなくて (N3, Not A but B, Conjunctive): ではなくて (formal) and じゃなくて (casual) are used with nouns and な-adjectives, while なくて is used with verbs and い-adjectives. Both connect negative forms to another idea and can express cause or reason. For example, 便利じゃなくて残念です ('It's unfortunate it's not convenient.') vs. 行けなくて残念です ('It's unfortunate I couldn't go.').

summary: A common way to indicate that (B) will be done without doing (A).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ないで
text: There are two primary ways in which ないで is used with verbs in Japanese. The first is to express 'without doing (A), (B)'. The second is to request that someone 'not do (A)'. We will examine the first in this write-up.
ないで is a combination of the auxiliary verb ない, and the particle で. Due to this, で keeps its standard meaning of 'with/by', in relation to 'not' doing something.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: なくて (N4, To not ~ and ~, Not ~ and ~ (Conjugations)): ないで and なくて are both negative connecting forms, but with different uses. ないで is used in negative requests or to mean 'without doing' something, e.g. 食べないでください ('Please don't eat it.'). and 朝ご飯を食べないで学校に行った ('I went to school without eating breakfast.'). なくて connects clauses to describe reasons or states, similar to 'and', e.g. 高くなくて便利です ('It's not expensive, and it's convenient.').

なくて (N4, Not ~ and, Not so, Because not (Examples)): ないで and なくて are both connecting forms of ない, but with different uses. ないで is used in negative requests or to mean 'without doing' something, e.g. 食べないでください ('Please don't eat it.') and 朝ご飯を食べないで学校に行った ('I went to school without eating breakfast.'). なくて can express a reason or cause, e.g. 行けなくて残念でした ('I couldn't go, which was disappointing.').

ともなく・ともなしに (N1, Absentmindedly, Mindlessly, Unconsciously, Without paying attention): Though these two phrases appear similar in form, both suggesting 'without doing', they differ in that ともなく・ともなしに is used figuratively to express that the action was performed, but in an absentminded manner, or ‘without even so much as the intention of doing (A), (B)’, e.g. 見るともなく見ていたら 'as I was absentmindedly looking...' whereas ないで literally means that action was not performed, e.g. 見ないでやる 'do without looking'.

ずに (N3, Without doing): ないで and ずに both express the idea of 'without doing (A)' and are used in similar ways. For example, 朝ご飯を食べないで学校に行った and 朝ご飯を食べずに学校に行った both mean 'I went to school without eating breakfast.', but ずに has a slightly more formal or literary tone, while ないで is more conversational. Unlike ないで, ずに cannot be used as a negative request form to say 'Don't (A).'.

な (N5, Do not, Don't (Prohibitive)): The dictionary/non-past form of a verb + な expresses a blunt command not to do something. Similarly, ないで attached to the negative stem of a verb is a more casual and gentle request. For example, するな is a strong way of saying 'Don't do it!' while しないで is a softer, more casual way of saying '[Please] don't do it.'

てください (N5, Please do (Polite request)): 〜てください is a polite way to say 'Please do (something),' as in 食べてください ('Please eat'). Its negative form, 〜ないで, means 'Don't do (something),' as in 食べないで ('Don't eat'). To make this negative request polite, simply add ください, as in 食べないでください means 'Please don't eat.'

Verb[ないで] (N4, (Please) do not (for me), Casual request): The ないで form combines a verb in the negative with で, and has two common uses: (1) to make a negative request, e.g. 食べないで ('Don't eat it.'), and (2) to express 'without doing' something, e.g. 晩ご飯を食べないで出かけた ('I went out without eating dinner.').

ないでください (N5, Please don't (Polite request)): ないでください is a polite way to ask someone not to do something. The shorter form, ないで, is more casual and typically used with close friends or family. While ないでください is appropriate for strangers or people of equal status, ないで has a softer, more informal tone. Adding the sentence-ending particle ね (e.g. 食べないでね) makes the request even gentler and more caring.

なさい (N4, Command to do): なさい is a firm but polite command form, often used by those in authority (like teachers or parents) toward subordinates. In contrast, ないで is a casual way to ask someone not to do something, e.g. 行かないで ('Don't go.'). It is typically used among close friends or family.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About Verb［れる・られる］
text: In Japanese, there are several ways to express that something 'passively' happens. All of these are done with the auxiliary verbs れる and られる. Japanese verbs in the passive form behave in a slightly different way than they do in English, so we will examine this difference more closely later. For now, let's focus on れる, られる, and される (the form used with する verbs).
Passivity in Japanese means that the person (or thing) that is the target of the action will be the subject of the sentence, rather than the person that is 'doing' whatever verb is being used.

You can conjugate any Japanese verb into the passive form in the following way. For う-Verbs (godan verbs), simply replace the last kana with the equivalent あ sound kana from the same row (す becomes さ, つ becomes た, ぶ becomes ば, う becomes わ, like with ない, and so on), then add れる. For る-Verbs (ichidan verbs), just replace the る with られる.
する and くる behave slightly differently than most other verbs. For する, it will become される, while くる will become こられる.
As can be seen in these examples, the 'doer' of the verb will be marked with に, but から can also be used in cases where there is no physical contact with the subject.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: られる can be used in several different situations. These are listed below.
Passive: {受|う}け{身|み} - Something happens to the subject as a result of an external force (sometimes sounds negative).
Possible: {可能|かのう} - There is the possibility for something to be done.
Spontaneous: {自発|じはつ} - Something happens by itself, or 'without instigation'.
Respectful: {尊敬|そんけい} - You are respecting someone by making them the subject of the sentence, despite someone else actually performing the verb.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: In Japanese, passivity focuses on the lack of control of the subject of the sentence. Due to this, the subject will sometimes be called the なる人, while the doer of the verb is called the する人.

Traditionally, many textbooks use the term 'passive', simply because there is no equivalent verb type in English (passive is the closest). However, we would like to introduce the term 'displacement verb'. This just means that the subject of the sentence is being described in a similar way to what happens in keigo (polite speech).

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: 他動詞・自動詞 (N4, Done through action vs. occurring on its own): 他動詞 (transitive) verbs act on something, while 自動詞 (intransitive) verbs describe actions that happen by themselves. The passive form (Verb［れる・られる］) can make transitive verbs behave like intransitive ones. For example, ケーキを食べた ('I ate cake.') vs. ケーキが食べられた ('The cake was eaten.'). But when the speaker is affected, the object stays, as in 兄にケーキを食べられた ('I had my cake eaten by my brother.').

れる・られる (Potential) (N4, To be able, Can (Potential)): Passive and potential forms have different meanings but can be confusing because some forms overlap. For う-verbs, the forms are distinct. For example, 言われる 'to be said' (passive) vs. 言える means 'can say' (potential). For る-verbs, a form like 食べられる can mean either 'to be eaten' (passive) or 'can eat' (potential), and which is intended must be determined from context.

Verb［せる・させる］ (N4, To make/let/have (somebody do something)): The passive (Verb［れる・られる］) and causative (Verb［せる・させる］) forms are both fundamental in Japanese. The passive shows that an action was done to someone, while the causative means to make or let someone do something. For example, 食べられた 'was eaten' vs. 食べさせた 'made/let someone eat'.

Causative-Passive (N4, Verbs (Causative-passive voice), To be made to do something, To be forced to do): The passive (Verb［れる・られる］) and causative-passive are two key verb forms in Japanese. The passive expresses that an action was done to someone, while the causative-passive means being made or forced to do something. For example, 食べられた 'was eaten' vs. 食べさせられた 'were made to eat'.

れる・られる + ままに (N1, Do as (one is told or ordered…), In accordance with, In compliance with, Just like): The passive form (Verb［れる・られる］) is used to show that an action was done to someone. For example, 言われた means 'was told'. When combined with ままに 'in that state', it can express following instructions exactly, e.g. 言われるままに買った ('I bought it just as I was told.').

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 他動詞・自動詞
text: The two most fundamental divisions that can be made with Japanese verbs are transitive verbs - the subject is moving/acting upon something else, and intransitive verbs - the subject themself is moving/acting. Sometimes these terms are simplified even further to 'other-move' (transitive), and 'self-move' (intransitive).
Basically, this is the difference between verbs that require an object marked with を (transitive verbs), and those that only require が, to show that the subject itself is moving (intransitive).
In Japanese, there are many transitive/intransitive pairs of verbs, and these will need to be memorized.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: In Japanese, the two ways in which all verbs can be described are an act/motion ({動作|どうさ}), and an act/motion upon something ({作用|さよう}).

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: する and なる can also be thought of as a transitive-intransitive pair

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: Verb［れる・られる］ (N4, Was done to ~ by ~, Done without consent, Done to one's dismay): 他動詞 (transitive) verbs act on something, while 自動詞 (intransitive) verbs describe actions that happen by themselves. The passive form (Verb［れる・られる］) can make transitive verbs behave like intransitive ones. For example, ケーキを食べた ('I ate cake.') vs. ケーキが食べられた ('The cake was eaten.'). But when the speaker is affected, the object stays, as in 兄にケーキを食べられた ('I had my cake eaten by my brother.').

Verb［せる・させる］ (N4, To make/let/have (somebody do something)): 他動詞 (transitive) verbs act on something, while 自動詞 (intransitive) verbs describe actions that happen by themselves. The causative form means to make or let someone do something, so intransitive verbs become transitive when changed, e.g. 人が走る 'a person runs' vs. 人を走らせる 'make a person run'.

summary: A common term which indicates that (A) will be redone, or fixed.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About なおす
text: {直|なお}す is a verb that means 'to fix', or 'to redo'. It is used when saying that something needs to be done a second time (usually due to the result/quality being insufficient the first time). To use {直|なお}す, it will need to be attached to the ます stem form of any verb.

With する verbs, the conjugation rules are slightly different. する will become し, and then {直|なお}す will be connected in the regular fashion. In some situations, する may be replaced with やる (a very casual equivalent of する). As やる is a う-Verb, it will be conjugated as やり{直|なお}す.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: {直|なお}す (to fix) should not be confused with {治|なお}す (to heal/mend). The kanji {直|ちょく} literally means 'straight', or 'direct', and implies that one should 'straighten out' something.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: つづける (N4, To continue): なおす can be attached to the stem of other verbs to express the idea of 're-doing' or doing something over. つづける can be attached to verb stems in the same way, but expresses the meaning of 'continuing' to do something. For example, やりなおす means 'to do over', while やりつづける means 'to keep doing'.

summary: A phrase used to create noun-like phrases, or sometimes ask questions about what (A) means.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ということ
text: One of the ways to perform nominalization (turning a phrase into a noun) in Japanese is through the use of the expression ということ. This grammar point is a combination of と (the particle), {言|い}う (the verb), and こと (the noun). Together, the literal translation is close to 'that (A) is said to be'. However, in reality, it sounds far less formal than this.
To use ということ, attach it to the end of any phrase (without です, or ます). In most cases it will be written using hiragana.
In conversation, という is regularly shortened to simply って. This form will be heard/seen much more frequently in conversation/manga and similar things.
ということ is also frequently used when clarifying what someone else has said. In these cases, it translates very similarly to 'you mean that (A)?', or 'you mean to say that (A)?'

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Although the kanji {言|い}う and {事|こと} may be used in this expression, the most common form does not use any kanji at all. This is a regular occurence in Japanese, as many set grammatical structures will not use kanji, simply because it makes the pattern easier to identify.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ということは (N2, That means, That is to say): ということ turns phrases into nouns and is often used to clarify what was said. When followed by は as ということは, it marks the phrase as a topic for further explanation or comment. ということは can also begin a sentence to restate or interpret what came before, like 'So what you're saying is (A)' in English.

こと (N4, Converting a verb into a noun): こと attaches to the dictionary form of verbs to turn them into nouns, e.g. 行くこと '(the act of) going'. ということ has a similar function, but adds the quoting phrase という, so it's often used to clarify information or reported speech, e.g. 日本に行くということ 'the fact that (he) is going to Japan'.

ことなの (N3, (A) is (Description of A), (A) means that (Description of A)): ことなの combines こと with the explanatory ～んです／のです form and is used to give or ask for background with an emphatic, explanatory tone. ということ also turns a phrase into a noun, meaning 'the fact that' or 'the act of (A)', but is typically used to clarify something without the added emphasis of ん／の.

というのは (N3, ~ Known as ~ is, ~ Called ~ is, ~ Means ~, Because): ということ and というのは both turn phrases into nouns. ということ is often used to clarify what was said, while というのは introduces a topic for further explanation or comment. というのは can also start a sentence to mean 'what I mean is (A)' or 'that is to say (A)'.

ということだ (N3, I heard that, Rumor has it that, It is said that, It means that): ということ turns phrases into nouns and often clarifies what was said, e.g. 日本に行くということ 'the fact that he's going to Japan'. Adding だ forms ということだ, which is used to report information second-hand, e.g. 来年から海外に住むということだ ('I hear he'll be living abroad from next year.').

という (N3, Called, Named, Known as, As much as): ということ turns phrases into nouns and is often used to clarify or restate something, e.g. 日本に行くということ 'the fact that (he) is going to Japan'. という by itself links a phrase or name to a noun, as in ポチという犬 'a dog named Pochi' or 来年日本に行くという学生 'a student who is going to Japan'.

summary: A common word, used for highlighting either broad or narrow time frames.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About とき
text: とき, or {時|とき} in kanji, is a noun that is regularly used to signify 'when' something happened (a verb). However, unlike some other time expressions, とき is mainly used to express things that happen at regular intervals (habits, hobbies, etc.), or at broad times/individual events (when it rains, when there is a sale at the shop, etc.)

Using とき is quite easy! You just need to attach it to the end of any independent word (verbs, nouns, or adjectives). As with most cases where a noun will be attached to another word in Japanese, we will also be required to use な after な-Adjectives, and の after nouns. The case-marking particle に will generally come directly after {時|とき}, signifying that another verb is about to follow.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: 最中に (N3, In the middle of): とき expresses the general time of an action or event, like 'when' in English. It can be used with nouns as in 雨の時 'when it rains', verbs as in 父が帰ってきた時 'when Dad came home', or adjectives as in 暑い時 'when it's hot', and can describe one-time or repeated actions. In contrast, 最中に describes something happening right in the middle of another action/event, e.g. 食事の最中に電話がなった ('My phone rang while I was in the middle of eating.').

際に (N2, When, At the time of, In case of, On the occasion of): Both とき and 際に express the time of an action or event, but with different nuances and levels of formality. とき is common in everyday conversation and broadly used, like the English 'when'. 際に is more formal and often appears in official contexts, such as instructions, advice, or warnings related to specific events.

ながら (N4, While ~ing, During, As): とき expresses the time of an action or event, like the English 'when'. It can be used with nouns as in 雨の時 'when it rains', verbs as in 父が帰ってきた時 'when Dad came home', or adjectives as in 暑い時 'when it's hot'. In contrast, ながら is used when doing something while performing another action. It is used only with verbs, and unlike とき, the subject of both phrases must be the same, e.g. 音楽を聴きながら走る 'listen to music while running'.

ているところだ (N4, In the process of doing ~ right now/at this moment): とき expresses the time of an action or event, like 'when' in English. It can be used with nouns as in 雨の時 'when it rains', verbs as in 父が帰ってきた時 'when Dad came home', or adjectives as in 暑い時 'when it's hot'. In contrast, ているところ uses the verb in て-form and emphasizes being in the middle of an action, often with a sense of being busy or focused, e.g. 晩ご飯を食べているところです ('I'm right in the middle of eating dinner.').

と同時に (N3, At the same time as, The instant, The moment, As well as): とき expresses the general time of an action or event, like 'when' in English. と同時に means 'at the same time as' and emphasizes simultaneity. For example, 帰ってきた時 means 'when (I) came home', while 帰ってきたと同時に means 'the moment (I) came home' or 'as soon as (I) came home'.

うちに (N3, While, During): とき expresses the time of an action or event, like 'when' in English. It can be used with nouns as in 雨の時 'when it rains', verbs as in 父が帰ってきた時 'when Dad came home', or adjectives as in 暑い時 'when it's hot', and can describe one-time or repeated actions. うちに means 'while' or 'during,' often with the nuance that it's the ideal or only time to act, e.g. 熱いうちに食べてね ('Eat it while it's hot.').

ことがある (N3, Something is possible, Sometimes, Occasionally, There are times when): とき marks the time of an action or event, like 'when' in English, e.g. 雨の時 or 雨が降るとき 'when it rains'. ことがある expresses something that happens occasionally, e.g. 雨が降ることがある ('There are occasions when it rains.'). Because they express different concepts, the two can be combined, as in: 時間がないとき、コンビニ弁当を食べることがある ('When I don't have time, there are occasions when I eat a convenience store lunch box.').

ているあいだに (N4, While, During the time that ~): とき expresses the time of an action or event, like the English 'when'. It can be used with nouns as in 雨の時 'when it rains', verbs as in 父が帰ってきた時 'when Dad came home', or adjectives as in 暑い時 'when it's hot'. In contrast, ているあいだに uses the て-form of verbs and refers to a period during which something occurs, e.g. 晩ご飯を食べている間に、父が帰ってきました ('While I was eating dinner, my father came home.').

ごろ (N4, Around, About): Both ごろ (or ころ) and とき indicate when something happened, but with key differences. ごろ is less specific and means 'around that time', as in 子どもの頃 'in my childhood days'. It also works as a suffix with time words, e.g. 11時ごろ 'around 11 o'clock', while とき cannot be used this way. By contrast, とき has a more precise nuance, as in 子どもの時 'when I was a child'.

折には (N1, When, Occasion, Opportunity, Time): Both とき and 折には express the time of an action or event, but differ in nuance and formality. とき is common in everyday conversation and broadly used, like the English 'when'. 折には is more formal, similar to 'on the occasion of', and is often used for special or less frequent (and often positive) events.

中 (N3, During, While, Throughout, In the process of): とき expresses the time of an action or event, like 'when' in English. It can be used with nouns as in 雨の時 'when it rains', verbs as in 父が帰ってきた時 'when Dad came home', or adjectives as in 暑い時 'when it's hot', and can describe one-time or repeated actions. 中 attaches to nouns and describes an action or state in progress, e.g. 勉強中 'now studying' or 使用中 'currently in use'.

の間に (N3, While, During, Between, Period): とき expresses the time of an action or event, like the English 'when'. It can be used with nouns as in 雨の時 'when it rains', verbs as in 父が帰ってきた時 'when Dad came home', or adjectives as in 暑い時 'when it's hot'. In contrast, の間に is used with nouns, and describes a period within which something happens, similar to the English 'while' or 'during', e.g. 冬休みの間に ('during winter break').

summary: An expression used to show that (A) will be done firstly, or before anything else.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About まず
text: Like many other adverbs in Japanese, まず can be used to modify a whole phrase/sentence. This means that it will regularly appear at the beginning of a statement. まず is associated with kanji {先|まず} and therefore carries the meaning of 'first', or 'starting with'.
まず is regularly used when you want to convey that something 'should' be done before anything else/discussed first, and not when something is first in rank.
In this kind of sentence, it would be far more natural to use a statement like {一番|いちばん}, {最初|さいしょ} or {一位|いちい} if discussing rank.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: て初めて (N3, For the first time, Not until, Only after, Only when, Only because): まず means 'first' or 'to begin with' and is used to express something that happens or should happen before something else. meaning: Even, To even, To the extent of
summary: A phrase which states that something is even to or until the surprising extent of (A).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About まで
text: The adverbial particle まで is used in the same way as many other adverbial particles, in that it is highlighting that the statement that comes after it as important in some way. However, unlike our first look at まで, which discussed its use as 'until', this use of まで has the nuance of 'even', or 'to the extent'.

Although using まで as 'even' may seem different to 'until', they are essentially the same thing in Japanese. This is because まで always means '(A) まで, (B)', where (A) is the 'limitation/extent', and (B) is the 'noteworthy factor'. This 'noteworthy factor' will usually be a descriptive word/phrase, such as a verb, adjective, or explanation.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: さえ (N3, Even): Both さえ and まで mean 'even,' but with different nuances. さえ is often used with negatives to express 'not even X,' e.g. 食べることさえできなかった ('I couldn't even eat.'). まで is usually affirmative and highlights something surprising or extreme, e.g. 骨まで食べた ('He even ate the bones.').

ほど (N3, The more, About, To the extent that, So much… that): まで and ほど both mean 'to the extent of,' but with different uses. まで emphasizes inclusion or a surprising limit, e.g. 骨まで食べた ('He even ate the bones.'). ほど means 'so much that' and often describes degree or intensity, e.g. 痛いほど分かる ('I understand to the point that it hurts.').

くらい ② (N3, To the extent that, So…that, About the only thing that...): Both まで and ほど share the core meaning of 'to the extent of,' but are used differently. まで emphasizes inclusivity or a surprising limit, e.g. 骨まで食べた ('He even ate the bones.'). In contrast, くらい② means 'to the point of' and often expresses degree, e.g. 叫びたいくらい怖かった ('It was so scary I wanted to scream.').

Noun + まで (N5, Until, Till, To (but no further than)): The particle まで has the core meaning of 'as far as.' It's commonly used with time expressions to mean 'until' (e.g. 月曜まで休む = 'rest until Monday') and with places to mean 'up to' or 'to (a location)' (e.g. 駅まで送る = 'see [someone] off to the station'). When used with verbs or non-location nouns, it can mean 'even' or 'as much as' (e.g. 骨まで食べる = 'eat even the bones').

ほど～ない (N3, Is not as…as, Isn't... like..., Not to the extent of...): Both grammar points share the idea of 'to the extent of,' but are used differently. ほど～ない makes negative comparisons, e.g. ジョンはトムほど強くない ('John isn't as strong as Tom.'). まで emphasizes something going beyond expectations, e.g. 骨まで食べた ('He even ate the bones.').

Verb + まで (N5, Until (something) happens): The particle まで has a core meaning of 'as far as' or 'to the extent of.' With verbs, it often means 'until A happens'—for example, 友達が来るまでテレビを見ていた ('I was watching TV until my friend came'). In other cases, it can mean 'even,' as in 骨まで食べた ('He even ate the bones'). Both uses reflect the core idea of reaching a certain extent or limit.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About までに
text: までに is a combination of two different types of particles. The adverbial particle まで, and the case marking particle に. までに is very similar to まで when it means 'until'. However, there is one very important distinction. This distinction is that までに means 'by', not 'until'.
To use までに, we will need to attach it to the end of a noun, or verb in the non-past form.

To understand the difference between まで, and までに, we need to remember that に usually marks a 'target', or a 'destination' for where something will happen. In this case, まで is the 'target' that に is marking. This is due to the fact that まで means 'as far as' (まで is sometimes written using kanji {迄|まで}, especially in older/formal texts, and newspapers).
In this way, までに more literally means '(A) as far as (に marks the target), (B).

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: Noun + まで (N5, Until, Till, To (but no further than)): The particle まで means 'until' when used with a time expression and a verb describing an ongoing action. For example, 8時までテレビを見る means 'watch TV until 8 o'clock.' In contrast, までに means 'by' and is used to express that an action is completed before a certain time. For example, 8時までに終わる means 'finish by 8 o'clock'.

Verb + まで (N5, Until (something) happens): The particle まで means 'until' when used with a verb that can describe a progressive or ongoing action, e.g. 8時までテレビを見る 'watch TV until eight o'clock'. In contrast, までに means 'by', 'before', or 'no later than', and is used with verbs that describe actions with a set completion point, e.g. 8時までに終わる 'to finish by/before eight o'clock.'

meaning: Also, As well, Moreover, Again, Additionally
summary: A structure which indicates that (A) will be done again, or in addition to (A).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About また
text: また, or {又|また} in its kanji form, is an expression which means 'again', 'additionally', 'also', or 'moreover'. This may seem confusing at first, but it may be easier to think of また as meaning 'repetition of (A)', where (A) is any particular course of action. This repetition is a bit different to English, in that it can express the same action, or an alternative option. また can be used as an adverb, or as a conjunction. In this lesson, we will focus on its use as a conjunction.
As with many other conjunctions in Japanese, a phrase/sentence can begin with また, so long as that sentence expresses a complete thought.

Due to また being quite different to any single word that we have in English, let's try to make the meaning a bit clearer. Imagine that '(A) action always has (B) result'. However, the action which leads to the (B) result could be many different things. Because of this, また can have the following meanings.
The same (A) action is taken - Has the nuance of 'again', or 'moreover'.
A different (A) action is taken - Has the nuance of 'also', and 'additionally'.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: 上に (N2, As well, Besides, In addition to): また and 上に both add information, but differ in usage and tone. また appears at the beginning of a sentence or phrase and means 'moreover' or 'again'. It's common in both speech and writing. 上に follows nouns, verbs, or adjectives and conveys a similar meaning, but with a more formal or written tone.

更に (N2, Even more or further, Again, More and more): また is common in both speech and writing, meaning 'again' or introducing additional information, like 'moreover' or 'additionally'. 更に is more formal and used in writing or structured speech, with the nuance of 'even more' or 'beyond that', often indicating further change or escalation.

再び (N3, Again, Once more, A second time): また and 再び both mean 'again', but differ in nuance and formality. また is common in speech and writing, used for repetition or to add information, like 'again' or 'additionally'. 再び is more formal and literary, often with a stronger sense of 'for the second time'.

それに (N4, And, Besides, Moreover, In addition): Both それに and また can be used to provide added information, like the English 'in addition' or 'moreover', but with slightly different nuances. また has a slightly formal tone, and adds information in a neutral sense. それに is more colloquial and has the nuance of adding information that supports or reinforces the previous statement.

summary: A construction that indicates that an action is being started.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About はじめる
text: To express that actions are beginning or ending in Japanese, the verbs {始|はじ}める (to commence), or {終|お}わる (to end) will need to be used. In this lesson, we will focus on actions that are 'beginning'.

To say that (A) is starting/beginning, we will need to attach はじめる to the ます stem of almost any verb. Whether you use the hiragana form, or the kanji form does not matter, as there will be no change in nuance.
Due to はじめる being a verb itself, the tense can be changed, to show that something will start, is starting, or has started.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: It can be easy to accidentally use {始|はじ}まる, the intransitive form of this verb. However, with this expression, the transitive form will always be used, due to the verb that はじめる is attached to being the thing that 'is started', by 'something' else.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: てしまう・ちゃう (N4, To do something by accident, To finish completely・totally, Unfortunately): はじめる attaches to verb stems to mean 'to begin' or 'start' doing something, e.g. 食べはじめる 'to start eating'. In contrast, てしまう・ちゃう follows the て-form and can express doing something unintentionally or completely, e.g. 食べてしまった・食べちゃった ('I ate it unintentionally.' or 'I ate it all.').

上がる・上げる (N3, Something is finished, To finish something, Something has come to an end, To do something completely, To do something through): はじめる attaches to verb stems to express 'beginning to' do something, e.g. 作りはじめる 'to start making'. In contrast, 上がる・上げる also attach to verb stems but express completing an action, e.g. 作りあげる 'to finish making', often with a sense of effort or finality.

おわる (N4, To finish, To end): はじめる and おわる can be attached to the stem of verbs to express the contrasting ideas of 'beginning' and 'finishing' an action, respectively. For example, 読みはじめる means 'to begin reading', while 読みおわる means 'to finish reading'.

だす (N4, To suddenly begin, To start doing): Both はじめる and だす attach to verb stems to mean 'to start doing (A)', but with different nuances. はじめる implies a deliberate or planned action, e.g. 学びはじめた ('I began to learn.'). In contrast, だす conveys a more spontaneous or unexpected beginning, e.g. 雨が降りだした ('It suddenly began to rain.').

ていく (N4, To ~ and go, To go on, To start): ていく expresses either literal movement away from the speaker or a change that begins now and continues into the future. In contrast, はじめる attaches to the verb stem to mean 'to start (A)'. The key difference is nuance: ていく highlights ongoing progression and continuation going forward, while はじめる focuses on the starting point and the idea of commencing an action.

かけ (N3, Half-, Not yet finished, About to, Begin to): はじめる attaches to verb stems to mean 'to begin' or 'start' doing something, e.g. 食べはじめる 'to start eating'. In contrast, かけ also attaches to verb stems but indicates something incomplete or in progress, e.g. 食べかけ 'half-eaten'. Forms with かけ function grammatically as nouns, as in 食べかけのバナナ 'a half-eaten banana'.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About おわる
text: To express that actions are beginning, or ending in Japanese, the verbs {始|はじ}める (to commence), or {終|お}わる (to end) will need to be used. In this lesson, we will focus on actions that are 'ending'.

To say that (A) is ending/finishing, we will need to attach おわる to the ます stem of almost any verb. Whether you use the hiragana form, or the kanji form does not matter, as there will be no change in nuance.
Due to おわる being a verb itself, the tense can be changed to show that something will end, is ending, or has ended.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Unlike はじめる, which uses the transitive form, {終|お}わる uses the intransitive form of its transitive/intransitive pair. This is due to most actions in Japanese being considered to be things that 'come to an end' naturally (intransitive), rather than forcefully (transitive). However, there are exceptions to this, and {終|お}える (the transitive version) may also be seen used as an auxiliary to other verbs.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: はじめる (N4, To start, To begin to): はじめる and おわる can be attached to the stem of verbs to express the contrasting ideas of 'beginning' and 'finishing' an action, respectively. For example, 読みはじめる means 'to begin reading', while 読みおわる means 'to finish reading'.

切る (N3, To do something completely to the end, Utterly, Resolutely): Both 切る and おわる attach to verb stems to express finishing an action, but with different nuances. おわる simply marks completion, e.g. 使いおわった ('I finished using it.'). In contrast, 切る often implies using something up, e.g. バターを使い切った ('I used up all the butter.') or doing something to the very end with full effort, e.g. ゴールまで走り切った ('I ran all the way to the finish line.').

上がる・上げる (N3, Something is finished, To finish something, Something has come to an end, To do something completely, To do something through): While おわる and 上がる・上げる both attach to verb stems to express finishing an action, their nuances differ. おわる can describe completing any action, e.g. ケーキを食べおわった ('I finished eating the cake.') or 映画を観おわった ('I finished watching a movie.'). 上がる・上げる is typically used when the action results in some completed product, e.g. 論文を書きあげた ('I finished writing the paper.').

てしまう・ちゃう (N4, To do something by accident, To finish completely・totally, Unfortunately): おわる attaches to verb stems to mean 'to finish doing (A)', e.g. 食べおわった ('I finished eating.'). In contrast, てしまう・ちゃう uses the て-form and can also mean doing something completely, but often adds a nuance of regret, finality, or lack of intention, e.g. 食べてしまった・食べちゃった ('I ate it and now it's gone.' or 'I didn't mean to eat it.').

だす (N4, To suddenly begin, To start doing): おわる and だす both attach to verb stems but express opposite ideas, like finishing vs. starting an action. おわる is used for completing almost any action, e.g. 本を読み終わった ('I finished reading the book.'). だす often describes actions that begin suddenly or unexpectedly, e.g. 雨が降り出した ('It started to rain.').

込む ② (N3, Remain, To do thoroughly, Deeply, Intensely): Both 込む and おわる attach to verb stems but express different nuances. おわる simply marks the end of an action, e.g. ケーキを食べおわった ('I finished eating the cake.') or 映画を観おわった ('I finished watching a movie.'). 込む adds the sense of doing something thoroughly and staying in that state, e.g. 黙り込んだ ('He fell completely silent and stayed that way.').

summary: A word that is often used to approximate large periods of time, but not very specific points.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ごろ
text: ころ, or ごろ (the colloquial pronunciation) is a word which carries the meaning of 'around', or 'about'. It is utilized in a similar way to くらい, but has a few differences. When ごろ is used, it will need to be attached to the end of a noun, or a noun followed by の.
The main difference between ころ and くらい is that ころ can be (and often is) used to express a broad point in time, while くらい is limited to expressing timeframes that are more specific.
Conversely, ころ will not be used when expressing approximate distances/lengths.

The primary reason for this is that ころ expresses a span of something, while くらい expresses an extent. In this way, ころ could also be translated as 'within the span of (A)', while くらい is closer to 'at the point of (A)'. As an easier way to think about it, if we have a one meter ruler, ころ could express anywhere between 1 to 100 centimeters (the span), but くらい can only express somewhere between 90 and 100 centimeters (the extent).

Just like with English, if the 'time' expressed is very specific, then either くらい or ころ could be used naturally. This is due to the 'span', and the 'extent' already being something that is a 'precise point' in these cases.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: The kanji form of {頃|ころ} is also very common, so it is worth learning as soon as possible, to save any confusion while reading.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: とき (N4, When, At the time of): Both ごろ (or ころ) and とき indicate when something happened, but with key differences. ごろ is less specific and means 'around that time', as in 子どもの頃 'in my childhood days'. It also works as a suffix with time words, e.g. 11時ごろ 'around 11 o'clock', while とき cannot be used this way. By contrast, とき has a more precise nuance, as in 子どもの時 'when I was a child'.

くらい ① (N5, About, Approximately): くらい (often ぐらい in speech) expresses an approximate degree or extent. A common use is with number + counter expressions, as in 10分くらいかかった ('It took about 10 minutes'). Unlike くらい, which can be used with durations or points in time (e.g. 10分くらい, 10時くらい), ごろ can only be used with points in time (e.g. 10時ごろ = 'around 10 o'clock').

summary: A phrase that simply highlights that one action will take place after another.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About あとで
text: In Japanese, あとで is a combination of the noun {後|あと} (behind), and the particle で (with). When these words are linked, they form an adverbial phrase which is used to express 'after', or 'later'. As with で's standard meaning of 'with', あとで is simply highlighting that something will happen, 'with' the 'after/behind' part of something.
To use あとで, attach it to the end of any past-tense verb, noun followed by の, or verb followed by のは (nominalization).
{後|あと}で
may also be used to alter the meaning of an entire phrase, by appearing at the front. This nuance is just that (A) will happen (at some point) after now.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: The reason that {後|あと} is translated as both 'after', and 'behind', is because sequences of events in Japanese behave similarly to a train. When the head of the train (one action) passes a specific point, there are still potentially many carriages (other actions) coming 'after', or 'behind' it.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: 前者は・後者は (N3, The former ~ the latter, The first ~ the second): 前者は and 後者は, like あとで, relate to sequence, but in different ways. あとで (also written in kanji as 後で) refers to the order of actions, like 'after doing (A)'. 前者 and 後者 mean 'the former' and 'the latter', pointing back to the previously mentioned items.

たら (N4, When, From when, Just when, If): Both あとで and たら can show that one action follows another, but their usage and nuance differ. あとで simply shows sequence, like 'after doing (A)'. たら adds a conditional nuance and can mean 'when' (temporal) or 'if' (hypothetical). Because of this, they are rarely interchangeable.

上で (N3, After, Upon): Both 上で and あとで express that one action follows another, but with different nuances. あとで simply shows sequence, like 'after doing (A)'. 上で implies the first action is a necessary step for the second, similar to 'upon doing (A)', and is more formal, often used in writing or business contexts.

てから (N5, Once...is done, Once...happens, After doing): てから and あとで both convey a sequence of events, but their nuances differ. てから uses the Verb + て form to show that one event follows another. In contrast, あとで follows the past tense (た form) and simply indicates that the second event occurred after the first, without implying any connection between the two.

まえに (N5, Before, In front of): あとで and まえに are both used to describe the timing of actions, but with opposite meanings. まえに usually follows a plain (non-past) verb and means 'before doing A' (e.g., 食べる前に = 'before eating'). In contrast, あとで typically follows the past tense form of a verb and means 'after doing B' (e.g., 食べたあとで = 'after eating').

summary: A phrase that shows when an action was continuing in the past.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ていた
text: To convey that '(A) was happening', or that somebody 'was doing (A)' in Japanese, ていた (or ていました) will be used. ていた is a construction which uses the conjunction particle て, and the ichidan verb いる (to exist), in its past tense form いた.

Sometimes ていた is used to express things that are still ongoing, but the speaker is not sure about, or would like to politely advise the listener about. This is very similar to the way in which English uses '(A) was doing (B)'.
In this example, although the action of 'sitting' is not finished, we can imagine that the speaker is suggesting that 'dad was sitting here, and he still is, but he just went to get a drink'.
The same kind of sentence could be used when the speaker has walked away from where their dad was sitting, and doesn't actually know if he is still sitting there or not.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: う-Verb (Past) (N5, う - Verbs (Past tense)): The う-Verb (Past) expresses a completed action or one that took place in the past, similar to '-ed' in English. The ていた form conveys an ongoing action or state in the past, similar to 'was -ing' in English. In other words, ていた indicates an action that was continuous or repeated, while the regular past form describes a single, completed action.

Verb + て (N5, And, Then (Linking events)): The Verb + て form connects verbs or parts of a sentence. When combined with いた, it describes a past state. For example, 食べていた means 'I was eating,' and 死んでいた means 'it was dead.' Whether ていた conveys an action ('was -ing') or a state depends on the verb. In casual speech, ていた is often shortened to てた.

meaning: Times (In each time period), Every, Frequency of
summary: A particle that often shows how frequently something occurs.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About に (Frequency)
text: When the case marking particle に is used, sometimes it has the nuance of 'frequency'. This means that it can be utilized to describe how often something happens/is done. In this grammatical construction, the 'time frame' is followed by に, then followed by the number of times that you would like to say that something happens.
In this way, に keeps its regular nuance of being a 'goal', or 'destination', within which something else takes place.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: おきに (N3, Repeated at intervals, Every other, Every, At intervals of): Both expressions show frequency, but in different ways. The に (frequency) construction combines a time period with a number to mean '(A) times per (B),' e.g. 一週間に２回 'twice a week'. おきに attaches to a number + counter to mean 'at intervals of (A),' e.g. 二日おきに学校に行く ('I go to school every three days.' meaning 'every third day').

ごとに (N4, Each, Every): Both expressions show frequency, but in different ways. The に (frequency) construction combines a time period with a number to mean '(A) times per (B),' e.g. 一週間に２回 'twice a week'. ごとに attaches to a number + counter to mean 'every X,' e.g. 二時間ごとに薬を飲む 'take medicine every two hours'.

summary: A phrase meaning finally, which focuses on arriving at the head of some long journey or effort.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About とうとう
text: とうとう is an adverb that is used to express that something 'finally' happens. In Japanese, there are a few ways to do this, but とうとう is one of the more common. Coming from the kanji {到頭|とうとう}, this structure literally means 到 (to arrive at), 頭 (the head of/crux of) something. Due to this, 'finally', and 'after all' are the two most common translations of とうとう. Like many other adverbs in Japanese, とうとう is often used at the beginning of a phrase/sentence.

While とうとう is written in hiragana the majority of the time, knowing the kanji will help when trying to remember the expression's nuance. That nuance is that something has 'ended', usually after some sort of long journey/effort.
This adverb may be used to express either positive or negative outcomes, as it focuses more on the time required to achieve the result, rather than the result being good or bad.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: 遂に (N3, Finally, At last): Both とうとう and 遂に mean 'finally', but with different nuances. とうとう emphasizes the long effort or struggle leading up to the result, while 遂に focuses more on the result itself and what may follow. In other words, both とうとう大学生になった and 遂に大学生になった mean 'I finally became a university student.', but the former is more backward-looking, while the latter is forward-looking.

いよいよ (N2, At last, Finally, More and more): Both とうとう and いよいよ can mean 'finally', but with different nuances. とうとう is used when something expected happens after effort or waiting, e.g. とうとう大学に入った ('I finally got into university'). いよいよ expresses anticipation for something imminent, e.g. いよいよ夏が来た ('At last, summer has come.').

summary: A word that is often used for highlighting comparisons between (A) and (B).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About より
text: In N5, we learned about the use of より that is seen when making comparisons in より～のほうが. However, in this lesson, we will take a look at how this case marking particle can be used by itself. When used alone, this particle expresses that (A) (a noun or verb) is being compared to (B) (a noun or verb that is regularly paired with an adjective). The word that より is directly attached to will always be 'less than' the comparison being made. However, the overall expression is used to describe that (B) is 'more' (something) than (A).

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: というより (N3, ...is more of a... than a..., Rather than saying that...): より expresses a general comparison, like 'more than (A)' or '~er,' e.g. 月曜日より水曜日がいい ('Wednesday is better than Monday.') or 走るより野球をするのが好き ('I prefer playing baseball to running.'). In contrast, というより specifically means 'more/rather than saying (A)' and is used primarily when rephrasing or clarifying something.

にもまして (N1, Even -er than, Even more than, More than anything, More than anybody, More than ever): Both express comparison meaning ‘more than,’ and they can overlap in meaning, but the tone differs. にもまして is a more formal, literary variant often used in writing or speeches to emphasize that something exceeds another in degree, as in 昨年にもまして今年は暑い ('This year is even hotter than last year.'). より is the neutral, everyday comparative used broadly in speech and writing without added emphasis, as in 去年より今年の方が暑い ('This year is hotter than last year.').

より～のほうが (N5, To be more ~ than ~): より is used to make comparisons, with Xより meaning 'more than X.' It often appears in the pattern より～のほうが, as in 'More than X, Y is...' but can also be used without のほうが. In any case, より always follows the thing being compared as 'less.' It can also directly precede adjectives—for example, より高い ('more expensive [than something]'), even if the item being compared isn't stated.

以上に (N2, More than, No less than, Even more): Both より and 以上に are used for comparisons. In some cases, their meaning and usage can overlap, e.g. 思っていたより and 思っていた以上に both mean 'more than I thought'. In other cases, they can differ in that 以上に suggests a shared quality between the two things being compared. For example, AはBより強い simply states that A is stronger than B, while AはB以上に強い suggests that A is even stronger than B (who is also strong).

こそ (N3, For sure, For certain, Even more so, Underlined or bolded text): より expresses a general comparison, like 'more than (A)' or '~er,' e.g. 月曜日より水曜日がいい ('Wednesday is better than Monday.') or 走るより野球をするのが好き ('I prefer playing baseball to running.'). In contrast, こそ adds emphasis, highlighting something as especially important, e.g. 月曜日こそ図書館に行きたい ('Monday is precisely when I want to go to the library.').

以上 ① (N4, More than (or equal to), Over・(and) above, Any more・Greater, Exceeding): Both 以上① and より express comparisons like 'more than (A)', but with different nuances. 以上 follows numbers or nouns like これ, and means '(A) or more,' e.g. ２時間以上かかる ('It will take two or more hours.'). より makes general comparisons and does not necessarily have a nuance of measuring some quantity.

ほど～ない (N3, Is not as…as, Isn't... like..., Not to the extent of...): Both expressions are used for comparisons. ほど～ない makes negative comparisons, e.g. ジョンはトムほど強くない ('John isn't as strong as Tom.'). より is used for positive comparisons, e.g. トムはジョンより強い ('Tom is stronger than John.'). Note that ほど follows the greater of the two options, while より follows the lesser.
