summary: A structure that highlights something occuring every (A), focusing on every individual interval.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ごとに
text: ごとに is a combination of the noun ごと, and the particle に. Together, they are used adverbially to express that something happens 'every (A)', or 'at intervals of (A)'. ごとに may be used after any verb (usually in non-past form), or noun.
Although ごとに may be used after verbs, the most common use is with nouns, or phrases that finish with nouns.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: Many native speakers make mistakes with the difference between おきに and ごとに, so there are quite a large number of people (especially in the younger generation) that will consider them completely interchangeable.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: につけ (N2, Whenever, Every time something happens): ごとに and につけ both express frequency, but differ in usage. In phrases like 失敗するごとに or 失敗するにつけ 'every time (you fail)', the meaning is similar, though the grammatical attachment is different. につけ is also more formal and literary, while ごとに is common and attaches directly to time or distance expressions, e.g. ３時間ごとに 'every 3 hours'.

おきに (N3, Repeated at intervals, Every other, Every, At intervals of): ごとに and おきに both express regular intervals, but with a key difference. ２日ごとに means 'every two days', i.e. the event happens on the second day. ２日おきに means 'at intervals of two days', or in other words every third day. A helpful tip: おきに comes from 置く, which can have the meaning of leaving a gap or space.

～ずつ (N3, One at a time, Per, Each, Gradually): Both express regular repetition, but in different structures. ～ずつ attaches to quantity phrases to mean 'each' or 'little by little', e.g. 一つずつください 'Give me one of each.' ごとに follows nouns and means 'every (A)', often time-based, e.g. ３０分ごとに体を動かす 'I move my body every thirty minutes.'

に (Frequency) (N4, Times (In each time period), Every, Frequency of): Both expressions show frequency, but in different ways. The に (frequency) construction combines a time period with a number to mean '(A) times per (B),' e.g. 一週間に２回 'twice a week'. ごとに attaches to a number + counter to mean 'every X,' e.g. 二時間ごとに薬を飲む 'take medicine every two hours'.

たびに (N3, Each time, Every time, Whenever): ごとに and たびに both express frequency, and can be interchangeable in cases like 失敗するたびに／ごとに 'every time (you) fail'. However, ごとに can directly follow time or distance expressions (e.g. ３時間ごとに), while たびに requires a verb indicating an action or event, e.g. ３時間が経つたびに 'every time 3 hours pass'. Their noun forms also differ, e.g. 発表の度に vs. 発表ごとに (both meaning 'with every announcement').

まい～のように (N4, Almost every ~, Nearly every ~, On a ~ basis): Both phrases express frequency but differ in usage. ごとに attaches to time expressions, nouns, or verbs to mean 'every (A),' e.g. ３時間ごとに 'every three hours' or 失敗するごとに 'every time (you) fail'. まい～のように is used only with time words that take 毎 and adds emphasis, meaning 'almost every (A)', e.g. 毎日のように 'nearly every day'.

summary: An expression which indicates that (A) should be done as often as possible, or whenever it becomes permissable.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About なるべく
text: Combining {成|な}る (to become), and {可|べ}く (to be permissible), なるべく is an expression that literally means 'as each opportunity becomes permissible/presents itself'. This is often simply translated as 'as much as possible', or 'whenever possible'.
なるべく (usually written in hiragana) is regularly used before an entire phrase, to express that (A) should happen as much as possible.

Due to なるべく expressing the 'possibility', or 'having the opportunity' to do something, it will sound considerably softer/more polite than できるだけ. できるだけ is a similar expression which more directly states that something will be done 'to the full extent possible'.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: できれば・できたら (N3, If possible): なるべく and できれば・できたら both mean 'to the extent possible', but differ in nuance. なるべく implies doing something as much or as often as possible over time, e.g. 'whenever possible.' できれば・できたら typically are used when referring to a single situation or request, like 'if possible'.

meaning: About to, On the verge of
summary: An expression that highlights the situation or place when an action is just about to start.
formation: Verb［る］ + ところ + です (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About るところだ
text: The noun ところ (sometimes shortened to とこ) is often used to describe the 'place' or 'situation' in which something happens. The primary determining factor for the nuance of ところ, is the tense of the verb it follows. When it is in the non-past form, ところ means 'about to (A)', or 'on the verge of (A)'.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: In this use, ところ means stage/level/situation

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: たところだ (N4, Just finished doing, Was just doing): たところだ and るところだ share the same structure, with the tense indicating whether the action is complete or not. るところだ uses the non-past form to mean 'about to do' something, e.g. 晩ご飯を食べるところだ ('I'm just about to eat dinner.'). たところだ uses the past form to mean 'just did' something, e.g. 晩ご飯を食べたところだ ('I just ate dinner.').

Verb[volitional]とする (N3, Try to, Attempt to, To be about to): Both can describe actions about to happen, but with different nuance. るところだ simply states that something is on the verge of occurring. Verb[volitional] + とする adds a sense of intent or effort, and is often used when the action may not actually happen, e.g. 子どもはなんでも食べようとする ('Kids will try to eat anything.'), where 食べるところだ wouldn't be appropriate.

かけ (N3, Half-, Not yet finished, About to, Begin to): ところだ and かけ both express incomplete actions, but with a key difference. るところだ emphasizes that the action is just about to happen, e.g. リンゴを食べるところだ ('I'm about to eat an apple.'). かけ indicates the action has started but isn't finished, e.g. 食べかけのリンゴ ('a half-eaten apple').

ところだった ① (N3, Almost, Nearly, About to, On the verge of): るところだ and ところだった① both express that an action is or was about to happen, but differ in outcome. るところだ means the action is about to occur and likely will. ところだった① means it was on the verge of happening, but didn't in the end.

summary: A word that often expresses mild frustration that (A) has not led to (B).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About のに
text: Although のに is often thought of as a simple combination of the particles の and に, it is actually its own particle, with the meaning of 'despite', or 'in order to'. In this lesson, we will focus primarily on the 'despite' nuance.

Due to のに being a conjunction particle, it can be linked to almost any word type, to show that 'despite (A), (B)'. As with many conjunction particles, な will be required after a noun/な-Adjective, but before のに.
It is also possible to see だのに, instead of なのに, but this is something that is only seen in certain dialects, and would be considered incorrect by the vast majority of native speakers.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: Regardless of having two quite different translations ('despite', and 'in order to'), のに always functions in the same way.
In the situation of '(A) のに, (B)', (B) is/will be the result.

The only difference between how the nuance will be read, is whether the (B) statement is a logical conclusion, or an illogical one. When logical, the meaning is usually 'in order to', when 'illogical', the meaning is usually 'despite'.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: それでも (N4, But still, And yet, Even so, Nevertheless): のに expresses contrast, similar to 'although,' and follows verbs, adjectives, or nouns (with な for nouns and な-adjectives). It's typically used at the end of a clause or sentence. それでも also shows contrast, but appears at the beginning of a sentence. The それ refers to the previous statement, giving it the meaning of 'Even so' or 'But still.'

それなのに (N2, And yet, Despite this): のに expresses contrast, similar to 'although,' and follows verbs, adjectives, or nouns (with な for nouns and な-adjectives). It's typically used at the end of a phrase or sentence. それなのに is a related form used at the beginning of a sentence, meaning 'and yet' or 'despite that,' with それ referring back to the previous statement.

くせに (N3, Even though, And yet, Despite): Both のに and くせに express contrast, but with different nuance. のに is relatively neutral, like 'although', while くせに adds a strong negative or critical tone. For example, 頭がいいのにやる気がない and 頭がいいくせにやる気がない both mean 'Although (he's) smart, (he) has no motivation.', the のに version is just stating a fact, while the くせに version implies that his lack of motivation is a negative trait and not befitting of him.

ものを (N1, But, Although, If only, I wish I had): ものを and のに both are used to express the sense of 'if only'. ものを is more formal and also typically used when the speaker is expressing their disappointment at something that should have happened, not happening, e.g. 事前に知らせてくれればいいものを ('if only you had informed me in advance'), while のに can be used for general wishes 晴れればいいのに ('if only the weather were nice').

ながらも (N3, But, Even while, Even though, Despite, Although): Both のに and ながらも express contrast, but with different focuses. のに is more general and used widely, like the English 'although.' ながらも is mainly used with state-expressing verbs and conveys surprise that something happened despite that state.

にしても (N3, Even though, Even if, Even when, Also): Both にしても and のに express contrast, but with different nuances. のに is a general contrastive expression, like 'although.' にしても often presents a hypothetical or assumed condition, followed by an unexpected result. Like other ～ても forms, it's commonly used with Wh-words, e.g. どこに行くにしても 'no matter where you go'.

ものの (N2, Although, But, Even Though): のに and ものの both express contrast, but differ in nuance and tone. のに is more casual and often conveys disappointment or regret. It can also end a sentence to imply 'If only (A)!'. ものの is more formal and means 'although (A), (B) didn't follow as expected,' often with an implicit contrast. Unlike のに, it is not generally used alone at the end of a sentence..

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About とおもう
text: To express that you 'think' something in Japanese, the common expression と{思|おも}う is regularly used. As you can probably guess, this is just a combination of the particle と, plus the う-Verb {思|おも}う. とおもう can be used after any verb, い-Adjective, な-Adjective, or noun, but will require だ after a noun or な-Adjective.
Although this structure usually requires だ after nouns and な-Adjectives, it is often omitted in casual speech.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: 〜ようと思う・〜おうと思う (N4, I think I will, I think I shall, Going to, Gonna (Volitional + と思う)): 〜よう・おうと思う uses the volitional form with と思う to express plans or intentions, like 'I intend to (A)' or 'I'm thinking of doing (A)' In contrast, plain と思う expresses a simple thought. For example, この本を読もうと思います means 'I intend to read this book.', while この本は面白いと思います means 'I think this book is interesting.'.

meaning: Such as, Things like, Etc., And so on
summary: A word that expresses (A), and things in the same category as (A).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About など
text: など is an adverbial particle that is used to express that something is being presented as an example, but that other things in the same category also exist. In this way, it is regularly translated as 'such as', 'things like', or 'and so on'.

など may be used after nouns, to describe that (A) is being presented as an example from within a group. Alternatively, など can be followed by の (B), to show that (A) is only one example from within a broader category related to (B).

など is regularly seen in its kanji form, {等|など}. This kanji itself has a similar meaning to 'etc' in English. Fun FactThe kanji for {等|など} is also used in the pluralizing suffix, ら. Due to this, we can see that this kanji is regularly utilized to highlight something that exists as part of a larger group.
In the first sentence, など presents (A) as being part of a larger group of similar things. This is exactly the same thing that happens in the second sentence with ら.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: など is also sometimes written as なんか, and has an interchangeable meaning in many situations. However, なんか will never use the kanji form of {等|など}.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: だの (N1, Things like, And so on, Or something, And whatnot): だの and など are similar in that both are used to list examples. They differ in that だの will often explicitly list multiple examples, while など can be used with a singular example to suggest 'and things like that'. Also だの often is used in statements with a negative implication, while など is more neutral and has no such limitations.

なんか・なんて (N3, Such as, Things like, Emphasis): Both なんか・なんて and など can be used to give examples, like '(A) and so on' or 'things like (A)', but they differ in nuance and formality. など is neutral and used in both speech and writing. なんか・なんて are more casual and often carry a dismissive or belittling tone, like '(A) and whatever' or 'unimportant things like (A)'.

といった (N2, Such as, Like, So much as): といった and など both give examples, but differ in usage. といった appears in the form AといったB, meaning '(B) such as (A),' e.g. サッカーといったスポーツ ('sports like soccer'). など can be used similarly as AなどのB, but also stands alone, e.g. サッカーなどが好き ('I like soccer and similar things.').

とか～とか (N4, Among other things, For example, Such as): など and とか～とか both list examples, but differ in nuance and structure. など usually follows a single noun or ends a list, implying the items are representative, like '(A) and so on' or 'things like (A).' とか～とか follows each noun and emphasizes specific, individual examples, like '(A) and (B), for example'.

summary: A confident, yet somewhat casual expression to highlight the way something looks.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About みたい
text: In Japanese, there are many ways to express that something happens in a way that is 'like' something else, or 'resembles' something else. One of these ways is through the use of the な-Adjective, みたい. みたい can be used after any word that a な-Adjective would usually follow, to express that something is 'like (A)', or 'similar to (A)'.
In the above examples, we can see that みたい should always be followed by だ (or です) when it is at the end of a statement, however, this is frequently omitted.
みたい is also often used to describe another noun, but needs to be followed by な in these cases. In this type of sentence, it is just expressing that something is '(B), but resembles (A)'.
みたい is used most often in conversational situations, and is based on direct, reliable information. It is far less formal than its counterpart, ようだ.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Despite みたい meaning 'to resemble', and being based on (usually) visual stimulus, it should not be confused with {見|み}たい 'to want to see'. This is a common mistake that learners make, as みたい itself does not have a kanji form.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: みたいだ is originally an abbreviation of the more formal phrase を見たような. As a result of this, we can see that ようだ kept its formal meaning, while みたい became the casual equivalent.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Conversational, Less formal than ようだ

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ようだ (N4, It seems that, It appears that, It looks like): Both みたい and ようだ express resemblance, like 'seems like' in English. みたい is more casual and common in speech, while ようだ is more formal and used in writing. みたい follows nouns directly (e.g. 春みたい), while ようだ requires の (e.g. 春のようだ). Both function grammatically as な-adjectives.

どうやら (N2, Apparently, Looks Like, Seems like): どうやら and みたい combine to convey a tentative impression or guess based on observed clues. どうやら adds a tone of cautious inference, while みたい expresses resemblance or appearance. For example: どうやら彼は来ないみたいだ (It seems like he’s not coming).

そうに・そうな (N4, Seem, Look like, Sound): Both みたい and そうに・そうな can mean 'seems like', but differ in nuance and usage. みたい expresses resemblance to something else, e.g. 春みたいな天気 'spring-like weather'. そうに・そうな is based on sensory cues and often used with verbs, e.g. 雨が降りそうな天気 'weather that looks like it's about to rain'.

みたいに・みたいな (N4, Like, Similar to, Resembling): The みたい in all these patterns means 'seems like (A)' or 'like (A)'. The difference lies in how it connects to other words. Examples include 春みたい or 春みたいだ／です ('It's like spring.'), 春みたいな天気 'spring-like weather', and 春みたいに暖かい ('It's warm like spring.').

にみえる (N4, To look, To seem, To appear): にみえる and みたい both express that something 'seems' a certain way, but with different nuance. にみえる specifically refers to visual appearance, e.g. 'looks like', and can be used with そうだ or ようだ. みたい means 'is like' or 'seems like' more in a more general sense, not necessarily related to appearance, and is more casual than にみえる.

そう (N4, Look like, Appear, Seem, Have a feeling that): Both みたい and そう can mean 'seems like', but differ in nuance and usage. みたい compares something to another, e.g. 春みたい ('It's like spring.') or is based on reliable evidence, e.g. 面白いみたい ('Apparently it's interesting.' i.e. based on something you've heard). そう is based on appearance or sensory impression, e.g. 面白そう ('It looks/sounds interesting.').

らしい ① (N4, Seems like, Apparently, I heard): Both らしい① and みたい express similarity, but with different nuances. らしい means something is typical or characteristic of what it represents, e.g. 春らしい天気 which implies 'weather that's just like spring should be'. In contrast, みたい suggests resemblance of one thing to something else that it is not, e.g. 春みたいな天気 'spring-like weather' such as an unseasonably warm day in winter.

ように・ような (N4, As・like, Just like): Both みたい and ように・ような express resemblance, similar to 'seems like' in English. みたい is more casual and common in everyday speech, while ように・ような is more formal and used in writing. みたい attaches directly to nouns, e.g. 春みたいな天気 'spring-like weather'. In contrast, よう requires の, e.g. 春のような天気 (same meaning).

meaning: Converting a verb into a noun
summary: A word that transforms whole phrases into single, noun-like expressions.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About こと
text: In a very similar way to のは, こと is used in Japanese for nominalization (creating a noun-like phrase). However, unlike のは, which is a combination of two particles, こと is a noun. To use こと, just add it to the end of a verb in its dictionary form.
こと (or {事|こと} in its kanji form) is a noun that is often translated as 'thing', and in this way, literally means 'the thing that is (A)' when used for nominalization.

As we can see from these examples, ない can also be used between the verb and こと, to form a 'not' statement. There are other auxiliary verbs that may be used with こと in this way, but ない is the most common.

Although this lesson discusses こと pairing with the dictionary form of verbs, it can actually pair with any standard verb form. Standard form just means anything that does not finish with the polite ます.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: Unlike もの (another noun used to describe 'things'), こと is a noun that is frequently used to describe things that are 'intrinsic'. This basically means things that are describable, but not necessarily always observable (feelings, conditions, events, etc.).

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Can also express something that is concrete - a fact.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ということ (N4, ~ing, The ~ that ~ (Nominalization)): こと attaches to the dictionary form of verbs to turn them into nouns, e.g. 行くこと '(the act of) going'. ということ has a similar function, but adds the quoting phrase という, so it's often used to clarify information or reported speech, e.g. 日本に行くということ 'the fact that (he) is going to Japan'.

のがすき (N5, Like doing, Love doing): This phrase combines the nominalizer の with the な-Adjective 好き to express liking an activity (e.g., 本を読むのが好き = 'I like to read books'). の can be replaced with こと, another nominalizer. The difference is subtle: の implies a concrete or tangible action, while こと is more abstract (e.g., 本を読むことが好き implies liking the 'act of reading').

ことなの (N3, (A) is (Description of A), (A) means that (Description of A)): These related expressions both use the noun こと, or 事 in kanji. On its own, こと turns a verb or adjective into a noun phrase, e.g. 食べる 'to eat' becomes 食べること 'the act of eating'. When combined with the explanatory/emphatic なの, it conveys meaning or definition, e.g. 'It means that (A)' or '(A) is how it is.'

の (N5, Verb nominalizer, The one who..., That which...): Both こと and の turn verbs or adjectives into noun phrases. こと is used for intangible or conceptual ideas, while の is used for more tangible or physical concepts. For example, 走るのが好きです and 走ることが好きです both mean 'I like running,' with の feeling more physical and こと more conceptual. However, they aren't interchangeable in set phrases like ことができる or ことがある.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About そう
text: そうだ is one of the 18 primary auxiliary verbs in Japanese, and can be used in two (2) different ways. The broad meaning in each of its applications is that something 'seems' to be a certain way. Due to this, そう is regularly translated as 'seems like', 'looks like', or 'appears as though'.
In this lesson, we will focus on the form that is used with the conjunctive (stem) form of words. Please examine the structure guide to see these forms.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Do not confuse with そうだ (I heard that...).

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: らしい ① (N4, Seems like, Apparently, I heard): The main difference between そう and らしい① lies in the source of information. そう implies speculation based on personal observation, e.g. 面白そう ('It looks interesting.'). らしい is based on secondhand information or inference, e.g. 面白いらしい ('I hear it's interesting.' or 'Apparently, it's interesting.').

のように・のような (N4, Like (Noun), Similar to (Noun)): のように・のような and そう both express impressions, but with different nuance. のように・のような show direct comparison, like 'like' or 'as if,' e.g. 春のように暖かい ('It's warm like spring.'). そう expresses a perceived impression based on observation, e.g. 暖かそう ('It seems warm.').

たい (N5, Want to do): The たい form expresses personal desires, such as 日本に行きたい ('I want to go to Japan'), though, the たい form is typically not used for expressing others' desires. One way that we can comment on another person's desires, however, is to use the そう form, meaning 'appears to.' For example 日本に行きたそう can be used to mean 'They seem to want to go to Japan.'

そうにない (N2, Unlikely to, Showing no signs of): そう expresses that something appears a certain way based on perception or indirect signs, e.g. 雨が降りそう ('It looks like it'll rain.'). In contrast, そうにない (or そうもない) indicates that something shows no signs of happening, e.g. 雨が降りそうにない ('It doesn't seem like it'll rain at all.').

みたい (N4, Like, Similar to, Resembling): Both みたい and そう can mean 'seems like', but differ in nuance and usage. みたい compares something to another, e.g. 春みたい ('It's like spring.') or is based on reliable evidence, e.g. 面白いみたい ('Apparently it's interesting.' i.e. based on something you've heard). そう is based on appearance or sensory impression, e.g. 面白そう ('It looks/sounds interesting.').

ように・ような (N4, As・like, Just like): ように・ような and そう both convey impressions, but with different nuance. ように・ような expresses direct comparison or similarity, like 'as if' or 'like,' e.g. 春が来たように暖かい ('It's warm as if spring had come.'). そう is based on the speaker's observation or feeling, e.g. 暖かそう ('It seems warm.').

っぽい (N3, -ish, -like, Characteristic of, Typical of, Tendency to): Both っぽい and そう express appearance or impression, but differ in nuance and usage. そう attaches to word stems and is neutral and often based on observation, e.g. 雨が降りそう ('It looks like it'll rain.'). っぽい is casual and attaches to nouns to mean '~ish' or '~like', e.g. 子供っぽい 'childish'. Unlike そう, it often carries a negative or demeaning tone.

そうもない (N3, Very unlikely to, Does not seem that, Does not appear that): そう is used to express that something seems likely based on perception or indirect signs, e.g. 雨が降りそう ('It looks like it's going to rain.'). In contrast, そうもない (or そうにない) indicates that there are no signs of something happening, e.g. 雨が降りそうもない ('It doesn't seem like it'll rain at all.').

にみえる (N4, To look, To seem, To appear): にみえる and そう both express that something 'seems' a certain way, but with different nuance. にみえる specifically refers to visual appearance and can be combined with そう, e.g. 面白そうにみえる ('It looks interesting.'). そう alone expresses general impression and doesn't necessarily rely on visual cues, e.g. 面白そう ('It seems interesting.'), which could be based on hearing about it, etc.

ような気がする (N3, Have a feeling that): ような気がする and そう both express impressions, but with different nuance. ような気がする conveys personal intuition or vague feeling, i.e. something you sense even without clear reason. On the other hand, そう is typically based on observable clues or appearance. In that sense, ような気がする is more subjective and less confident than そう.

summary: An expression that can turn adjectives into nouns that express an amount.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About さ
text: さ is a suffix in Japanese that can be attached to the stem form of い-Adjectives and な-Adjectives. When this happens, it transforms the target adjective into a noun that illustrates the 'amount' of that particular adjective. This commonly translates as '-ness' in English (sweetness, tallness, spiciness, etc), but is referred to as degree in Japanese.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: み (N3, ~ness, Used to indicate conditions or nature): さ and み both nominalize adjectives, similar to '~ness' in English, but differ in nuance and usage. さ works with both い and な-adjectives and expresses measurable degree, e.g. 高さ 'height' or 大変さ 'difficulty'. み is typically used with い-adjectives and focuses on quality or characteristics rather than degree, e.g. 面白み 'that which makes (something) interesting'.

meaning: Among other things, For example, Such as
summary: A word which may be used with either verbs or nouns, to express a variety of non-specific actions or things.
formation: Adjective (A) + (だ) + とか + Adjective (B) + (だ) +（とか）

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About とか～とか
text: とか is a word that belongs to a unique family of particles in Japanese called listing particles. As the name suggests, these particles are used for listing groups of items that share similarities. とか can be used after verbs, or nouns, to express 'among other things, (A)'.
When multiple things are listed, the last item in the list can (and often does) have とか omitted.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: とか is used to list items in a non-exhaustive way. What this means is that the listener will assume that there are other items in the list, apart from what is stated directly. The speaker is just providing a few examples of a (potentially much larger) category.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: For non-exhaustive lists

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: やら～やら (N2, Whether or, Things like, And … so on): While both やら～やら and とか～とか list examples, they differ in nuance. やら～やら often has an uncertain tone or a presents contradictory possibilities, e.g. 行くのやら行かないのやら ('whether he's going or not'). とか is more neutral and casual, simply listing examples without a strong nuance of uncertainty.

たり～たりする (N5, Things like ~ and ~): Both たり～たりする and とか～とか are used to give examples of actions, similar to the English '(doing) things like A and B.' The key difference is how they attach to words. たり is made by adding り to the た (past tense) of a verb, while とか follows the dictionary form. Also, とか can follow nouns directly, while たり requires だ to become だったり.

たとえば (N4, For example): たとえば and とか～とか both introduce examples, but differ in usage. たとえば comes at the start of a sentence or clause, like 'for example'. In contrast, とか～とか is used to list multiple items and follows each noun. Because they differ in function, they can be used together in the same sentence, e.g. たとえば本とか雑誌とか ('For example, things like books, magazines, and so forth.').

といった (N2, Such as, Like, So much as): といった and とか～とか both give examples, but differ in structure and nuance. といった is used in the form AといったB to mean '(B) such as (A)', e.g. サッカーといったスポーツ ('sports such as soccer'). とか～とか follows each noun to list examples, e.g. サッカーとか野球とか ('things like soccer and baseball').

など (N4, Such as, Things like, Etc., And so on): など and とか～とか both list examples, but differ in nuance and structure. など usually follows a single noun or ends a list, implying the items are representative, like '(A) and so on' or 'things like (A).' とか～とか follows each noun and emphasizes specific, individual examples, like '(A) and (B), for example'.

なんか・なんて (N3, Such as, Things like, Emphasis): なんか・なんて and とか～とか both give examples, but differ in tone and usage. なんか・なんて usually follows a single noun to imply 'things like (A)', often with a dismissive or belittling nuance. とか～とか is used after each item in a list and simply means 'things like (A), (B), and so forth' without any negative implication.

し～し (N4, And, Giving reasons): し～し and とか～とか both list things, but with a different nuance. し～し lists reasons or causes, like 'because of things like (A) and (B)'. とか～とか simply lists items without implying they are a cause for something else, i.e. 'things like (A), (B), and so forth'. Also, とか～とか is very casual, while し～し will be found in both speech and writing.

～なり～なり (N1, Or, Either or): While both ～なり～なり and とか～とか present examples, they differ in formality and nuance. ～なり～なり is more formal and presents possible choices without preference. とか～とか is casual and used in everyday speech to mean 'things like (A) and (B),' often implying there are other possible examples.

や (N5, Things like, And the like): Both や and とか～とか are used to list items non-exhaustively, implying that other, unmentioned items are also included. や is more common in writing or formal speech, while とか is more colloquial. や must follow nouns, while とか can also be used with actions or events involving verbs. Additionally, とか can follow each item in the list, whereas や is not used after the final item.

summary: A phrase that highlights things which can be said are this (A), or that (A), or whatever (A), focusing on describable features.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About そういう
text: Coming from the こそあど{言葉|ことば} family of words, こう, そう, ああ, or どう may be used with the verb {言|い}う to form an expression which literally means 'in the way of (A)'. (A) being 'this' これ, 'that' それ, 'that over there' あれ, or 'what' どれ (in questions). As with all pre-noun adjectival words, this expression will be used directly before a noun.

Although こう, そう, ああ, and どう share a relationship with これ, それ, あれ, and どれ, they are their own individual words, which each have a meaning similar to 'as such'. These words are all adverbs when used by themselves.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: そう (the adverb), should not be confused with そう, the auxiliary verb. そう (the adverb) comes from the kanji {然|そ}う, while the auxiliary verb does not have a kanji form.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: そんな・こんな・あんな・どんな (N4, Such a・Kind of, Something like ~): そういう (and its variants こういう, ああいう, どういう) and そんな・こんな・あんな・どんな both modify nouns to mean 'that sort of,' 'this sort of,' etc. While often similar in meaning, そういう tends to be a bit more formal or polite. In contrast, depending on context そんな can be used with a negative or dismissive tone, which is not true of そういう.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About Verb[よう]
text: よう (and う) are grammar constructions that function in a similar way to ましょう, or to be more precise, ましょう is the polite (conjugated) form of these auxiliary verbs. They are used as a casual way of expressing 'let's' when making suggestions, or 'I shall' when making statements.
よう is only one of the potential forms of this grammar point, and can actually be divided into two separate auxiliary verbs, う (used with う-Verbs), and よう (used with る-Verbs, する, and くる).

When attaching う to う-Verbs, simply replace the last kana with the equivalent お sound kana from within the same column (く becomes こ, う becomes お, す becomes そ, etc.), before adding う. For る-Verbs, replace る with よう.
As with many other verb conjugations, する and くる behave in a slightly different way to regular う-Verbs and る-Verbs. する will become しよう, while くる will become こよう.
The type of statements that う, and よう can be used for in Japanese are usually divided into three categories.
{推量|すいりょう} - Expresses guesses (has a similar meaning to だろう, which itself is the よう form of だ)
{意志|いし} - Expresses intentions (has a similar meaning to ～するつもりだ)
{勧誘|かんゆう} - Expresses invitations or encouragement (has a similar meaning to {誘|さそ}う 'to invite')

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Although よう is used with る-Verbs, する, and くる, it should not be confused with ようだ, another auxiliary verb that is used when describing likeness (in a similar way to そうだ).

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: まい (N2, Won't, Intend not to, Probably not): まい and the volitional form (〜よう) both express the speaker’s intent or decision, but in opposite directions. 〜よう indicates intention or willingness to do something, as in 行こう (Let’s go), while まい expresses a strong negative intention or refusal, as in 行くまい (I will not go).3

〜ようと思う・〜おうと思う (N4, I think I will, I think I shall, Going to, Gonna (Volitional + と思う)): Both use the volitional Verb [よう] form. On its own, it expresses a suggestion, e.g. 食べよう ('Let's eat.'). When combined with と思う, it expresses an intention or plan, e.g. 食べようと思う ('I'm thinking of eating.'). The key difference is that Verb [よう] includes others in the action, while ～ようと思う expresses the speaker's personal intent.

〜ようとしない (N3, Not willing to, Not make an effort to, To not attempt or try to, Volitional + としない): Both of these use Verb [よう], the volitional form. By itself, it expresses a suggestion, e.g. 食べよう ('Let's eat'.). Combined with としない, it means 'doesn't even try to,' e.g. 野菜を食べようとしない ('He/she doesn't even make an effort to eat vegetables.'). The key difference is between making a proposal vs. showing a lack of intent or effort.

～ましょうか (N5, Shall we, Shall I): ましょうか and Verb [よう] are both volitional forms, with ましょうか being polite and Verb [よう] (sometimes with か) casual. ～ましょうか is used to make polite suggestions like 'Shall we...?' (e.g. 行きましょうか = 'Shall we go?') 行こうか is more casual and introspective, often expressing the speaker's internal thoughts (e.g. 'Should I go?')

Verb[volitional]とする (N3, Try to, Attempt to, To be about to): Both of these use Verb [よう], the volitional form. On its own, it expresses a suggestion, e.g. 食べよう ('Let's eat.'). When combined with とする, it shows an attempt to do something, often one that fails, e.g. 食べようとしたけど ('I tried to eat it, but...'). The key difference is suggestion/proposal vs. attempted action.

〜ようではないか (N2, Let's do something, Why don't we): Both of these use Verb [よう], the volitional form, to express suggestions like 'Let's do (A).' The core meaning is the same, but they differ in tone. Verb [よう] is casual and used in everyday speech among friends. In contrast, ～ようではないか has a tone that sounds more formal and grandiose, and will be found in media or situations where the speaker is looking for dramatic effect.

ましょう (N5, Let's, Shall we (Polite volitional)): ましょう and Verb[よう] are both volitional forms that mean 'Let's (do something).' The difference is tone: ましょう is polite, while Verb[よう] is casual. For example, 行きましょう (polite) and 行こう (casual) both mean 'Let's go.' The casual Verb[よう] form is also used in other grammar patterns to express intent, such as 行こうと思う ('I think I'll go' / 'I'm planning to go').

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ようだ
text: In a similar way to みたい, ようだ is used when making observations about something in Japanese. This auxiliary verb is used to express three primary things.
たとえ - Using (A) as an example to highlight the way that (B) looks/is acting.
{推定|すいてい} - Using (A) as a reason for an assumption made about (B).
{例示|れいじ} - Presenting (A) as an example of what (B) is.
ようだ is usually based on direct information/experience, and shows that the speaker has high confidence in what they are saying. It may also frequently appear in its kanji form, {様|よう}だ.
ようだ can be used with any verb, い-Adjective, な-Adjective, or noun. However, it requires な before it when used with な-Adjectives, or の when used with nouns.

Although ようだ and そうだ are often used in similar situations, そうだ shows that the speaker has a lot less confidence in their statement than ようだ. Because of this, ようだ is a much better choice when stating things that are obvious/observable by anyone.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: そうだ (N3, I heard that, It is said that): While both of these forms express information indirectly, they differ in the source of the information. ようだ simply means 'it appears that...', and can cover information gleaned from a variety of sources. In contrast, (だ)そうだ is typically used specifically to indicate hearsay (i.e. 'I heard that...'/'someone said that...').

そうに・そうな (N4, Seem, Look like, Sound): そうに・そうな and ようだ can both mean 'seems' or 'appears', but differ in nuance and usage. そうに・そうな is based on sensory observation and attaches to verbs/adjectives (in the case of そうに) or nouns (in the case of そうな). In contrast, ようだ is based on information or inference and typically appears at the end of a sentence, e.g. 雨が降るようだ ('It looks like it will rain.').

らしい ① (N4, Seems like, Apparently, I heard): Both forms express observations similar to 'seems' or 'appears,' but differ in nuance. ようだ is based on direct information or experience, e.g. 雨が降るようだ ('It seems it will rain.', based on people carrying umbrellas). らしい① implies indirect or secondhand information, e.g. 雨が降るらしい ('I heard it will rain.' or 'Apparently, it will rain.')

みたい (N4, Like, Similar to, Resembling): Both みたい and ようだ express resemblance, like 'seems like' in English. みたい is more casual and common in speech, while ようだ is more formal and used in writing. みたい follows nouns directly (e.g. 春みたい), while ようだ requires の (e.g. 春のようだ). Both function grammatically as な-adjectives.

ように・ような (N4, As・like, Just like): ようだ and ように・ような share the meaning of 'seems' or 'appears', but differ in usage. ようだ is used at the end of a sentence to express observations or inferences, e.g. 雨が降るようだ ('It looks like it will rain.'). ように・ような connect to verbs or nouns to show similarity, e.g. 春のように暖かい ('It's warm like spring.') and 春のような天気 'spring-like weather'.

とみえる (N4, It seems that, It can be deduced, One can conclude that): Both ようだ and と見える express observations, but differ in nuance and formality. ようだ is commonly used to say something appears a certain way, based on various cues. と見える is more formal or literary and implies a deduction based on specific evidence, which is usually mentioned, e.g. 慌てているところを見ると、何かあったと見える ('Judging by how flustered he looks, something must've happened.').

かのようだ (N2, As if, Just like): Both ようだ and かのようだ express appearance or resemblance, but with different nuance. ようだ means 'It seems' or 'It appears,' and can be used whether the speaker believes the thing is actually as it appears or not. かのようだ adds a stronger, often figurative tone like 'just as if (A)', and is typically used when the speaker knows it is it not actually that thing.

にみえる (N4, To look, To seem, To appear): Both ようだ and に見える express observations, but differ in nuance. ようだ means 'appears to be' based on various cues, e.g. 虫のようだ ('It seems to be an insect.', based on looks, behavior, or context). に見える focuses specifically on visual appearance, e.g. 虫に見える ('It looks like an insect.'), without implying that the speaker thinks it actually is one.

ときいた (N4, I heard that): ようだ expresses that something appears a certain way, based on various cues that are not always explicitly stated, e.g. 雨が降るようだ ('It seems it will rain.', perhaps because people are carrying umbrellas, etc.). In contrast, ときいた specifically means 'I heard (A)', and indicates that the information is hearsay directly obtained by the speaker.

ようでは・ようじゃ (N2, If, If it is true that): While both use よう, their meanings differ. ようだ expresses a neutral observation, e.g. 雨が降るようだ ('It seems it will rain.'). ようでは／ようじゃ introduces a hypothetical or ongoing situation that leads to an undesirable outcome, e.g. 雨が降るようじゃ、試合ができない ('If it rains, we can't hold the game.').

どうやら (N2, Apparently, Looks Like, Seems like): どうやら and ようだ are frequently used together to express the speaker’s tentative judgment based on evidence or context. どうやら introduces the inference, while ようだ states the conclusion in a neutral or formal tone. For example: どうやら電車が遅れているようだ (It seems the train is delayed).

summary: A casual way to express that something is not (A) at all, but also often used in positive phrases in modern Japanese.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ぜんぜん
text: In Japanese, there are several adverbs that are traditionally used exclusively with negative expressions (containing ない). {全然|ぜんぜん} is one of them. When used at the beginning of a ない (or ません) containing phrase, 全然（ぜんぜん) has the meaning of 'completely not (A)', or 'not (A) at all'.
In writing, it is equally as natural to use either {全然|ぜんぜん} as kanji, or hiragana only, so both forms may be used confidently.
ぜんぜん is more flexible (and friendly sounding) in casual conversation than {全|まった}く, a similar expression which has a formal (often negative) nuance.

While both of these sentences have the meaning of 'not (A) at all', まったく could give the listener the impression that you are not pleased with the situation. This will depend quite a bit on tone of voice, though.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Slang: totally・completely, exceptionally

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: とても～ない (N3, Not ~ at all, Cannot ~ at all): Both ぜんぜん (with a negative form) and とても～ない can mean 'not at all', but differ slightly in nuance. とても～ない emphasizes impossibility, e.g. とてもできない and ぜんぜんできない both mean 'I absolutely can't do it.'. With adjectives like 美味しくない, where there is no sense of potential, 全然 is preferred, e.g. 全然美味しくない ('It's not tasty at all.').

すこしも～ない (N4, Not even a little, Not at all, Not in the least, Never): ぜんぜん and すこしも～ない both emphasize negation and mean 'not at all.' A key difference is that ぜんぜん, especially in casual speech, can also appear in affirmative phrases, e.g. ぜんぜん大丈夫 ('It's totally fine.'). In contrast, すこしも～ない is more formal and strictly used in negative contexts, e.g. すこしも寒くない ('It's not even a little cold.').

全く～ない (N3, Not~at all): Both ぜんぜん (with a negative verb) and 全く～ない mean 'not at all,' e.g. ぜんぜんできない and 全くできない both mean 'I can't do it at all.', with ぜんぜん being more casual in tone. In modern speech, both can occasionally appear with affirmative forms, e.g. ぜんぜん大丈夫 ('It's completely fine.'), though this was traditionally considered improper use.

summary: A word used to casually express uncertainty, or soften personal opinions.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About かな
text: Originally a mixture of the sentence ending particles か, and な, かな evolved over time to become its own (singular) sentence ending particle, which roughly translates as 'I wonder if (A)?'.

As it is a sentence ending particle, かな can be added to the end of almost any sentence. However, in the case of な-adjectives, both だ and です will usually be omitted, with かな simply following the word stem itself.

Combining the meanings か and な, we can see where かな gets its original meaning. か presents questions (usually to other people), while な shows that a statement is related purely to the speaker's own thoughts/opinions. In this way, かな expresses that the speaker's own thoughts are being questioned.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: はたして (N2, Wonder if ~ (really)?, Wonder how ~ (actually)?, Sure enough, As expected): Both かな and はたして express doubt, but their usage differs. かな is a casual sentence-ending particle meaning 'I wonder,' e.g. 寒いかな？ ('I wonder if it's cold?'). はたして appears at the beginning of a sentence for emphasis, often with かな or ～のだろうか, e.g. はたして来るのだろうか？ ('Will they really come, I wonder?').

～のだろうか (N4, I wonder...): Both かな and ～のだろうか express doubt or curiosity, like 'I wonder if (A)' かな is casual and common in everyday speech or texting. ～のだろうか also can be used in conversation but conveys a more thoughtful or serious tone, suggesting deeper consideration as compared to かな, which can be used for offhand comments.

かしら (N4, I wonder): Both かな and かしら can express doubt, similar to the English 'I wonder if (A)'. Comparing the two, かな is the more common and casual expression, used by both genders in a wide variety of contexts and settings. In contrast, かしら has a softer tone that can come off as more polite and feminine.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About あまり～ない
text: あまり is a very flexible word in Japanese, that is used in several different grammar points. When paired with the ない form of a word, it translates to 'not very (A)', or 'hardly (A)'. To pair あまり (or the casual form, あんまり) with another word, we just need to place it at the beginning of a phrase, or directly before the ない statement.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: あまり has this meaning of 'excessive' in all of its grammar points, and the nuance will only change based on whether the sentence itself is positive (does not use ない), or negative (uses ない).

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: 別に〜ない (N3, Not really, Not particularly, It's not like...): Both 別に〜ない and あまり〜ない are used to qualify negative statements, but differ in nuance. あまり〜ない expresses a lesser degree, e.g. あまり痛くない ('It doesn't hurt much.'). In contrast, 別に〜ない adds a tone of indifference or dismissal, e.g. 別に痛くない ('It's not like it hurts.', implying that there is no need to worry, etc.).

全く～ない (N3, Not~at all): Both 全く～ない and あまり～ない express negation, but differ in degree. 全く～ない indicates a complete absence, e.g. 全く寒くない ('It's not cold at all.'). あまり～ない suggests a lesser degree, e.g. あまり寒くない ('It's not very cold.').

めったに〜ない (N3, Hardly, Rarely, Seldom): Both めったに〜ない and あまり〜ない are used to qualify negative expressions, but differ in nuance. めったに〜ない means 'rarely' or 'almost never' and focuses on frequency, e.g. めったに行かない ('I rarely go.'). あまり〜ない is less strong, e.g. あまり行かない ('I don't go often.'). It can also qualify a degree or amount, e.g. あまり寒くない ('It's not very cold.'), while めったに cannot.

なかなか (N3, Very, Quite, Considerably): なかなか and あまり～ない both express degree, but in opposite directions. なかなか implies exceeding expectations, e.g. なかなか美味しい ('It's quite tasty.'). In contrast, あまり～ない suggests a lesser degree, or falling short of expectations, e.g. あまり美味しくない ('It's not very tasty.').

あまり (N3, So much...that): あまり has the base meaning of 'excess', but its nuance changes with context. Together with a negative word in the form あまり～ない, it means 'not very (A)', e.g. あまり寒くない ('It's not very cold.'). Used affirmatively, it implies something of an excessive degree, e.g. 緊張のあまりうまくできなかった ('I was so nervous I couldn't do it well.').

なかなか～ない (N3, Not really, Hardly, Not easily or readily, By no means, Far from): なかなか～ない and あまり～ない both express negation, but with different nuance. なかなか～ない implies difficulty or delay despite effort, e.g. なかなか話せない ('I can't speak easily.', implying difficulty despite effort). あまり～ない simply indicates a lower degree, e.g. あまり話せない ('I can't speak very much/well.').

すこしも～ない (N4, Not even a little, Not at all, Not in the least, Never): Both あまり～ない and すこしも～ない are used in negative statements, but differ in degree and tone. あまり～ない means 'not very (A)' and is fairly colloquial, e.g. あまり寒くない ('It's not very cold.'). すこしも～ない is more formal and emphatic, e.g. 少しも寒くない ('It's not the least bit cold.').

たくさん (N5, Many, A lot of, Plenty, Enough): たくさん is a noun meaning 'many' or 'a lot,' often used with verbs (e.g. たくさん食べた = 'I ate a lot'). To express the opposite idea ('not much' or 'not many'), the pattern あまり～ない is used (e.g. あまり食べなかった = 'I didn't eat much'). Note that あまり originally means 'excess' and can also appear in affirmative forms (see あまりに).

そんなに (N4, So (much), That much, Like that): Both あまり～ない and そんなに express a negative degree, but with different nuance. あまり～ない means 'not very' in a general sense, e.g. あまり寒くない ('It's not very cold.'). そんなに (literally 'that much') can imply comparison to a standard and can be used with both negative and affirmative phrases, e.g. そんなに好きなら 'if you like [it] that much...' and そんなに好きじゃない ('I don't like it that much.').

summary: A grammar point that expresses hypothetical situations and their potential, sometimes expected outcomes.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ば
text: There are several different ways to express 'if' in Japanese. One of these is through using the conjunction particle ば. ば presents hypothetical situations (possibilities), and pairs with verbs using an う to え sound-change conjugation method on the terminal (last) kana. Let's examine this with a few verbs first.

As we can see with these verbs, the final kana will change to an え sound, from its original う (る to れ, う to え, く to け, す to せ, etc.) before adding ば. It is important to practice these, to not get them mixed up with verbs that use れる, and られる. Unlike with these verbs, the base form of する and くる will not change when using ば.
To conjugate い-Adjectives with ば, the い will be replaced with けれ, one of the standard い-Adjective conjugation forms. After this, just add ば.
For な-Adjectives, and nouns, なら (another standard conjugation form of these words) will be added, before attaching ば.
In the negative form (using ない), both the auxiliary verb ない, and the い-Adjective ない will conjugate in the same way. Simply replace い with けれ, and then add ば.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: The なら in ならば is often used by itself to mean 'if', and is an abbreviation of the classical auxiliary verb なり 'to be'. In its hypothesis form, なり will become ならば. However, なり is very irregularly used by itself in modern Japanese, with なら, and ならば being far more common.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Hypothetical

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: と (N4, If, When, Whenever, And, [Conditional]): ば and と are both conditional expressions, but differ in nuance. ば emphasizes the condition that leads to a result, often with an 'if and only if' tone. と is used for habitual or automatic outcomes, suggesting that what follows happens naturally or inevitably when the condition is met.

たら (N4, When, From when, Just when, If): ば and たら are both conditional forms, but with different nuances. ば emphasizes the condition itself, often with an 'if and only if' feel, e.g. 田中さんが来てくれれば何とかなる ('If Tanaka comes, it'll work out.'). たら sets up an hypothetical condition, which can be followed by a result, comment, or request, e.g. 田中さんが来てくれたら教えてね ('If/when Tanaka comes, let me know.').

なら (N4, Were it, If, If it's the case, As for (Conditional)): ば and なら are both conditional forms, but with slightly different nuances. ば focuses on the condition itself, e.g. 田中さんが来てくれれば何とかなる ('If Tanaka comes, it'll work out.'). In contrast, なら has the nuance that the speaker has some reason to believe the condition is likely, e.g. 田中さんが来てくれるなら 'if Tanaka comes (as I expect he might)'.

もし (N4, If (For emphasis)): もし and ば are both used in conditional expressions, but play different roles. ば is a grammatical ending that turns verbs into 'if' statements, e.g. 食べる 'eat' becoming 食べれば 'if (you) eat'. In contrast, もし is used at the start of sentences or phrases to emphasize that a hypothetical statement follows, and therefore is often paired with ば, たら, or なら, e.g. もし食べれば 'if (you) were to eat...'.

ば〜ほど (N3, The more…the more): ば is a conditional form that emphasizes the condition needed for a result, e.g. 勉強すればうまくなるよ ('If you study, you'll get better.'). ば〜ほど builds on this to mean 'the more (A), the more (B)' e.g. 勉強すればするほど、うまくなる ('The more you study, the better you'll get.').

meaning: Were it, If, If it's the case, As for (Conditional)
summary: A phrase that expresses something hypothetical, but is often used in same way as は.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About なら
text: As mentioned in our lesson about ば, なら is often used by itself to mean 'if'. This is considered to be an abbreviation of ならば, the hypothetical form of なり, a classical auxiliary verb that is not used much in modern Japanese.

Because なり originally meant 'to be', it functions in a similar way to the auxiliary verb だ. This means that it regularly pairs with nouns, or phrases that have been nominalized (become noun-like), through the use of の.
However, unlike だ (or です), なら is also regularly used without the extra help of の for nominalization, and can be attached directly to verbs or い-Adjectives.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: Although なら comes from the classical auxiliary verb なり, it should not be confused with the particle なり, which often has the meaning of 'as soon as', or 'just after'. Thankfully, the particle なり is also quite uncommon in modern Japanese.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: なら replaces だ when used with nouns or な-adjectives

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ばあいは (N4, In the event of, In the case of): なら and ばあいは (often in kanji as 場合は) both correspond to 'if', but with different nuances. なら expresses 'if it's the case that (A)', often implying the speaker believes it will happen, e.g. 来るなら 'if it's the case that (they) come'. In contrast, ばあいは means 'in the event that (A)', presenting a possible situation without assumption, e.g. 来る場合は 'in the event that (they) come'.

もしも～なら・もしも～でも (N3, If, Supposing): なら is a conditional that follows phrases to mean 'if it's the case that (A)', often implying the condition is likely or assumed. もしも adds emphasis to the hypothetical nature of a situation and is placed at the beginning, e.g. もしも雨なら 'if it were to rain'. It can also appear with でも, e.g. もしも雨でも 'even if it rains' (implying 'I'll still go', etc.).

としたら・とすれば・とすると (N3, If it were the case that, Assuming that...): Both としたら・とすれば・とすると and なら express 'if,' but with different nuance. としたら (and its variants) emphasize a strongly hypothetical condition, like the English 'if we suppose that (A)'. In contrast, なら can imply that the speaker believes the condition likely to happen, e.g. 'if it's true that (A)', or 'if it's the case that (A)'.

もし (N4, If (For emphasis)): なら and もし are both used in conditional expressions but have different roles. なら follows phrases to mean 'If it's the case that (A)', often implying the speaker believes it will happen. もし is used at the start of sentences or phrases to emphasize that a hypothetical statement follows, and is often paired with conditionals like なら, ば, or たら, e.g. もし雨なら行かない ('If it rains, I won't go.').

ば (N4, If… then, (Conditional)): ば and なら are both conditional forms, but with slightly different nuances. ば focuses on the condition itself, e.g. 田中さんが来てくれれば何とかなる ('If Tanaka comes, it'll work out.'). In contrast, なら has the nuance that the speaker has some reason to believe the condition is likely, e.g. 田中さんが来てくれるなら 'if Tanaka comes (as I expect he might)'.

こそ (N3, For sure, For certain, Even more so, Underlined or bolded text): こそ and なら can look similar after a noun, e.g. 彼こそできる vs. 彼ならできる, but differ in nuance. こそ is emphatic, suggesting that something someone is 'the one', e.g. 彼こそできる ('He's exactly the one who can do it.'). なら implies a conditional focus, e.g. 彼ならできる ('If it's him we're talking about, he can do it.'), without the nuance of excluding other possibilities that こそ can have.

それなら (N2, Then, If that's the case): なら follows a phrase or noun to express a condition, as in 田中さんが行かないなら、私も行かない (If Tanaka isn’t going, I won’t go either). The なら of それなら is the same particle, but the phrase それなら is used sentence-initially to refer back to something previously mentioned, as in 行かないの？それなら私も行かない (You’re not going? In that case, I won’t go either).

と (N4, If, When, Whenever, And, [Conditional]): Both と and なら are conditional expressions, but differ in nuance. と is used for habitual or automatic results, e.g. 春になると花が咲く ('When it becomes spring, flowers bloom.'). なら is used for one-time or assumed situations and implies the speaker believes the condition is likely, e.g. 雨なら出かけない ('If it's going to rain, I won't go out.').

たら (N4, When, From when, Just when, If): なら and たら are both conditional expressions but differ in nuance and usage. なら means 'if it's the case that (A)', often implying the speaker believes it will happen, e.g. 来るなら 'if it's the case that (they) come'. たら covers the ideas of both 'if' and 'when', expressing both hypothetical conditions or guaranteed events, e.g. 駅に着いたら電話してください ('Call me when/if you arrive at the station.').

meaning: To feel, To think, To act as if, To want, To desire
summary: A word that describes the way that others are acting, or may be feeling.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About がる
text: がる is a う-Verb that is primarily used as a suffix in Japanese. When used in this way, it means 'to act like (A)', or 'to show signs of being (A)', where (A) is the word that it is attached to.
To use がる, you will need to link it to the stem form of an い-Adjective (simply remove the い), or to the stem form of a な-Adjective (do not include the な).

がる is a verb which means 'to give the impression of (A)', or 'to act like (A)'. This is very important in Japanese, as you would not usually say how somebody else feels, unless they told you directly and you are simply repeating what you heard (in which case you would use the quotation particle と).

When you want to express the way you 'think' that someone else feels, but don't have any direct information about it, that is when がる would be natural to use. For example, if you see someone shivering in the cold, you would say something like the following.

The main difference between がる, and がっている, is that がる will be used when a person usually/always acts a certain way, whereas がっている is more about the way someone/something is acting in any specific moment.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: がる is used in たがる construction, which is simply たい + がる.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: たい (N5, Want to do): The たい form expresses personal desires, like バナナが食べたい ('I want to eat a banana'). がる, on the other hand, is used to show that someone else seems to want something, like 食べたがっている ('[He/she] seems like they want to eat'). The たい form is generally not used for others' desires unless the subject has explicitly made their desire clear.

たがる (N4, To want to (Third person)): がる attaches to adjectives to describe the observed feelings or desires of another person, e.g. 寒がる 'seems cold', ほしがる 'seems to want (A)', and so on. When combined with the たい-form of verbs, it becomes たがる, expressing observed desire, e.g. 飲みたがる 'seems to want to drink'.

がほしい (N4, To want something, To be in need of): がほしい and がる both express desire but differ in usage. がほしい straightforwardly expresses the speaker's own wants, e.g. 車がほしい ('I want a car.'). In contrast, がる attaches to adjectives (e.g. ほしい becomes ほしがる) to describe what someone else appears to feel, e.g. 田中さんは車をほしがっている ('Mr. Tanaka seems to want a car.').

てほしい (N4, I want you to): てほしい and がる both relate to expressing desire but are used differently. てほしい is used when you want someone to do something, e.g. これを買ってほしい ('I want you to buy this.'). がる describes what another person appears to feel, e.g. 田中さんは車を買いたがっている ('Mr. Tanaka seems to want to buy a car.').

meaning: To give off, Smell, Sound, Taste, Sensation
summary: An expression used to highlight that something is causing a specific sensory experience, or that that sense is going.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About がする
text: In Japanese, describing things that can be experienced with the senses (excluding visual), is a little bit different to the way that we would convey it in English. Traditionally, we would use unique verbs for each of these situations, such as 'smells like (A)', 'tastes like (A)', 'feels like (A)', etc. While this is still possible in Japanese, it is not the most common way.

がする is a grammar construction that focuses on the source of the smell, sound, taste, or feeling, and makes the sensory experience itself the subject of the sentence. To use がする, simply attach it to the end of any phrase that expresses which type of 'sense' is being created/given off by the subject.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: 聞こえる (N4, To be audible, To sound (like), (Can) hear, To be heard): がする and 聞こえる both express sensory experiences, but differ in nuance. がする is used with sensory words, e.g. 音がする 'I hear', 匂いがする 'I smell', and 味がする 'I taste' (literally, 'It gives off a sound/smell/taste.'). 聞こえる focuses specifically on sound and means 'to be heard' or 'to sound like', e.g. 音楽が聞こえる ('I hear music.') or 音楽に聞こえる ('It sounds like music.').

にみえる (N4, To look, To seem, To appear): がする and にみえる (often written in kanji as に見える) both describe sensations, but differ in usage. がする is used with sensory words, e.g. 音がする 'I hear', 匂いがする 'I smell', and 味がする 'I taste' (literally, 'It gives off a sound/smell/taste.'). に見える specifically describes visual sensations and means 'looks like', e.g. 石に見える ('It looks like a rock.'), without implying that it is the thing it visually resembles.

summary: An expression used to describe wearing accessories or similar items. It is also sometimes used to describe a person’s facial expression or appearance.
formation: Noun + を + しています (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About する (Have/Wear)
text: Although する is most often translated as 'to do', it has some other uses in Japanese which may not be immediately intuitive. One such use is to say that someone is 'wearing' something, or that someone 'has' a certain type of physical feature or expression.
Grammatically, the clothing or physical feature will be marked by を, as in a regular active sentence. する will normally be used in combination with ている, when used in this sense.
The sort of physical features that are used with する are generally limited. The most common is a type of face or expression, but it may also be seen with eyes, build (of a body), or voices.

Equally, when used with 'worn' items, the usage is limited, normally with accessories or items which are added or 'fastened', not with items which cover whole areas. Other verbs are normally more natural for clothing.

summary: A phrase used to make guesses about what others want to do, or speak in the third person.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About たがる
text: As we explored in our lesson about がる, this verb can be used with adjectives, to express the way in which people are acting. However, it can also be partnered with the auxiliary verb たい, to form たがる. This grammar construction is used when expressing that someone is acting like they 'want' to do something.
To use this structure, attach たい to the ます stem form of any verb, then replace the い in たい with がる.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: がほしい (N4, To want something, To be in need of): がほしい and たがる both express desire but differ in usage. がほしい is used for the speaker's own wants, e.g. 車がほしい ('I want a car.'). たがる combines the たい-form of verbs with がる to describe a third person's apparent desire to do something, e.g. 田中さんは車を買いたがっている ('Tanaka seems to want to buy a car.').

てほしい (N4, I want you to): てほしい and たがる both express desire but in different ways. てほしい is used when the speaker wants someone else to do something, e.g. これを買ってほしい ('I want you to buy this.'). たがる combines the たい-form with がる to describe a third person's apparent desire, e.g. 田中さんは車を買いたがっている ('Tanaka seems to want to buy a car.').

がる (N4, To feel, To think, To act as if, To want, To desire): がる attaches to adjectives to describe the observed feelings or desires of another person, e.g. 寒がる 'seems cold', ほしがる 'seems to want (A)', and so on. When combined with the たい-form of verbs, it becomes たがる, expressing observed desire, e.g. 飲みたがる 'seems to want to drink'.

たい (N5, Want to do): The たい form expresses personal desires, such as 日本に行きたい ('I want to go to Japan'). がる, on the other hand, is a suffix that shows when someone else appears to want something, like 日本に行きたがっている ('They seem like they want to go to Japan'). The たい form is typically not used for expressing others' desires unless quoting the subject.

summary: A phrase that expresses uncertainty, but is also frequently shortened.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About かもしれない
text: かもしれない is an expression in Japanese that is often treated as a single word, but is actually the combination of the particle かも, and the potential form of the う-Verb {知|し}る (to know) with the auxiliary verb ない attached. かもしれない is regularly translated simply as 'might', or 'maybe', but the literal translation is much closer to 'even (A), we cannot know'.
To use かもしれない, attach it to the end of any verb, noun, な-Adjective or い-Adjective, in their non-polite (keigo) forms.
As the う-Verb {知|し}る is part of this construction, it may also be altered to its polite-potential form, creating かもしれません.
Due to かもしれない being such a common grammar pattern in daily speech for expressing uncertainty about various things, several colloquial forms also exist. These are かも, かもしらん, and かもしれん.
かも is by far the most common of these colloquial forms, with かもしらん potentially sounding a little bit rough/boyish.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Colloquial: かも or かもしらん, Polite: かもしれません

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: もしかしたら (N3, Perhaps, Maybe, Possibly): かもしれない and もしかしたら both express possibility, but differ in placement and nuance. かもしれない appears at the end of sentences or phrases and means 'might' or 'may', e.g. 行くかもしれない ('I might go.'). もしかしたら comes at the beginning to emphasize the uncertainty, e.g. もしかしたら行くかもしれない ('Perhaps I might go.').

だろう (N5, Right?, Probably, Isn't it?): かもしれない (polite form かもしれません) and だろう (polite form でしょう) are both casual phrases used to express uncertainty or possibility, but with different degrees of certainty. かもしれない is less certain, similar to 'maybe' or 'might,' while だろう expresses a higher degree of certainty, like 'probably' or 'I guess.'

じゃないか (N4, Isn't it?, Is it not?): かもしれない and じゃないか can both appear at the end of a sentence, but differ in nuance. かもしれない expresses uncertainty, e.g. おいしいかもしれない ('It might be tasty.'). じゃないか is more emphatic and seeks agreement, e.g. おいしいじゃないか ('It's tasty, isn't it?' or 'I'm telling you it's tasty, don't you agree?').

おそらく (N2, Probably, Perhaps, (Most) likely, (I) fear that): おそらく and かもしれない both express possibility, but differ in certainty and placement. かもしれない comes at the end of sentences or phrases and means 'might' or 'may', e.g. 行くかもしれない ('I might go.'). おそらく appears at the beginning and expresses a stronger likelihood, e.g. おそらく行くだろう ('Most likely, I'll go.').

でしょう (N5, Right?, Probably, Isn't it?): かもしれない (polite form かもしれません) and でしょう both express uncertainty or possibility, softening a statement. The main difference is the degree of certainty: かもしれない expresses less certainty, similar to 'maybe' or 'might,' while でしょう (casual だろう) expresses a higher degree of certainty, similar to 'probably' or 'I guess.'

chapterTitle: Do it Like this, Did it Like that

summary: A somewhat casual expression that highlights the way something looks, or is acting.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About みたいに・みたいな
text: As learned in our previous lesson about みたい, it is a な-Adjective. This means that it can be used in conjunction with nouns, or with verbs. In each of these cases, it will carry the meaning of 'like (A)', or 'resembling (A)'. The difference between みたい describing a verb or a noun can be identified by whether it is followed by な (describes a noun), or に (describes a verb). Let's take a look at some examples.
This difference is important to know, as (B), the thing that みたい is describing, does not always come directly after みたい.

In the second example sentence, we can see that {泳|およ}ぐ (the verb that に is linked to), does not actually come until later in the sentence. This is quite a regular occurrence, especially in longer passages.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Despite みたい meaning 'to resemble', and being based on (usually) visual stimulus, it should not be confused with {見|み}たい 'to want to see'. This is a common mistake that learners make, as みたい itself does not have a kanji form.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: のように・のような (N4, Like (Noun), Similar to (Noun)): のように・のような and みたいに・みたいな both express comparisons, 'like' or 'similar to,' but differ in formality and structure. みたい is more casual and attaches directly after nouns, e.g. 春みたいな天気 'spring-like weather'. よう is more formal and uses の before it, e.g. 春のような天気, which has the same meaning.

と同じで・と違って (N3, Like, Similar to, Unlike, Dissimilar to): みたいに・みたいな and と同じで both express comparison but differ in nuance. みたいに・みたいな suggests similarity or resemblance, e.g. ‘like’ or ‘seems like'. と同じで states something is explicitly the same, showing a stronger degree of similarity. Conversely, と違って means ‘unlike’ or ‘different from'.

みたい (N4, Like, Similar to, Resembling): The みたい in all these patterns means 'seems like (A)' or 'like (A)'. The difference lies in how it connects to other words. Examples include 春みたい or 春みたいだ／です ('It's like spring.'), 春みたいな天気 'spring-like weather', and 春みたいに暖かい ('It's warm like spring.').

風 (N4, -style, Way, Fashion): 風 (ふう) and みたいに・みたいな both express resemblance or appearance. 風 attaches directly to nouns, e.g. アメリカ風料理 'American-style food' and can sound more formal. みたいな also attaches to nouns, but is more casual and makes a more straightforward comparison, e.g. ハンバーガーみたいな料理 = 'food like a hamburger'.

ように・ような (N4, As・like, Just like): ように・ような and みたいに・みたいな both express similarity, meaning 'like' something else. The main difference is formality and structure. みたい is more casual and attaches directly, e.g. 春みたいな天気 'spring-like weather' in a season that is not actually spring. よう is more formal and requires の, e.g. 春のような天気, which has the same meaning.

らしい ① (N4, Seems like, Apparently, I heard): みたいに・みたいな and らしい① both convey a sense of 'seems', but differ in nuance and usage. みたい compares something to something else, e.g. 春みたいに暖かい ('It's warm like spring.'). らしい expresses hearsay or inference, e.g. 暖かいらしい ('Apparently it's warm.' or 'It seems warm.' based on what was heard or observed.).

そうに・そうな (N4, Seem, Look like, Sound): そうに・そうな and みたいに・みたいな both attach to verbs and adjectives and express appearance, but differ in nuance. そうに・そうな is based on observable signs, e.g. 雨が降りそうな天気 'weather that looks like it's about to rain'. みたいに・みたいな compares something to another thing, e.g. 春みたいな天気 'spring-like weather' in a season that is not actually spring.

らしい ② (N4, typical of, -ish・like, appropriate for, becoming of, befitting): みたいに・みたいな and らしい② both express likeness but differ in nuance. みたい suggests resemblance despite being different, e.g. 春みたいな天気 ('spring-like weather' in another season). らしい describes something that fits the typical image of what it actually is, e.g. 春らしい天気 ('weather that's just like you'd expect in spring', when it is actually spring.).

chapterTitle: Do it Like this, Did it Like that

summary: An expression used when something seems to look a certain way, but the speaker isn't sure.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About そうに・そうな
text: そうだ is one of the 18 auxiliary verbs in Japanese, and can be used in the same way as な-Adjectives (may be followed by な when acting as an adjective, or に when acting as an adverb). This is a unique characteristic of そうだ and ようだ. It is not something that can be done with all auxiliary verbs. As with そうだ, そうに and そうな carry the meaning of 'seeming like (A)', or 'looking like (A)'.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Negative Verb[ない] + そう, い-Adj [ない] + さ + そう

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ようだ (N4, It seems that, It appears that, It looks like): そうに・そうな and ようだ can both mean 'seems' or 'appears', but differ in nuance and usage. そうに・そうな is based on sensory observation and attaches to verbs/adjectives (in the case of そうに) or nouns (in the case of そうな). In contrast, ようだ is based on information or inference and typically appears at the end of a sentence, e.g. 雨が降るようだ ('It looks like it will rain.').

のように・のような (N4, Like (Noun), Similar to (Noun)): Both そうに・そうな and のように・のような describe appearances, but with different nuances. そうに・そうな conveys a subjective impression or an event that seems about to happen, e.g. 優しそうな目 'kind-seeming eyes' or 雨が降りそうな天気 'weather that seems like it's about to rain'. ように・ような, in contrast, expresses comparison, e.g. 春のような天気 'spring-like weather'.

げ (N2, Seemingly, Giving appearance of, [Expresses emotions or feelings]): そうに・そうな and げ both describe appearances, but with some differences. Both can be used with adjectives like 優しそうな目 'kind-looking eyes' and 優しげな目 (same meaning), though げ is more subjective and poetic. Unlike げ, そう can also describe things that seem about to happen, e.g. 雨が降りそうな空 'a sky that looks like it's about to rain'.

みたい (N4, Like, Similar to, Resembling): Both みたい and そうに・そうな can mean 'seems like', but differ in nuance and usage. みたい expresses resemblance to something else, e.g. 春みたいな天気 'spring-like weather'. そうに・そうな is based on sensory cues and often used with verbs, e.g. 雨が降りそうな天気 'weather that looks like it's about to rain'.

にみえる (N4, To look, To seem, To appear): Both そうに・そうな and にみえる express appearance, but with different nuances. そうに・そうな conveys a subjective impression of a state, e.g. 優しそうな目 'kind-seeming eyes', or an event about to happen, e.g. 雨が降りそうな天気 'weather that seems like it's about to rain'. にみえる, used with そう or alone, e.g. 優しそうにみえる ('He/she seems kind.') or 虫にみえる ('It looks like a bug.'), specifically emphasizes visual appearance.

みたいに・みたいな (N4, Like, Similar to, Resembling): そうに・そうな and みたいに・みたいな both attach to verbs and adjectives and express appearance, but differ in nuance. そうに・そうな is based on observable signs, e.g. 雨が降りそうな天気 'weather that looks like it's about to rain'. みたいに・みたいな compares something to another thing, e.g. 春みたいな天気 'spring-like weather' in a season that is not actually spring.

ように・ような (N4, As・like, Just like): Both そうに・そうな and ように・ような describe appearances, but with different nuances. そうに・そうな conveys a subjective impression or an event about to happen, e.g. 優しそうな目 'kind-seeming eyes' or 雨が降りそうな天気 'weather that looks like it's about to rain'. ように・ような, in contrast, expresses comparison, e.g. 春が来たような天気 'weather that feels like spring has arrived'.
