chapterTitle: Do it Like this, Did it Like that

summary: A slightly formal expression that highlights that (B) is being done in the manner, or like (A).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About のように・のような
text: The auxiliary verb ようだ is used for making observations. It states that something is 'in the manner/way of (A)'. Like the auxiliary verb そうだ, ようだ may be used in a similar way to な-Adjectives (can be followed by な when acting as an adjective, or に when acting as an adverb). の is required before these constructions when it is describing a noun.

Because よう (coming from the kanji {様|よう}) usually expresses the 'manner' in which something is existing/happening, it is regularly used when the speaker has direct personal experience from which they are drawing a comparison. This means that よう will sound far more confident than みたい, or そう.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: When ようだ is describing another word (in its ような, or ように form), this is known as 'presenting an example' ({例示|れいじ} in Japanese), and means that '(A) is an example of (B)'.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: This is a version using nouns, みたい(に・な)→appearance of, のよう(に・な)→in the manner of

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: まるで…ようだ (N3, It is entirely as if, It is just as though): These are two closely related grammar points that both use 様 to make an explicit comparison. まるで～様だ is an emphatic expression that makes a statement that one thing is almost exactly comparable to something else (despite actually being different). In comparison, のように is used adverbially, likening a particular state or action to a similar one.

そうに・そうな (N4, Seem, Look like, Sound): Both そうに・そうな and のように・のような describe appearances, but with different nuances. そうに・そうな conveys a subjective impression or an event that seems about to happen, e.g. 優しそうな目 'kind-seeming eyes' or 雨が降りそうな天気 'weather that seems like it's about to rain'. ように・ような, in contrast, expresses comparison, e.g. 春のような天気 'spring-like weather'.

そう (N4, Look like, Appear, Seem, Have a feeling that): のように・のような and そう both express impressions, but with different nuance. のように・のような show direct comparison, like 'like' or 'as if,' e.g. 春のように暖かい ('It's warm like spring.'). そう expresses a perceived impression based on observation, e.g. 暖かそう ('It seems warm.').

みたいに・みたいな (N4, Like, Similar to, Resembling): のように・のような and みたいに・みたいな both express comparisons, 'like' or 'similar to,' but differ in formality and structure. みたい is more casual and attaches directly after nouns, e.g. 春みたいな天気 'spring-like weather'. よう is more formal and uses の before it, e.g. 春のような天気, which has the same meaning.

ように・ような (N4, As・like, Just like): Both のように・のような and ように・ような use よう to express similarity, but with different structures and uses. のように・のような follows nouns for comparisons, e.g. 日本人のような話し方 'a manner of speaking like a Japanese person's'. ように・ような follows verbs and conveys the meaning of doing something 'as if' or 'in a way that is like,' e.g. 日本人が話すように話す 'to speak like a Japanese person speaks'.

ふうに (N2, ~ way, In a way that suggests, Like ~): のように・のような and ふうに both express similarity, but with different usage and nuance. のように・のような follows nouns, e.g. 春のような天気 'spring-like weather', and expresses a general comparison. ふうに, on the other hand, typically follows verbs or words like こんな and そんな, implying 'in a way' or 'giving the feel of,' e.g. こんなふうに話す 'to speak in this way'.

にみえる (N4, To look, To seem, To appear): Both のように・のような and にみえる express how something 'appears,' but with different nuances. のように・のような is used for comparisons and connects to nouns or the rest of the sentence, e.g. 春のような天気 'spring-like weather'. にみえる specifically refers to visual appearance and can be used alone, e.g. その虫は葉っぱに見える ('That bug looks like a leaf.').

chapterTitle: Do it Like this, Did it Like that

slug: ようと思う-おうと思う
reading: う・よう + と{思|おも}う
meaning: I think I will, I think I shall, Going to, Gonna (Volitional + と思う)
summary: A phrase that expresses when someone thinks that they are resolved to do (A).
formation: Verb［よう］ + と思（おも）います(1) (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 〜ようと思う・〜おうと思う
text: The combination of a verb with the auxiliary verb う, or よう, followed by the う-Verb {思|おも}う gives us the common expression ようと{思|おも}う. This expression is often translated as 'I think I will (A)', or 'I shall (A)'. It is also close to the casual expression 'I'm gonna (A)'.

Remembering that う and よう can have one of three possible meanings in Japanese (as discussed in the よう grammar point), ようと{思|おも}う is usually only used to express one of those three. That 'one' is as follows:
{意志|いし} - Expresses intentions (has a similar meaning to ～するつもりだ).
This expression is also often used with {思|おも}っている. In these cases, it highlights that the intention of the speaker is something that they regularly think, or have been thinking about for some time.
{思|おも}っている may also be used when describing the intentions of another person, as discussed in our lesson about と{思|おも}う.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Let's be careful to remember the difference between the auxiliary verbs よう, and ようだ. They are different constructions that have different meanings, and behave in unique ways grammatically.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: とおもう (N4, I think): 〜よう・おうと思う uses the volitional form with と思う to express plans or intentions, like 'I intend to (A)' or 'I'm thinking of doing (A)' In contrast, plain と思う expresses a simple thought. For example, この本を読もうと思います means 'I intend to read this book.', while この本は面白いと思います means 'I think this book is interesting.'.

てみる (N4, To try to): 〜ようと思う・〜おうと思う expresses intention, similar to 'I'm thinking of doing X,' e.g. 行こうと思います ('I plan to go.') てみる conveys the idea of trying something to see what it's like, e.g. 行ってみる ('I'll go and see.'). These forms can be combined, e.g. 行ってみようと思います ('I plan to go and see what it's like.')

Verb[よう] (N4, Let's, I shall (Casual volitional)): Both use the volitional Verb [よう] form. On its own, it expresses a suggestion, e.g. 食べよう ('Let's eat.'). When combined with と思う, it expresses an intention or plan, e.g. 食べようと思う ('I'm thinking of eating.'). The key difference is that Verb [よう] includes others in the action, while ～ようと思う expresses the speaker's personal intent.

つもりだ (N5, To plan to, To intend to): Both つもりだ and 〜ようと思う・〜おうと思う can both be used to express intentions or plans for the future. つもりだ feels slightly more 'official' or definite, similar to the English 'I intend to' or 'I hope to'. In contrast, 〜ようと思う・〜おうと思う has a more casual and less definitive feel, similar to the English 'I'm thinking of (doing something)'.

chapterTitle: Do it Like this, Did it Like that

summary: An inflectional ending used when turning い-adjectives or な-adjectives into adverbs.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About く・に
text: Adverbs can be used before verbs to indicate the way in which an action is being done. This is translated in a similar way to '~ly' in English, where the adjective 'quick' would become 'quickly' when describing a verb.

Both い-Adjectives and な-Adjectives have different rules for being used adverbially.
For い-Adjectives, remove the い and replace it with く. This is also known as the conjunctive form. For な-Adjectives, に will be added directly after.
In most cases, adverbs that are modifications of an い-Adjective or a な-Adjective should come directly before the verb they are modifying.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: There are many adverbs in Japanese that are modifications of neither い-Adjectives nor な-Adjectives. For ease, we will call these 'true adverbs'. True adverbs may appear in different parts of the sentence depending on the information they are conveying. However, this is an advanced topic that will be covered at another stage.

chapterTitle: Do it Like this, Did it Like that

summary: A binding particle used to emphasize that something is not necessarily a specific thing, but could be something else.
formation: ［い］Adjective［く］+ は + ありません (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About くは
text: Besides marking the topic of a sentence in a straightforward way, the は particle can also be used to indicate contrast or comparison. One way it does this is with い-Adjectives, in the pattern ～くは.
Grammatically, this is the continuative form of an い-Adjective (く), plus the particle は.

～くは is most often used with negatives, to emphasize that something isn't necessarily one thing, but there is an implication that it still may be another. This looks similar to the regular negative form of い-Adjectives but with は inserted after く.
As は is being used contrastively here, often the contrast will be explicitly stated, although this isn't always the case.
Although this pattern of inserting は for contrast is most common with negatives, it can also be seen in positive sentences.

chapterTitle: Do it Like this, Did it Like that

meaning: Adjective + する, To make something/someone (more)
summary: A construction indicating that something is being made to have the characteristic of (A).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ～にする・～くする
text: When combined with a な-Adjective, にする (or くする in the case of い-Adjectives) carries the meaning of 'to make more (A)'.
Just like the にする grammar point that is used for highlighting decisions, this にする construction implies that the speaker has a high level of control over the action.
Basically, this changes the adjective into an adverb, and then uses する to show that the adjective itself is the thing that is being done.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: にする is one of four regularly repeating grammar patterns in Japanese that highlight the level of control that the speaker has over the action/result of an action. From highest to lowest level of control, these are as follows:
にする - High level of control, the speaker/subject can perform this action themselves.
になる - High level of control, the speaker/subject can perform this action themselves, but there is no external target.
とする - Medium level of control, the speaker/subject can perform this action, but some outside factors may need to be considered (difficulty, other people, time, etc.).
となる - Low level of control, the speaker/subject has almost no control over these actions, and something that came about purely due to external factors is being discussed.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ことにする (N3, To decide on, Have decided to): ～にする・～くする and ことにする both involve making something a certain way, but differ in usage. ～にする and ～くする are used with nouns and な-Adjectives, e.g. 綺麗にする 'make clean' and 甘くする 'make sweet'. ことにする, used with verbs, implies deciding on an action, e.g. いくことにする 'decide to go'.

ようにする (N4, To try to, To make sure to, To endeavor to): ～にする・～くする and ようにする both mean making something a certain way, but differ in usage. ～にする・～くする is used with nouns and adjectives to mean ‘make into (A)’, e.g. 綺麗にする ‘make clean’ and 甘くする ‘make sweet’. ようにする is used with verbs and conveys the idea of making sure to do something, e.g. 走るようにする ‘make sure to (or make an effort to) run’.

～になる・～くなる (N5, To become (Adjective)): ～にする・～くする and ～になる・～くなる express change but differ in focus. ～にする and ～くする imply making something a certain way, e.g. 綺麗にする 'make clean', 甘くする 'make sweet'. ～になる and ～くなる describe something changing on its own, e.g. 綺麗になる 'become clean', 甘くなる 'become sweet'. The difference is between focusing on the agent causing the change, or simply framing it in terms of the thing itself changing.

chapterTitle: Do it Like this, Did it Like that

meaning: I hope, I wish, You should, It would be good
summary: A fairly casual phrase to express hopes for yourself, or for others.
formation: Noun + だ + と + いい
(Desired Outcome) Phrase + といい + ね
(Desired Outcome) Phrase + といい + なぁ
(Desired Outcome) Phrase + といい+んだ(1) + けど(2)
(2) けれど、けども、けれども、が
Verb + と + いい + です (polite)
［い］Adjective + と + いい + です (polite)
［な］Adjective + だ + と + いい + です (polite)
Noun + だ + と + いい + です (polite)
(Desired Outcome) Phrase + といい + です + ね (polite)
(Desired Outcome) Phrase + といい + です+なぁ (polite)
(Desired Outcome) Phrase + といい+んです(1) + けど(2) (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About といい
text: One of the regular uses of the と particle is to express 'if'. However, unlike some other structures (like なら, たら, and ば), と implies that the 'if' result of と is something that will definitely happen, or is a natural consequence of (A) happening. When combined with the い-Adjective いい, it means 'if (A), it would be good'.
This construction may be used with any phrase ending in a word in its standard form.
Because と expresses a 'certain' outcome, the 'good' in this grammar construction often sounds quite strong, leading to といい regularly being translated closer to 'I hope (A)', or 'I wish (A)'.

There are several situations in which this grammar point can be used to express that you are hoping something for yourself, or hoping something for someone else. This is primarily determined by the use of な, or んだけど (hoping for yourself), or ね (hoping for others/mutual benefit).

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ばいい (N3, Can, Should, It'd be good if): When followed by いい, both ば and と express 'if you do (A), it would be good', but with different nuances. ば conveys uncertainty and is used for unlikely events, e.g. 'It would be nice if (A)', implying that it probably won't happen. と is stronger, often implying hope, e.g. 'I hope (A) happens.' Depending on context, といい can also suggest 'You should (A).'.

たらいい・といい (N3, It would be nice if, It would be good if, Should, I hope): Both といい and たらいい can express 'if you do (A), it would be good'. but differ in nuance. たら is less certain, often used for things that may or may not happen, e.g. 'It would be nice if (A).'. と is more definite and can imply hope, e.g. 'I hope (A).'. Depending on the context, といい can also suggest 'You should (A).'.

chapterTitle: Do it Like this, Did it Like that

meaning: To reach the point that, To come to be that, To turn into
summary: A grammar point that expresses something becoming the manner or style of (A).
formation: Verb［できる］(1) + ように + なる
Verb［できる］(1) + ように + なります (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ようになる
text: When combined with the particle に, and the う-Verb なる, よう expresses that a particular action has reached the point of being completed/able to be completed. Because of this, ようになる is regularly translated as 'to reach the point that (A)', or 'to turn into (A)'.
To use ようになる, it will need to be added to the plain-potential, non-past form of a verb.
However, ようになる is not limited to being used in affirmative sentences, and may also be used after a verb with ない. This shows that something has reached the point of 'not' being able to be completed.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ように (N4, So that, In order to, In such a way that): ように means 'in such a way' and expresses doing something to achieve a certain result, e.g. 忘れないようにメモした ('I took a memo so I wouldn't forget.'). ようになる, on the other hand, describes a situation changing to a certain state, without specifying the cause, e.g. 話せるようになった ('I became able to speak.').

ようにする (N4, To try to, To make sure to, To endeavor to): Both ようになる and ようにする express something becoming a certain way, but differ in nuance. ようになる describes a situation becoming that way, e.g. 行けるようになった ('I became able to go.', implying external or internal factors allowed it). ようにする focuses on someone actively making it possible, e.g. 行けるようにする ('I'll make sure I can go.').

ことになる (N3, It will end up being, It is the result of, It has been decided that): Both ようになる and ことになる express something becoming a certain way, but with different nuances. ようになる describes a change in state, e.g. 話せるようになった ('I became able to speak.') ことになる, on the other hand, conveys a decision made, often outside the speaker's control, e.g. 辞めることになった ('It was decided that I/he/she would quit.').

chapterTitle: Do it Like this, Did it Like that

meaning: Almost every ~, Nearly every ~, On a ~ basis
summary: A grammar point which highlights when something is done in the manner of every (A), but not necessarily every (A).
formation: 毎（まい） + Time Expression + のように

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About まい～のように
text: In a similar way to のように, まい～のように states that something is happening 'in the manner/way of (A)'. まい means 'every' (coming from the kanji {毎|まい}), and will always be followed by (A). (A) being a word that expresses some kind of measurement (usually time).
まい～のように is often translated as 'almost every (A)', 'nearly every (A)', or 'on an (A) basis'.

Because よう (from the kanji {様|よう}) usually expresses the 'manner' in which something is existing/happening, this phrase literally highlights that something occurs 'in the manner of every (A)', and is therefore up to the interpretation of the listener as to whether the speaker means 'every', or 'almost every'.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Although みたいに and のように are regularly interchangeable, that is not the case with まい～のように. This is because みたいだ is originally an abbreviation of the more formal phrase を見たような, and therefore can sound unnatural when used to describe things that cannot be seen, like time.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: おきに (N3, Repeated at intervals, Every other, Every, At intervals of): Both まい～のように and おきに express frequency, but in different ways. まい～のように is used with 'every~' time expressions to mean 'almost every (A)', e.g. 毎日のように 'almost every day'. In contrast, おきに attaches to a number + counter expression to mean 'at intervals of (A),' e.g. 一日おきに 'every other day' or 'at intervals of one day'.

ように・ような (N4, As・like, Just like): These expressions are related through the ように in まい～のように, which is the same as in ように・ような, both expressing comparison. まい～のように is used with 'every~' time expressions to mean 'almost every (A)', e.g. 毎日のように 'almost every day'. In contrast, ように・ような is used for general comparisons, e.g. 春のように暖かい ('It's warm like spring.').

ごとに (N4, Each, Every): Both phrases express frequency but differ in usage. ごとに attaches to time expressions, nouns, or verbs to mean 'every (A),' e.g. ３時間ごとに 'every three hours' or 失敗するごとに 'every time (you) fail'. まい～のように is used only with time words that take 毎 and adds emphasis, meaning 'almost every (A)', e.g. 毎日のように 'nearly every day'.

たびに (N3, Each time, Every time, Whenever): Both まい～のように and たびに express frequency and the idea of 'every,' but with different nuances. まい～のように is used with 'every~' time expressions to mean 'almost every (A)', e.g. 毎日のように 'almost every day'. In contrast, たびに follows verbs or noun phrases to mean 'every time (A)', e.g. 彼に会うたびに 'every time I see him' or 旅行のたびに 'every time I take a trip'.

につき (N2, Due to, On account of, Each or every): まい～のように and につき both express frequency, but in different ways. まい～のように is used with 'every~' time expressions to mean 'almost every (A)', e.g. 毎日のように 'almost every day'. In contrast, につき follows time/quantity expressions to mean 'each' or 'every,' e.g. 30分につき 'for every 30 minutes'. につき can also mean 'due to', which is unrelated to frequency.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About じゃないか
text: When learning じゃない and ではない, we briefly mentioned that these constructions are regularly partnered with the particle か, in order to form a (usually casual) question. In this lesson, we will further explore this usage.

Unlike じゃない and ではない (which need to come after a noun or な-Adjective), じゃないか is able to be attached to the end of almost any phrase, to indicate a question. This is very similar to finishing a sentence with 'isn't it?' in English.
When じゃないか is too casual, ではないか will be used instead. Despite being more formal, this may sound a bit stiff at times, so is best only used when politeness is expected.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: じゃない (N5, Is not, Isn't): じゃない follows a noun or な-Adjective to express 'is not' or 'are not.' じゃないか, with the addition of か, changes the meaning to 'Isn't it...?' as in 本じゃない ('It isn't a book') vs. 本じゃないか ('It's a book, isn't it?') While じゃない is used only after nouns or な-Adjectives, じゃないか can follow い-Adjectives and verbs as well.

だろう (N5, Right?, Probably, Isn't it?): だろう, in addition to expressing conjecture ('It's probably…'), can seek confirmation or agreement from the listener (e.g., 面白いだろう = 'It's interesting, right?'). じゃないか is more forceful and assertive, suggesting the speaker strongly believes something and expects agreement (e.g., 面白いじゃないか = 'It's interesting, isn't it!'). Both are casual forms and should be avoided in polite conversation.

かもしれない (N4, Might, Maybe, Probably): かもしれない and じゃないか can both appear at the end of a sentence, but differ in nuance. かもしれない expresses uncertainty, e.g. おいしいかもしれない ('It might be tasty.'). じゃないか is more emphatic and seeks agreement, e.g. おいしいじゃないか ('It's tasty, isn't it?' or 'I'm telling you it's tasty, don't you agree?').

のではないだろうか (N2, I think ... isn't it?, It might be that..., Don't you agree?): Both じゃないか and のではないだろうか are negative questions similar to the English '...isn't it?' but differ in nuance. じゃないか is used to confirm something the speaker believes to be true, often with a confrontational or challenging tone, e.g. 'It's (A), isn't it!?' In contrast, のではないだろうか is more tentative, expressing uncertainty and seeking confirmation, e.g. 'Do you suppose it's (A)?'.

ね (N5, Isn't it?, Right? (Sentence ending particle) ): じゃないか and ね both seek agreement at the end of a sentence, but they have different nuances and levels of politeness. じゃないか is casual and assertive, often strongly insisting on an opinion, and can feel confrontational, making it best suited for use among close friends. In contrast, ね is softer and used widely to seek gentle agreement or confirmation in various contexts.

でしょう (N5, Right?, Probably, Isn't it?): でしょう, in addition to expressing conjecture, can also seek confirmation or agreement from the listener (e.g., 面白いでしょう = 'Interesting, right?'). じゃないか is more forceful and casual, implying the speaker strongly believes something and expects the listener to agree (e.g., 面白いじゃないか = 'Interesting, isn't it!'). Note that でしょう is polite, while じゃないか is very casual.

～のだろうか (N4, I wonder...): Both ～のだろうか and じゃないか seek confirmation, but with different levels of confidence. のだろうか expresses uncertainty, used for low-confidence guesses or suppositions, e.g. 'I wonder if (A)?'. In contrast, じゃないか is used to confirm something the speaker believes to be true, often with a confrontational or challenging tone, e.g. 'It's (A), isn't it!?'.

chapterTitle: Do it Like this, Did it Like that

summary: A structure that presents a presumption based on information about (A) having the appearance that one would expect of (A).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About らしい ①
text: The auxiliary verb らしい is very similar to the auxiliary verbs そうだ and ようだ, in that it expresses something that the speaker 'thinks' is true. This use is known as {推定|すいてい} (presumption) in Japanese. However, despite being a presumption/assumption, らしい usually sounds relatively confident.
らしい is regularly translated as 'it seems like (A)', or 'I heard that (A)'.
To use らしい, attach it to the end of any (non-polite) verb, adjective, or noun.

In these examples, らしい indicates that the speaker has some reason to believe that (A) is true. This could be that they heard, saw, or read something, but are still not 100% sure whether their understanding is correct or not. In this way, it sounds very similar to 'it appears as though (A)' in English.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: そう (N4, Look like, Appear, Seem, Have a feeling that): The main difference between そう and らしい① lies in the source of information. そう implies speculation based on personal observation, e.g. 面白そう ('It looks interesting.'). らしい is based on secondhand information or inference, e.g. 面白いらしい ('I hear it's interesting.' or 'Apparently, it's interesting.').

とみえる (N4, It seems that, It can be deduced, One can conclude that): らしい ① and にみえる both express observations, but differ in nuance and formality. らしい ① suggests hearsay or information from a third-party source, e.g. 知っていたらしい ('Apparently he/she knew.'). In contrast, とみえる is more formal and expresses the speaker's deduction based on evidence, e.g. 知っていたと見える ('It appears he/she knew.', as if drawing a conclusion based on evidence).

ようだ (N4, It seems that, It appears that, It looks like): Both forms express observations similar to 'seems' or 'appears,' but differ in nuance. ようだ is based on direct information or experience, e.g. 雨が降るようだ ('It seems it will rain.', based on people carrying umbrellas). らしい① implies indirect or secondhand information, e.g. 雨が降るらしい ('I heard it will rain.' or 'Apparently, it will rain.')

らしい ② (N4, typical of, -ish・like, appropriate for, becoming of, befitting): らしい has two related but distinct functions. らしい ① conveys information heard from a third-party source with a nuance that the speaker believes it to be true, e.g. 雨が降るらしい ('Apparently, it's going to rain.'). らしい ② serves as an adjective, describing a typical characteristic, e.g. 春らしい天気 'spring-like weather'.

そうだ (N3, I heard that, It is said that): らしい ① and そうだ both convey information heard from another source, but with different nuances. らしい ① suggests hearsay with some degree of certainty, implying the speaker believes it to be true, e.g. 'Apparently it's (A)'. In contrast, そうだ is more neutral, simply meaning 'I heard (A).' or 'They say (A).'. They also connect differently to nouns and な-Adjectives, e.g. 大変らしい vs. 大変だそうだ (both meaning 'It seems difficult.').

どうやら (N2, Apparently, Looks Like, Seems like): どうやら and らしい are often used together to express conjecture based on indirect evidence. どうやら softens the statement and suggests uncertainty, while らしい indicates that the information is based on hearsay or external sources. For example: どうやら雨が降るらしい (Apparently, it’s going to rain).

ときいた (N4, I heard that): らしい ① and ときいた both convey information obtained from another source, but with different nuances. らしい ① expresses hearsay, with the nuance that the speaker is relatively confident about the information, e.g. 雨が降るらしい ('Apparently, it's going to rain.'). In contrast, ときいた literally means 'I heard (A)', with no implication about the speaker's belief, and it cannot be used for information obtained from e.g. written sources.

っぽい (N3, -ish, -like, Characteristic of, Typical of, Tendency to): っぽい and らしい ① both describe being 'like' something, but with different nuances and formality. っぽい, similar to the English '-ish,' refers to having the characteristics of something without being that thing, and is very casual, e.g. 子どもっぽい態度 'childish behavior', e.g. from an adult. In contrast, らしい ① implies embodying a characteristic in a more fitting or expected way, e.g. 子どもらしい笑顔 'a smile just as you'd expect from a child'.

にみえる (N4, To look, To seem, To appear): Both らしい ① and にみえる can convey observations, but with different nuances. らしい ① implies hearsay or information from a third-party source, e.g. 雨が降るらしい ('Apparently it's going to rain.'). In contrast, にみえる expresses a direct visual observation, e.g. 雨が降るようにみえる ('It looks like it's going to rain.', based on visual cues like the sky).

みたい (N4, Like, Similar to, Resembling): Both らしい① and みたい express similarity, but with different nuances. らしい means something is typical or characteristic of what it represents, e.g. 春らしい天気 which implies 'weather that's just like spring should be'. In contrast, みたい suggests resemblance of one thing to something else that it is not, e.g. 春みたいな天気 'spring-like weather' such as an unseasonably warm day in winter.

みたいに・みたいな (N4, Like, Similar to, Resembling): みたいに・みたいな and らしい① both convey a sense of 'seems', but differ in nuance and usage. みたい compares something to something else, e.g. 春みたいに暖かい ('It's warm like spring.'). らしい expresses hearsay or inference, e.g. 暖かいらしい ('Apparently it's warm.' or 'It seems warm.' based on what was heard or observed.).

んだって (N3, I heard that, He or She said that): んだって and らしい ① both convey information from another source, but with different nuances and levels of formality. らしい ① suggests hearsay with a nuance of certainty, indicating the speaker believes it to be true, e.g. 'Apparently it's (A).'. In contrast, んだって is highly casual and includes an explanatory nuance, similar to 'He/she/they said/say (A), you know.'.

ということだ (N3, I heard that, Rumor has it that, It is said that, It means that): ということだ and らしい ① both convey information from another source, but differ in nuance and formality. らしい ① conveys hearsay with a nuance of confidence, e.g. 雨が降るらしい ('Apparently, it's going to rain.'). In contrast, ということだ literally means 'It is said that (A).' or 'The word is that (A).', and sounds more formal and confident than らしい ①.

chapterTitle: Do it Like this, Did it Like that

summary: A grammar point that expresses an action done either to enable or prevent something else.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ておく
text: When the conjunction particle て is followed by the う-Verb {置|お}く in Japanese, it regularly has the meaning of 'to do (A) in advance'. {置|お}く as a verb itself means 'to place something' (down), but also has the nuance 'to leave something alone', or to 'drop something' (like a topic). In this way, ておく can be thought of as meaning 'to do (A) and leave it (until later)'.

When using ておく, the 'future event' that the (A) action is being done for may be something that is coming soon, or may be something that the speaker doesn't want to ever come. Due to this, ておく is also regularly used when the speaker is doing something specifically to prevent another thing from happening.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: てある (N4, Something is done, Has been done, Remaining state): Both てある and ておく express actions done for future purposes, but with key differences. てある focuses on the resulting state after the action is performed, e.g. 窓が開けてある ('The window has been opened.', when it remains open for some purpose). In contrast, ておく emphasizes the action itself, focusing on preparation, e.g. 窓を開けておいた ('I opened the window.', implying that it was for future benefit.). Note also the different particles used.

chapterTitle: Do it Like this, Did it Like that

meaning: To want something, To be in need of
summary: A common structure that identifies things that are desired.
formation: Noun + が + ほしい + です (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About がほしい
text: To say that you want something in Japanese, the が particle will be combined with the い-Adjective {欲|ほ}しい 'to want (A)', or 'to desire (A)'. This is exactly the same way as other い-Adjectives behave when describing nouns.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Do not confuse:, ほしくなかった [past negative], with, ほしくなった => ほしい+なる

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: たがる (N4, To want to (Third person)): がほしい and たがる both express desire but differ in usage. がほしい is used for the speaker's own wants, e.g. 車がほしい ('I want a car.'). たがる combines the たい-form of verbs with がる to describe a third person's apparent desire to do something, e.g. 田中さんは車を買いたがっている ('Tanaka seems to want to buy a car.').

がる (N4, To feel, To think, To act as if, To want, To desire): がほしい and がる both express desire but differ in usage. がほしい straightforwardly expresses the speaker's own wants, e.g. 車がほしい ('I want a car.'). In contrast, がる attaches to adjectives (e.g. ほしい becomes ほしがる) to describe what someone else appears to feel, e.g. 田中さんは車をほしがっている ('Mr. Tanaka seems to want a car.').

ように～てほしい (N4, Want ~ to ~ like ~, Want ~ to be able to ~, Want ~ to ~ in the way of ~): These two patterns using ほしい to express a 'want' differ in meaning and usage. がほしい follows nouns to express the speaker's desire for something, whether physical (金がほしい = 'I want money.') or figurative (自由がほしい = 'I want freedom.'). ようにしてほしい combines ようにする and てほしい to express a desire for someone to act in a certain way, e.g. 忘れないようにしてほしい ('I want you to make sure not to forget.').

たい (N5, Want to do): Both the たい form and がほしい express desires, similar to the English 'want.' The difference is that たい is used with verbs to express one's desire to perform some action, while がほしい is used after nouns to express one's desire for an object. For example, 日本に行きたい means 'I want to go to Japan' (desire to do something), while お金がほしい means 'I want money' (desire for an object).

てほしい (N4, I want you to): Both がほしい and てほしい express a want, but differ in meaning and usage. がほしい follows nouns to express the speaker's desire for something, whether physical, e.g. 金がほしい ('I want money.') or figurative, e.g. 自由がほしい ('I want freedom.'). In contrast, てほしい uses the て form of a verb to express a desire for someone else to do something, e.g. これを見てほしい ('I want you to look at this.').

chapterTitle: Do it Like this, Did it Like that

summary: A phrase which expresses that the speaker wants someone else to do something.
formation: Verb［て］+ ほしい + です (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About てほしい
text: As mentioned in our lesson about 'saying that you want something' with がほしい, sometimes ほしい can be used as auxiliary adjective (an adjective that needs to be connected to another word in order to have meaning). In these cases, it will follow the conjunction particle, て. When used this way, てほしい expresses that the speaker 'wants somebody to do something'.
To use てほしい, simply change the verb that you 'want someone to do' into its て-form, and then add ほしい.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: たい (N5, Want to do): Both たい and てほしい express a desire, with one key difference. The たい form is used to express your own desires, similar to the English 'I want to...' while てほしい expresses your desires for other people, or in other words, 'I want you to…' For example, 見たい would express your desire to see something, while 見てほしい would be used if you want someone else to take a look.

たがる (N4, To want to (Third person)): てほしい and たがる both express desire but in different ways. てほしい is used when the speaker wants someone else to do something, e.g. これを買ってほしい ('I want you to buy this.'). たがる combines the たい-form with がる to describe a third person's apparent desire, e.g. 田中さんは車を買いたがっている ('Tanaka seems to want to buy a car.').

がる (N4, To feel, To think, To act as if, To want, To desire): てほしい and がる both relate to expressing desire but are used differently. てほしい is used when you want someone to do something, e.g. これを買ってほしい ('I want you to buy this.'). がる describes what another person appears to feel, e.g. 田中さんは車を買いたがっている ('Mr. Tanaka seems to want to buy a car.').

がほしい (N4, To want something, To be in need of): Both がほしい and てほしい express a want, but differ in meaning and usage. がほしい follows nouns to express the speaker's desire for something, whether physical, e.g. 金がほしい ('I want money.') or figurative, e.g. 自由がほしい ('I want freedom.'). In contrast, てほしい uses the て form of a verb to express a desire for someone else to do something, e.g. これを見てほしい ('I want you to look at this.').

ように～てほしい (N4, Want ~ to ~ like ~, Want ~ to be able to ~, Want ~ to ~ in the way of ~): Both ように～てほしい and てほしい express wanting someone else to do something, with the key difference being the presence of よう. よう adds a nuance of doing something in a certain way. For example, 忘れないでほしい ('I want you not to forget.') vs. 忘れないようにしてほしい ('I want you to make sure to not forget.', in the sense of doing what needs to be done to ensure you do not forget).

chapterTitle: Do it Like this, Did it Like that

summary: A phrase that specifically expresses that you have heard something from someone or somewhere.
formation: Noun + （だ） + と聞（き）きました (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ときいた
text: When the particle と is used for citation in Japanese, it is regularly partnered with other verbs, to form set phrases. One of these set expressions is と{聞|き}いた, which means 'I heard that (A)'.
と{聞|き}いた may be used after any phrase expressing the thing that was heard.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: んだって (N3, I heard that, He or She said that): Both ときいた and んだって express hearsay, but with different nuances and formality. ときいた means 'I heard (A).' and conveys information directly heard by the speaker, e.g. 高いときいた ('I heard it was expensive.'). In contrast, んだって is casual and adds an explanatory nuance, like 'They say (A).' or 'I heard that (A).', e.g. 高いんだって ('They say it's expensive, you know.').

らしい ① (N4, Seems like, Apparently, I heard): らしい ① and ときいた both convey information obtained from another source, but with different nuances. らしい ① expresses hearsay, with the nuance that the speaker is relatively confident about the information, e.g. 雨が降るらしい ('Apparently, it's going to rain.'). In contrast, ときいた literally means 'I heard (A)', with no implication about the speaker's belief, and it cannot be used for information obtained from e.g. written sources.

だって (N3, I heard/was said, Because, But, Even or also, Even if or even though): Both ときいた and だって express hearsay, but differ in tone and formality. ときいた means 'I heard that (A)' and is neutral and conveys information directly heard by the speaker, while だって is casual and emphatic, often used in conversation to mean something like 'They say (A).' or 'I'm telling you (A).'.

ようだ (N4, It seems that, It appears that, It looks like): ようだ expresses that something appears a certain way, based on various cues that are not always explicitly stated, e.g. 雨が降るようだ ('It seems it will rain.', perhaps because people are carrying umbrellas, etc.). In contrast, ときいた specifically means 'I heard (A)', and indicates that the information is hearsay directly obtained by the speaker.

そうだ (N3, I heard that, It is said that): Both ときいた and そうだ express hearsay, but with different nuances. ときいた means 'I heard (A).' and conveys information directly heard by the speaker, e.g., 高いときいた ('I heard it was expensive.'). In contrast, そうだ reports hearsay in a more abstract fashion, similar to 'They say (A).' in English.

chapterTitle: Do it Like this, Did it Like that

meaning: To be audible, To sound (like), (Can) hear, To be heard
summary: An expression highlighting that (A) is audible, due to it making some specific sound. Does not require concentration to hear.
formation: Noun + が + 聞（き）こえる
Noun + に + 聞（き）こえる
Noun + が + 聞（き）こえます (polite)
［な］Adjective + に + 聞（き）こえます (polite)
Noun + に + 聞（き）こえます (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 聞こえる
text: {聞|き}こえる is a verb that is often used to describe things that can be heard, or the way in which something is heard. Because of this, the most common translations of this verb are 'to be audible', or 'to sound like (A)'. {聞|き}こえる is an intransitive verb, and literally means 'to give off sound'.

When using {聞|き}こえる, (A) will always be followed by が. (A) is considered to be the 'source' of the sound (a noun). However, the 'way that something sounds' will be marked adverbially. This means that an い-Adjective will be changed to its く form, and な-Adjectives/nouns will be followed by に.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: 聞こえる was originally a conjugation of 聞く、but nowadays it is treated as a standalone intransitive verb

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: がする (N4, To give off, Smell, Sound, Taste, Sensation): がする and 聞こえる both express sensory experiences, but differ in nuance. がする is used with sensory words, e.g. 音がする 'I hear', 匂いがする 'I smell', and 味がする 'I taste' (literally, 'It gives off a sound/smell/taste.'). 聞こえる focuses specifically on sound and means 'to be heard' or 'to sound like', e.g. 音楽が聞こえる ('I hear music.') or 音楽に聞こえる ('It sounds like music.').

れる・られる (Potential) (N4, To be able, Can (Potential)): Both 聞こえる and 聞ける can mean 'can hear,' but differ in nuance. 聞こえる refers to a sound being audible, while 聞ける indicates the ability to hear or listen. For example, a bird chirping nearby would be 聞こえる, but being able to stream a song would be 聞ける.

chapterTitle: Do it Like this, Did it Like that

meaning: To be visible, To seem, To be in sight
summary: A phrase showing that (A) is something that is visible and in plain sight. Does not require searching to see.
formation: Noun + が + 見（み）えます (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 見える
text: In the same way that {聞|き}こえる is used to describe things that are 'audible', {見|み}える can be used to describe things that are 'visible'. {見|み}える itself is an intransitive verb, meaning that the object that is 'visible' will be marked with が.

When using {見|み}える, (A) will always be followed by が. However, the 'way that something looks' will be marked adverbially. This means that an い-Adjective will be changed to its く form, and な-Adjectives/nouns will be followed by に.
This usage of {見|み}える will be covered more in our focused lesson on this particular grammar structure.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: 見える was originally a conjugation of 見る, but nowadays we treat it as a standalone intransitive verb. It is also used in honorific speech, meaning “to come.”

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: れる・られる (Potential) (N4, To be able, Can (Potential)): Both 見える and 見られる mean 'can see' (potential form) but their nuances differ. 見える describes something being visible, while 見られる refers to the ability to view something. For example, stars in the sky are 見える, but being able to watch a movie on a streaming service would be 見られる.

がみられる (N4, Can see, Can be seen, Can observe, Can be observed, Be evident, Chance to see something): Both みられる and 見える mean 'can see' (potential form) but differ in nuance. 見える means something is visible, while 見られる refers to the ability to watch or view. For example, stars on a clear night would be 見える, but being able to watch a movie on a streaming service would be 見られる.

chapterTitle: Do it Like this, Did it Like that

meaning: To suddenly begin, To start doing
summary: An expression that highlights that (A) starts suddenly, or unintentionally.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About だす
text: だす, or {出|だ}す in its kanji form is a verb that is regularly attached to the conjunctive form of other verbs. When it is connected in this way, it has the meaning of 'to suddenly do (A)', or 'to burst into (A)'.
To use this construction, simply add だす to the ます stem (conjunctive form) of the verb that you want to highlight as happening 'suddenly'.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: はじめる (N4, To start, To begin to): Both はじめる and だす attach to verb stems to mean 'to start doing (A)', but with different nuances. はじめる implies a deliberate or planned action, e.g. 学びはじめた ('I began to learn.'). In contrast, だす conveys a more spontaneous or unexpected beginning, e.g. 雨が降りだした ('It suddenly began to rain.').

かけ (N3, Half-, Not yet finished, About to, Begin to): かけ and だす both attach to verb stems and can express the start of an action, but their nuance differs. かけ emphasizes that the action has begun but remains incomplete. For example, 書きかけの小説 'a partially written/incomplete novel.' In contrast, だす highlights the beginning of the action, often with a sense of suddenness. For example, 書き出した ('He suddenly started writing.').

おわる (N4, To finish, To end): おわる and だす both attach to verb stems but express opposite ideas, like finishing vs. starting an action. おわる is used for completing almost any action, e.g. 本を読み終わった ('I finished reading the book.'). だす often describes actions that begin suddenly or unexpectedly, e.g. 雨が降り出した ('It started to rain.').

いきなり (N2, For no reason, Suddenly, All of a sudden): Both だす and いきなり express sudden action, but they differ in usage. だす attaches to verb stems to mean 'to suddenly start doing something.' For example, 動き出す 'begin to move'. In contrast, いきなり appears before verbs or phrases, like 'suddenly' in English. They can also be used together, as in いきなり動き出した ('It suddenly started moving.').

summary: A suffix highlighting a specific group of years, eras, or generations.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ～代
text: The suffix ～{代|だい} is used for several different things. One of the most common uses is for highlighting someone's decade of age. In the same way that English says teens, twenties, and thirties. All that is required is adding {代|だい} after the age (in tens), in Japanese.
In addition to someone's decade of age, ～{代|だい} can be used to express a chronological decade, such as the 1960's, 70's, or 80's. In these cases, {年|ねん}{代|だい} will be used after the decade.

summary: An intransitive verb that indicates the burden or the conditions necessary to complete something. Mainly used in sentences about money or time.
formation: Noun + が + かかります (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About かかる (Time/Price)
text: かかる is a verb that has many different uses. One common use is to say that something takes time or money. The core meaning of かかる is 'to hang', or 'to rest (weigh) upon'. When applied to time or money, the idea is that something weighs upon the subject, acting as a burden or requirement for completion.
As かかる is an intransitive verb, a general noun representing time/money/value will be marked by the subject-marking particle が.

Specific amounts of time/money expressed with counter words can also be used. However, when used with counter words, が is normally dropped entirely (a common pattern for counters in general). It may help to think of the counter as being used adverbially here, describing the verb/action itself and not acting as a noun.

meaning: Cost (money), Run you about (a certain price)
summary: A verb used to express the value of a specific object. Often used to emphasize that something is expensive.
formation: Noun + が(1) + Price + します (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About する (Cost)
text: Although する is most often translated as 'to do', it has some other uses in Japanese which may not be immediately intuitive. One such use is to say the price of something. Because する is an active verb, it can be thought of as being similar to English phrases where an item actively holds its value, such as 'commanding a price' or 'exhibiting a certain worth'.
When used in this way, the item in question will be marked by は or が. The price itself acts adverbially, so has no particle attached, and する directly follows it.
Compared to simply stating the cost of something, using する can sound similar to saying 'It will run you about...' in English. It implies something worth noting, often signifying something expensive.
When used in this way, する can also be used in questions to ask how much something costs.

summary: An adverbial particle that expresses surprise about the number of something.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About Number + も
text: The adverbial particle も is often used for labeling (A) as part of a category, when it would not usually be considered part of that group. In this way, it emphasizes that (A)'s inclusion is something that is surprising/unexpected in some way.

When も is used after a specific number + counter, it shows that the number itself is surprising. This can be when the actual number is lower, or higher than what was expected. Due to this, も can translate as 'as much as (A)', or 'not even (A)', and other similar phrases in this expression.

At first glance, this may seem different than も's translation as 'too' or 'also', but in those cases, も is also just pointing out that the something unexpected is part of whatever group was initially highlighted.
The above sentence just shows that the (B) speaker is unexpectedly putting themselves in the group that the (A) speaker initially only considered themselves to be a part of.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: からする (N1, About, Or more, Over, Starts at): からする can be thought of as a more formal equivalent of もする when following number (or number+counter) expressions, e.g. 100万円からする時計 ('a watch that costs as much as 1,000,000 yen') vs. 100万円もする時計 (same meaning, but more colloquial).

Number + しか〜ない (N4, No more than, Not exceeding, As few as・as little as, Only): Number + も emphasizes a large quantity, like 'as many as (A)' or 'a whole (A)' in English. In contrast, Number + しか〜ない emphasizes a small quantity. For example, おにぎりを３個も食べた ('I ate three whole rice balls.') vs. おにぎり１個しか食べなかった ('I only ate one rice ball.').

Number/Amount + は (N4, At least, Sort of, Or so): Both forms emphasize quantity, but with contrasting nuance. Number/Amount + は implies 'at least' that amount, with a contrastive tone. For example, ３０分はかかると思うけど ('I think it'll take at least 30 minutes.', implying that it won't be less, but might be more.). In contrast, Number + も emphasizes the amount as if the speaker believes it is a lot, e.g., ３０分もかかった ('It took thirty whole minutes.').

なん + counter + か (N4, Some, Several, A few): These patterns are similar in that both combine a counting expression with a particle. なん + counter + か combines the question word 何 (なん or なに) with a counter to mean 'a few (A)' or 'some amount of (A)', for example 何人か 'a few people.' In contrast, Number + も emphasizes that the number is large, e.g. １０００人も来た ('A whole 1000 people came.')

meaning: Almost all, Most, Hardly any, Few (Adverbial noun)
summary: A common phrase that highlights that (A) is mostly or hardly something, depending on if the sentence is positive or negative.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ほとんど
text: The adverb ほとんど is used in many situations in Japanese, and often translates as 'most', 'hardly any', 'almost all', and similar expressions. The nuance will always depend on the rest of the sentence. The most accurate translation for the word ほとんど itself is simply 'almost', where the thing that it is describing is always considered to be a full group, rather than a single thing.
As with many other adverbs that highlight an 'amount' in Japanese, ほとんど can modify a whole phrase, or can be used before の, to further specify a single noun.
In negative sentences, ほとんど translates as 'hardly any'. This is mainly due to the 'full group' that ほとんど is describing being highlighted as almost 'not' existing.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Generally written in kana, though 殆ど form can also be seen

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: めったに〜ない (N3, Hardly, Rarely, Seldom): めったに〜ない and ほとんど can be used similarly, but with key differences. めったに〜ない means 'rarely', much like ほとんど with a negative verb. For example, めったに行かない ('I rarely go.') and ほとんど行かない ('I almost never go.') are close, though めったに suggests even lower frequency. Unlike めったに, ほとんど can also be positive, as in ほとんどみんな 'almost everyone'

だいたい (N4, Most・mostly, Adequately・generally, For the most part, Roughly・approximately, In the first place): Both だいたい and ほとんど can express 'most' or 'almost all,' but they also have distinct uses. For example, だいたいの人 and ほとんどの人 both mean 'most people', and だいたい一緒 and ほとんど一緒 both mean 'almost the same'. However, they diverge when ほとんど is used negatively as in ほとんどない 'almost none', as well as when だいたい means 'generally' or 'approximately' (だいたい５時に起きる), as ほとんど cannot be used here.

slug: そんな-こんな-あんな-どんな
pattern: そんな・こんな・あんな・どんな
summary: A casual phrase that highlights things such as this (A), or that (A), or whatever (A), focusing on likeness.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About そんな・こんな・あんな・どんな
text: One of the most common ways to convey that something is 'like' something else in casual conversation, is through the use of そんな, こんな, あんな, or どんな (when asking a question). These are not officially words themselves, but are abbreviations that come from そのような, このような, あのような, and どのような.
To use this casual expression, simply say it directly before the noun that you are describing, or enquiring about.
Because these abbreviations originally come from a longer (more formal) variation, that form may also be used in situations where you would like to sound a little bit more polite.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: そういう (N4, Like that, Kind of): そういう (and its variants こういう, ああいう, どういう) and そんな・こんな・あんな・どんな both modify nouns to mean 'that sort of,' 'this sort of,' etc. While often similar in meaning, そういう tends to be a bit more formal or polite. In contrast, depending on context そんな can be used with a negative or dismissive tone, which is not true of そういう.

いかなる (N1, What kind of, No matter what kind of, No … (with a negative verb), Any... (with a negative verb)): そんな・こんな・あんな・どんな are used before nouns and mean 'that/this/what kind of' or 'something like (A)'. This is a common and fairly casual pattern in everyday speech. いかなる is similar to どんな, but with a much more formal or literary tone. For example, いかなることがあっても and どんなことがあっても both mean 'no matter what happens', but the いかなる version sounds much more formal.

そんなに (N4, So (much), That much, Like that): そんな・こんな・あんな・どんな come before nouns and mean 'that/this/what kind of (A)' or 'something like (A)'. そんなに is the same そんな, but followed by に. そんなに (as well as こんなに, あんなに, どんなに) is used with verbs or adjectives to add emphasis, similar to 'that much' or 'to that extent' in English. For example, そんな本 means 'a book/books like that,' and そんなに面白い means 'that interesting' or 'so interesting'.

summary: A slightly formal word which highlights each respective (A) in a group or series.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 各
text: One of the slightly more formal ways to say that something is happening 'each', or 'every' (A) in Japanese, is by using the prefix {各|かく}. While there is no strict rule for when this prefix can be used, it is almost always seen before words of Chinese origin (kanji compounds), or katakana words.
Although this kanji is used to mark 'each', it is very rarely used to mark units of time. The most common/natural usage of {各|かく} is for identifying things that are part of a sequence. For example:
Each/Every stop, on a train line that has many stops.
Each/Every page, in a book that has many pages.
Each/Every floor, in a building that has many floors.
Each/Every house, in a street of many houses.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: それぞれ (N3, Each, Respectively): Both 各 and それぞれ express the idea of 'each' or 'every', but they differ in usage. 各 always goes before a noun, for example, 各部屋 'each room', 各階 'each floor', and so on. それぞれ, on the other hand, can stand alone at the start of a sentence or be attached to a noun with の. For example, 人はそれぞれ違う意見がある ('People each have differing opinions.').

～ずつ (N3, One at a time, Per, Each, Gradually): Both mean 'each', but with different usage. ～ずつ follows quantity expressions to mean 'each' or 'at a time', e.g. 一つずつください 'Give me one of each.' or ちょっとずつよくなってきた 'It's gotten better a little at a time.' 各 appears before nouns and means 'every' or 'each', e.g. この電車は各駅にとまります 'This train stops at every station.'

meaning: Next to (rank), Second to, Ranked after
summary: An expression indicating that one thing follows another. It is used to express the relative order of things.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About の次に
text: の{次|つぎ}に is a phrase that is used to express that something comes 'after' something else. It shows the relative order of things.
It is composed of the case-marking particle の, the noun {次|つぎ} 'next', and the case-marking particle に. A noun or noun phrase must always come before の, as it is a case-marking particle.
The most basic use of の{次|つぎ}に is to show literal sequence in time, saying what comes 'next'.

However, の{次|つぎ}に can also show a relative ranking or order. In this usage, it will mean 'second (only) to...' or 'ranked after...'. This ranking can express things like preference or importance, not just numbers and figures.

meaning: More than (or equal to), Over・(and) above, Any more・Greater, Exceeding
summary: A phrase which expresses that (A) is the minimum amount, for which something is greater than or exceeds.
formation: Noun + Amount + 以上（いじょう）
それ(1) + 以上（いじょう）

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 以上 ①
text: In order to mark something as 'equal to, or more than (A)', {以上|いじょう} will be used. This is simply a combination of the kanji {以|い} which means 'by means of', and {上|じょう} 'above'. This expression may also be translated as 'greater than (A)', or 'exceeding (A)'.
To use {以上|いじょう}, attach it to the amount that you want to highlight as the 'minimum' amount.
{以上|いじょう} is also regularly used as a statement that translates roughly as 'the end', or 'that's it', and is a very common way to say that something has finished.
Although saying 'the end' would sound a bit rude in English in this situation, it is completely natural in Japanese, and literally means 'the above (list of things I said) is all'.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Actual Amount ≥ Amount + Counter

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: からある (N1, As much as, As many as, At least): からある and 以上① both emphasize large numbers or amounts, but differ in nuance and usage. からある means 'as many as', usually with inanimate objects (due to the use of ある), and attaches directly to nouns, e.g. ５００枚からあるチケット ('as many as 500 tickets'). 以上① means 'X or more', can be used with people, and attaches to nouns with の, e.g. 500人以上の学生 = '500 or more students'.

より (N4, More than, Over): Both 以上① and より express comparisons like 'more than (A)', but with different nuances. 以上 follows numbers or nouns like これ, and means '(A) or more,' e.g. ２時間以上かかる ('It will take two or more hours.'). より makes general comparisons and does not necessarily have a nuance of measuring some quantity.

いか (N4, Less than (or equal to), Under・(and) below, Any less・fewer, Not exceeding): 以上① and いか (written as 以下) both attach to amounts or nouns like それ, but express opposite meanings: 以上① means 'X or more', while いか means 'X or less'. For example, １００円以上 '100 yen or more' vs. １００円以下 means '100 yen or less'. In both cases, the stated number is included. 以上 and 以下 can also refer to earlier or later content in a document.

以上に (N2, More than, No less than, Even more): 以上① and 以上に are related patterns that both mean 'more than or equal to', but are used differently. 以上① typically attaches to amounts or nouns like それ, meaning 'X or more'. For example, １００円以上 means '100 yen or more'. In contrast, 以上に follows nouns, verbs, or adjectives, and means 'more than (A)'. For example, 必要以上に means 'more than necessary'.

meaning: Less than (or equal to), Under・(and) below, Any less・fewer, Not exceeding
summary: A structure which highlights that (A) is the maximum amount, for which something is less than or under.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About いか
text: In order to mark something as 'equal to, or less than (A)', {以下|いか} will be used. This is simply a combination of the kanji {以|い} which means 'by means of', and {下|か} 'below'. This expression may also be translated as 'under (A)', or 'fewer than (A)'.
To use {以下|いか}, attach it to the amount that you want to highlight as the 'maximum' amount.
Similarly to the way that {以上|いじょう} can be used to mark 'everything up until now', {以下|いか} can and often is used to highlight 'everything after now', 'the rest', or 'the following'.

text: 以上 ① (N4, More than (or equal to), Over・(and) above, Any more・Greater, Exceeding): 以上① and いか (written as 以下) both attach to amounts or nouns like それ, but express opposite meanings: 以上① means 'X or more', while いか means 'X or less'. For example, １００円以上 '100 yen or more' vs. １００円以下 means '100 yen or less'. In both cases, the stated number is included. 以上 and 以下 can also refer to earlier or later content in a document.

meaning: Except・besides, Other than, With the exception of
summary: A word which indicates everything outside of (A), or except for (A).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About いがい
text: In order to mark something as 'except (A)', or 'besides (A)', {以外|いがい} will be used. This construction is a combination of the kanji {以|い} which means 'by means of', and {外|がい} 'outside'. This expression can most accurately be translated as 'with the exception of (A)', or 'everything outside of (A)'.
To use {以外|いがい}, attach it to the thing that you want to highlight as being the 'all inclusive' amount/area.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: はともかく (N2, Setting aside, Apart from): はともかく carries the nuance of setting something aside to focus on the rest. For example, 田中さんはともかく、みんな来ると思う means 'Setting Tanaka aside, I think everyone will come.'. In contrast, いがい emphasizes exclusion, 田中さん以外はみんな来ると思う means 'I think everyone but Tanaka will come.' So, はともかく avoids commenting on Tanaka, while いがい explicitly excludes him.

を除いて (N2, Except, With the exception of, Unless): いがい and を除いて both express exclusion, similar to 'other than' or 'with the exception of' in English. Their meanings are very close and often interchangeable. The main difference is that を除いて is more formal and mainly used in writing, while いがい appears in both casual speech and writing. 土日以外毎日働いています and 土日を除いて毎日働いています both mean 'I work every day except Saturday and Sunday.'.

ほかに(も)・ほか(に)は (N4, Other, Another, Any other, Anything else, As well as, Besides, In addition): Both forms can express the idea of 'other than', but their nuance and usage differ slightly. いがい emphasizes exceptions, like 'except for' or 'other than,' and attaches directly after nouns, e.g. バナナ以外の果物 means 'fruits other than bananas.' In contrast, ほかに highlights the presence of alternatives, takes の when linking to nouns, e.g. バナナの他に 'other than bananas', and can also start a sentence or phrase.

をおいてほかに〜ない (N1, No...but, Nothing else but, None other than): Both forms express exclusion, but with key differences. いがい (often written in kanji as 以外) attaches directly to nouns, e.g. サッカー以外 'other than soccer'. It's common in both speech and writing. In contrast, をおいてほかに〜ない is much more formal and academic. It's also used almost exclusively to positively highlight something, while いがい carries no such nuance.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ずっと ①
text: The adverb ずっと has two primary meanings in Japanese. The first is that something keeps going in a constant state, without ever stopping/resting, and the second is to emphasize an amount of something. We will examine the first meaning in this lesson.
To use ずっと, add it to the beginning of the phrase that you want to highlight as being ongoing.
Alternatively, ずっと can be used after から, to express that something has been continuing 'ever since' some specific event/point in time.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: ずっと literally means that something is 'unwavering', or 'unfaltering'. Due to this, the statement that ずっと is attached to will always be perceived as being 'far more (A)', or 'to the maximum amount possible for (A)', regardless of whether it is highlighting a noun, verb, or an adjective.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ずっと ② (N3, By far, Way, Far...er, Far...more): ずっと is an adverb with two main uses that are related but differ in nuance. ずっと① emphasizes a continuous action or state over time, for example, ずっと好きだった ('I always liked you/her/etc.'). In contrast, ずっと② is used in comparisons to show degree, for example, バスケより野球のほうがずっと好き ('I like baseball much more than basketball.').

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About だいたい
text: {大体|だいたい} is an adverb that is used to highlight the 'main point' of something in Japanese, and therefore has several different nuances. {大体|だいたい} will regularly be translated as 'mostly', 'generally', or 'for the most part'.
As with other adverbs that highlight amounts, {大体|だいたい} can be used to modify entire phrases, or can be used directly before a noun as {大体|だいたい}の + noun.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ほとんど (N4, Almost all, Most, Hardly any, Few (Adverbial noun)): Both だいたい and ほとんど can express 'most' or 'almost all,' but they also have distinct uses. For example, だいたいの人 and ほとんどの人 both mean 'most people', and だいたい一緒 and ほとんど一緒 both mean 'almost the same'. However, they diverge when ほとんど is used negatively as in ほとんどない 'almost none', as well as when だいたい means 'generally' or 'approximately' (だいたい５時に起きる), as ほとんど cannot be used here.

おおよそ (N2, Approximately, Roughly, About, Outline, Gist): Both can mean 'most', as in だいたいの人／おおよその人 'most people'. They can also both mean 'approximately', e.g. だいたい３時間／おおよそ３時間 'about three hours'. However, おおよそ is much more formal and mainly used in writing. だいたい can also express 'in the first place', e.g. だいたいなんでいるの？ ('Why are you here in the first place?)' or 'roughly/adequately', e.g. だいたいでいいから ('Roughly is fine.), while おおよそ cannot.

summary: A phrase used to select one thing from within a group, and then describe it further.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About のなかで
text: Just like the grammar point の{中|なか}で～が{一番|いちばん}～, this grammar point may be used when marking one thing from within a group, and then further describing it. The only difference is that の{中|なか}で by itself simply marks something as being 'among (A)', or 'within (A)', rather than being the 'most (A)'.
の{中|なか}で is also frequently used to describe things that are happening within a place, and will translate simply as 'in (A)', in these cases.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ～のうち(で) (N2, Of the, Among(st)): ～のうち(で) and のなかで are similar expressions that both mean 'among', but their usage can differ. ～のうち(で) is most often used with number + counter phrases. For example, 5人のうち4人が合格した ('Out of 5 people, 4 passed.'). With non-numerical groupings, like スポーツの中でどれが一番好き？ ('Among sports, which do you like best?'), のなかで is more common, especially in speech.

同士 (N3, Fellow, With each other, Mutually, Between, Among, Together, With): のなかで and 同士 can both refer to groups or relationships, but their meanings and usage differ. のなかで means 'among' and is used to highlight one or more members within a group, e.g. サッカー選手の中で誰が好き？ ('Among soccer players, who do you like?'). 同士, on the other hand, emphasizes mutual relationships, e.g. サッカー選手同士で話し合った means 'They talked as fellow soccer players.'.

なかなか (N3, Very, Quite, Considerably): Though both contain なか, their meanings are different. なかなか is often used in negatives to express difficulty, like 'not easily' (なかなかできません), or in positives to mean 'quite' (なかなかいい). In contrast, のなかで means 'among' and is used when referring to one or more members of a group. For example, 果物の中でりんごが一番好き means 'Among fruits, I like apples the best.'.

summary: A semi-formal expression used to confidently describe the manner in which something appears.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ように・ような
text: We have seen many cases now where the auxiliary verb ようだ may be modified slightly to show that something is being done 'in a way' that will bring about a specific outcome. In this lesson, we will look at how ような (when used with nouns), or ように (when used with verbs) may be used with almost any noun/verb, to show that they are being done/existing in a particular manner.

Sometimes, this structure is used purely to express the speaker's uncertainty about whether (B) really is being done/existing in the way of (A). In these cases, ように (or ような) will be translated as 'as if', or 'as though'.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ような気がする (N3, Have a feeling that): ように・ような follows the plain form of a verb or adjective, and expresses similarity in a general sense. For example, 春が来たような日 'a day that is like as if spring had come'. ような気がする is a common idiom that uses this pattern, meaning 'have a feeling.' For example, 誰かが来たような気がする ('I have a feeling that someone came.').

ように～てほしい (N4, Want ~ to ~ like ~, Want ~ to be able to ~, Want ~ to ~ in the way of ~): ように・ような follows the plain form of a verb or adjective and expresses general similarity. For example, 日本人のように話す 'speak like a Japanese person'. The same よう appears in ように～てほしい, which expresses wanting someone to act a certain way. For example, 日本人のように話してほしい ('I want you to speak like a Japanese person.').

ようだ (N4, It seems that, It appears that, It looks like): ようだ and ように・ような share the meaning of 'seems' or 'appears', but differ in usage. ようだ is used at the end of a sentence to express observations or inferences, e.g. 雨が降るようだ ('It looks like it will rain.'). ように・ような connect to verbs or nouns to show similarity, e.g. 春のように暖かい ('It's warm like spring.') and 春のような天気 'spring-like weather'.

風 (N4, -style, Way, Fashion): 風 (ふう) and ように・ような both express resemblance. 風 attaches directly to nouns, e.g. アメリカ風料理 'American-style food', while ような requires の before nouns, e.g. ハンバーガーのような料理 'food like a hamburger'. 風 often has a more stylistic nuance, while ような is a more neutral comparison.

まい～のように (N4, Almost every ~, Nearly every ~, On a ~ basis): These expressions are related through the ように in まい～のように, which is the same as in ように・ような, both expressing comparison. まい～のように is used with 'every~' time expressions to mean 'almost every (A)', e.g. 毎日のように 'almost every day'. In contrast, ように・ような is used for general comparisons, e.g. 春のように暖かい ('It's warm like spring.').

という風に (N2, As if to say, As if to suggest that, In such a way that, Things like): Both という風に and ように・ような can be used to express similarity or comparison, but their nuance differs. という風に suggests doing something in a way 'as if to say' something else, meaning that the comparison can be uncertain or abstract. In contrast, ように・ような expresses a more direct comparison, implying similar qualities.

ふうに (N2, ~ way, In a way that suggests, Like ~): ふうに and ように・ような both express similarity or comparison, but their nuance differs. ふうに suggests appearing a certain way or having a certain style (literally, a certain 'air'). In contrast, ように・ような implies a more direct comparison or resemblance. Their usage also differs: ふうに is followed by verbs or phrases, while ように connects to phrases and ような to nouns.

みたい (N4, Like, Similar to, Resembling): Both みたい and ように・ような express resemblance, similar to 'seems like' in English. みたい is more casual and common in everyday speech, while ように・ような is more formal and used in writing. みたい attaches directly to nouns, e.g. 春みたいな天気 'spring-like weather'. In contrast, よう requires の, e.g. 春のような天気 (same meaning).

そう (N4, Look like, Appear, Seem, Have a feeling that): ように・ような and そう both convey impressions, but with different nuance. ように・ような expresses direct comparison or similarity, like 'as if' or 'like,' e.g. 春が来たように暖かい ('It's warm as if spring had come.'). そう is based on the speaker's observation or feeling, e.g. 暖かそう ('It seems warm.').

みたいに・みたいな (N4, Like, Similar to, Resembling): ように・ような and みたいに・みたいな both express similarity, meaning 'like' something else. The main difference is formality and structure. みたい is more casual and attaches directly, e.g. 春みたいな天気 'spring-like weather' in a season that is not actually spring. よう is more formal and requires の, e.g. 春のような天気, which has the same meaning.

そうに・そうな (N4, Seem, Look like, Sound): Both そうに・そうな and ように・ような describe appearances, but with different nuances. そうに・そうな conveys a subjective impression or an event about to happen, e.g. 優しそうな目 'kind-seeming eyes' or 雨が降りそうな天気 'weather that looks like it's about to rain'. ように・ような, in contrast, expresses comparison, e.g. 春が来たような天気 'weather that feels like spring has arrived'.

のように・のような (N4, Like (Noun), Similar to (Noun)): Both のように・のような and ように・ような use よう to express similarity, but with different structures and uses. のように・のような follows nouns for comparisons, e.g. 日本人のような話し方 'a manner of speaking like a Japanese person's'. ように・ような follows verbs and conveys the meaning of doing something 'as if' or 'in a way that is like,' e.g. 日本人が話すように話す 'to speak like a Japanese person speaks'.

とおり (N3, In that way, Exactly, Precisely, Just as): Both とおり and ように・ような can express doing something in a similar way, but their nuance differs. とおり implies doing something exactly as described, while ように・ような suggests general similarity. For example, 言われたとおりにした ('I did exactly as I was told.') vs. 言われたようにした ('I did it as I was told.'), where the latter is less precise and emphatic about how closely the speaker followed instructions.

かのようだ (N2, As if, Just like): かのようだ and ように・ような both use よう, meaning 'seems', but have different specific uses. かのようだ carries a strong hypothetical nuance and is often used to mean 'just like' or 'as if' when comparing to obviously different things. In contrast, ように・ような expresses comparison in a more direct or neutral way and can be used whether the similarity is hypothetical or real.

にみえる (N4, To look, To seem, To appear): ように・ような and にみえる can both describe similarities in appearance, but differ in usage. ように・ような follows the plain form of a verb or adjective and expresses general similarity. にみえる follows a noun or な-adjective (note: よう functions as a な-adjective) and means 'looks like'. The two can be used together, for example, 台風が来たように見える ('It looks as if a typhoon had come.').

meaning: At least, Sort of, Or so
summary: A structure which implies a general or approximate amount of (A). Often meaning at least.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About Number/Amount + は
text: The は particle has two primary functions. The first is to mark the topic of a sentence, as learned very early in our Japanese language journey. However, the second common usage of は is to highlight contrast (making a comparison). When は is used after a number/counter, it regularly has this comparison meaning. This can be translated as 'or so', or 'at least'.
Before は, the counter is regularly followed by くらい (or ぐらい). This just softens the statement, and further highlights the 'or so' meaning.

Despite being translated as 'at least', the comparative meaning of は itself is what creates the nuance of this grammar structure. The thing before は is being highlighted as an amount, while also implying that there are other amounts. This implication of another amount makes は sound as if it could mean 'as opposed to (B)'. So in essence, this grammar structure sounds like 'As for (A), as opposed to (B)', where (B) is not usually mentioned.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: は is pronounced "わ"

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: Number + も (N4, Emphasis, As ~ as, Not even): Both forms emphasize quantity, but with contrasting nuance. Number/Amount + は implies 'at least' that amount, with a contrastive tone. For example, ３０分はかかると思うけど ('I think it'll take at least 30 minutes.', implying that it won't be less, but might be more.). In contrast, Number + も emphasizes the amount as if the speaker believes it is a lot, e.g., ３０分もかかった ('It took thirty whole minutes.').

は (N5, As for... (Highlights sentence topic)): When は follows a number or amount, it often adds a contrastive nuance like 'at least' or 'no more than.' For example, １回は行ったけど means 'I went once, but no more than that.' This is similar to contrastive uses of は, like in 田中さんは行ったけど ('Tanaka went, but no one else did'). If there's no contrast, the number is usually used without a particle, as in 三つ買った ('I bought three').

なん + counter + か (N4, Some, Several, A few): These patterns are similar in that both combine a counting expression with a particle. Number/Amount + は has a contrastive nuance, implying 'at least' that amount. For example, １０人は来ると思うけど ('I think at least 10 people will come.', implying the speaker is uncertain if any more will.). In contrast, なん + counter + か means 'a few (A)' or 'several (A)', e.g. 何人か 'a few people.'

summary: A common phrase used when exactly what amount of (A) is uncertain, so a rough estimate of several or some is given.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About なん + counter + か
text: The expression なん + counter + か in Japanese is a way of highlighting an uncertain number of something, and comes across similarly to 'some', 'several', or 'a few' in English. Literally, the meaning is much closer to 'what + counter + I wonder?', as it shows the speaker's uncertainty about the number.

In addition to なん; いく, from the kanji {幾|いく} (how many/much) may be used as part of this construction. While both are fairly common, {幾|いく} is more common as part of set expressions, like {幾|いく}ら (how much) and {幾|いく}つ (how many/old), while なん is more common for counting specific things, like people.
Both {何|なん} and {幾|いく} are regularly seen in plain hiragana and their kanji forms, so it is worth remembering both.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: Number + も (N4, Emphasis, As ~ as, Not even): These patterns are similar in that both combine a counting expression with a particle. なん + counter + か combines the question word 何 (なん or なに) with a counter to mean 'a few (A)' or 'some amount of (A)', for example 何人か 'a few people.' In contrast, Number + も emphasizes that the number is large, e.g. １０００人も来た ('A whole 1000 people came.')

Number/Amount + は (N4, At least, Sort of, Or so): These patterns are similar in that both combine a counting expression with a particle. Number/Amount + は has a contrastive nuance, implying 'at least' that amount. For example, １０人は来ると思うけど ('I think at least 10 people will come.', implying the speaker is uncertain if any more will.). In contrast, なん + counter + か means 'a few (A)' or 'several (A)', e.g. 何人か 'a few people.'

誰か・どこか・誰も・どこも (N5, Someone, Somewhere, Not anyone, Not anywhere): なん + counter + か is a pattern that combines the question word 何 (なん or なに) with a counter to mean 'a few (A)' or 'some amount of (A)'. For example, 何人か 'a few people.' This is essentially the same as the question word + particle, or 誰か・どこか・誰も・どこも, structure, which is used in expressions such as 何か 'something', 誰か 'someone', and so forth.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 真(っ)
text: The prefix ま, coming from the kanji {真|ま} (true), is attached to words in Japanese to express that something is 'completely', 'exactly', 'genuinely' (A). Depending on the word that follows {真|ま}, several different conjugation patterns will be used. This conjugation depends on which column the first kana of the word after {真|ま}comes from. ま comes from the ま, み, む, め, も column, for example.
When linked with a ま column, or な column word, {真|ま} will become {真|ま}ん.
When linked with a か column, さ column, or しゃ sound word, {真|ま} will become {真|ま}っ.
When linked with a は column, {真|ま} will become {真|ま}っ, and the first kana of the following word will change to a 'P' sound.
