meaning: No more than, Not exceeding, As few as・as little as, Only
summary: A phrase showing that the only things that exist are a specific number of (A).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About Number + しか〜ない
text: The adverbial particle しか is often compared to だけ, in that it also expresses 'only'. However, unlike だけ, しか can only be used in negative statements. Due to this, しか～ない is regularly translated as 'there's only (A)', or 'there's nothing but (A)'. しか～ない may be used to express numbers, or nouns. In this lesson we will examine numbers.
To use this construction, the number that you want to express as being 'all that exists' will go before しか, then しか will be followed by a verb in its ない, or ありません form.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: Number + も (N4, Emphasis, As ~ as, Not even): Number + も emphasizes a large quantity, like 'as many as (A)' or 'a whole (A)' in English. In contrast, Number + しか〜ない emphasizes a small quantity. For example, おにぎりを３個も食べた ('I ate three whole rice balls.') vs. おにぎり１個しか食べなかった ('I only ate one rice ball.').

しか～ない (N4, There's only, Nothing but): しか～ない expresses the meaning of 'only' or 'nothing but'. For example, バナナしか食べなかった ('I only ate a banana', or literally 'I didn't eat anything but a banana.'). When used with numbers in the Number + しか〜ない pattern, it emphasizes that the quantity is small, e.g., ５人しか来なかった ('Only 5 people came.', or literally 'No one came but five people.').

summary: An expression which shows that (A) is only one thing from within the whole category of (B).
formation: Noun (A) + は + (Category) Noun (B) + の一つ + だ
Noun (A) + は + (Category) Noun (B) + の一つ + です (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ～は～の一つだ
text: In order to express that something is only one thing from within a larger category, the construction ～は～の{一|ひと}つだ will be used. In this expression, (A), the thing that there is one of, will be followed by は. After this, (B) + の{一|ひと}つだ will highlight the broader category to which (A) belongs.
In this grammar point, の{一|ひと}つ is a standard counter. This means that other counters can and will be used, when they are more appropriate than {一|ひと}つ.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ～のうち(で) (N2, Of the, Among(st)): Both ～のうち(で) and ～は～の一つだ are used to identify things within a group or category. ～のうち(で) is most often paired with number + counter phrases to mean 'among', for example, ５人のうち４人が合格した ('Out of 5 people, 4 passed.'). In contrast, ～は～の一つだ identifies something as part of a group, e.g., バナナは果物の一つだ ('A banana is one type of fruit.').

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ～ない～はない
text: ～ない～はない is an example of a double negative in Japanese, and is a grammar construction that requires careful attention in order not to incorrectly interpret. Both the い-Adjective ({形容詞|けいようし}), and auxiliary verb forms of ない may be used in this construction, depending on what type of word is being negated. Let's take a look at a few examples.
Literally, this grammar pattern is very similar to 'there isn't an (A) that doesn't (B)' in English.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ないことには～ない (N2, Unless you do something): Both forms use a double negative but differ in nuance and usage. ～ない～はない means 'There is no (A) that is not (B).' For example, 書けない漢字はない ('There are no kanji he can't write.') emphasizes complete ability. In contrast, ないことには～ない means 'unless', or literally 'If (A) can't happen, then (B) can't.'. For example, 漢字が書けないことには試験は合格できない ('You can't pass the test unless you can write kanji.').

ないことはない (N3, Is not impossible, It doesn't mean that it isn't): Both forms use a double negative to convey a positive meaning, but differ in nuance and usage. ～ない～はない means 'There is no (A) that isn't (B).', e.g. 書けない漢字はない ('There are no kanji he can't write.'), strongly affirming his ability. In contrast, ないことはない softens a statement, implying 'It's not that (A) isn't true,' e.g., 書けないことはないけど ('It's not that I can't write.', i.e. I can, but perhaps not easily or well.).

meaning: Not even a little, Not at all, Not in the least, Never
summary: A structure highlighting that something is not even a little (A).
formation: すこしも + ［な］Adjective + ではない(1)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About すこしも～ない
text: Coming from the word {少|すこ}し (a little bit), すこしも～ない is an expression which translates almost exactly to 'not even a little bit (A)' in English. Due to this, it indicates that there is 'no (A)', '(A) never happens', or 'not (A) at all', depending on whether a verb or an adjective is the word that is being negated. すこしも can come at the beginning of the sentence, or directly before the word/statement it is referring to.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: とても～ない (N3, Not ~ at all, Cannot ~ at all): とても～ない is an emphatic negative used to show that something is far beyond one's ability. For example, とてもできない ('I can't do that at all.'). In contrast, すこしも～ない means 'not even a little bit (A)' and isn't limited to ability. For example, すこしも面白くない ('It's not interesting at all.'). Unlike すこしも, とても can be used without ない if the meaning is still negative, e.g. とても無理だ ('It's completely impossible.').

決して〜ない (N3, Never, By no means): 決して〜ない and すこしも～ない are both emphatic negatives, but differ in nuance and formality. 決して〜ない is more formal and mainly used in writing, with the sense of 'by no means' or 'never'. For example, 決して危険ではない ('It is by no means dangerous.'). すこしも～ない is less formal and emphasizes absence of degree or amount, e.g., 少しも危険ではない ('It's not even a little bit dangerous.').

なかなか～ない (N3, Not really, Hardly, Not easily or readily, By no means, Far from): なかなか～ない expresses that something is not easily done, often implying difficulty or repeated effort. For example, なかなかうまく話せない ('I just can't speak well.') has the nuance that the speaker is trying but not succeeding. In contrast, すこしも～ない means 'not even a little.' 少しも話せない means 'I can't speak at all.', focusing on the absence of ability without any implication of effort or struggle.

全く～ない (N3, Not~at all): 全く～ない and すこしも～ない are emphatic negatives that can both mean 'not at all' or 'not even a little'. For example, 全く飲まない and 少しも飲まない both mean 'I don't drink at all.' or 'I don't drink even a little.'. While often interchangeable, すこしも may sound unnatural when there's no nuance of amount or degree. For example, 全く行ったことがない ('I haven't gone at all.'), which wouldn't fit with すこしも.

ことはない (N3, There is no need to, Never happens): ことはない and すこしも～ない are both emphatic negatives, but with different nuances. ことはない means 'There's no need to (A).' or 'There are no instances of (A).'. For example, 心配することはない ('There's no need to worry.'), and 彼と話すことはない ('There are no occasions when I talk to him.'). In contrast, すこしも～ない emphasizes absence of degree or amount, e.g., すこしも心配していない ('I'm not even a little bit worried.').

ぜんぜん (N4, (Not) at all): ぜんぜん and すこしも～ない both emphasize negation and mean 'not at all.' A key difference is that ぜんぜん, especially in casual speech, can also appear in affirmative phrases, e.g. ぜんぜん大丈夫 ('It's totally fine.'). In contrast, すこしも～ない is more formal and strictly used in negative contexts, e.g. すこしも寒くない ('It's not even a little cold.').

あまり～ない (N4, Not very, Not much, Not really, Hardly): Both あまり～ない and すこしも～ない are used in negative statements, but differ in degree and tone. あまり～ない means 'not very (A)' and is fairly colloquial, e.g. あまり寒くない ('It's not very cold.'). すこしも～ない is more formal and emphatic, e.g. 少しも寒くない ('It's not the least bit cold.').

すくなくない (N4, Quite a few, Quite a lot, Many, Not a few, Not a little): These expressions look similar but have opposite meanings. すくなくない is a double negative meaning 'not a few', which implies 'many' or 'a lot'. For example, そういう人はすくなくない ('There are many people like that.', or literally 'not just a few'.). In contrast, すこしも～ない emphasizes absence. For example, すこしも面白くない ('It's not interesting at all.'), which implies 'not even a little bit'.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About すくなくない
text: Another expression that utilizes the {少|すく} kanji (meaning 'few'), in its い-Adjective form, is {少|すく}なくない. This is an example of a double negative in Japanese, as {少|すく}ない 'a few' is being negated in {少|すく}なくない. Therefore, the meaning is 'not a few', and translates more closely to 'quite a few', or 'quite a lot'.
To use this expression, simply pair a noun with は, が, or も, and then follow it with {少|すく}なくない (or {少|すく}なくありません).

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: すこしも～ない (N4, Not even a little, Not at all, Not in the least, Never): These expressions look similar but have opposite meanings. すくなくない is a double negative meaning 'not a few', which implies 'many' or 'a lot'. For example, そういう人はすくなくない ('There are many people like that.', or literally 'not just a few'.). In contrast, すこしも～ない emphasizes absence. For example, すこしも面白くない ('It's not interesting at all.'), which implies 'not even a little bit'.

meaning: In the event of, In the case of
summary: A phrase which often highlights a potential occasion, or person in question.
formation: ［な］Adjective + な + 場合（ばあい）(は)
Noun + の + 場合（ばあい）(は)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ばあいは
text: {場合|ばあい}は is a phrase in Japanese that is often translated to 'in the event of (A)', or 'in the case of (A)'. It can be used with almost any type of word, but will require な when following a な-Adjective, or の when following a noun.
{場合|ばあい} by itself is usually translated as 'case', or 'situation'. It is frequently used to highlight a hypothetical situation, or a viewpoint/characteristic of another person.

When {場合|ばあい}は is highlighting a viewpoint/characteristic of another person, this is almost always in contrast/comparison to something that is already being discussed. This is an example of the contrastive nuance of the は particle.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: なら (N4, Were it, If, If it's the case, As for (Conditional)): なら and ばあいは (often in kanji as 場合は) both correspond to 'if', but with different nuances. なら expresses 'if it's the case that (A)', often implying the speaker believes it will happen, e.g. 来るなら 'if it's the case that (they) come'. In contrast, ばあいは means 'in the event that (A)', presenting a possible situation without assumption, e.g. 来る場合は 'in the event that (they) come'.

万が一 (N2, Just in case, In the worst-case scenario, In the unlikely event, By any chance): ばあいは and 万が一 are related in that both refer to potential situations. ばあいは (often written in kanji as 場合は) means 'in the case of' or 'in the event that'. For example, 行く場合は 'in the event that you go'. On the other hand, 万が一 is typically used at the start of a sentence to highlight a rare or unlikely case. Because they serve different roles, the two can even be used together, e.g. 万が一の場合は 'in the unlikely event that (A)'.

としたら・とすれば・とすると (N3, If it were the case that, Assuming that...): ばあいは and としたら・とすれば・とすると both express the idea of 'in the case of' or 'in the event that'. In general, ばあいは (often written in kanji as 場合は) is more concrete and used for specific situations that might arise. For example, 行く場合 'in the event that you go'. In contrast, としたら・とすれば・とすると is typically used to discuss more hypothetical scenarios.

と (N4, If, When, Whenever, And, [Conditional]): と and ばあいは can both express conditions, but differ significantly in usage. と describes something that happens habitually or as a natural result, e.g. お酒を飲むとすぐ酔っ払ってしまう ('When I drink alcohol, I get drunk quickly.'). ばあいは is used more for situational instructions, like お酒を飲む場合は運転しないほうがいい ('In the event that you drink alcohol, you shouldn't drive.').

に取って (N3, To, For, Concerning): ばあいは (often written in kanji as 場合は) and に取って (often written in kana as にとって) can overlap in some cases, but not all. For example, 私の場合は and 私にとって can both mean 'as far as I'm concerned' or 'in my case'. However, since にとって simply means 'concerning', it can't replace ばあいは for the meaning of 'in the event that', e.g. 行く場合は気をつけたほうがいい ('In the event that you go, you should be careful.').

summary: A casual, simple conjunctive form used as an abbreviated way of saying please do (A).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About Verb[て]
text: In casual speech, てください is often shortened to て. This usually comes across as being a friendly way to say 'please do (A)', but may sound like a very soft order, so is best used with friends/toward people of lower status.
This nuance of て is usually able to be identified by appearing at the end of a sentence.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: Verb + て (N5, And, Then (Linking events)): The Verb + て form connects verbs or parts of a sentence. It can also be used by itself as a casual request. For example, 食べて would mean 'Please eat [this.]' These casual requests are often followed by the sentence-ending particle ね to further soften them. To express a more polite request, the てください form should be used.

てください (N5, Please do (Polite request)): Both the 〜て and 〜てください are used to make requests. てください is polite and neutral, and can be used with strangers or people of equal status. In contrast, the 〜て form is more casual and is used when speaking with friends or family. Requests using either form, especially the plain 〜て, can be softened further by adding the sentence-ending particle ね (e.g. 食べてね), which adds a gentle, caring tone.

命令形 (N4, (Verb)!, Do (something)!): The imperative or command form (命令形) gives blunt commands, e.g. 止まれ ('Stop!'), often sounding forceful. Verb[て] form is softer and used for casual requests, e.g. 見て 'Look!'. Adding よ or ね softens it further, e.g. 見てね ('Take a look, okay?'), which is commonly done in friendly, everyday speech.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About てよかった
text: When て (or で when following ない) is paired with the past form of the い-Adjective, いい; てよかった, なくてよかった, or ないでよかった will have the meaning of 'I'm glad that (A)' (when positive), or 'I'm glad that I didn't (A)' (when negative).

The primary difference between なくてよかった and ないでよかった in this expression, is that ないでよかった will be used far more frequently in casual speech. Comparatively, なくてよかった tends to be reserved for books, and may even be considered old-fashioned by some people.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ばよかった (N4, Should have, I wish, It would have been better to): Though they may look similar, てよかった and ばよかった express opposite feelings. てよかった conveys relief or happiness about something that happened, e.g. 行ってよかった ('I'm glad I went.' or literally 'It was good that I went.'). In contrast, ばよかった expresses regret about something that didn't happen, e.g., 行けばよかった ('I wish I had gone.' or literally, 'It would have been nice if I went.').

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About Verb［せる・させる］
text: In order to express that someone was 'made to do', or 'let do' something, the auxiliary verbs せる and させる will be used. The meaning that せる and させる will convey (when attached to a verb) is called {使役|しえき} (causative, employment, or using) in Japanese.

A common misconception is that せる and させる are standard conjugations of each verb. However, these auxiliary verbs should be thought of as having their own meaning, in a similar way to how たい, ない, だ, です, and other auxiliaries each have their own meanings.

In order to use these grammar structures, remove the る from る-Verbs, and then add させる. For う-Verbs, change the last kana to the あ sound kana from within the same column (except for う, which becomes わ), and then add せる (る becomes ら, む becomes ま, く becomes か, etc.).

As usual, する and {来|く}る have special conjugation rules. する will be replaced completely by させる (in a similar way to how できる completely replaces する in the 'potential' form). {来|く}る will become {来|こ}させる.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: Because the actual 'doer' in causative verb sentences will be marked with が (as is always the case), the literal translation of せる and させる is closer to the following:
(A) が (B) に楽しませる - For (A) to cause fun 'in' (B).
(A) が (B) を楽しませる - For (A) to cause fun 'through' (B).
It is these standard meanings of the particles に (a location) and を (a target) that will create the 'let', or 'make' nuance when using せる, or させる.

text: Causative-Passive (N4, Verbs (Causative-passive voice), To be made to do something, To be forced to do): The causative (Verb［せる・させる］) and the causative-passive are two related verb forms. Verb［せられる・させられる］ is used to express either 'letting' or 'making/forcing' someone do something. For example, the causative of 行く 'go' is 行かせる 'let/make (someone) go'. The causative-passive is the passive form of this, meaning 'to be made to do (A)', e.g., 行かせられた (or the contracted form 行かされた) means 'I was made/forced to go.'.

Verb［れる・られる］ (N4, Was done to ~ by ~, Done without consent, Done to one's dismay): The passive (Verb［れる・られる］) and causative (Verb［せる・させる］) forms are both fundamental in Japanese. The passive shows that an action was done to someone, while the causative means to make or let someone do something. For example, 食べられた 'was eaten' vs. 食べさせた 'made/let someone eat'.

他動詞・自動詞 (N4, Done through action vs. occurring on its own): 他動詞 (transitive) verbs act on something, while 自動詞 (intransitive) verbs describe actions that happen by themselves. The causative form means to make or let someone do something, so intransitive verbs become transitive when changed, e.g. 人が走る 'a person runs' vs. 人を走らせる 'make a person run'.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About といってもいい
text: と{言|い}ってもいい is a common expression in Japanese which literally means 'even if you say (A), it is good/ok'. This is translated more naturally as 'you could say (A)', or 'you might say (A)'.
As the と at the beginning of the phrase is the 'quotation' use of the と particle, と{言|い}ってもいい may be used after almost any statement that the speaker wants to quote.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: Most grammatical structures in Japanese that use {言|い}う will often appear without kanji. This is simply to make them easier to recognize as a grammar pattern, rather than a standard word in a sentence. This is also true for patterns that include {行|い}く, or {来|く}る.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: と (N5, Quotation): と is a quoting particle used to mark the content of direct or indirect speech, thoughts, or feelings. For example, 行くと言っていた means '[He] was saying [he] will go.' といってもいい combines と with 言う and the い-Adjective いい, meaning 'You/one could say' (literally, 'It's fine even if one says...').

と言える (N3, Would or could say that..., Can probably say that..., Fair to say that...): Both と言える and といってもいい can express a meaning similar to the English 'it can/might be said that (A)' with the difference being the degree of assertiveness. と言える is a firmer statement, literally meaning '(A) can be said.'. In contrast, といってもいい sounds more tentative, implying that it would be fine/acceptable to say the thing in question, but allowing for the possibility that other views/opinions may also be valid.

Verb + てもいい (N5, It's okay to, It's alright to, Can/may): The ても form has the core meaning of 'even if.' One common use is Verb + てもいい, which gives or asks for permission—for example, 食べてもいいですか？ literally means 'Is it okay even if I eat this?' but works like 'Can/May I eat this?' in English. Similarly, といってもいい means 'It's okay even if you say...' but is used to express 'You could say' or 'One might say.'

ないでもない (N1, Kind of, Might, Slightly, It’s not (impossible) that, Somewhat, In some respects): These forms are similar in that both can make a statement sound less certain, but their nuance differs. ないでもない uses a double negative, literally 'It's not not (A).', to express a somewhat unsure positive, e.g., 分からないでもない ('I kind of understand.', or literally 'It's not that I don't understand.'). といってもいい suggests 'you could say (A)', e.g. 問題ないといってもいい ('You could say there's no problem.').

って (N5, Casual quotation): って (a contracted form of と) is a casual quoting particle used to mark direct or indirect speech, thoughts, feelings, or to introduce a topic casually. For example, 行くって言っていた means '[They] were saying [they] will go.' といってもいい combines と with 言う and いい, meaning 'You/one could say' (literally: 'It's fine even if one says...').

summary: A phrase that may be used with many types of words, to express that even though (A), (B).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ても
text: The combination of the conjunction particle て (or the case-marking particle で), with the adverbial particle も, often has the nuance of 'even if (A)', or 'even though (A)'.
To use this structure, simply conjugate a verb or い-Adjective into its て-form, and then add も.
For nouns and な-Adjectives, でも will be used instead.
This grammar pattern may also be used for highlighting negative sentences, and will translate similarly to 'even if not (A)', or 'even though not (A)' in these cases.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: でも (the form after nouns and な-Adjectives) is often considered to be an adverbial particle itself, and there is often debate amongst native speakers as to whether でも is actually a word, or simply a standard grouping of で, the case marking particle and も, the adverbial particle. However, It may be easier to remember でも as its own word, for learning purposes.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: てもいい (N5, It is alright/fine/okay even if, Can/may, ~ is also okay): てもいい is a common grammatical pattern used to give or ask for permission. At the core of this expression is the ても conditional pattern. Though てもいい is often translated as 'Can I…' or 'May I…' in English, the literal meaning is 'Is it okay even if I...?' In this sense, the basic ても pattern has an even wider range of uses. For example, 負けてもあきらめない means '(I) won't give up even if (I) lose.'

たとえ〜ても (N3, Even if…is the case, Supposing that): たとえ～ても is a stronger and more limited version of ても used in hypothetical situations. For example, たとえどこに行っても 'no matter where you might go' is a more emphatic version of どこに行っても 'wherever you go'. However, in cases where ても expresses permission, e.g. てもいい 'you can (A)', たとえ would not be used, since the meaning is not strongly hypothetical.

でも (N4, Or something, Any... (with question words), No matter (who)): The particle でも can attach to question words to mean 'any~' as in 誰でも 'anyone' or なんでも 'anything', or follow nouns to suggest a casual option, like in お茶でも飲みませんか？ ('Want some tea or something?'). This looks similar to ても, which becomes でも after nouns and な-adjectives, but means 'even if', as in 日本語でも大丈夫です ('It's fine even if it's in Japanese.').

もしも～なら・もしも～でも (N3, If, Supposing): ても is a highly versatile structure meaning 'even if,' used widely in both speech and writing. In contrast, ようが～まいが is much more formal and mainly found in written or academic contexts. Both forms can express 'whether or not'. For example, 食べても食べなくても and 食べようが食べまいが both mean 'whether or not (you) eat', but the latter is more emphatic and formal.

もし (N4, If (For emphasis)): もし and ても both express hypothetical situations, but in different ways. もし appears before a clause to emphasize the condition, similar to 'if' or 'supposing that', while ても is attached to the verb itself. Because they fill different roles, they can be used together, e.g., もし雨が降っても 'even if it rains'. もし can also pair with other conditionals like たら or ば.

にしたところで (N1, Even, Even for, Even from the perspective of, Even in the case of): Both express concession meaning ‘even if,’ but the tone and strength differ. にしたところで is a more emphatic and formal way to say ても, often used to stress that the result will not change despite the condition, sometimes implying resignation or futility, as in 急いだところで間に合わない ('Even if we were to hurry now, we won’t make it in time.'). ても is the neutral, everyday way to say 'even if', and is used broadly without added emphasis, as in 急いでも間に合わない ('Even if we hurry, we won’t make it.').

さえ (N3, Even): さえ and ても can both express the meaning of 'even' and sometimes overlap, especially with nouns. For example, 子どもでもできる and 子どもさえできる both mean 'Even a child can do it.'. However, they diverge when ても expresses permission, such as in 行ってもいい ('You can go.') or when さえ means 'if only', e.g. お金さえあれば 'as long as you have money'. In these cases, the two expressions are not interchangeable.

Verb + てもいい (N5, It's okay to, It's alright to, Can/may): ても has the core meaning of 'even if.' One common use is in Verb + てもいい to ask or give permission. For example, 食べてもいいですか？ means 'Can/May I eat this?' (literally, 'Is it okay even if I eat this?') More broadly, ても can also express contrast. For example, 寒くても行きます means 'I'll go even if it's cold.'

にせよ・にしろ (N2, Even if, Even though, No matter, Whether… or): Both forms can express the meaning of 'even if'. ても is more versatile and commonly used in both everyday speech and writing, while にせよ・にしろ is more limited in usage, with にせよ sounding especially formal. Note that ても is often used in the pattern てもいい 'it's okay to (A)' to ask or give permission, whereas にせよ・にしろ is not used this way.

たって (N2, Even if, Even though, No matter how): ても and たって both mean 'even if' or 'even though,' with the main difference being tone and formality. ても is widely used in both everyday speech and writing, while たって is more casual and emphatic, typically found in informal conversation. Aside from tone, their meaning is nearly identical, e.g., 行っても and 行ったって both mean 'Even if I/you/etc. go...'

ようが～まいが (N1, Even if, No matter what, Whether or not, [Emphatic], Volitional + が): ても is an extremely versatile expression used to mean 'even if' in a wide variety of contexts, both in everyday speech and writing. In contrast, ようが～まいが is a highly formal expression that specifically means 'whether or not' and occurs primarily in written or academic language. For example 食べようが食べまいが and 食べても食べなくても both mean 'whether or not (you) eat', but the former is far more formal and emphatic.

としても (N2, Even if (we assume), Assuming, Also as): Both forms can express the meaning of 'even if' or 'even though.' ても is more versatile and commonly appears in expressions like てもいい 'it's okay to (A)' to ask or give permission. としても has a stronger hypothetical nuance similar to 'Even assuming that…', and can also serve as a more emphatic version of として. For example, 私としても大変だ ('It's tough even for me.').

にしても (N3, Even though, Even if, Even when, Also): Both forms can mean 'even if' or 'even though,' but differ in nuance. ても is more versatile and often appears in expressions like てもいい 'it's okay to (A)' for asking or giving permission. にしても carries a stronger hypothetical tone, like 'Even supposing that...' which ても alone doesn't necessarily convey. Both are used with question words, e.g. どこに行っても and どこに行くにしても 'no matter where you go', with the latter sounding more hypothetical.

meaning: To do something by accident, To finish completely・totally, Unfortunately
summary: A structure that expresses that (A) is done completely, or unfortunately.
formation: (*) Used when Verb［て］ends with で

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About てしまう・ちゃう
text: By combining the conjunction particle て, with the verb しまう (sometimes written as {終|しま}う), you are able to express that something was done 'by accident', 'completely', or 'unfortunately'. These meanings may seem quite different, but we will discuss their similarities in a moment. Let's look at a few examples of てしまう first.
As we can see, verbs that usually take
で
instead of
て
will be no different when using
てしまう
Sometimes, てしまう or でしまう will be shortened to a more casual form, which are often used in speech. These forms are as follows:
てしまう will become ちゃう
でしまう will become じゃう

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: てすみません (N4, I'm sorry for): てすみません is used to apologize for doing something, e.g. 遅れてすみません ('Sorry for being late.'). It often pairs with てしまう・ちゃう, which adds a nuance of regret or accident. For example, 遅れてしまってすみません・遅れちゃってすみません ('I'm sorry I was late.'), which implies that you didn't mean to do so and feel bad it happened.

はじめる (N4, To start, To begin to): はじめる attaches to verb stems to mean 'to begin' or 'start' doing something, e.g. 食べはじめる 'to start eating'. In contrast, てしまう・ちゃう follows the て-form and can express doing something unintentionally or completely, e.g. 食べてしまった・食べちゃった ('I ate it unintentionally.' or 'I ate it all.').

切れない (N3, Being unable to finish or complete): てしまう・ちゃう and 切れない can express opposite meanings. One nuance of てしまう・ちゃう is to do something completely, e.g. 食べてしまった has one potential meaning of 'I ate it all.'. In contrast, 食べ切れなかった would mean 'I couldn't eat all of it.'. Note that てしまう・ちゃう can also express regret or an unintentional action, which 切れない does not. For example, 食べてしまった could also mean 'I ate it (even though I didn't intend to).'.

おわる (N4, To finish, To end): おわる attaches to verb stems to mean 'to finish doing (A)', e.g. 食べおわった ('I finished eating.'). In contrast, てしまう・ちゃう uses the て-form and can also mean doing something completely, but often adds a nuance of regret, finality, or lack of intention, e.g. 食べてしまった・食べちゃった ('I ate it and now it's gone.' or 'I didn't mean to eat it.').

つい (N3, Accidentally, Unconsciously, Against one's better judgement): つい and てしまう・ちゃう can both express doing something unintentionally or against one's better judgment. つい appears at the beginning of a sentence or phrase, while てしまう・ちゃう is a verb ending. They are often used together to emphasize the nuance of regret or unintentionally, e.g. つい食べてしまった・つい食べちゃった would imply 'I ended up eating it (even though I didn't mean to).'.

切る (N3, To do something completely to the end, Utterly, Resolutely): 切る conveys the idea of doing something completely, which overlaps with one nuance of てしまう・ちゃう, but their usage differs. てしまう・ちゃう can imply that the action was unintentional or against one's will, which 切る cannot. In other words, 食べ切った simply means 'I ate all of it.', while 食べてしまった・食べちゃった also can have the meaning of mean 'I ended up eating it (even though I didn't intend to).', which 食べ切った cannot.

上がる・上げる (N3, Something is finished, To finish something, Something has come to an end, To do something completely, To do something through): 上がる・上げる can express the idea of completing an action, which overlaps with てしまう・ちゃう, but they differ in nuance. てしまう・ちゃう can express regret or lack of control, while 上がる・上げる focuses on the act of producing a finished result. For example, 書き上げる 'finish writing'. In contrast, てしまう・ちゃう can be used with any verb, regardless of whether a tangible result is produced.

meaning: And・and so, Due to, Because of, Since, Conjunctive
summary: A casual, simple conjunctive form indicating (A) as being the reason or cause of (B).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About Verb[て] + B
text: One of the functions that the conjunction particle て performs in Japanese is very similar to 'since', or 'due to', in English. Phrases that use this particular (A) て (B) nuance of the て-form primarily express something that is beyond the control of the speaker in the (B) statement.
To use this grammar construction, pair the て-form of a verb or い-Adjective with the (B) phrase. In the case of nouns and な-Adjectives, で (the particle) will be used instead.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: The 'because' nuance of て (or で) in this grammar construction is primarily influenced by the (B) phrase being something that is uncontrollable, rather than being a different meaning of the particles て, or で themselves. Literally the meaning is closer to the following:
(A) て {困|こま}る - Being troubled cannot be controlled, so (A) must have caused it.
(A) て {嬉|うれ}しい - Being happy cannot be controlled, so (A) must have caused it.
(A) て {大変|たいへん} - Having a problem cannot be controlled, so (A) must have caused it.
(A) て びっくり - Being surprised cannot be controlled, so (A) must have caused it.
(A) て {疲|つか}れている - Being worn-out cannot be controlled, so (A) must have caused it.
(A) て {心配|しんぱい} - Feeling anxiety cannot be controlled, so (A) must have caused it.

Many other words, such as the ones listed above will cause て (or で) to have a similar nuance. てすみません also uses this meaning of て, as すみません is a feeling that the speaker cannot control, relating to the situation being left unfinished.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Notice that Verb[て] + すみません uses this version of て

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: なくて (N4, Not ~ and, Not so, Because not (Examples)): Both structures use the て-form to express cause or reason. Verb [て] + B uses the affirmative form to explain a positive reason, e.g. 行けてよかったです ('I'm glad I could go.'). In contrast, なくて is the て-form of the negative ない and expresses a negative reason, e.g. 行けなくて残念でした ('It was unfortunate I couldn't go.').

Adjective + て・Noun + で (N5, And... (Conjunctive)): Both of these patterns involve connecting a word or phrase (adjectives and nouns in one case, verbs in the other) to the rest of the sentence using the て form. The meaning of the connection depends on context. Sometimes it simply links words, as in 大きくてきれい ('big and pretty'), while in other cases, the て form expresses reason or method, as in 歩いて行った ('went by walking').

し～し (N4, And, Giving reasons): Both forms can express reasons, but their usage differs. Verb[て] + B shows that the stated action is the direct reason for what follows, while し～し implies that multiple reasons exist, even if only one is mentioned. For example, 犯人が捕まって安心です ('I'm relieved because the criminal was caught.') vs. 犯人が捕まったし、安心です ('The criminal was caught, and I'm relieved.'), where the し version suggests there may be other factors for the relief.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About Causative-Passive
text: When the auxiliary verb せる (or させる) 'to make/let do' is combined with the auxiliary verb られる 'to be the receiver of', it creates the causative-passive form of verbs in Japanese. These sentences will be from the perspective of the person who has 'been made to do' something, and are very often negative (against the will of the speaker).

First, verbs must be conjugated in the same way that they would be with せる, or させる. After that simply remove the る, and then add られる. This will create the verb form させられる (linked with る-Verbs), or せられる (linked with う-Verbs).
As with the causative form, する and {来|く}る have special conjugation rules. する will be replaced completely by させられる, while {来|く}る will become {来|こ}させられる.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: れる may not be used in place of られる in causative-passive sentences. This is because せる and させる both have せ (an え sound kana) at the point where they will connect with られる. This is a rule for all verbs with an え sound kana at their conjugation point (excluding the 'potential' use of れる and られる).

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: Verb［せる・させる］ (N4, To make/let/have (somebody do something)): The causative (Verb［せる・させる］) and the causative-passive are two related verb forms. Verb［せられる・させられる］ is used to express either 'letting' or 'making/forcing' someone do something. For example, the causative of 行く 'go' is 行かせる 'let/make (someone) go'. The causative-passive is the passive form of this, meaning 'to be made to do (A)', e.g., 行かせられた (or the contracted form 行かされた) means 'I was made/forced to go.'.

Verb［れる・られる］ (N4, Was done to ~ by ~, Done without consent, Done to one's dismay): The passive (Verb［れる・られる］) and causative-passive are two key verb forms in Japanese. The passive expresses that an action was done to someone, while the causative-passive means being made or forced to do something. For example, 食べられた 'was eaten' vs. 食べさせられた 'were made to eat'.

meaning: By, With, On, By means of, ~ing with
summary: A casual, simple conjunctive form showing that (B) was done in the way of (A).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About Verb[て]・Noun[で] + B
text: The conjunction particle て, or the case marking particle で are often used to highlight when something is being 'used'. The thing being used does not necessarily need to indicate a tool, but can also indicate a circumstance/situation. In these cases, '(A) で (B)' translates as 'with/by means of (A), (B)'.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: With て (and で), the nuance is quite often that '(A) allowed/led to (B)'. This may be a simple sequence of events, or may be through the direct use of a tool/situation. The nuance that is being highlighted will always depend on the (B) phrase. Due to this, it is important to always read the (B) clause, before deciding what the speaker is trying to convey.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: で (N5, With, By (using)): The particle で follows a noun to describe the means or method of an action (e.g., ペンで書く = 'to write with a pen'). A verb in the て form can express a similar nuance (e.g., ペンを使って書く = 'to write using a pen,' 歩いて行く = 'to go by walking'). The meaning is the same, but the form differs depending on whether the 'method' is expressed with a noun or a verb.

meaning: Something is done, Has been done, Remaining state
summary: An expression that is used with transitive verbs, to show that something has been left a certain way.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About てある
text: Like 'verb + ている', 'verb + てある' is a structure that will convey an ongoing state. However, てある may only be used with transitive verbs, and highlights the object itself as being the subject of the sentence (rather than the initial person/thing that performed the action).

As ある is being used, it highlights the object as being inanimate (or unable to undo the action that was performed on it). Due to this, てある is regularly translated as 'to be left (A)', or 'to remain (A)', where (A) is the original verb that somebody performed on the object.

Whether the sentence uses が or を to mark the object will depend on what is being emphasized. In cases where を is used, the emphasis is on the whoever performed the action, regardless of whether they are strictly mentioned in the sentence. However, が focuses more on the ongoing state of the object, without any emphasis being placed on the person who may have performed that action originally. Additionally, を may mark the object in sentences where the action itself involves some kind of preparation. For example:
{予約|よやく} - Reservation (requires time investment to reserve).
{準備|じゅんび} - Preparation (requires time investment to prepare).
{録音|ろくおん} - Recording (requires time investment to make the recording).

In situations that involve no real preparation (opening a door, for example), が will be preferred when marking the object. This 'preparation' can be thought of as a time investment, where the invested time of the doer leads to the sentence more naturally expressing that person as the subject, and the object as what will take を.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Only used with transitive verbs!

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: っぱなし (N3, Leaving something in a certain state, Left as is, Keep on -ing): てある and っぱなし both describe ongoing states, but differ in tone. てある suggests something was done intentionally for future benefit. For example, 窓が開けてある means 'The window has been opened (for a reason).'. In contrast, っぱなし often implies carelessness. For example, 窓を開けっぱなしにして家を出た means 'I (carelessly) left the house with the window open.'.

ておく (N4, To do something in advance): Both てある and ておく express actions done for future purposes, but with key differences. てある focuses on the resulting state after the action is performed, e.g. 窓が開けてある ('The window has been opened.', when it remains open for some purpose). In contrast, ておく emphasizes the action itself, focusing on preparation, e.g. 窓を開けておいた ('I opened the window.', implying that it was for future benefit.). Note also the different particles used.

まま(に) (N3, As is, While remaining, Left in a state): てある and まま(に) both describe continuing states, but differ in nuance. てある implies an action was done for a reason and that the result remains. For example, 窓が開けてある ('The window has been opened.') implies that it has been left open for a purpose. In contrast, まま(に) emphasizes that the state remains unchanged, without implying purpose, e.g. 窓を開けたまま家を出てしまった ('I left the house with the window open.').

summary: A phrase used to highlight that someone wants another person to do something in the manner of (A).
formation: Verb + ように + Verb［て］ + ほしい

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ように～てほしい
text: (A) ように～てほしい is an expression in Japanese which combines the auxiliary verb, ようだ, with the てほしい structure (indicating that you/someone else wants someone to do something). As ようだ is being linked to a verb which comes later in the sentence, it will take on the adverbial form ように.
This expression is used to highlight that you (or someone else) want someone to do something 'in the way of (A)'.
Note that when ように follows a noun, の will be required.
Either に or が may mark the thing that the speaker 'wants' to do. It is more common for に to be used to mark people, while が will often mark events/objects.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ように・ような (N4, As・like, Just like): ように・ような follows the plain form of a verb or adjective and expresses general similarity. For example, 日本人のように話す 'speak like a Japanese person'. The same よう appears in ように～てほしい, which expresses wanting someone to act a certain way. For example, 日本人のように話してほしい ('I want you to speak like a Japanese person.').

ようにする (N4, To try to, To make sure to, To endeavor to): ようにする means 'to make an effort to ensure something happens a certain way' and expresses intention or habit. For example, 遅れないようにする ('I'll try not to be late.'). In contrast, ように～てほしい expresses a desire for someone else to behave a certain way. For example, 遅れないようにしてほしい ('I want you to make an effort not to be late.').

がほしい (N4, To want something, To be in need of): These two patterns using ほしい to express a 'want' differ in meaning and usage. がほしい follows nouns to express the speaker's desire for something, whether physical (金がほしい = 'I want money.') or figurative (自由がほしい = 'I want freedom.'). ようにしてほしい combines ようにする and てほしい to express a desire for someone to act in a certain way, e.g. 忘れないようにしてほしい ('I want you to make sure not to forget.').

てほしい (N4, I want you to): Both ように～てほしい and てほしい express wanting someone else to do something, with the key difference being the presence of よう. よう adds a nuance of doing something in a certain way. For example, 忘れないでほしい ('I want you not to forget.') vs. 忘れないようにしてほしい ('I want you to make sure to not forget.', in the sense of doing what needs to be done to ensure you do not forget).

ように (N4, So that, In order to, In such a way that): The core meaning of ように is 'so that' or 'in order to', and it is commonly used in patterns like ようにする 'make an effort to (A)' or ようにいう 'ask someone to (A)'. When used together with the ～てほしい form, it expresses wanting someone else to do the action. For example, 忘れないようにする ('I'll try not to forget.') vs. 忘れないようにしてほしい ('I want you to try not to forget.').

ようにいう (N4, To tell, request, or order to do (in such a way)): ようにいう means 'to tell or ask someone to do something.' It is often used for indirect or general requests. For example, 来るようにいう 'tell (someone) to come'. When paired with てほしい, it shows a desire for someone else to make the request. For example, 来るようにいってほしい ('I want you to tell him/her/them to come.').

summary: A phrase that highlights when something happens during the broad time frame of (A).
formation: Verb［ている］+ 間（あいだ）に

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ているあいだに
text: When (A) ている is paired with {間|あいだ}に (B), it expresses that '(B) is happening/happened within the timeframe of (A)'. These events do not need to be related in any specific way, but the (B) action must happen somewhere within the duration of (A). This construction translates naturally as 'during the time that (A), (B)'.
ている{間|あいだ}に will often be used when the (B) action is somehow beyond the control of the speaker. However, this is not always the case.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: {間|あいだ} literally means an 'interval', and therefore highlights the (A) event as being the 'whole' span of time, within which (B) happened/will happen at some point.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: の間に (N3, While, During, Between, Period): 間(あいだ) means 'period' or 'space', and in addition to its literal meaning, it is used in expressions meaning 'while' or 'between', e.g. 1月と4月の間に 'between January and April'. In the ているあいだに form, the focus is on something happening during another ongoing action. For example, 勉強しているあいだに電話がかかってきた ('The phone rang while I was studying.').

中 (N3, During, While, Throughout, In the process of): Both patterns express being in the middle of an action, but differ in how they are used. 中 attaches to nouns to indicate 'in the process of' or 'during.' For example, 今、食事中です means 'I'm in the middle of eating.' ているあいだに refers to something happening while another action or state is ongoing. For example, ご飯を食べているあいだに電話が鳴った and 食事中に電話が鳴った are equivalent in meaning.

ながら (N4, While ~ing, During, As): Both forms involve the idea of simultaneous or ongoing actions, but differ in structure and nuance. ているあいだに expresses that something happened during another ongoing action, e.g. 勉強しているあいだに電話がかかってきた ('The phone rang while I was studying.'). ながら shows one subject doing two things at once, e.g. 音楽を聴きながら勉強するのが好き ('I like to study while listening to music.').

～ところに・～ところへ (N2, At the time, When, While, Timing): Both express something happening during an ongoing action, but differ in focus. Compared to ているあいだに, which states in a straightforward manner one thing happening in the middle of another thing, ～ところに・～ところへplaces more of a focus on the 'scene' or situation, and is therefore often used to express a surprising or disturbing event.

とき (N4, When, At the time of): とき expresses the time of an action or event, like the English 'when'. It can be used with nouns as in 雨の時 'when it rains', verbs as in 父が帰ってきた時 'when Dad came home', or adjectives as in 暑い時 'when it's hot'. In contrast, ているあいだに uses the て-form of verbs and refers to a period during which something occurs, e.g. 晩ご飯を食べている間に、父が帰ってきました ('While I was eating dinner, my father came home.').

ついでに (N3, While you are at it, On the occasion): Both can mean 'while,' but the nuance differs. ついでに implies doing something extra during another task, e.g. 買い物のついでに郵便局に寄った ('While shopping, I stopped at the post office.'). ているあいだに just marks that something happened during another action, as in 買い物しているあいだに電話がかかってきた ('I got a call while shopping.').

つつある (N2, -ing, Be -ing): Both forms involve the idea of an ongoing process, but with different nuance and focus. ているあいだに refers to something happening while another action or state is ongoing. For example, 勉強しているあいだに電話がかかってきた ('The phone rang while I was studying.'). In contrast, つつある expresses something in the process of changing, e.g. 病気が治りつつある ('My illness is in the process of healing.').

ているところだ (N4, In the process of doing ~ right now/at this moment): Both patterns express ongoing actions but differ in focus. ているところだ means being in the middle of something, often with a sense of being occupied. For example, 勉強をしているところだ ('I'm in the middle of studying.').ているあいだに highlights something that happens during another action, e.g. 勉強しているあいだに電話がかかってきた ('The phone rang while I was studying.').

ている① (N5, Is, Am, Are (~ing)): The ている① form describes an ongoing action or state. When combined with あいだに (meaning 'while doing something'), it expresses the idea of 'while doing A, B happened.' This is typically used for events outside the speaker's control. For example, 映画を見ている間に、電話が掛かってきました means 'While I was watching a movie, a phone call came in.'

うちに (N3, While, During): Both patterns can express the idea of 'while,' but differ in nuance. ているあいだに refers to something happening during another ongoing action. For example, 勉強しているあいだに電話がかかってきた means 'The phone rang while I was studying.' うちに emphasizes doing something while a particular state still lasts. For example, 早いうちに帰ろう means 'Let's go home while it's still early.'

summary: A grammar point used to highlight that not doing something is okay.
formation: Verb［なくて］ + （も） + いい + です (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About なくてもいい
text: なくてもいい is simply the opposite of てもいい, and highlights that it is 'ok even if (A) is not done'. This usually comes across as being quite polite, and sounds like 'don't worry about doing (A)' in English.
なくてもいい is a combination of the auxiliary verb ない in its conjunction form, with てもいい.

In order to make this phrase sound even more casual, the adverbial particle も may be omitted. This does not change the nuance at all, but will sound a bit more friendly (when used with people that you know well).

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: も can be dropped in casual speech

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: てはいけない (N5, Must not, May not): なくてもいい means something is optional; 'it's okay not to (do something).' In contrast, てはいけない expresses prohibition; 'you must not' or 'cannot' do something. For example, 食べなくてもいい means 'It's okay not to eat it,' while 食べてはいけない means 'You must not eat it.' The first gives freedom; the second sets a rule.

てはならない (N2, Must not, Cannot, Should not): なくてもいい means there is no obligation to do something, like the English 'you don't have to (A)' (or literally, 'it's okay even without'). For example, 食べなくてもいい means 'You don't have to eat it.' In contrast, てはならない expresses prohibition, like 'must not (A)' or 'cannot (A)'. For example, 食べてはならない means 'You must not eat it.'.

ことはない (N3, There is no need to, Never happens): ことはない and なくてもいい can overlap when expressing 'There is no need to...' or 'You don't have to...' For example, 心配することはない and 心配しなくてもいい both mean 'There's no need to worry.' However, ことはない can also be used to express that something never happens. For example, 彼と話すことはない means 'I never talk to him,' which is not a use for なくてもいい.

なくてはいけない (N5, Must do, Have to do): なくてはいけない expresses obligation or necessity, saying something 'must' or 'needs to' be done. なくてもいい has the opposite meaning, saying that one doesn't have to do something (literally, 'it's okay not to do'). For example, 食べなくてはいけない means '(You) must eat it', while 食べなくてもいい means '(You) don't have to eat it.'

summary: A common way to express that (A) will be attempted. To do (A) and see how it goes.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About てみる
text: In order to express that you will (or someone else should) try something, the conjunction particle て will be paired with {見|み}る (almost always without kanji). While this is translated as 'to try to (A)', the actual meaning is closer to 'to do (A), and see (whether the result is good or not)'.
This grammar construction is usually only used when someone tries something for the first time.
As mentioned above, this phrase is also used when suggesting that someone else should try something. In these situations, (A) + てみて, or more formally, (A) + てみてください will be used.
Sometimes, in very casual requests, even the て of みて will be dropped, and (A) + てみ will be used by itself. This usually has the nuance of 'come on, just give it a go!'

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: While the kanji for {見|み}る may be used in this grammar point, it will result in the 'see' meaning being heavily stressed (rather than 'try'). This may cause a misunderstanding on the part of the person listening/reading.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: 〜ようと思う・〜おうと思う (N4, I think I will, I think I shall, Going to, Gonna (Volitional + と思う)): 〜ようと思う・〜おうと思う expresses intention, similar to 'I'm thinking of doing X,' e.g. 行こうと思います ('I plan to go.') てみる conveys the idea of trying something to see what it's like, e.g. 行ってみる ('I'll go and see.'). These forms can be combined, e.g. 行ってみようと思います ('I plan to go and see what it's like.')

ようにする (N4, To try to, To make sure to, To endeavor to): Both can be translated in English as 'try (doing)', but differ in nuance. ようにする means to make an effort or form a habit, e.g. 毎朝走るようにしている ('I try to run every morning.') has the nuance of making a point of doing so. In contrast, てみる means to try something out to see the result, e.g. 走ってみた ('I tried running.'), which has the nuance of doing so to see what it was like.

Verb[volitional]とする (N3, Try to, Attempt to, To be about to): Verb[volitional]とする and てみる are both translated as 'try', but the former implies attempting something that may not succeed, e.g. 話そうとした ('I tried to speak.'), which implies that maybe the attempt was unsuccessful. In contrast,てみる focuses on trying something to see the result, as in 話してみた ('I tried speaking.'), which has the nuance of doing so to see what it was like.

てごらん (N3, (Please) try to, (Please) look): てみる expresses trying something to see what it's like, similar to the English 'try (doing)', e.g. 食べてみる ('I'll try eating it.'). てごらん is a more directive form that encourages someone else to try something, e.g. 食べてごらん ('Try eating it.' as a gentle request). てごらん is often used by adults to children, or superiors to subordinates. Among peers, something like 食べてみて would be more common.

summary: A polite phrase that expresses the speaker's apologetic feelings for doing (A).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About てすみません
text: てすみません is a grammar construction that expresses the speaker's regret about (A). It is often translated directly to 'I'm sorry for (A)'. As discussed in one of our previous lessons on て, we examined the 'since', or 'due to' meaning that it can have. Let's look at a few examples.

Phrases that use this particular (A) て (B) nuance of the て-form primarily express something that is beyond the control of the speaker in the (B) statement. Coming from the verb {済|す}む (to finish), すみません (the negated form) means 'to be unfinished'. In this way, てすみません literally means that the speaker feels that something is 'unfinished due to (A)'. This is very similar to phrases like 'having unfinished business' in English.

Although the translation is 'I'm sorry', perhaps it would be easier to remember this grammar structure as highlighting someone's regret/unfinished feelings about (A), and simply showing that to the person that is being apologized to.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: てしまう・ちゃう (N4, To do something by accident, To finish completely・totally, Unfortunately): てすみません is used to apologize for doing something, e.g. 遅れてすみません ('Sorry for being late.'). It often pairs with てしまう・ちゃう, which adds a nuance of regret or accident. For example, 遅れてしまってすみません・遅れちゃってすみません ('I'm sorry I was late.'), which implies that you didn't mean to do so and feel bad it happened.

てくれてありがとう (N4, Thank you for ~ ing): These て-form patterns are opposites. てすみません expresses apology for your action, e.g., 遅れてすみません ('Sorry for being late.'), while てくれてありがとう expresses gratitude for someone else's action, e.g., 来てくれてありがとう ('Thank you for coming.'), implying that the person's coming benefitted you.

meaning: To do something for someone, As a favor for
summary: A polite, yet sometimes insulting expression, used when giving something to another.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About てあげる
text: When joining the
conjunction particle
て
, with the
る-Verb
あげる

(to give), it implies that someone is doing something for the benefit of someone else. Literally, this expression means 'to give/bestow the action of (A) upon (B)', but translates more naturally as 'to do (A) for (B)', or 'to do (A) as a favor for (B)'.
The receiver of the てあげる action will be marked with に, while the doer will be marked with が (if mentioned).

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Might sound patronizing and can be rude especially if used with elderly people!

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: あげる (N5, To give (away), To present, To provide): あげる is a basic verb meaning 'to give,' often used when the giver is the speaker or someone in the speaker's in-group, and the receiver is outside that group. For example, プレゼントをあげる means 'to give a present.' When used as てあげる after a verb in the て form, it means doing something for someone's benefit. For example, 英語を教えてあげる means 'to teach English (to someone as a favor).'

てくれる (N4, To do something for someone (usually you)): Both use the て form with a giving verb to describe doing a favor. てあげる is used when you or someone close to you does something for someone else, e.g. 友達に日本語を教えてあげた ('I taught my friend Japanese.'). In contrast, てくれる is used when someone else does something for you or someone close to you, e.g. 友達が日本語を教えてくれた ('My friend taught me Japanese.').

てもらう (N4, To get someone to do, To have someone do): Both use the て form to talk about favors, but with different perspectives. てあげる focuses on the giver (you or someone close to you) doing something for someone else. てもらう focuses on the receiver having something done for them. For example, ケンに教えてあげた ('I taught/told Ken.') vs. ケンに教えてもらった ('Ken taught me.').

meaning: To do something for someone (usually you)
summary: A phrase used to highlight that the speaker or someone close to them is having a favor done for them.
formation: Verb［ないで］+ くれますか (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About てくれる
text: The verb {呉|く}れる in Japanese, is very similar to {与|あた}える (to bestow). The primary difference is that {呉|く}れる (primarily written in hiragana) means to 'bestow to the speaker' (or someone in the speaker's inner circle).

In this way, てくれる is the opposite of てあげる, which conveys that someone (usually the speaker) gives (an action) to another person that is outside of their inner circle. てくれる is commonly translated as 'would you do (A) for me', as a question, or 'someone did (A) for me', as a statement.

When asking for a favor, てくれる can be shortened to てくれ. However, this is very casual, and should not be used with strangers (or anyone that you do not know well). As an English equivalent, てくれ sounds similar to phrases like 'would ya do (A)', or 'could ya do (A)?'

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Receiver's point of view

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: くれる (N5, To give (me), To be given): くれる means 'to give' and is used when someone outside the speaker's group gives something to the speaker or their in-group. For example, プレゼントをくれた means '(someone) gave me a present.' As てくれる, it shows someone did something for the speaker's benefit, as in 日本語を教えてくれた ('(someone) taught me Japanese').

てあげる (N4, To do something for someone, As a favor for): Both use the て form with a giving verb to describe doing a favor. てあげる is used when you or someone close to you does something for someone else, e.g. 友達に日本語を教えてあげた ('I taught my friend Japanese.'). In contrast, てくれる is used when someone else does something for you or someone close to you, e.g. 友達が日本語を教えてくれた ('My friend taught me Japanese.').

てくれてありがとう (N4, Thank you for ~ ing): てくれる describes someone doing something that benefits you, like 来てくれた ('He/you/they came for me.'), implying that their coming helped you. てくれてありがとう specifically expresses gratitude for the action, e.g. 来てくれてありがとう ('Thank you for coming.'). The base meaning is the same, but one contains an explicit message of thanks.

ないでください (N5, Please don't (Polite request)): ないでください is used to ask someone not to do something in a polite way. It's relatively neutral and can be used with strangers or people of equal status. In contrast, てくれる, when said with a rising question intonation, is a casual and gentle way to ask a favor from someone close, such as a friend or family member. It feels softer and more familiar than standard polite forms.

ていただけませんか (N4, Won't you, Could you please (Humble request)): てくれる shows someone did something for your benefit, like 教えてくれた ('They taught/told me.'). ていただけませんか is a humble and polite way to make a request, e.g. 教えていただけませんか？ ('Would you kindly teach/tell me?'). Both involve benefits for the speaker but differ in tone and usage.

てもらう (N4, To get someone to do, To have someone do): Both express receiving a favor, but from different perspectives. With てくれる, the subject is the giver and they do something for you. With てもらう, the subject is the receiver and they get someone to do something. For example, ケンが教えてくれた frames the action as 'Ken taught/told me.', while ケンに教えてもらった frames it as 'I had Ken teach/tell me.'.

てください (N5, Please do (Polite request)): てください is a basic way to express a polite request (e.g., 'Please do...') For example, 食べてください would mean 'Please eat (this).' It is polite and neutral, and can be used with strangers or people equal in status to you. In comparison, てくれる (when used with rising question intonation), is a casual, gentle way of making a request to a close friend or family member.

meaning: To get someone to do, To have someone do
summary: An expression used when someone is getting another person to do something for them.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About てもらう
text: Being slightly more direct than てくれる, てもらう removes the meaning of 'to bestow' (to the speaker), and focuses on the meaning of 'to receive' (from the giver). With てもらう, に will mark the person that 'did something' for the subject, while が (or は) will highlight the receiver themselves.
In English, this grammar structure is regularly translated as 'to have (someone) do (A) for you', or 'to get (someone) to do (A) for you'. Literally, it means 'to receive the action of (A)'.
てもらう is also regularly used when receiving a service from someone, as てくれる would imply that the action was a favor.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ていただけませんか (N4, Won't you, Could you please (Humble request)): てもらう describes getting someone to do something for you, e.g. 教えてもらった ('I had them teach/tell me.'). ていただけませんか is a polite way to ask for such a favor, as in 教えていただけませんか？ ('Would you kindly teach/tell me?'). Both involve receiving help but differ in politeness and usage.

もらう (N5, To receive, To get, To obtain): もらう is a basic verb meaning 'to receive,' often used when the speaker or someone in their in-group receives something from someone outside the group. For example, プレゼントをもらった means 'I received a present.' When used as てもらう after a verb in the て form, it shows that the speaker received the benefit of an action, as in 日本語を教えてもらった ('I had someone teach me Japanese').

てあげる (N4, To do something for someone, As a favor for): Both use the て form to talk about favors, but with different perspectives. てあげる focuses on the giver (you or someone close to you) doing something for someone else. てもらう focuses on the receiver having something done for them. For example, ケンに教えてあげた ('I taught/told Ken.') vs. ケンに教えてもらった ('Ken taught me.').

てくれる (N4, To do something for someone (usually you)): Both express receiving a favor, but from different perspectives. With てくれる, the subject is the giver and they do something for you. With てもらう, the subject is the receiver and they get someone to do something. For example, ケンが教えてくれた frames the action as 'Ken taught/told me.', while ケンに教えてもらった frames it as 'I had Ken teach/tell me.'.

summary: A stern but semi-polite way to request that someone do something.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About なさい
text: なさい is the imperative form of なさる, an honorific language verb which specifically highlights and respects the actions of another person (never the speaker).

Despite being respectful, the fact that this is a 'command' means that it would never be used toward a superior. Due to this, なさい is most frequently used toward peers, or people of lower status, like children.
To use なさい, simply connect it to the ます stem of any verb.
なさい may be shortened further to な, which becomes an even more casual form that is used most frequently toward peers.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: When casual, can be shortened to just な

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ないで (N4, Without doing, Not ~ and ~): なさい is a firm but polite command form, often used by those in authority (like teachers or parents) toward subordinates. In contrast, ないで is a casual way to ask someone not to do something, e.g. 行かないで ('Don't go.'). It is typically used among close friends or family.

お～願う (N2, Please, Could you please): Both forms are used to ask someone to do something, but with different levels of formality. なさい is a polite command often used from superiors to subordinates, as in 待ちなさい ('Wait.'). お～願う is extremely humble and formal, used in business or public announcements, as in お待ち願います ('We request that you to wait.').

な (N5, Do not, Don't (Prohibitive)): The dictionary/non-past form of a verb + な expresses a blunt command not to do something. In contrast, a verb stem + なさい expresses a strong but respectful command. For example, 食べるな means 'Don't eat it!' while 食べなさい means 'Eat it!' Despite being derived from an honorific verb, なさい is still a command and is used with lower-status people or children, not superiors.

ないでください (N5, Please don't (Polite request)): ないでください is a polite way to ask someone not to do something. It is relatively neutral, and could be used with strangers or people equal in status to you. In contrast, なさい is a command form, similar to the English 'Do (this),' typically used when one person is in a higher position, such as teachers to students, adults to children, etc.

なさる (N4, To do (Honorific)): なさる and なさい are derived from the same verb but used differently. なさる is an honorific form of する, used for respectful reference to someone's actions, as in 明日仕事なさいますか？ ('Will you be working tomorrow?'). なさい is the imperative form, used to firmly but politely instruct someone, as in 宿題をしなさい ('Do your homework.').

命令形 (N4, (Verb)!, Do (something)!): The imperative or command form (命令形) gives strong, direct commands, e.g. 食べろ ('Eat!'). On its own, it sounds harsh, so it's often softened. なさい is a more polite alternative, often used by parents or teachers toward children, e.g. 野菜を食べなさい ('Eat your vegetables!'). Both forms command action but differ in tone.

てください (N5, Please do (Polite request)): てください and なさい are both used to tell or ask someone to do something in Japanese. てください is a polite request, similar to 'Please (do this),' and is appropriate in neutral or formal situations, such as with strangers or people of equal status. なさい, on the other hand, is a firm command, closer to 'Do (this),' and is typically used by someone in a higher position, like teachers to students or adults to children.

お～ください (N4, Please do (Honorific)): Both forms ask someone to do something, but the tone is different. なさい is a polite but direct command, often used by parents or teachers, as in これを使いなさい ('Use this.'). お～ください is a respectful request form, used to politely encourage someone like a customer or superior to do something, as in これをお使いください ('Please use this.').

てごらん (N3, (Please) try to, (Please) look): Both are command forms, but with different tones. なさい is a polite but direct command, often used by teachers or parents, e.g. 食べなさい ('Eat.'). てごらん is softer and gently encourages someone to give something a try, e.g. 食べてごらん ('Try eating it'). Both are typically used from adults to children, or superiors to subordinates.

summary: A casual, simple conjunctive form highlighting non-sequence, but contrasting states.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About Verb[て] + B
text: One of the common functions that the conjunction particle て has, is that it can contrast things that share some sort of relationship. This is similar to the contrastive use of は. In order to identify this nuance of て, we will need to think about whether the things being described are happening one after the other, or are simply describing '(A), and then (B)'. Let's look at some examples.

Due to this 'contrast' that is shown with て, sometimes it is translated as 'while (A), also (B)'. The primary difference between this nuance of て, and other 'while' or 'but' grammar points, is that (A) and (B) will always have equal weight/importance in a て sentence. Comparatively, structures like けど, のに, だが and similar points will usually imply that either (A) or (B) is more important in some way.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: Verb + て+ B (N5, And, And then, After that (sequence)): Both patterns use the て form to link a verb or verb phrase to the next part of the sentence, but the nuance varies. It can either simply connect actions, as in パンを買って食べた ('I bought bread and ate it'), or suggest a cause or effect, as in 人が多くて入れなかった ('There were too many people, so I couldn't get in'). This interpretation depends on the context.

summary: A casual, simple conjunctive form used as an abbreviated way of saying please don't do (A).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About Verb[ないで]
text: ないでください is a polite way to express 'please don't do (A)'. However, such politeness is often not required, like in conversations between close friends. In these cases, ないで by itself may be used for the same purpose. Although grammatically the same as the ないで with the meaning of 'without doing (A), (B)', rather having a part (A) and a part (B) to the sentence, this ないで acts more like a simple statement.

ないで combines the auxiliary verb ない, with the case marking particle, で. To use this structure, simply attach it to the negative stem of the verb that you wish to request someone not to do. The sentence itself usually finishes with ないで.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ないで (N4, Without doing, Not ~ and ~): The ないで form combines a verb in the negative with で, and has two common uses: (1) to make a negative request, e.g. 食べないで ('Don't eat it.'), and (2) to express 'without doing' something, e.g. 晩ご飯を食べないで出かけた ('I went out without eating dinner.').

ないでください (N5, Please don't (Polite request)): Both Verb[ないで] and ないでください are used to express requests not to do something. While ないでください is polite, and can be used with strangers or people equal in status to you, Verb[ないで] (without ください) is more casual, and typically used to make requests of friends or family members in a casual tone. Requests with てください and especially Verb [て] can be followed by ね (e.g. 食べてね) for a softer, more gentle feeling.

summary: A polite expression used to thank someone for doing something for you.
formation: Verb［て］ + くれて + ありがとう
Verb［て］ + くれて + ありがとう + ございます (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About てくれてありがとう
text: As an extension of てくれる, which expresses that something was done for the speaker, or someone within their immediate circle, てくれてありがとう thanks someone for that action.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: てすみません (N4, I'm sorry for): These て-form patterns are opposites. てすみません expresses apology for your action, e.g., 遅れてすみません ('Sorry for being late.'), while てくれてありがとう expresses gratitude for someone else's action, e.g., 来てくれてありがとう ('Thank you for coming.'), implying that the person's coming benefitted you.

てくれる (N4, To do something for someone (usually you)): てくれる describes someone doing something that benefits you, like 来てくれた ('He/you/they came for me.'), implying that their coming helped you. てくれてありがとう specifically expresses gratitude for the action, e.g. 来てくれてありがとう ('Thank you for coming.'). The base meaning is the same, but one contains an explicit message of thanks.

Verb + て (N5, And, Then (Linking events)): The Verb + て form connects verbs or parts of a sentence. A common use is to express thanks by combining it with the giving verb くれる (also in the Verb + て form) and ありがとう. For example, 教えてくれてありがとう means 'Thank you for teaching me.' This is a casual form, and a more polite version would use honorific verbs (くださる or いただく) and add ございます.

くれる (N5, To give (me), To be given): くれる is a basic verb meaning 'to give,' usually used when someone from outside the speaker's group gives something to the speaker or their in-group. For example, プレゼントをくれた means '(someone) gave me a present.' It also appears in the pattern てくれてありがとう to thank someone for a favor. For example, 日本語を教えてくれてありがとう means 'Thank you for teaching me Japanese.'

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About てくれない・てもらえない
text: When used in the negative, てくれない (coming from てくれる), and てもらえない (coming from てもらえる, the potential form of てもらう), are similar to the negative question form of じゃないか. They express the following:
てくれない - Would you not do (A) for me?
てもらえない - Could I not have you do (A) for me?
In both of these constructions, か (the question particle) may be omitted. However, they do sound slightly more polite when か is used.
Let's examine the following list, for a scale of the level of politeness.
てくれ, てくれる, てもらえる, てくれない (か), てもらえない (か)

sections.label: Caution

summary: A somewhat casual phrase to express that the speaker is wondering about (A), because it is uncertain.
formation: Noun +（な + の(1)）+ だろうか
［な］Adjective +（な + の(1)）+ でしょうか (polite)
Noun +（な + の(1)）+ でしょうか (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ～のだろうか
text: When だろう (the conjugated auxiliary verb) is grouped with か (the question particle), it presents the statement before it as something that the speaker is unsure about. In this way, it sounds similar to 'I wonder if (A)' in English.
To use this construction, the statement before だろうか must be nominalized (turned into a noun-phrase). This is done through the use of の, or なの (in the case of な-Adjectives and nouns).
Despite the grammatical rule relating to nominalization using の (or なの), this part of the phrase is often omitted.
だろうか is quite masculine, so in order to sound more polite/ladylike, でしょうか may also be used instead.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Although だろうか is quite masculine, it does not strictly mean that でしょうか is feminine. でしょうか may be used confidently by either women or men.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Versions without ん/の are also acceptable but sound old-fashioned

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: かしら (N4, I wonder): Both express uncertainty or internal questioning, like 'I wonder'. ～のだろうか (or the polite ～のでしょうか) is neutral and used by all genders. かしら has a softer, feminine tone and is rarely used by men. The explanatory の adds a nuance of seeking an answer, which かしら does not.

はたして (N2, Wonder if ~ (really)?, Wonder how ~ (actually)?, Sure enough, As expected): ～のだろうか means 'I wonder...' and is used at the end of a sentence to express doubt. はたして adds emphasis and often appears at the start of a sentence to heighten that feeling. They're often used together, as in 果たして勝てるのだろうか？ ('Can we actually win?').

かな (N4, I wonder): Both かな and ～のだろうか express doubt or curiosity, like 'I wonder if (A)' かな is casual and common in everyday speech or texting. ～のだろうか also can be used in conversation but conveys a more thoughtful or serious tone, suggesting deeper consideration as compared to かな, which can be used for offhand comments.

じゃないか (N4, Isn't it?, Is it not?): Both ～のだろうか and じゃないか seek confirmation, but with different levels of confidence. のだろうか expresses uncertainty, used for low-confidence guesses or suppositions, e.g. 'I wonder if (A)?'. In contrast, じゃないか is used to confirm something the speaker believes to be true, often with a confrontational or challenging tone, e.g. 'It's (A), isn't it!?'.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About お～になる
text: お～になる (or ご～になる) is an honorific language expression which is used to pay respect to the actions of the person that is being spoken to/another person (never the speaker). In this expression, になる is used in exactly the same way that する would be, except that it will be attached to the ます stem of the verb that it is referring to.

The primary difference between お and ご, is that お will be used with words/readings of Japanese origin (kun-yomi), and ご will be used with words/readings of Chinese origin (on-yomi). In fact, お and ご are both represented by the same kanji. For this kanji, {御|お} is one of the kun-yomi, and {御|ご} is one of the on-yomi.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: Some verbs, like いでる, are used almost exclusively with honorific language. おいでになる (the お～になる form of いでる) is an example of this, and can mean 'to come', 'to go', or 'to be'. This is due to the perspective of the speaker when using honorific language, and something that we will discuss in more detail later.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Remember not to use honorific language when speaking about yourself and your actions!

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: なさる (N4, To do (Honorific)): Both are honorific forms. お～になる is used for regular verbs, like 答える 'answer' becoming お答えになる (same meaning, but showing respect to the answerer). なさる is the specific honorific form of する, e.g. ゴルフをなさる means '(He/she) plays golf.' in an honorific/respectful sense. Since する is irregular, it does not use the お～になる pattern.

いらっしゃる (N4, To be (Honorific), To come (Honorific), To go (Honorific)): These are honorific forms used to respectfully describe others' actions. お～になる is used with regular verbs, e.g. 書く 'write' becoming お書きになる (same meaning, but showing respect to the writer). いらっしゃる is a special honorific form that replaces 行く, 来る, and いる, for which the お～になる form is not used.
