sections.label: About
sections.heading: About なさる
text: なさる is an honorific language verb which acknowledges and respects the actions of another (never the speaker). Like お～になる, なさる has exactly the same meaning as する.

なさる can be utilized in any situation where する would be used, as a direct replacement. It is a special-class verb, which means that it has some unique conjugation rules. In its casual form, it will conjugate in exactly the same way as a う-Verb.
However, in the polite form, instead of る changing to り (as would be expected of a う-Verb), it will change to い instead.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: なさる is considered a little bit old fashioned in modern Japanese, and お～になる is the preferred form used by most native speakers.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Remember not to use honorific language when speaking about yourself and your actions!

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: お～になる (N4, To do (Honorific)): Both are honorific forms. お～になる is used for regular verbs, like 答える 'answer' becoming お答えになる (same meaning, but showing respect to the answerer). なさる is the specific honorific form of する, e.g. ゴルフをなさる means '(He/she) plays golf.' in an honorific/respectful sense. Since する is irregular, it does not use the お～になる pattern.

いたす (N4, To do (Humble), To venerably do): いたす is the humble form of する, used when talking about your own actions to someone respected. For example, 連絡いたします means 'I'll contact you.' in a deferential way. なさる is the opposite: the honorific form used when referring to the respected person's actions, as in ゴルフをなさいます ('He/she plays golf.').

する (N5, To do, To make into): Both なさる and する express performing an action, similar to the English 'do.' The key difference is politeness: する is the standard, neutral term used in everyday contexts, while なさる is an honorific expression used to 'elevate' someone else's actions with respect to you (or your in-group).

なさい (N4, Command to do): なさる and なさい are derived from the same verb but used differently. なさる is an honorific form of する, used for respectful reference to someone's actions, as in 明日仕事なさいますか？ ('Will you be working tomorrow?'). なさい is the imperative form, used to firmly but politely instruct someone, as in 宿題をしなさい ('Do your homework.').

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About お～ください
text: お～ください is an honorific language expression in Japanese which is used in a similar way to なさい. It is the imperative form of くださる, which itself is the honorific language equivalent of くれる. In this way, it conveys 'please do (A) for me'.
お～ください is more polite than なさい, and may be used when making requests to almost anybody, regardless of if they are higher, or lower status than you.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: ご～ください will only be used as part of the humble speech expression, ご～する (or お〜する). In these cases, it becomes ご～してください.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: お気をつけください is quite commonly used and accepted. This comes from treating 気をつける as one expression.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ないでください (N5, Please don't (Polite request)): ないでください is a polite way to ask someone not to do something. It's neutral and can be used with strangers or people of equal status. In contrast, お〜ください is an honorific request form used with superiors, customers, or others of higher status. Some verbs, like 食べる and 行く, have special honorific forms such as 召し上がる and いらっしゃる, which are used instead of the お〜ください structure.

なさい (N4, Command to do): Both forms ask someone to do something, but the tone is different. なさい is a polite but direct command, often used by parents or teachers, as in これを使いなさい ('Use this.'). お～ください is a respectful request form, used to politely encourage someone like a customer or superior to do something, as in これをお使いください ('Please use this.').

お～願う (N2, Please, Could you please): お～ください and お～願う are both honorific request forms but differ in nuance and setting. お～ください is often used when politely encouraging someone to take an action, such as お上がりください ('Please come in.'). お～願う is more formal and is typically used in public announcements or formal situations. For example, ご注意願います ('Please be careful.') might be used in a train announcement.

てください (N5, Please do (Polite request)): てください is a polite, neutral way to say 'Please do (something),' and is used with strangers or equals. The honorific form, お〜ください, is used for superiors or customers. However, some verbs like 食べる and 行く have special honorific forms, such as 召し上がる and いらっしゃる, which are used instead.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About いらっしゃる
text: いらっしゃる is another of the common honorific language expressions in Japanese. This means that it elevates the status of another person, in order to pay them respect. It will never be used when referring to the speaker themselves, or their own actions.

いらっしゃる can be used to replace {居|い}る 'to be', {来|く}る 'to come', or {行|い}く 'to go'. This is due to the unique perspective that honorific language places the speaker in, in relation to the person that is being respected. This is a slightly advanced concept that we will discuss more later.
To use いらっしゃる, simply replace いる, くる, or いく with いらっしゃる.
Alternatively, いらっしゃる may also be used to replace いる, くる, or いく when they are attached to the て-form of another verb.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Remember not to use honorific language when speaking about yourself and your actions!

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: がいる (N5, To be, There is, To remain (in a state)): がいる combines the particle が with the verb いる to express the existence of living or animate beings, like people or animals. いらっしゃる is the honorific equivalent of いる, as well as 行く and 来る. In other words, がいらっしゃる is the honorific version of がいる, and いらっしゃいますか is the honorific equivalent of いますか, 行きますか, or 来ますか.

お～になる (N4, To do (Honorific)): These are honorific forms used to respectfully describe others' actions. お～になる is used with regular verbs, e.g. 書く 'write' becoming お書きになる (same meaning, but showing respect to the writer). いらっしゃる is a special honorific form that replaces 行く, 来る, and いる, for which the お～になる form is not used.

くる (N5, To come): Both いらっしゃる and くる express movement toward the speaker, similar to the English 'come.' The key difference is politeness: くる is the neutral verb used in everyday contexts, while いらっしゃる is an honorific verb used to show respect for someone's movement. Note that いらっしゃる also serves as the honorific form of いる, いく, and くる.

へいく (N5, To go to, To head toward): Both いらっしゃる and いく express movement away from the speaker, similar to the English 'go.' The key difference is politeness: いく is a neutral verb used in everyday contexts, while いらっしゃる is a polite, honorific verb used to show respect for someone's movement. Note that いらっしゃる also serves as the honorific form of いる, くる, and いく.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ございます
text: ございます is a combination of the (special-class) verb, ござる ({御座|ござ}る in its kanji form), and the auxiliary verb ます. It is considered polite speech, and is directly equivalent to ある (or いる).

ござる itself is almost never used in daily conversation in modern Japanese, due to the preference of the polite form, ございます. However, ござる is regularly used in dramas, manga, and other forms of media (especially historical dramas).

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: がある (N5, To be, There is): ある and ございます are both verbs of existence. ある is the plain form used in everyday conversation, while ございます is the polite form used in formal settings or speeches. For example, 本がある means 'I have / there is a book' in casual speech, while 本がございます is the same phrase in a more polite and formal context (note that が must be used in both cases).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About でございます
text: As mentioned briefly in the ございます lesson, でございます is a structure which can be used as a replacement for であります, the polite form of である (which itself is the formal equivalent of だ). Both です and でございます are considered polite speech. However, でございます is the more polite of the two. Let's take a look at a few examples.

でござる may also be seen, as it is the base form of で + ございます a (special-class) verb. However, in modern Japanese, this is primarily restricted to historical dramas, or characters that have a somewhat 'quirky' personality.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: Using でございます to introduce yourself is considered quite polite, however, when referring to other people, いらっしゃる 'to be' is preferred, as honorific language is more respectful than polite speech.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: です (N5, To be, Is): です and でございます are both polite forms of 'is' or 'to be.' です is polite but commonly used in everyday conversation. でございます is extremely polite and formal, used in customer service, ceremonial speech, or other situations requiring a high level of respect.

だ (N5, To be, Is): だ conveys a casual, informal, or blunt tone, except when required by certain grammatical patterns. In contrast, でございます is a highly polite form, primarily used in business settings or when addressing someone of higher social status such as a boss or customer.

why.いらっしゃいます: いらっしゃる is an honorific verb used in place of いる, 来る, or 行く, and is only used for people or living things. However, in this sentence, we're not talking about the presence or movement of the person, but rather their status (being out), so we need the polite form of the copula だ, not an honorific verb of existence.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About お〜する
text: お〜する comes from a form of polite speech in Japanese called humble speech. This type of speech is used to refer to the speaker and their actions. This is opposed to honorific language, which refers exclusively to the listener and their actions. お〜する is almost exactly the same as お～になる, as in it simply means する.
お〜する is regularly used with words of Japanese origin, while ご～する will be used with words of Chinese origin. The する in this compound will attach directly to the ます stem of almost any verb.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: いたす (N4, To do (Humble), To venerably do): These are both humble forms used to describe one's own actions politely. お～する is used with regular verbs, such as 手伝う 'help' becoming お手伝いする (same meaning, but in a deferential sense). In contrast, いたす is the humble form of する and is used instead of お～する when using する itself. For example, 連絡いたします 'I will contact you.' is the humble form of 連絡する (same meaning).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About いたす
text: いたす, or {致|いた}す as it is often written, is a humble speech う-Verb, which refers to the actions of the speaker (or people within the speakers inner circle, like their company). Similarly to お〜する, いたす means 'to do'.

In the case of する verbs themselves, simply replace する with いたす. For other verbs, add いたす to the ます stem of the verb, while attaching お, or ご to the beginning (depending on whether it is a word of Japanese or Chinese origin).

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: いたす is considered to be slightly more humble than お〜する, which means that it will be heard more frequently in advertisements, or being used by company employees.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: It is more humble than お〜する

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: なさる (N4, To do (Honorific)): いたす is the humble form of する, used when talking about your own actions to someone respected. For example, 連絡いたします means 'I'll contact you.' in a deferential way. なさる is the opposite: the honorific form used when referring to the respected person's actions, as in ゴルフをなさいます ('He/she plays golf.').

する (N5, To do, To make into): Both いたす and する express performing an action, similar to the English 'do.' The key difference is politeness: する is the standard, neutral term used in everyday contexts, while いたす is a humble expression used to show respect by 'lowering' your actions (or those of your in-group) in relation to another person.

お〜する (N4, I humbly do, I am obliged to do, Humble speech): These are both humble forms used to describe one's own actions politely. お～する is used with regular verbs, such as 手伝う 'help' becoming お手伝いする (same meaning, but in a deferential sense). In contrast, いたす is the humble form of する and is used instead of お～する when using する itself. For example, 連絡いたします 'I will contact you.' is the humble form of 連絡する (same meaning).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ていただけませんか
text: ていただけませんか is the humble speech form of てもらえませんか, which itself is the negative potential form of てもらう 'to have (A) done by someone else'.
This structure is a combination of て (the conjunction particle), the う-Verb いただく 'to be topped with', the polite-negative auxiliary verb ません, and the question particle, か.
Generally, it is translated in a similar way as てもらえませんか 'won't you (A)', or 'could you please (A)'.

This construction and いただく itself can regularly be seen as {頂|いただ}く, its kanji form. Due to this kanji literally meaning 'to be topped with', it is just acknowledging that the person that is doing the action for you (or someone in your group), is doing so from 'above' (sounds more respectful).
Here we can see how the 'to be topped/capped with' meaning is used in a standard sentence.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: てもらう (N4, To get someone to do, To have someone do): てもらう describes getting someone to do something for you, e.g. 教えてもらった ('I had them teach/tell me.'). ていただけませんか is a polite way to ask for such a favor, as in 教えていただけませんか？ ('Would you kindly teach/tell me?'). Both involve receiving help but differ in politeness and usage.

てください (N5, Please do (Polite request)): てください is a basic way to express a polite request (e.g., 'Please do…'). It is polite and neutral, and can be used with strangers or people equal in status to you. For more formal situations, ていただけませんか is a more polite and humble request, often used when speaking to clients, customers, or superiors. It softens the tone further—similar to saying 'Would you mind doing...for me?' in English.

てくれる (N4, To do something for someone (usually you)): てくれる shows someone did something for your benefit, like 教えてくれた ('They taught/told me.'). ていただけませんか is a humble and polite way to make a request, e.g. 教えていただけませんか？ ('Would you kindly teach/tell me?'). Both involve benefits for the speaker but differ in tone and usage.

てくれない・てもらえない (N4, Won't you?, Will you?, Could you?, Can you?, Would you?): All three are used to request something, like 'Can you do (A) for me?', but differ in tone. てくれない and てもらえない are casual and used with friends, as in 日本語を教えてくれない？ ('Can you teach me Japanese?'). ていただけませんか is much more polite, and therefore appropriate when asking someone like a boss or teacher.

ないでください (N5, Please don't (Polite request)): ないでください is a polite way to ask someone not to do something. It's neutral and appropriate for strangers or people of equal status. In contrast, 〜ていただけませんか is a more respectful and humble way to ask someone to do something, typically used with clients, customers, or superiors when 〜てください might sound too direct.

summary: A word that often highlights the specific time that an event may hypothetically happen.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About たら
text: The conjunction particle たら is used as a kind of 'halfway point' between 'if' and 'when' in Japanese. It expresses the completion of an (A) action, and then a (B) action that is considered to be the result of (A). It may be hypothetical, or it may be presenting a one-time result of something that happened in the past.
To use たら, it will replace た in the simple past form of verbs, い-Adjectives, な-Adjectives, and nouns.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: もし (N4, If (For emphasis)): もし and たら are often used together to form conditional ('if') sentences. もし typically comes at the start of a sentence to emphasize the hypothetical nature of what follows, while たら gives the verb its conditional form. For example, もし宝くじが当たったら車を買おうと思います means 'If I win the lottery, I think I'll buy a car.'.

あとで (N4, After, Later): Both あとで and たら can show that one action follows another, but their usage and nuance differ. あとで simply shows sequence, like 'after doing (A)'. たら adds a conditional nuance and can mean 'when' (temporal) or 'if' (hypothetical). Because of this, they are rarely interchangeable.

たらどう (N4, Why don't you...?, What if you did...?): たら expresses a condition or hypothetical, and when combined with どう, forms a casual suggestion. For example, 散歩に行ったらどう？ means 'How about going for a walk?'. Similar to the English phrase 'Why don't you (A)?' or 'How about (A)?', it isis common in informal conversation.

ば (N4, If… then, (Conditional)): ば and たら are both conditional forms, but with different nuances. ば emphasizes the condition itself, often with an 'if and only if' feel, e.g. 田中さんが来てくれれば何とかなる ('If Tanaka comes, it'll work out.'). たら sets up an hypothetical condition, which can be followed by a result, comment, or request, e.g. 田中さんが来てくれたら教えてね ('If/when Tanaka comes, let me know.').

なら (N4, Were it, If, If it's the case, As for (Conditional)): なら and たら are both conditional expressions but differ in nuance and usage. なら means 'if it's the case that (A)', often implying the speaker believes it will happen, e.g. 来るなら 'if it's the case that (they) come'. たら covers the ideas of both 'if' and 'when', expressing both hypothetical conditions or guaranteed events, e.g. 駅に着いたら電話してください ('Call me when/if you arrive at the station.').

と (N4, If, When, Whenever, And, [Conditional]): たら and と are both conditional forms, but they differ in nuance and usage. たら expresses both 'if' and 'when', and can describe hypotheticals or one-time events, such as 雨が降ったら行きません ('If it rains, I won't go.'). と is used for regular or expected outcomes, as in 春になると桜が咲く ('When spring comes, the cherry blossoms bloom.').

それなら (N2, Then, If that's the case): それなら expresses a response to a condition, as in それなら行きません (In that case, I won’t go). The conditional たら form can also mark conditions at the end of verbs, adjectives, or nouns. それだったら can convey a similar meaning to それなら, but with a slight nuance: それなら assumes the condition will or has happened, while それだったら tends to be more hypothetical.3

てから (N5, Once...is done, Once...happens, After doing): てから and たら both convey a sequence of events, but their nuances differ. てから simply indicates that one event follows another. In contrast, たら is similar to the English 'when' or 'if' and suggests that the second event is a result of the first. たら can be used in both hypothetical situations ('if A, then B') and past events ('When I did A, B happened').

上で (N3, After, Upon): Both 上で and たら can describe sequences or conditions, but with different nuance. 上で implies that one action is a prerequisite for another, such as 社長と相談した上で決めましょう ('Let's decide after discussing it with the president.'). たら is more general and covers a wider range of temporal and conditional uses, as in 晴れたら散歩に行こう ('If it's sunny, let's go for a walk.').

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ほかに(も)・ほか(に)は
text: {他|ほか}に is regularly considered to be one of the more difficult structures to master in Japanese, so let's take a thorough look at it. Basically, {他|ほか} by itself just means 'another', or 'other'. に highlights {他|ほか} 'another thing' as being the target of what comes next in any particular sentence. The possibilities are as follows:
{他|ほか}に - Another thing.
{他|ほか}に（も） - Even another thing (sounds less certain).
{他|ほか}に（は） - Was there another thing (focuses on something pre-existing, which someone may have forgotten).
{他|ほか}
の
+ Noun - Another 'specific thing'.
{他|ほか}に（は） may be used in either positive or negative sentences, but it tends to appear in negative sentences more often.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: ほかにも cannot be used in negative sentences, with the exception of questions
外 is another way to write ほか

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: をおいてほかに〜ない (N1, No...but, Nothing else but, None other than): Both use ほか (他, other) to express contrast or exclusivity. ほかに(も) and ほか(に)は mean 'other than' and are used to compare or list alternatives. をおいてほかに〜ない is a stronger expression meaning 'no one/nothing else but', as in 彼をおいてほかに適任者はいない ('There's no one more suitable than him.').

いがい (N4, Except・besides, Other than, With the exception of): Both forms can express the idea of 'other than', but their nuance and usage differ slightly. いがい emphasizes exceptions, like 'except for' or 'other than,' and attaches directly after nouns, e.g. バナナ以外の果物 means 'fruits other than bananas.' In contrast, ほかに highlights the presence of alternatives, takes の when linking to nouns, e.g. バナナの他に 'other than bananas', and can also start a sentence or phrase.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About がひつよう
text: が{必要|ひつよう} is a common expression in Japanese which is used to highlight the 'need' or 'necessity' of something. It is a structure that may only be used with nouns, which means that verbs will need to be nominalized (turned into noun-phrases) in order to use this construction.
Both が and だ may sometimes be omitted from this expression in casual speech. However, it is a good idea to at least use が, to clarify the thing that is 'necessary'.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ひつようがある (N4, It is necessary to): Both expressions use 必要 'necessary' to show that something is needed. が必要 attaches to nouns or nominalized verbs, as in 金が必要 ('Money is necessary.') or 覚えることが必要 ('It's necessary to memorize.'). 必要がある connects only to verbs and uses the form 覚える必要がある ('There is a need to memorize.'), which means essentially the same thing but fits more naturally with verb phrases.

summary: A word that is used to show the surprising extent of something. To that extent.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About そんなに
text: そんなに, like そんな, is one of the most common ways to express that one thing is 'like' something else in casual conversation. The addition of the particle に just highlights そんな as being the 'destination' of the 'like' amount. This construction is regularly translated as 'so much', 'that much', or simply 'like that'.
As a word, そんなに is used adverbially. This means that it may come before any verb, い-Adjective, or な-Adjective.
Almost any そんなに based sentence can be translated literally as '(A) to an extent like that', where (A) is the word that comes after そんなに, and に indicates 'to'.
As そんなに is another example of こそあど{言葉|ことば} (words like これ, それ, あれ, and どれ), it means that こんなに, あんなに, and どんなに may also be used.

Despite this, そんなに is almost considered a set phrase, and is therefore the most common out of all of the possibilities (except for どんなに, which is often used when explaining/giving reasons for something).

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: そんな・こんな・あんな・どんな (N4, Such a・Kind of, Something like ~): そんな・こんな・あんな・どんな come before nouns and mean 'that/this/what kind of (A)' or 'something like (A)'. そんなに is the same そんな, but followed by に. そんなに (as well as こんなに, あんなに, どんなに) is used with verbs or adjectives to add emphasis, similar to 'that much' or 'to that extent' in English. For example, そんな本 means 'a book/books like that,' and そんなに面白い means 'that interesting' or 'so interesting'.

あまり～ない (N4, Not very, Not much, Not really, Hardly): Both あまり～ない and そんなに express a negative degree, but with different nuance. あまり～ない means 'not very' in a general sense, e.g. あまり寒くない ('It's not very cold.'). そんなに (literally 'that much') can imply comparison to a standard and can be used with both negative and affirmative phrases, e.g. そんなに好きなら 'if you like [it] that much...' and そんなに好きじゃない ('I don't like it that much.').

summary: A phrase that highlights a specific action as being required.
formation: Verb + 必要（ひつよう） + が + ある
Verb + 必要（ひつよう） + が + あります (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ひつようがある
text: Like が{必要|ひつよう}, {必要|ひつよう}がある is an expression which is used to highlight the 'need' or 'necessity' of something. The primary difference being that {必要|ひつよう}がある highlights the need to 'do (A)', and will therefore be used with verbs (without the need for nominalization).
To use {必要|ひつよう}がある, just attach it after the plain form of the verb that you want to highlight the 'need' for.

As we can see, this construction is simply the combination of a verb + {必要|ひつよう} (creating a verb modified noun), the case marking particle が, and the う-Verb ある. In this way, it just means 'the need of doing (A) exists'.
Naturally, this grammar pattern may also be used negatively, to highlight that there is 'no need to do (A)', or that 'doing (A) is not necessary'.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: がひつよう (N4, Need, Necessary): Both expressions use 必要 'necessary' to show that something is needed. が必要 attaches to nouns or nominalized verbs, as in 金が必要 ('Money is necessary.') or 覚えることが必要 ('It's necessary to memorize.'). 必要がある connects only to verbs and uses the form 覚える必要がある ('There is a need to memorize.'), which means essentially the same thing but fits more naturally with verb phrases.

ことはない (N3, There is no need to, Never happens): These forms are opposites in meaning. ひつようがある shows something must be done, as in 行く必要がある ('You need to go.'). ことはない reassures that something doesn't need to be done, as in 行くことはない ('You don't need to go.'). One expresses necessity, the other expresses lack of it.

sections.heading: About たとえば
text: たとえば (or {例|たと}えば in its kanji form) is an adverb in Japanese that is used at the beginning of a sentence, or an individual statement, in order to present an example. It can be translated almost directly as 'for example'.

sections.label: Compare

text: とか～とか (N4, Among other things, For example, Such as): たとえば and とか～とか both introduce examples, but differ in usage. たとえば comes at the start of a sentence or clause, like 'for example'. In contrast, とか～とか is used to list multiple items and follows each noun. Because they differ in function, they can be used together in the same sentence, e.g. たとえば本とか雑誌とか ('For example, things like books, magazines, and so forth.').

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About れる・られる (Potential)
text: In addition to 'passive' verbs, れる and られる (the auxiliary verbs) are used when expressing possibility '{可能|かのう}'.

られる will be attached to the base form of る-Verbs (the form after る has been removed). Note also that れる and られる themselves behave like standard る-Verbs, so can be conjugated into a variety of different tenses in the same way as a standard verb.

A common sight in modern Japanese is words where the ら may be removed, 'ラ{抜|ぬ}き{言葉|ことば}', and れる may be used by itself. However, this is not technically correct Japanese, and may cause confusion in cases where ら is required (with る-Verbs and くる, when られる is expressing 'passivity', 'respect', or 'spontaneous occurrence').

For う-Verbs, they will behave a little differently. Instead of the final kana of the verb changing to an あ sound, and then adding れる (as would be the case with passive verbs), the final kana of the verb will change to an え sound (る will become れ, う will become え, す will become せ, etc.) before adding る.
Interestingly, する verbs do not have a 'potential' form, and the verb できる will be used in its place.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: ことができる and られる (when used in its 'potential' meaning) have exactly the same nuance. However, many people consider ことができる to be slightly more polite.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: In Japanese, the potential is considered to be something beyond the control of a person.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ことができる (N4, Can, Be able to): Both express potential or ability, like 'can do'. ことができる is more formal and common in writing, e.g. 書くことができる 'can write', while the potential form れる・られる is shorter and used in conversation, e.g. 書ける 'can write'. The meaning is the same, but usage differs by tone and context.

Verb［れる・られる］ (N4, Was done to ~ by ~, Done without consent, Done to one's dismay): Passive and potential forms have different meanings but can be confusing because some forms overlap. For う-verbs, the forms are distinct. For example, 言われる 'to be said' (passive) vs. 言える means 'can say' (potential). For る-verbs, a form like 食べられる can mean either 'to be eaten' (passive) or 'can eat' (potential), and which is intended must be determined from context.

見える (N4, To be visible, To seem, To be in sight): Both 見える and 見られる mean 'can see' (potential form) but their nuances differ. 見える describes something being visible, while 見られる refers to the ability to view something. For example, stars in the sky are 見える, but being able to watch a movie on a streaming service would be 見られる.

聞こえる (N4, To be audible, To sound (like), (Can) hear, To be heard): Both 聞こえる and 聞ける can mean 'can hear,' but differ in nuance. 聞こえる refers to a sound being audible, while 聞ける indicates the ability to hear or listen. For example, a bird chirping nearby would be 聞こえる, but being able to stream a song would be 聞ける.

得る・得る (N2, Is able to, Can, Possible): 得る・得る and the れる・られる (Potential) form both indicate possibility or ability, but differ in nuance. れる・られる is used for general ability, as in 話せる 'can speak', and is conversational. 得る is more formal and written-style, and is typically that something is possible or conceivable, like 起こり得る ('It could happen.').

summary: A casual way of expressing but, with the focus on giving reasons, elongating a pause, or leaving something unsaid due to awkwardness.
formation: (2) けれども、けれど、けども、けど
Phrase (A) + のです(1) + が(2) + Phrase (B) (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About んだけど・んですが
text: んだけど is an expression that combines んだ (explaining/giving cause), with けど (but). Together they translate simply as 'but...', although the nuance is actually closer to 'but with (A) as the reason… (B)', while (B) is sometimes left unsaid. This implies that the speaker is looking for a reply, or does not want to say the (B) part of the sentence out of politeness/awkwardness.
There are several different forms of this construction that are mostly interchangeable with each other. From most casual, to most formal, they are as follows:
んだけど、んだけれど、んだけれども、んだが、んですが
ん may be replaced with の in any of the above expressions. However, it will again make it slightly more formal.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: んだが, or simply だが is probably the 'strongest' out of these possibilities, and is considered quite masculine. If you are going to use this form, we recommend making sure that your tone is a bit softer, so that it does not sound too authoritative.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Versions without ん/の are also acceptable but ん/の version is more common nowadays.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: が (N5, But, However): Both express contrast, but が is more formal and used in writing, like 面白いが難しい ('It's interesting, but difficult'). When combined with ～んだ・～んです, as in 行きたいんですが, it softens the sentence and invites a response or action from the listener.

～んです・のです (N5, Explanatory, Emphasis, The fact is): ～んです・のです adds an explanatory tone to a statement, like 難しいんです ('It's difficult, I'm telling you.'). When paired with contrastive particles like けど or が, the speaker often implies something left unsaid, as in 難しいんですけど ('It's hard, but...', implying 'and that's why I can't do it', etc.).

けど・だけど (N5, But, However): Both introduce contrast, like the English 'but'. けど・だけど are common in speech, as in 難しいけど面白い ('It's difficult, but interesting.'). Adding ～ん to this pattern adds an explanatory nuance, often used to imply a request or hesitation, e.g. 難しいんですけど 'It's difficult, but...(do you want me to do it anyway?, etc.)'.

meaning: Bound to (be), Expected to (be), Should be (able)
summary: A phrase that expresses when the speaker thinks that (A) is bound to be true.
formation: Noun + の + はず + だ
［な］Adjective + な + はず + です (polite)
Noun + の + はず + です (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About はずだ
text: はず, coming from the kanji {筈|はず}, is a word in Japanese that is very similar to 'bound' in English. This means that it expresses something that the speaker is 'quite sure is true', but cannot confirm. The most common translations of はず are 'bound to be (A)', and 'should be (A)'.
As はず is a noun, it may be used in any place that a noun would usually be used. It will often be followed by だ, or です.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Despite はず sometimes being translated as 'should', this is only when you think that something 'should be true', and cannot be used when making suggestions/giving advice. Due to this, 'bound' is the more accurate translation of {筈|はず}, in almost all situations.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: There is also another, even less used kanji for はず：弭。

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: に決まっている (N2, Surely, Bound to, Certainly, Be decided): While both of these grammar points express a belief or expectation, and can function similar to the English 'should (be)', はずだ conveys a more general assertion typically based upon some information or evidence, while に決まっている sounds more decisive/absolute and sometimes emotional, and can be based simply on the speaker's personal opinion.

ことになっている (N2, To be expected to, To be scheduled to): Both can describe future events, but differ in source. はずだ shows the speaker's expectation, like 来るはずだ ('He should come.'). ことになっている refers to something officially decided, often outside the speaker's control. For example, 来ることになっている ('It has been decided that he will come.')

べきではない (N3, Should not, Must not, Ought not to): はずだ expresses an assumption or expectation based on reason or context, e.g. 雨が降るはずだ ('It should rain.'). In contrast, べきではない expresses a strong sense of moral or social obligation not to do something, e.g. 嘘をつくべきではない ('You shouldn't lie.').

わけだ (N3, For that reason, No wonder, As you'd expect, Naturally, Thus, This is why): Both express logical conclusions, but with different emphasis. はずだ conveys expectation or prediction, as in 来るはずだ ('He should come.'). わけだ explains a reason behind something known or observed, like 来るわけだ ('So that's why he's coming.'). はずだ leans future-oriented, わけだ explanatory.

べき (N3, Must, Should, Ought to): はずだ and べき can both be translated as 'should', but they differ in nuance. はずだ expresses an expectation based on evidence or reasoning, like 明日来るはずだ ('He should come tomorrow.'). In contrast, べき expresses obligation or social correctness, as in 来るべきだ ('You should come.').

はずがない (N4, Hardly possible, Cannot be, Highly unlikely, Improbable): These forms are opposites. はずだ expresses positive expectation, as in 来るはずだ ('He should come.'), while はずがない strongly denies a possibility based on logic or knowledge, as in 来るはずがない ('There's no way he'll come.'). Both are grounded in reasoning, but the conclusions differ.

つもりだ (N5, To plan to, To intend to): つもりだ is used to express personal intentions or plans, similar to 'I hope to' or 'I intend to' in English. In contrast, はずだ expresses an expectation or belief that something will happen, based on logic or evidence. While つもりだ is subjective and often refers to the speaker's own plans, はずだ is more objective and is used for expectations about others or events outside the speaker's control.

ばいい (N3, Can, Should, It'd be good if): はずだ indicates something is expected based on information or logic, as in 行けるはずだ ('I should be able to go.'). ばいい expresses hope or a hypothetical good outcome, like 行ければいい ('It'd be nice if I could go.'). One is based on reasoning, the other on desire.

たらいい・といい (N3, It would be nice if, It would be good if, Should, I hope): はずだ expresses confident expectation, as in 雨が降るはずだ ('It should rain.'). たらいい and といい express hope or desire without implying it will happen, e.g. 雨が降るといい ('I hope it rains.'). The difference lies in expectation vs. wish. Thus, といい is often used even when the speaker is not confident the thing will happen.

ものだ (N3, Supposed to, Should, That's the way it is): はずだ conveys a specific expectation or prediction based on current evidence, like 雨が降るはずだ ('It should rain.'). ものだ expresses a general rule or common tendency, like 雨は春によく降るものだ ('It often rains in spring.'). The former is situational, while the latter is habitual or cultural.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About かどうか
text: かどうか is an expression in Japanese which combines the 'or' meaning of か, with the 'how' meaning of どう. (A) かどうか (B) is regularly translated as 'whether or not (A), (B)'.
To use かどうか, simply attach it to the end of any phrase that you want to express the 'or' use of か about, then add the (B) phrase.
Although 'whether or not' is the standard translation, the more literal translation of かどうか is 'if it's (A), or however it is, (B)'.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: か何か (N2, Or something, Or something like that): か何か and かどうか look similar but are used differently. か何か follows a noun and means 'or something,' as in お茶か何か飲みますか？ ('Would you like some tea or something?'). かどうか means 'whether or not' and expresses uncertainty, like 面白いかどうか分からない ('I don't know whether or not it's interesting.').

にしても～にしても (N2, Regardless of whether): Both can suggest contrastive options, but with different usage. かどうか focuses on 'whether or not' something is true. にしても～にしても means 'regardless of which', and is used for comparing two alternatives. For example, 楽しいにしてもつまらないにしても行く ('Whether it's fun or boring, I'll go.').

〜でも 〜でも (N4, Whether ~ or, Neither ~ or): かどうか expresses uncertainty, as in 来るかどうか分からない ('I don't know whether or not they'll come.'). 〜でも〜でも lists multiple alternatives and suggests the outcome is unchanged. For example, 雨でも晴れでも行く ('Whether it rains or shines, I'll go.').

にしても (N3, Even though, Even if, Even when, Also): かどうか expresses binary uncertainty, like 'whether or not', as in 行くかどうか分からない ('I don't know whether or not they'll go.'). にしても adds a tone of concession or contrast, like 'even if'. For example, どこに行くにしても 'no matter where (you) go'. The former asks a yes/no-type question, the latter implies acceptance of a situation.

か否か (N1, Whether or not): Both か否か and かどうか express 'whether or not,' but differ in tone and usage. か否か is highly formal and mostly seen in legal documents, academic writing, or formal reports. かどうか is more common in daily conversation and general writing, making it the default choice in most situations.

にしろ～にしろ (N2, Whether… or): Both express the sense of 'whether', but in different ways. かどうか is used to present uncertainty, as in 面白いかどうか分からない ('I don't know whether or not it's interesting.'). にしろ～にしろ expresses that something applies regardless of the case, like 面白いにしろつまらないにしろ観たい ('Whether it's interesting or boring, I want to watch.').

Question-phrase + か (N4, Including questions within sentences): Both are embedded question forms. A question phrase plus か makes an indirect question, like 何時に来るか分からない ('I don't know what time they'll come'). かどうか focuses specifically on yes/no questions, like 来るかどうか分からない ('I don't know whether or not they'll come.').

～ても～なくても (N3, Whether ~ or not): かどうか expresses uncertainty, like 'whether or not', as in 行くかどうか分からない ('I don't know whether or not they'll go.'). ～ても～なくても presents two opposite possibilities and says the result is unchanged, like 降っても降らなくても行く ('Whether it rains or not, I'm going.').

summary: A conditional that expresses known or certain outcomes.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About と
text: In the same way as the case marking particleと means 'and', sometimes it is translated as 'if'. In these cases, it is considered to be far stronger than ば, なら, or たら (which express hypothetical outcomes). This is because one of the primary uses of と is highlighting a result. In these cases, と is actually a conjunction particle, and shows one of three things.
{仮定|かてい}の{順接|じゅんせつ} - A result that is assumed to be true, and obvious.
{確定|かくてい}の{順接|じゅんせつ} - A result that is known to be true.
{仮定|かてい}の{逆接|ぎゃくせつ} - The opposite of a result that is assumed to be true.
Due to this, the (B) part of a phrase using と as 'if', will always occur when (A) happens, as it is considered to be the result of (A).
と may not be used in situations where the (B) result 'might' happen. It must be definite (or close to definite).
In this particular nuance of と, despite being translated as 'if', the actual meaning is much closer to 'and', as と is expressing that (A) and (B) will always go together.

text: もし (N4, If (For emphasis)): と is used to express natural or habitual results, as in 春が来ると花が咲く ('When spring comes, flowers bloom.'). もし adds emphasis to conditionals and can appear before と or other conditionals like たら and ば. For example, もし雨が降ったら 'if it rains' has a more hypothetical tone than if もし were not present.

そうすると (N3, Having done that..., If that is done..., (And/just) then, Thereupon, If so): と marks a natural condition, while そうすると is used to explain what would happen in that case. It means 'if that happens' or 'then...' and often introduces a result. For example, 早く寝なさい。そうすると、明日は元気になるよ ('Go to bed early. Then you'll feel good tomorrow.')

すると (N3, Having done..., If...is done..., (And/just) then, Thereupon, If so): と marks a natural result, while すると is a transition word meaning 'thereupon' or 'and then'. It's often used at the beginning of a new sentence to show what happened next. For example, ドアを開けた。すると、猫がいた ('I opened the door. And there was a cat.'

ばあいは (N4, In the event of, In the case of): と and ばあいは can both express conditions, but differ significantly in usage. と describes something that happens habitually or as a natural result, e.g. お酒を飲むとすぐ酔っ払ってしまう ('When I drink alcohol, I get drunk quickly.'). ばあいは is used more for situational instructions, like お酒を飲む場合は運転しないほうがいい ('In the event that you drink alcohol, you shouldn't drive.').

ば (N4, If… then, (Conditional)): ば and と are both conditional expressions, but differ in nuance. ば emphasizes the condition that leads to a result, often with an 'if and only if' tone. と is used for habitual or automatic outcomes, suggesting that what follows happens naturally or inevitably when the condition is met.

なら (N4, Were it, If, If it's the case, As for (Conditional)): Both と and なら are conditional expressions, but differ in nuance. と is used for habitual or automatic results, e.g. 春になると花が咲く ('When it becomes spring, flowers bloom.'). なら is used for one-time or assumed situations and implies the speaker believes the condition is likely, e.g. 雨なら出かけない ('If it's going to rain, I won't go out.').

たら (N4, When, From when, Just when, If): たら and と are both conditional forms, but they differ in nuance and usage. たら expresses both 'if' and 'when', and can describe hypotheticals or one-time events, such as 雨が降ったら行きません ('If it rains, I won't go.'). と is used for regular or expected outcomes, as in 春になると桜が咲く ('When spring comes, the cherry blossoms bloom.').

summary: A casual, hypothetical structure showing that one must do (A). Often with the nuance of if (A) is not done, something bad may happen.
formation: Verb［ない］+ と + （いけません(1)） (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ないと
text: As an extension of the 'if' meaning of と, attaching the auxiliary verb ない to the verb before it will express 'if (A) is not done, (B)'. (B) is most frequently いけない 'cannot go', which makes ないといけない a double negative phrase, which translates to 'must do (A)', or 'have to do (A)'.
いけない may be replaced with だめ, to make the phrase more casual, but ならない is generally not used with ないと.
ないといけない
is regularly abbreviated to
ないと
, but has exactly the same meaning in these cases.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: ないとならない is generally not used and is best avoided

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: なければならない (N4, Must do, Have to do): Both express obligation, but differ in tone. ないと is casual and often shortened in speech, as in 行かないと ('I've got to go.'). なければならない is more formal, used in writing or polite conversation. Both convey the idea of needing to do something.

なくてはいけない (N5, Must do, Have to do): ないと, なくちゃ, and なくてはいけない express obligation, meaning something 'must' or 'needs' to be done. なくてはいけない is more formal, while ないと (the negative form plus conditional と) is a casual alternative. While いけない can be replaced with ならない, ないと is usually used on it's own or followed by いけない or だめ, the more casual option.

なければいけない (N4, Must do, Have to do): These expressions mean the same thing but differ in formality. ないと is used casually in speech, as in もう行かないと ('I need to go soon.'). なければいけない is more polite and suitable for formal contexts. Both mean 'I must (A).' or 'I have to (A).'.

べき (N3, Must, Should, Ought to): ないと and べき both express a sense of necessity, but with different nuances. ないと focuses on immediate or practical obligation, like 行かないと ('I've got to go.'). べき expresses moral or logical duty, as in 行くべきだ ('You should go.').

なくちゃ・なきゃ (N5, Must do, Have to do): Both ないと and なくちゃ・なきゃ express necessity or obligation in casual speech, similar to 'I have to' or 'I need to' in English. They are very close in meaning and formality, and are generally interchangeable in everyday conversation with little to no difference in nuance.

なくてはならない (N5, Must do, Have to do): Both ないと and なくてはならない both express obligation or necessity, meaning something 'must' or 'needs' to be done. なくてはならない is more formal, while ないと (negative form with a condition と) is a more casual alternative. While ないと can be used alone or followed by either いけない (more formal) or だめ (more casual), it's generally not used with the more formal ならない.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About はずがない
text: Like はず, coming from the kanji {筈|はず}, which suggests that something is 'bound' to be true, はずがない suggests that something is 'not bound' to be true. This expression is usually translated as 'hardly possible', 'improbable', or 'unlikely', but in reality, it is a bit weaker than these, and translates more literally to '(A) is not the only possibility'.
As はずがない (a combination of {筈|はず}, the case-marking particle が, and the い-Adjective ない) is a phrase that starts with a noun, it may be used after any word that could usually connect with a noun.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ようがない・ようもない (N2, There's no way to, It's impossible to): These both express impossibility, but in different ways. はずがない asserts a strong disbelief based on knowledge, like 雨が降るはずがない ('It can't possibly rain.'). ようがない・ようもない focuses on the lack of a method, as in 連絡のしようがない ('There's no way to contact them.').

わけではない (N3, It doesn't mean that, It is not the case, It's not like): はずがない strongly rejects something as being true. わけではない denies an assumption while leaving room for nuance. For example, 雨が降るはずがない ('There's no way it will.') vs. 雨が降るわけではない ('It's not that it will rain.'), implying e.g. that the weather might be poor in other ways, etc.

そうもない (N3, Very unlikely to, Does not seem that, Does not appear that): そうもない and はずがない both express the improbability of something happening. そうもない is the less confident of the two and carries the nuance that something seems unlikely, e.g. 雨が降りそうもない ('It doesn't appear that it's going to rain.'). In contrast, はずがない is a stronger denial, with a nuance of disbelief or surprise, e.g. 負けるはずがない ('There's no way / It's highly unlikely [we] will lose.').

わけがない (N3, There is no way, There is no reason, It is impossible, Cannot be): はずがない and わけがない are similar in that they both express a strong denial of a possibility, similar to the English 'There's no way that (A)', but with slightly different nuances. はずがない gives the sense that the speaker is drawing a conclusion based on their own reasoning, often with a sense of surprise or disbelief. In contrast, わけがない expresses an even stronger denial, as if the impossibility is an obvious fact.

ないことはない (N3, Is not impossible, It doesn't mean that it isn't): はずがない strongly denies something, as in そんなことがあるはずがない ('That can't possibly be true.'). In contrast, ないことはない suggests that something is technically possible, but maybe unlikely or difficult, as in 行けないことはない ('It's not that I can't go.').

わけだ (N3, For that reason, No wonder, As you'd expect, Naturally, Thus, This is why): はずがない denies something based on logic or evidence, while わけだ draws a conclusion or explains a reason. For example, 来るはずがない ('There's no way he'll come.') vs. 来るわけだ ('So that's why he's coming.'). One rejects a possibility, while the other clarifies it.

はずだ (N4, Bound to (be), Expected to (be), Should be (able)): These forms are opposites. はずだ expresses positive expectation, as in 来るはずだ ('He should come.'), while はずがない strongly denies a possibility based on logic or knowledge, as in 来るはずがない ('There's no way he'll come.'). Both are grounded in reasoning, but the conclusions differ.

ことはない (N3, There is no need to, Never happens): ことはない has two primary uses: one is to express that there is no need to do something, e.g. 心配することはない ('There's no need to worry.'), and the other is to say that something simply doesn't happen, e.g. 彼と会うことはない ('There are no cases where I meet him.'). In contrast, はずがない expresses the speaker's strong denial or disbelief regarding some possibility, e.g. 負けるはずがない ('There's no way / It's highly unlikely we will lose.').

ものか (N2, Definitely not, Absolutely not, Impossible, Do you really think~?): Both express strong denial, but ものか is more emphatic and emotional. はずがない states something is unlikely or impossible, based on logic, e.g. 来るはずがない ('There's no way he'll come.'). ものか rejects something outright, as in 君にできるものか！ ('As if you could!').

まじき (N1, Unbecoming of, Unworthy of, Not proper for, Should not, Must not, Cannot): Both express strong denial, but their usage differs. まじき is a formal, literary expression usually found in fixed phrases such as あるまじき, and is used to judge that something is morally or socially unacceptable rather than logically impossible, as in 指導者としてあるまじき行為だ ('It is behavior unbecoming of a leader.'). はずがない denies possibility based on logic, evidence, or common sense, stating that something cannot be true, as in 彼がそんなことをするはずがない ('There is no way he would do such a thing.').

summary: A phrase that highlights that one specific thing is all that exists.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About しか～ない
text: The adverbial particle しか is often compared to だけ, in that it also expresses 'only'. However, unlike だけ, しか can only be used in negative statements. Due to this, しか～ない is regularly translated as 'there's only (A)', or 'there's nothing but (A)'. しか～ない may be used to express numbers, or nouns. In this lesson we will examine nouns.

Like しか～ない, the construction used for expressing numbers, when used before a noun, this expression will mean that nothing apart from that one 'thing' exists. Any verb may be used after しか, but it must be in its ない (or ありません) form.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: だらけ (N3, Completely covered in, Full of): だらけ and しか～ない are used differently and express contrasting meanings. だらけ follows nouns and expresses the idea of 'covered with' or 'full of', e.g. 泥だらけ 'covered in mud'. In contrast, しか～ない is used with a noun and negative verb to mean 'only' or 'nothing but', e.g. １００円しかない ('I have only 100 yen.'). They are similar in that both can often carry a negative or undesirable nuance.

にほかならない (N2, Nothing but, None other than, Simply): しか～ない and にほかならない are similar in that both can be translated as 'nothing but' or 'only', but with a different nuance. しか～ない means 'nothing but' in the sense of 'nothing else exists', e.g. １００円しかない ('I only have 100 yen.'). In contrast, にほかならない means 'nothing but' in the sense of 'simply' or 'definitely', e.g. 彼は犯罪者に他ならない ('He's simply / nothing but a criminal.').

を余儀なくされる (N1, To be forced to do something): を余儀なくされる and しかない are similar in that both express having no choice but to do something, though their usage differs. を余儀なくされる follows nouns and has a nuance of being forced by circumstances, e.g. 中止を余儀なくされる 'be forced to cancel.' In contrast, しかない follows verbs and focuses on lack of choice rather than external pressure, e.g. 行くしかない ('There's no choice but to go.').

をおいてほかに〜ない (N1, No...but, Nothing else but, None other than): Both convey the idea of 'nothing but,' but with different nuances. をおいてほかに～ない almost always has a positive nuance, suggesting that the thing in question is the only one that possesses some good quality, e.g. 日本語を学ぶなら文プロをおいてほかにない ('If you want to learn Japanese, there's nothing but Bunpro.'). In contrast, しか～ない emphasizes lack and is often used with a negative nuance, e.g. １００円しかない ('I only have 100 yen.').

きり (N3, Only, Just, Since): きり and しか～ない can both express the idea of 'only,' but in different ways. きり is used primarily with number+counter expressions, like 一度きり 'only one time' or 二人きり 'only/just the two of us'. In contrast, しか～ない is used with a noun and negative verb to mean 'only' or 'nothing but', e.g. １００円しかない ('I have only 100 yen.'). In some cases, the two can be used together, e.g. 一度きりしか行っていない ('I only went just the once.').

でしかない (N2, Merely, Nothing but, No more than): しか～ない uses the particle しか and a verb in the negative (ない) form to convey the idea of 'only' (literally, 'nothing but'), e.g. １００円しかない ('I only have / have nothing but 100 yen.') and バナナしか食べなかった ('I only ate / ate nothing but a banana.'). でしかない is a version of this using a form of だ・です 'is', and means 'it is only' or 'it's nothing but', e.g. ゴミでしかない ('It's nothing but garbage.').

ばかり (N3, Just, Only, Nothing but): ばかり and しか～ない can both mean 'only' or 'nothing but', but their usage and nuance differ. ばかり is used with affirmative verb forms and can imply excess. For example, 漫画ばかり読む 'to read only manga' has a sense of reading manga all the time. In contrast, しか～ない is used with negative verbs and expresses 'nothing but' in a more objective sense. For example, 漫画しか読まない simply states that nothing else is read.

しかない (N3, Have no choice but, Only, Just): When used with a noun and a negative verb, しか～ない expresses the idea of 'only' (literally, 'nothing but'), e.g. １００円しかない ('I only have / have nothing but 100 yen.') and バナナしか食べなかった ('I only ate / ate nothing but a banana.'). When used at the end of a sentence following a verb in the affirmative form, しかない has the related meaning of 'there's no choice but to do (A)', e.g. 行くしかない ('I have no choice but to go.').

だけしか (N3, To emphasize '~only', Nothing but): だけしか is essentially an emphatic version of しか～ない, combining だけ 'only' and しか～ない 'nothing but' to strongly emphasize that there is nothing else. For example, １００円だけしかない ('I only have / have nothing but 100 yen.) is a more emphatic version of 100円しかない (same meaning), and 日本語だけしか話せない ('I can only speak / can speak nothing but Japanese.') is a more emphatic version of 日本語しか話せない (same meaning).

だけ (N5, Only, Just): だけ conveys 'only' or 'just.' しか～ない combines the particle しか with a negative verb to express 'nothing but.' While the two have similar meanings, their structures differ. For example, the equivalent of バナナだけ食べた ('I ate only a banana') would be バナナしか食べなかった ('I ate nothing but a banana'). Compared to だけ, しか～ない emphasizes the limitation or lack of other options more strongly.

Number + しか〜ない (N4, No more than, Not exceeding, As few as・as little as, Only): しか～ない expresses the meaning of 'only' or 'nothing but'. For example, バナナしか食べなかった ('I only ate a banana', or literally 'I didn't eat anything but a banana.'). When used with numbers in the Number + しか〜ない pattern, it emphasizes that the quantity is small, e.g., ５人しか来なかった ('Only 5 people came.', or literally 'No one came but five people.').

summary: A somewhat casual expression used to show that something is not just (A), but also (B).
formation: ［な］Adjective + な + だけ + でなく(1)
(1) ではなく（て）、じゃなく（て）

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About だけでなく
text: だけでなく (an abbreviation of だけではなく) is a common construction in Japanese which translates to 'not only (A), but also (B)'. Sometimes the (B) statement may be left unsaid. This expression may connect to any (A) phrase that だけ would usually be able to connect to.
The conjunction particle て should follow なく, as it is the conjunctive form of the い-Adjective ない. However, the て in this particular construction is very often omitted.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: It is often used together with second noun + particle も (meaning "also") in main clause.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ばかりでなく (N3, Not only…but also, As well as): だけでなく and ばかりでなく convey the same essential meaning of 'not only'. Both expressions are often followed by another noun + も, which gives the added meaning of 'not only (A), but also (B)'. The main difference is that ばかりでなく is more formal and appears primarily in written or academic language. In everyday speech, the だけ version is more common, particularly in the variant form だけじゃなくて.

だけ (N5, Only, Just): だけ conveys the meaning of 'only' or 'just'. だけでなく (or variant forms like だけではなく, だけじゃなくて, etc.) is a negation of this, combining だけ with で (the conjuctive form of だ) and なく (the conjunctive form of ない) to express the meaning of ‘not only (A)...but also (B)’. Unlike だけ, だけでなく will always be followed by a continuation of the sentence providing additional information, e.g. バナナだけでなく、リンゴも食べました (‘I ate not only a banana, but also an apple.’).

だけでなく(て)～も (N3, Not only ~ but ~ also, Not just ~ but ~ also): だけでなく (or だけでなくて, だけじゃなくて, etc.) is a common expression that means 'not only'. It is often followed by another noun + も in the expression だけでなく(て)～も, which has the meaning of 'not only (A), but also (B)', e.g. 肉だけでなく、魚も食べる ('I eat not only meat, but also fish.'). In other words, だけでなく(て)～も is an extension of the だけでなく pattern when you want to specify the additional thing or quality.

にとどまらず (N1, Not limited to, Not only...but also, Not stopping at): Both add information beyond an initial point, but the nuance differs. にとどまらず means ‘not limited to’ and emphasizes that the scope goes further than expected, often used in formal or written contexts to highlight expansion, as in 影響は国内にとどまらず海外にも及んだ ('The impact extended beyond the country to overseas.'). だけでなく is more neutral and conversational, simply adding another item without emphasizing scale or extension, as in 英語だけでなく日本語も話せる ('He can speak not only English but also Japanese.').

に限らず (N2, Not just, Not only… but also): だけでなく and に限らず both express non-exclusivity, but differ in nuance and formality. だけでなく is a straightforward expression meaning 'not only (A), but also (B)', and is often used in everyday conversation (especially in the variant form だけじゃなくて). In contrast, に限らず has a more formal and academic tone, and carries a slightly different nuance, suggesting that whatever follows is 'not limited to' the thing in question.

をはじめ (N3, Not only...but also..., Starting with): だけでなく and をはじめ both express non-exclusivity, but differ in nuance. だけでなく simply means 'not only (A), but also (B)', e.g. 英語だけでなく、日本語も話せる ('He can speak not only English, but also Japanese.'). In contrast, をはじめ implies that something is the first in a list of many, e.g. 日本語をはじめ、様々な外国語が話せる ('He can speak many foreign languages, starting with Japanese.').

はもちろん (N3, Not only but also, Let alone, Not to mention, Of course): だけでなく and はもちろん both express non-exclusivity, but differ in nuance and emphasis. だけでなく simply means 'not only (A), but also (B)', e.g. 英語だけでなく、日本語も話せる ('He can speak not only English, but also Japanese.'). In contrast, はもちろん implies the first thing is obvious, while the second is more notable, e.g. 英語はもちろん、日本語も話せる ('He can speak English of course, but also Japanese.').

のみならず (N2, Not only...but, Not just...but, What is more): のみならず and だけでなく are essentially synonymous in that they both express non-exclusivity (i.e. 'not only'), but differ in formality. While だけでなく is common in both everyday speech (often appearing as だけじゃなくて) and writing, のみならず is a highly formal expression used primarily in writing and academic contexts. Both phrases are often followed by a noun + も to convey 'not only (A), but also (B)'.

summary: A grammar point that can highlight an entire phrase as being possible.
formation: Verb + こと + が + できる
Verb + こと + が + できます (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ことができる
text: Like ことがある, ことができる is an expression that nominalizes what comes before it (turns it into a noun-phrase), and then highlights something about that (A) phrase. In the case of ことができる, the thing being highlighted about (A) is that it is 'possible'. This translates as 'can do (A)', or 'to be able to do (A)'.
However, こと is only required when the (A) phrase needs nominalization (is not a noun to begin with). Due to this, ができる may be used by itself when following a noun, without changing the meaning.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: のが (or のは) is also frequently used for nominalization, but this is rarely the case when a verb follows it. Some other expressions where のが may not be swapped for こと are as follows:
ことがある - For (A) to exist.
ことにする - To make something (A).
ことになる - For (A) to come to be.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: れる・られる (Potential) (N4, To be able, Can (Potential)): Both express potential or ability, like 'can do'. ことができる is more formal and common in writing, e.g. 書くことができる 'can write', while the potential form れる・られる is shorter and used in conversation, e.g. 書ける 'can write'. The meaning is the same, but usage differs by tone and context.

summary: A very casual, blunt way to ask questions, that is usually only used by men.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About かい
text: The sentence ending particle かい is a grammar structure that is used in Japanese to highlight a question. Despite commonly being thought of as one word, it is actually the combination of か (the sentence-ending particle) and い, another sentence-ending particle that is primarily used by men (in a similar way to ね and よ).

かい will usually be used directly after the word or phrase that it is highlighting. In the case of verbs and い-Adjectives, の may be inserted before かい. For な-Adjectives and nouns, なの may be inserted directly before it. However, の (or なの) are frequently omitted, due to how casual かい is.
When it is not omitted, の (or なの) may be shortened to ん (or なん）. This is in the same way that の and なの would behave in the のです and なのです grammar structures.
Although there are some exceptions, かい will almost always be used to ask simple yes/no questions.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: Outside of かい, the sentence ending particle い is not commonly used in modern Japanese, and therefore will only appear in a few very specific structures (like だい). Despite being similar to ね, い is considered to be fairly ぞんざい 'rough', and should only be used with people that you are very familiar with, and never to someone above you.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: か (N5, Question marking particle): か is the standard question particle, used at the end of sentences to form questions (e.g., どんな本が好きですか？ = 'What kind of books do you like?'). It also appears in the middle of other grammar patterns. かい is a casual, informal question particle often used by older men at the end of yes/no questions (e.g., 元気かい？ = 'Are you feeling okay?').

summary: A short word which emphasizes hypothetical sentences even further.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About もし
text: もし is an adverb used to emphasize the nuance of 'if', with expressions like と, ば, なら, たら, and ても. Literally, the meaning of もし is close to 'while slight', or 'while small'.
To use もし, simply add it to the beginning of any phrase that uses one of the conditional expressions listed above.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: もし is sometimes seen written as {若|も}し, a kanji which has the meaning of 'low in (A)', (also seen in the word {若|わか}い 'young'). It is from this kanji that もし gets its meaning of 'while low in (probability, number, age, experience)'.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: と (N4, If, When, Whenever, And, [Conditional]): と is used to express natural or habitual results, as in 春が来ると花が咲く ('When spring comes, flowers bloom.'). もし adds emphasis to conditionals and can appear before と or other conditionals like たら and ば. For example, もし雨が降ったら 'if it rains' has a more hypothetical tone than if もし were not present.

たとえ〜ても (N3, Even if…is the case, Supposing that): もし and たとえ are similar in that both can be used at the beginning of a sentence to emphasize a hypothetical situation or condition. The primary difference is that while もし can be followed by a wide variety of conditionals, including なら, たら, ば, and ても, たとえ is almost always followed by a ても expression, giving it the meaning of 'even if (A)' or 'even supposing that (A)'.

もしも～なら・もしも～でも (N3, If, Supposing): もし is typically used at the beginning of a sentence to emphasize that what follows is a hypothetical situation or condition, similar to the English 'if' or 'supposing that (A)'. もしも is a more emphatic version of this, and sentences with もしも almost always contain a conditional expression, as seen in the もしも～なら・もしも～でも pattern. The specific meaning is determined by the conditional, e.g. もしも～なら 'if (A)' vs. もしも～でも 'even if (A)'.

たら (N4, When, From when, Just when, If): もし and たら are often used together to form conditional ('if') sentences. もし typically comes at the start of a sentence to emphasize the hypothetical nature of what follows, while たら gives the verb its conditional form. For example, もし宝くじが当たったら車を買おうと思います means 'If I win the lottery, I think I'll buy a car.'.

なら (N4, Were it, If, If it's the case, As for (Conditional)): なら and もし are both used in conditional expressions but have different roles. なら follows phrases to mean 'If it's the case that (A)', often implying the speaker believes it will happen. もし is used at the start of sentences or phrases to emphasize that a hypothetical statement follows, and is often paired with conditionals like なら, ば, or たら, e.g. もし雨なら行かない ('If it rains, I won't go.').

ても (N4, Even if, Even though): もし and ても both express hypothetical situations, but in different ways. もし appears before a clause to emphasize the condition, similar to 'if' or 'supposing that', while ても is attached to the verb itself. Because they fill different roles, they can be used together, e.g., もし雨が降っても 'even if it rains'. もし can also pair with other conditionals like たら or ば.

ば (N4, If… then, (Conditional)): もし and ば are both used in conditional expressions, but play different roles. ば is a grammatical ending that turns verbs into 'if' statements, e.g. 食べる 'eat' becoming 食べれば 'if (you) eat'. In contrast, もし is used at the start of sentences or phrases to emphasize that a hypothetical statement follows, and therefore is often paired with ば, たら, or なら, e.g. もし食べれば 'if (you) were to eat...'.

summary: A very short, casual expression that is frequently used for listing reasons.
formation: ［な］Adjective (A) + だ + し + （［な］Adjective (B) + だ + し）
Noun (A) + だ + し + （Noun (B) + だ + し）

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About し～し
text: Like て, し is a conjunction particle. This means that it is used for linking the (A) and (B) parts of a sentence, and describing that link in some way. The 'description' that し will highlight is 'reasons'. Regularly it is translated simply as 'and'.

し may be connected to the end of almost any word, but will require a だ before it when it comes after nouns or な-Adjectives. し will follow every 'reason' that is being listed in a sentence. However, the last し may be replaced with から or ので, before the 'result' is stated.

Using し will indicate that each 'reason' being listed is of equal weight/importance. Because of this, it would not be appropriate to use in sentences where one of the reasons clearly far outweighs everything else.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: In all of its uses, し indicates things that are {矛盾|むじゅん}{無|な}く{共存|きょうぞん}する, which basically means 'things that coexist, without contradicting each other'. This is the primary reason why each thing listed must be of equal importance (in terms of the overall story that the speaker is trying to convey).

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: The last し in a sentence can be replaced with から or ので

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ことだし (N1, (And) so, Because, Since): Both give reasons, but the structure and emphasis differ. ことだし presents a reason as a settled or obvious circumstance that naturally justifies a decision, often sounding calm and explanatory, as in 雨も降っていることだし、今日は家にいよう ('Since it’s raining anyway, let’s stay home today.'). By contrast, し～し lists multiple reasons side by side, emphasizing accumulation rather than inevitability, as in 雨だし寒いし、出かけたくない ('It’s raining and cold, so I don’t want to go out.').

上に (N2, As well, Besides, In addition to): 上に (literally, 'on top of') can be used as a slightly formal way to express 'in addition to (A), (B)', e.g. 安い上に、美味しい ('In addition to being inexpensive, it's tasty.'). While し～し is similar in that it lists multiple things, it specifically does so in the context of giving reasons for something, e.g. 安いし、美味しいし、一番好きなお店です ('It's inexpensive, it's tasty too, and so it's my favorite shop.').

じゃあるまいし (N1, You are not ~ so..., it isn't ~ so...): じゃあるまいし is a combination of the まい form that is equivalent to ないだろう and し used to list reasons. Technically, it could be rephrased as じゃないだろうし, or even simply じゃないし for a more direct way of expressing the sentiment of 'You're/It's not (A), so...', e.g. 子どもじゃあるまいし ('You're not a child, so...').

Adjective + て + B (N5, And..., Both and (Conjunctive)): し～し lists multiple reasons, similar to 'because of A, B, and so on' in English. In contrast, Adjective + て + B just connects adjectives. While it can imply the first quality supports the second (e.g. 甘くておいしい = 'sweet and delicious'), it doesn't suggest a broader conclusion. し often implies one, as in 甘いし、おいしいし, meaning 'It's sweet and delicious… (so I like it).'

から (N5, Because, Since): Both し～し and から express reasons, similar to 'so' or 'because' in English. The reason (A) for outcome (B) is always followed by し or から, e.g. (A) し/から (B). The key difference is that から focuses on a single reason, while し～し lists multiple reasons. Even with one reason, し implies other unstated or implied reasons.

ので (N5, Because, So, Since, The reason being): Both し～し and ので express reasons, similar to 'so' or 'because' in English, with the reason coming before し or ので. The main difference is that ので focuses on a single, objective reason, while し～し lists multiple reasons and often has a more personal or subjective feel. Even with one reason, し implies that there are other unstated or implied reasons.

とか～とか (N4, Among other things, For example, Such as): し～し and とか～とか both list things, but with a different nuance. し～し lists reasons or causes, like 'because of things like (A) and (B)'. とか～とか simply lists items without implying they are a cause for something else, i.e. 'things like (A), (B), and so forth'. Also, とか～とか is very casual, while し～し will be found in both speech and writing.

Verb[て] + B (N4, And・and so, Due to, Because of, Since, Conjunctive): Both forms can express reasons, but their usage differs. Verb[て] + B shows that the stated action is the direct reason for what follows, while し～し implies that multiple reasons exist, even if only one is mentioned. For example, 犯人が捕まって安心です ('I'm relieved because the criminal was caught.') vs. 犯人が捕まったし、安心です ('The criminal was caught, and I'm relieved.'), where the し version suggests there may be other factors for the relief.

pattern: でできる・からできる
meaning: Made of, Made from, Produced from, Come from
summary: A grammar point which shows what something is made from, or made with. Brought about with (A).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About でできる・からできる
text: でできる, or からできる are two structures that share very similar meanings. Basically, they both mean '(B) was made from/out of (A)'. These constructions highlight the 'ingredients', or 'materials' that something is/was made out of. Let's look at some examples.

から and で are both case marking particles in this grammar point, and while they express much the same thing when translated into English, there is a slight nuance difference. These differences are as follows:
から - Literally 'prepared from'. Tends to be used more frequently when the material is not obvious at first glance. May also put focus on the ingredients/materials before there was any alteration.
で - Literally 'prepared with'. Tends to be used more frequently when the materials are more obvious.

Despite this, recent generations use で in most situations, regardless of if the material is visible at first glance or not. As a result, でできる and からできる are almost indistinguishable in modern Japanese.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: できている → more specific, できる → more general

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: によって・による (N3, By means of, According to, Depending on, Because of, Due to): でできる・からできる expresses that something is made or composed of a certain ingredient, e.g. この家は木でできている ('This house is made from wood.'). In one usage, によって can be used with verbs like 作る or できる with a similar meaning, e.g., 木によって作られた家 'a house made from wood'. In other uses, によって can also mark the person or method by which something is made, while でできる・からできる cannot.
