chapterTitle: Do it Like this, Did it Like that - Advanced

summary: A word used to show that (B) happens during (A), with (B) being more important.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ながら
text: ながら is another conjunction particle in Japanese that has two primary different meanings. These meanings are as follows:
{同時|どうじ}の{動|うご}き - Two things that are existing/happening simultaneously.
{確定|かくてい}の{逆説|ぎゃくせつ} - Two things that are unexpectedly existing/happening simultaneously.

We will focus purely on the {同時|どうじ}の{動|うご}き meaning in this grammar point. To use ながら, simply add it to the ます stem of verb (A), and then highlight verb (B) as part of the following clause. This may be translated simply as 'while' in English.
Grammatically, the (B) action is considered to be the 'important' action, while the (A) action expresses the timeline within which (B) takes place.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: The subject of A and B must be the same.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: つつある (N2, -ing, Be -ing): つつ (when used by itself) and ながら both attach to verbs to express 'while doing', but つつある differs in usage. Specifically, ながら describes two actions performed simultaneously by the same subject, e.g. 音楽を聴きながら走る 'listen to music while running'. In contrast, つつある refers to a continuing process and is not typically used with physical actions, e.g. 物価が上がりつつある ('Prices are continuing to rise.').

ながらに (N1, While being, Born (with), Traditional (old-fashioned, as it was long ago), As always, While crying or in tears, (Burned) alive): Though these two expressions appear similar, ながらに is much more limited in usage and primarily found in set expressions. ながら can convey a simply 'while doing (A), (B)', e.g. 音楽を聴きながら勉強する ('study while listening to music'), while ながらに (or variant forms like ～ながらの) expresses 'while' or 'although' in terms of states, e.g. 生まれながらに持っている権利 ('a right you have simply by virtue of being born').

がてら (N1, On the occasion of, While … as well, While … (one is) at it, During, Along the way): がてら and ながら both convey performing two actions together, but differ in nuance. がてら expresses a secondary or incidental activity done in addition to a main one, e.g. 犬の散歩がてら、コンビニに寄った ('I stopped at the convenience store while taking my dog for a walk.'). In contrast, ながら typically describes two actions of relative importance performed simultaneously, e.g. テレビを観ながらご飯を食べた ('I watched TV while eating dinner.').

つつ (N2, While, And): ながら and つつ overlap in some uses but not in others. When used to express simultaneous actions, e.g. コーヒーを[飲みながら・飲みつつ]本を読む 'read a book while drinking coffee', they are essentially identical in meaning, with the only difference being that つつ is more formal and literary. There are certain phrases, however, e.g. 生まれながら 'from birth', where only ながら works and つつ cannot be used.

中 (N3, During, While, Throughout, In the process of): ながら attaches to verb stems to express performing one action simultaneously with another, e.g. 音楽を聴きながら勉強する 'listen to music while studying'. In contrast, 中 attaches to nouns to express 'while doing X,' and there is no requirement that what follows must be an action performed by the same subject, e.g. 会議中に電話がかかってきた ('A phone call came in while I was in a meeting.').

かたわら (N1, While, Besides, In addition to): かたわら and ながら are similar in that both can describe performing two tasks at once, but differ in nuance and usage. かたわら follows noun + の or the dictionary form of verbs, and typically implies performing a secondary action alongside a main one. It is often used with habitual actions, such as doing a side job or hobby along with a main job. In contrast, ながら is a more versatile way of expressing two simultaneous actions.

ているところだ (N4, In the process of doing ~ right now/at this moment): ているところだ and ながら both can express ongoing actions or states, but are used differently. ているところだ focuses on being 'in the middle of' something and implies that the speaker is occupied with that action, e.g. ご飯を食べているところだ ('I'm in the middle of eating.'). In contrast, ながら expresses simultaneous actions, e.g. テレビを観ながらご飯を食べる 'watch TV while eating'.

うちに (N3, While, During): ながら attaches to verb stems to express performing one action simultaneously with another, e.g. 音楽を聴きながら走る 'listen to music while running'. In contrast, うちに can follow various words or phrases to express doing something while a certain state or condition persists, e.g. 若いうちにマラソンを走りたい ('I want to run a marathon while I'm young.').

の間に (N3, While, During, Between, Period): ながら attaches to verb stems to express performing one action simultaneously with another, e.g. 音楽を聴きながら走る 'listen to music while running'. In contrast, 間に can follow various words or phrases to express doing something while a certain state or condition persists, e.g. 若い間にマラソンを走りたい ('I want to run a marathon while I'm young.').

ているあいだに (N4, While, During the time that ~): Both forms involve the idea of simultaneous or ongoing actions, but differ in structure and nuance. ているあいだに expresses that something happened during another ongoing action, e.g. 勉強しているあいだに電話がかかってきた ('The phone rang while I was studying.'). ながら shows one subject doing two things at once, e.g. 音楽を聴きながら勉強するのが好き ('I like to study while listening to music.').

ついでに (N3, While you are at it, On the occasion): ながら attaches to verb stems to express performing one action simultaneously with another, e.g. 音楽を聴きながら走る 'listen to music while running'. In contrast, ついでに follows various words or phrases to convey the idea of taking advantage of the opportunity to do another thing at the same time, e.g. 買い物に行くついでに走ってきた ('On the occasion of going shopping, I went for a run.').

とき (N4, When, At the time of): とき expresses the time of an action or event, like the English 'when'. It can be used with nouns as in 雨の時 'when it rains', verbs as in 父が帰ってきた時 'when Dad came home', or adjectives as in 暑い時 'when it's hot'. In contrast, ながら is used when doing something while performing another action. It is used only with verbs, and unlike とき, the subject of both phrases must be the same, e.g. 音楽を聴きながら走る 'listen to music while running'.

chapterTitle: Do it Like this, Did it Like that - Advanced

meaning: Just finished doing, Was just doing
summary: A phrase that expresses the situation or place when an action has just been, or is just about to be completed.
formation: Verb［た］(1) + ところ + です (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About たところだ
text: In a similar way to how ところ (sometimes shortened to とこ) means 'about to (A)', or 'on the verge of (A)', when following the non-past form of a verb, when following the auxiliary verb た, ところ will mean 'just did (A)'.
To use this structure, make the past tense of any verb, and then add ところ.
While this expresses 'just did (A)', ていた may be used when you would like to express that you were 'just doing (A)'.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: When the kanji form of {所|ところ} is used, it is often referring to an actual physical location, rather than a situation/standpoint. However, this is something that native speakers will sometimes mistake. Therefore, seeing the kanji form and the hiragana form are both relatively common.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: ところ can be contracted to とこ in casual conversations. In this use ところ means "stage/level/situation"

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: るところだ (N4, About to, On the verge of): たところだ and るところだ share the same structure, with the tense indicating whether the action is complete or not. るところだ uses the non-past form to mean 'about to do' something, e.g. 晩ご飯を食べるところだ ('I'm just about to eat dinner.'). たところだ uses the past form to mean 'just did' something, e.g. 晩ご飯を食べたところだ ('I just ate dinner.').

たとたんに (N3, The instant or moment, As soon as, Just as): たところだ and たとたんに are similar in that both refer to something that has just happened, but with different usage and nuance. たところだ simply describes the timing, e.g. 家に帰ってきたところだ ('I just got home.'). In contrast, とたんに expresses that something else happened immediately at that moment. For example, 家に帰ってきたとたんに雨が降ってきた ('The instant I got home, it started to rain.').

たて (N3, Freshly ~ed, Just ~ed): たところだ and たて are similar in that both refer to something that has just happened, but they differ in usage and nuance. たところだ uses the past tense of a verb and simply describes the timing, e.g. パンを焼いたところだ ('I just baked some bread.'). In contrast, たて attaches to verb stems and has the nuance of 'freshly done/finished', e.g. 焼きたてのパンが一番美味しい ('Freshly baked bread is the most delicious.').

たばかり (N4, Just did, Something just happened): たところだ and たばかり are similar in that both refer to something that has just happened, but with slightly different nuances. Both 晩ご飯を食べたところです and 晩ご飯を食べたばかりです essentially mean 'I just ate dinner.', but while the version with ところ focuses solely on the timing, the version with ばかり carries a nuance of continued relevance, e.g. implying '...and that's why I'm not hungry now' or '...and so I want to rest before working out'.

chapterTitle: Do it Like this, Did it Like that - Advanced

meaning: In the process of doing ~ right now/at this moment
summary: A phrase that highlights the situation or place in which another action is in the middle of occuring.
formation: Verb［ている］+ ところ + だ
Verb［ている］+ ところ + です (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ているところだ
text: In the previous grammar point, we learned that たところ (or ていたところ) will mean 'just did (A)', or 'was just doing (A)'. ているところ works in a similar way, but expresses that someone is right in the middle of doing something. It is regularly translated as 'doing (A) right now', or 'in the process of (A)'.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: In this use ところ means "stage/level/situation"

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: 途中に・途中で (N2, On the way, Partway, In the middle of): ているところだ conveys that an action is currently in progress, often with a sense of immediate involvement, e.g. 朝ご飯を食べているところだ ('I'm in the middle of eating breakfast.'). In contrast, 途中に・途中で expresses doing something 'on the way' or 'in the middle' of another activity, e.g. 通勤の途中で朝ご飯を食べた ('I ate breakfast on my commute to work.').

ながら (N4, While ~ing, During, As): ているところだ and ながら both can express ongoing actions or states, but are used differently. ているところだ focuses on being 'in the middle of' something and implies that the speaker is occupied with that action, e.g. ご飯を食べているところだ ('I'm in the middle of eating.'). In contrast, ながら expresses simultaneous actions, e.g. テレビを観ながらご飯を食べる 'watch TV while eating'.

中 (N3, During, While, Throughout, In the process of): ているところだ and 中 are similar in that both express being in the middle of doing something, but they function differently grammatically. ているところだ is used with verbs, e.g. 今、食事をしているところです ('Now I'm in the middle of eating.'). In contrast, 中 attaches to the end of nouns and expresses a similar meaning, e.g. 今、食事中です, which means essentially the same thing but is more concise.

うちに (N3, While, During): ているところだ conveys that an action is in progress at that moment, with the nuance that the speaker is occupied with it, e.g. 晩ご飯を食べているところだ ('I'm in the middle of eating dinner.'). In contrast, うちに describes doing an action while a certain state is ongoing, often with the nuance that it's the ideal time, e.g. 熱いうちに食べましょう ('Let's eat it while it's hot.').

～ところに・～ところへ (N2, At the time, When, While, Timing): ているところだ conveys that an action is in progress at that moment, with the nuance that the speaker is occupied with it, e.g. ゲームをしているところだ ('I'm in the middle of playing a video game.'). In contrast, ～ところに・～ところへ describes something happening at the moment of another action, e.g. ゲームをしているところに母に呼ばれた ('I was called by my mother while I was in the middle of playing a game.').

最中に (N3, In the middle of): ているところだ conveys that an action is in progress at that moment, with the nuance that the speaker is busy with it, e.g. 晩ご飯を食べているところだ ('I'm in the middle of eating dinner.'). In contrast, 最中に is used to express that something else happened during that action, e.g. 晩ご飯を食べている最中に電話がかかってきた ('The phone rang while I was right in the middle of eating dinner.').

ている① (N5, Is, Am, Are (~ing)): The ている① form describes an ongoing action or state. ているところだ conveys the same meaning but emphasizes being 'right in the middle' of doing something. For example, 食べている means 'I am eating,' while 食べているところだ emphasizes 'I'm in the middle of eating,' which could explain why you can't talk long on the phone, for example.

ついでに (N3, While you are at it, On the occasion): ているところだ and ついでに both relate to ongoing actions but differ greatly in usage. ているところだ describes an action in progress at that moment, with the nuance that the speaker is currently occupied (e.g. 昼ご飯を食べているところだ = 'I'm in the middle of eating lunch'). In contrast, ついでに describes performing an 'extra' action on the same occasion as another (e.g. 散歩のついでに昼ご飯を買ってきた = 'While on a walk, I bought lunch').

の間に (N3, While, During, Between, Period): ているところだ conveys that an action is in progress at that moment, with the nuance that the speaker is occupied with it, e.g. 映画を観ているところだ ('I'm in the middle of watching a movie.'). In contrast, の間に is used to express that something else happened at some point during the duration of that action, e.g. 映画を観ている間に父が帰ってきました ('My father came home while I was watching a movie.').

とき (N4, When, At the time of): とき expresses the time of an action or event, like 'when' in English. It can be used with nouns as in 雨の時 'when it rains', verbs as in 父が帰ってきた時 'when Dad came home', or adjectives as in 暑い時 'when it's hot'. In contrast, ているところ uses the verb in て-form and emphasizes being in the middle of an action, often with a sense of being busy or focused, e.g. 晩ご飯を食べているところです ('I'm right in the middle of eating dinner.').

ているあいだに (N4, While, During the time that ~): Both patterns express ongoing actions but differ in focus. ているところだ means being in the middle of something, often with a sense of being occupied. For example, 勉強をしているところだ ('I'm in the middle of studying.').ているあいだに highlights something that happens during another action, e.g. 勉強しているあいだに電話がかかってきた ('The phone rang while I was studying.').

chapterTitle: Do it Like this, Did it Like that - Advanced

summary: An expression that presents two choices, and then asks the speaker to choose one.
formation: Noun (A) + と + Noun (B) + （と） + どちら(1) + が
Verb1 + こと(2) + と + Verb2 + こと(2) + （と） + どちら(1) + が
(1) どちらのほう、どっち、どっちのほう

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About と～と、どちらが
text: と～と、どちらが is an expression in Japanese that is made from the following parts:
と - The particle (x2) in its meaning of 'and'.
どちら - The polite speech form of {誰|だれ} 'who', and a slightly newer form of どっち that basically means 'which'.
が - The case marking particle.
This structure is used when the speaker is asking a question about whether someone will choose (A) or (B). It is only used when there are no more than two possible choices.

As can be seen above, verbs may be used as part of this structure if they are nominalized with こと, or の. Additionally, the polite form does not specifically need to be used, and どっち may be used instead.
The second と itself is quite often omitted, as どちら (or どっち) implies that both (A) and (B) are part of the same structure.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: のなかで～がいちばん～ (N5, Out of ~, ~ is the best/most ~): Both of these patterns can be used to express preferences or comparisons. The main difference is that the と～と、どちらが pattern is used when asking about or expressing a choice between two options, while のなかで～がいちばん～ involves comparing a group of three or more options.

chapterTitle: Do it Like this, Did it Like that - Advanced

meaning: To try to, To make sure to, To endeavor to
summary: A phrase that expresses attempting to do something in the manner of (A).
formation: Verb［る］(1) + ように + する
Verb［る］(1) + ように + します (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ようにする
text: (A) ようにする is an expression in Japanese which combines the auxiliary verb ようだ, with する (indicating that you will 'try' to do something). As ようだ is being linked to the verb する, it will take on its adverbial form, ように. This structure emphasizes that the (A) action (always a verb) is something that the speaker is going out of their way to do, and implies effort.
Naturally, this structure may also be used with a negative verb, to imply that (A) being done is something that is actively being avoided. This translates as 'to make sure not to do (A)'.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: Because ようだ comes from the kanji {様|よう} 'manner', it carries the nuance that the 'way' that someone is doing (A) is specifically in a way that has success as the goal. Literally it translates quite closely to 'to do (A) in the manner of getting it done', and therefore just strengthens the (A) action, by using 'to do' twice.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Specifies end goals

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ように (N4, So that, In order to, In such a way that): The core meaning of ように is 'in such a way'. It's used to show an action done to achieve a result, e.g. 勉強できるように新しい本を買った ('I bought a new book so I can study.'). ようにする builds on this to express making a habit or effort, like 毎日、日本語を勉強するようにしている ('I try to study / make a habit of studying Japanese every day.').

Verb[volitional]とする (N3, Try to, Attempt to, To be about to): ようにする (literally, 'do things in such a way as to X') expresses taking care to perform a certain action and often indicates a habitual effort. In contrast, Verb[volitional] + とする implies a one-time attempt to do something, often implying the attempt may not succeed. For example, 毎朝走るようにしている ('I'm making a habit of running every morning.') vs. １０キロ走ろうとしたけど ('I tried to run 10k, but...' implying 'but I couldn't finish', etc.).

〜ようとしない (N3, Not willing to, Not make an effort to, To not attempt or try to, Volitional + としない): ようにする (literally, 'do things in such a way as to X') can express the idea of taking care to perform a certain action and often describes intentions or habits. 〜ようとしない conveys the opposite, not making an effort to do something. For example, 毎日野菜を食べるようにしている ('I'm making a habit of eating vegetables every day.') vs. うちの子どもは野菜を食べようとしない ('My child doesn't even try to eat vegetables.').

ようになる (N4, To reach the point that, To come to be that, To turn into): Both ようになる and ようにする express something becoming a certain way, but differ in nuance. ようになる describes a situation becoming that way, e.g. 行けるようになった ('I became able to go.', implying external or internal factors allowed it). ようにする focuses on someone actively making it possible, e.g. 行けるようにする ('I'll make sure I can go.').

ように～てほしい (N4, Want ~ to ~ like ~, Want ~ to be able to ~, Want ~ to ~ in the way of ~): ようにする means 'to make an effort to ensure something happens a certain way' and expresses intention or habit. For example, 遅れないようにする ('I'll try not to be late.'). In contrast, ように～てほしい expresses a desire for someone else to behave a certain way. For example, 遅れないようにしてほしい ('I want you to make an effort not to be late.').

ことにする (N3, To decide on, Have decided to): ことにする and ようにする are closely related but have different nuances. ことにする is used to express a resolution or decision, e.g. 来年、マラソンを走ることにした ('I decided to run a marathon next year.'). In contrast, ようにする expresses making an effort to carry out an action and is often used for ongoing intentions or habits, e.g. 毎朝走るようにしている ('I'm trying to run every morning.').

てみる (N4, To try to): Both can be translated in English as 'try (doing)', but differ in nuance. ようにする means to make an effort or form a habit, e.g. 毎朝走るようにしている ('I try to run every morning.') has the nuance of making a point of doing so. In contrast, てみる means to try something out to see the result, e.g. 走ってみた ('I tried running.'), which has the nuance of doing so to see what it was like.

～にする・～くする (N4, Adjective + する, To make something/someone (more)): ～にする・～くする and ようにする both mean making something a certain way, but differ in usage. ～にする・～くする is used with nouns and adjectives to mean ‘make into (A)’, e.g. 綺麗にする ‘make clean’ and 甘くする ‘make sweet’. ようにする is used with verbs and conveys the idea of making sure to do something, e.g. 走るようにする ‘make sure to (or make an effort to) run’.

chapterTitle: Do it Like this, Did it Like that - Advanced

summary: A formal, hypothetical way to say that something must be done.
formation: Verb［ない］ + なければ + いけない
Verb［ない］ + なきゃ + いけない
Verb［ない］ + なければ + いけません (polite)
Verb［ない］ + なきゃ + いけません (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About なければいけない
text: Like なくてはいけない, なければいけない is a structure that implies that something 'must be done'. However, it is important to remember that this is actually a double negative, and therefore means 'If (A) is not done, it cannot go', or more simply '(A) cannot not be done'.
To make this construction, the auxiliary verb ない will need to be conjugated with ば, creating なければ (if not). After this, いけない (to not be able to go) will be added to the end.
As learned in the なきゃ lesson, なければ may be shortened to なきゃ. This structure is frequently used either with or without the added いけない.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: While いけない (to not be able to go) and ならない (to not become) are quite similar, ならない will rarely be used outside of formal situations, or in writing. Due to this, いけない will be heard much more frequently in speech (when it is not omitted).

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Verb[ない]+と+いけない/ならない is also used to express duty or necessity.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: なければならない (N4, Must do, Have to do): These two patterns both express obligation (i.e. 'must do' or 'have to do'). For example, 行かなければならない and 行かなければいけない both express an obligation to go, but the ならない version is slightly more formal and found more often in writing. In everyday conversation, contractions like なきゃ (e.g. 行かなきゃ) are more common.

べきではない (N3, Should not, Must not, Ought not to): These express contrasting meanings: なければいけない 'must' vs. べきではない 'should not'. The former implies necessity or rule, while the latter carries a tone of moral or social advice, e.g. 行かなければいけない ('You must go.') vs. 行くべきではない ('You shouldn't go.').

なくてはいけない (N5, Must do, Have to do): なくてはいけない and なければいけない express obligation or necessity, saying something 'must' or 'needs to' be done. They are equivalent in meaning, with the only difference being that the なければ version is slightly more formal, though the difference is not highly significant. Note that in casual speech, these forms are often shortened to なくちゃ and なきゃ, respectively.

ねばならない (N2, Must, Have to, Should): Both express obligation ('must do' or 'have to do') with a nuance of necessity. 行かねばならない and 行かなければいけない both express an obligation to go, and while なければいけない is already formal, ねばならない is even more formal and old-fashioned, often seen in academic or historical contexts. In daily speech, the contracted form なきゃ is more common than either.

てはならない (N2, Must not, Cannot, Should not): These are opposites: なければいけない expresses obligation (i.e. 'must'), while てはならない means prohibition (i.e. 'must not'). For example, 行かなければいけない ('You must go.') vs. 行ってはならない ('You must not go.'). Both are formal and common in writing or structured speech, while in conversation casual forms like なきゃ and ちゃ are more common.

なくてはならない (N5, Must do, Have to do): なくてはならない and なければいけない express obligation, meaning something 'must' or 'needs' to be done. The two forms are equivalent. The level of formality is similar, with なければ being slightly more formal than なくては and ならない being slightly more formal than いけない. The parts are interchangeable, and in casual speech, these forms are often shortened to なくちゃ and なきゃ, respectively.

なくちゃ・なきゃ (N5, Must do, Have to do): Both なくちゃ・なきゃ and なければいけない express obligation or necessity, meaning something 'must' or 'needs to' be done. なければいけない is more formal and often appears in writing or official contexts, while なくちゃ・なきゃ are casual contractions (of なくては and なければ) used in everyday speech with friends and family.

てはいけない (N5, Must not, May not): てはいけない is used to express prohibition, meaning that something 'must not' or 'cannot' be done. In contrast, なければいけない expresses obligation, something 'must' be done. These forms can be tricky for learners, as なければいけない is negative in form but means 'must' (literally, 'it's not good if you don't'), while てはいけない is affirmative in form but means 'must not' (literally, 'it's not good if you do').

ないと (N4, Must, Have to): These expressions mean the same thing but differ in formality. ないと is used casually in speech, as in もう行かないと ('I need to go soon.'). なければいけない is more polite and suitable for formal contexts. Both mean 'I must (A).' or 'I have to (A).'.

chapterTitle: Do it Like this, Did it Like that - Advanced

summary: A very formal, hypothetical way to say that something must be done, that is usually only written.
formation: Verb［ない］ + なければ + ならない
Verb［ない］ + なきゃ + ならない
Verb［ない］ + なければ + なりません (polite)
Verb［ない］ + なきゃ + なりません (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About なければならない
text: Like なければいけない, なければならない is a structure that implies that something 'must be done'. However, it is important to remember that this is actually a double negative, and therefore means 'If (A) is not done, it cannot become', or more simply '(A) cannot not be done'.
To make this construction, the auxiliary verb ない will need to be conjugated with ば, creating なければ (if not). After this, ならない (to not become) will be added to the end.
As we learned in the なきゃ lesson, なければ may be shortened to なきゃ. This structure is frequently used, either with or without the added ならない.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: While いけない (to not be able to go) and ならない (to not become) are quite similar, ならない will rarely be used outside of formal situations, or in writing. Due to this, いけない will be heard much more frequently in speech (when it is not omitted).

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Verb[ない]+と+いけない/ならない is also used to express duty or necessity.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ないと (N4, Must, Have to): Both express obligation, but differ in tone. ないと is casual and often shortened in speech, as in 行かないと ('I've got to go.'). なければならない is more formal, used in writing or polite conversation. Both convey the idea of needing to do something.

なければいけない (N4, Must do, Have to do): These two patterns both express obligation (i.e. 'must do' or 'have to do'). For example, 行かなければならない and 行かなければいけない both express an obligation to go, but the ならない version is slightly more formal and found more often in writing. In everyday conversation, contractions like なきゃ (e.g. 行かなきゃ) are more common.

なくてはならない (N5, Must do, Have to do): なくてはならない and なければならない both express obligation or necessity, meaning something 'must' or 'needs' to be done. They are equivalent in meaning, but なければならない is slightly more formal and common in written rules or official language. In casual speech, these forms are often shortened to なくちゃ and なきゃ, respectively.

なくちゃ・なきゃ (N5, Must do, Have to do): Both なくちゃ・なきゃ and なければならない express obligation or necessity, meaning something 'must' or 'needs to' be done. なければならない is more formal and commonly found in writing or official statements. In contrast, なくちゃ・なきゃ are casual contractions (of なくては and なければ) used in everyday speech with friends and family.

ねばならない (N2, Must, Have to, Should): Both express obligation with a nuance of rule or necessity, e.g. 行かねばならない and 行かなければならない both mean 'must go'. なければならない is formal; ねばならない is even more formal and often appears in academic or historical texts. In conversation, contractions like なきゃ are more common.

てはいけない (N5, Must not, May not): てはいけない is used to express prohibition, meaning that something 'must not' or 'cannot' be done. なければならない expresses the opposite meaning, i.e., that something 'must' be done. These forms can be tricky for learners, as なければならない appears negative but means 'must' (literally, 'it's not good if you don't'), while てはいけない appears affirmative but means 'must not' (literally, 'it's not good if you do'). (いけない and ならない themselves are essentially synonymous, though ならない is somewhat more formal/written-style.)

なくてはいけない (N5, Must do, Have to do): なくてはいけない and なければいけない express obligation or necessity, saying something 'must' or 'needs to' be done. They are equivalent in meaning, but the なければならない version is slightly more formal, and thus more likely to be found in written rules, etc. Note that in casual speech, these forms are often shortened to なくちゃ and なきゃ, respectively.

べきではない (N3, Should not, Must not, Ought not to): These are opposites: なければならない 'must' vs. べきではない 'should not'. The former suggests a rule or necessity; the latter implies social or moral advice, e.g. 行かなければならない ('You must go.') as compared to 行くべきではない ('You ought not to / shouldn't go.').

てはならない (N2, Must not, Cannot, Should not): These express opposites: なければならない 'must' vs. てはならない 'must not'. For example, 行かなければならない 'must go' is the opposite of 行ってはならない 'must not go'. Both are formal and typically used in writing or structured speech. Casual speech favors shorter forms like なきゃ and ちゃ.

ことだ (N3, Should, Ought): ことだ is used for light advice ('should' or 'ought to'), e.g. 毎日早起きすることだ ('You should get up early every day.'). なければならない expresses stronger obligation, like 'must' or 'have to', often implying consequences. ７時に起きなければならない ('You must get up at 7.').

chapterTitle: Do it Like this, Did it Like that - Advanced

summary: A phrase that highlights (A) as an action that is being continued, or occuring over and over.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About つづける
text: By attaching the verb {続|つづ}ける 'to continue' to the conjunctive form of another verb, we will be able to express that '(A) is continuing'. Let's have a look at a few examples of this structure.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: てくる (N4, To come to, To become, To continue, To be starting to, Has been ~ing): Both つづける and てくる can show the progression of an action over time. つづける attaches to the verb stem and focuses on the continuation of the action itself. てくる uses the て-form and emphasizes that the action started in the past and has continued up to the present.

ばかりだ (N3, (Only) continue to, Keep on -ing, More and more): つづける and ばかりだ both show continuation, but with different nuances. つづける attaches to verb stems and shows simple ongoing action, e.g. 減り続けている 'is continuing to decrease'. ばかりだ adds the sense of 'more and more,' often negatively, e.g. 減るばかりだ 'keeps on decreasing'.

ている① (N5, Is, Am, Are (~ing)): ている is a common structure in Japanese to express an ongoing action or state. つづける attached to the verb stem expresses a similar meaning, but with a greater emphasis on the idea of continuation. For example, 増えている means that something is increasing or has increased, while 増えつづけている carries the additional nuance that it is continuing to increase.

一方だ (N3, More and more, Continue to, Keep on, -er and -er): つづける and 一方だ both indicate continuation but differ in tone. つづける means a simple ongoing action, e.g. 減り続けている 'is still decreasing'. 一方だ follows dictionary-form verbs and adds a sense of progression in one direction, often negatively, e.g., 減る一方だ 'is getting worse and worse'.

ている② (N5, State of being, Has (have) done): ている expresses an ongoing action or state. つづける attached to the verb stem expresses a similar meaning, but with a greater emphasis on the idea of continuation. For example, 増えている means that something is increasing or has increased, while 増えつづけている carries the additional nuance that it is continuing to increase.

なおす (N4, To do over, To redo): なおす can be attached to the stem of other verbs to express the idea of 're-doing' or doing something over. つづける can be attached to verb stems in the same way, but expresses the meaning of 'continuing' to do something. For example, やりなおす means 'to do over', while やりつづける means 'to keep doing'.

chapterTitle: Do it Like this, Did it Like that - Advanced

meaning: To tell, request, or order to do (in such a way)
summary: A slightly formal way to state that something is said, requested, or ordered in the manner of (A).
formation: Verb + ように + 言（い）う(1)
Verb + ように + 言（い）います (polite)
(1) 頼たのみます、命めいじます (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ようにいう
text: ようにいう is an expression which combines the auxiliary verb ようだ, with the う-Verb {言|い}う. This indicates that something is being said in a way that instigates (A). As ようだ is being linked to the verb {言|い}う, it will take on its adverbial form, ように.

As ようにいう means 'to be said in the way of (A) being done', it is regularly translated as 'to tell', 'to request', or 'to order'. In the case of requesting, {頼|たの}む may substitute for {言|い}う. For ordering, {命|めい}じる may substitute for it instead.
{言|い}う itself is the most versatile of these three verbs, as it may imply 'to order', or 'to request'. This will depend on the tone of the speaker/overall context of the request/order.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ように (N4, So that, In order to, In such a way that): The core meaning of ように is 'in such a way.' It shows doing something to achieve a result, e.g. 間に合うように早めに出かけた ('I left early so I could be on time.'). ようにいう builds on this and means 'to instruct someone to do something', e.g. 間に合うように言っておいた ('I told them to be on time.').

ように～てほしい (N4, Want ~ to ~ like ~, Want ~ to be able to ~, Want ~ to ~ in the way of ~): ようにいう means 'to tell or ask someone to do something.' It is often used for indirect or general requests. For example, 来るようにいう 'tell (someone) to come'. When paired with てほしい, it shows a desire for someone else to make the request. For example, 来るようにいってほしい ('I want you to tell him/her/them to come.').

chapterTitle: Do it Like this, Did it Like that - Advanced

summary: An expression that highlights a specific plan that someone has made.
formation: Noun + の + 予定 + だ
Noun + の + 予定 + です (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About よていだ
text: {予定|よてい}だ is an expression that functions very similarly to つもりだ 'to intend to do'. The primary difference being that {予定|よてい} is a 'plan', rather than an 'intention'. Due to this, {予定|よてい} is used far more frequently for things that you have formal plans to do (like meeting a friend for lunch).
To use {予定|よてい}, just attach it to the non-past form of a verb, or to a noun (after inserting の).

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: つもりで (N2, With the intention of doing, Instead of..., Act as if or pretend, Believing that..., Thinking that...): 予定だ expresses a concrete future plan, e.g. 来年日本に行く予定だ ('I plan to go to Japan next year.'). つもり is often less concrete and, in つもりで form, connects actions with intention, e.g. 遊ぶつもりで行った 'went with the intention of having fun'. It can also mean 'believing (A)' as in 俳優になったつもりで話す 'speak as if you were (lit. with the belief that you had become) an actor'.

つもりだ (N5, To plan to, To intend to): Both つもりだ and よていだ express future intentions or plans, but with different nuances. つもりだ emphasizes personal intent or decision, such as 'I intend to' or 'I hope to,' without necessarily implying a set timeframe. よていだ focuses more on planning or scheduling, suggesting that the action is expected to happen at a specific time.

chapterTitle: Do it Like this, Did it Like that - Advanced

meaning: Pray that/for, Hope that/for, Keep fingers crossed that
summary: A structure indicating that one hopes that (A) will happen, so is praying in that manner.
formation: Verb［る］ + ように + 祈（いの）る
Verb［ない］ + ように + 祈（いの）る
Verb［る］ + ように + 祈（いの）ります (polite)
Verb［ない］ + ように + 祈（いの）ります (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ようにいのる
text: As we have seen several times now, the auxiliary verb ようだ is frequently used with verbs, to express that the 'completion' of an action is the specific goal/wish of the speaker. It does this implicitly through the meaning of the kanji {様|よう} 'manner of doing'.

ようにいのる (or {祈|いの}る in its kanji form) is no different, and will imply that the speaker is praying for (A) to be done/completed. This comes from the meaning of the う-Verb {祈|いの}る itself, which can be translated as 'to pray', or 'to beg'. Despite being able to be used when actually praying, this grammar point is used most often to express a 'hope'.
In a similar way to other ように structures, ないように may also be used with {祈|いの}る, to show that someone is praying for something 'not' to happen.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ように (N4, So that, In order to, In such a way that): The core meaning of ように is 'in such a way'. In general usage, this conveys performing a certain action in order to achieve a stated result, e.g. 合格できるように毎日勉強した ('I studied every day so I could pass.'). ようにいのる (often written in kanji as 祈る 'pray') is one form of this and expresses a wish or hope, e.g. 合格できるように祈っているよ ('I'm hoping/praying you'll pass.').

chapterTitle: Do it Like this, Did it Like that - Advanced

summary: A semi-formal construction that subjectively expresses when something has just happened.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About たばかり
text: As an adverbial particle, ばかり usually has one of three basic meanings.
Degree: {程度|ていど} - Highlights the 'rough' amount/degree of something (similar to くらい).
Limit: {限定|げんてい} - Highlights the 'limit' of something (similar to だけ).
Completion: {完了|かんりょう} - Highlights the 'end', or 'completion' of something.

In this lesson, we will focus primarily on the completion meaning. When connecting ばかり to the past form of a verb (using た), it will imply that a specific action has 'just finished', 'just stopped', or 'just been completed'.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: Despite having three different meanings, ばかり can be thought of as always highlighting how close one thing is to another.
Degree: {程度|ていど} - Highlights (A)'s degree of closeness (to a stated amount).
Limit: {限定|げんてい} - Highlights (A)'s degree of closeness (to a description).
Completion: {完了|かんりょう} - Highlights (A)'s degree of closeness (to a point in time).

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: ばっかり, ばっか, ばかし, and ばっかし are all fairly common casual variations of ばかり

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: たところだ (N4, Just finished doing, Was just doing): たところだ and たばかり are similar in that both refer to something that has just happened, but with slightly different nuances. Both 晩ご飯を食べたところです and 晩ご飯を食べたばかりです essentially mean 'I just ate dinner.', but while the version with ところ focuses solely on the timing, the version with ばかり carries a nuance of continued relevance, e.g. implying '...and that's why I'm not hungry now' or '...and so I want to rest before working out'.

たとたんに (N3, The instant or moment, As soon as, Just as): Both refer to something that just happened, but differ in nuance. たばかり describes the state after completion, e.g. 帰ってきたばかり 'just got home'. とたんに means something happened the moment another did, e.g. 帰ってきたとたんに雨が降った ('The moment I got home, it started to rain.').

たて (N3, Freshly ~ed, Just ~ed): Both express recency but differ in usage. たばかり follows た-form verbs to show something just happened, e.g. 焼いたばかり 'just baked'. たて attaches to stems and means 'freshly done', e.g. 焼きたてのパン 'freshly-baked bread'.

chapterTitle: Do it Like this, Did it Like that - Advanced

meaning: -ification, -ization, To make something, To change, To become, Transform into
summary: A suffix showing that something will change or transform into (A). Similar to (A)ification, or (A)ization in English.
formation: Noun + 化（か） + する(1) + Noun

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 化する
text: {化|か} by itself is a suffix in Japanese which means 'to change', or 'to transform'. When paired with する, it means 'to transform into (A)', where (A) is the noun that {化|か} is connected to. This structure is regularly translated as '~ification', or '~ization', and similar suffixes in English.
When the する is connected to another noun, it may occasionally appear as した, or with の attached to the end of it. This will indicate that there is a relationship between (B) and (A).
However, in formal/scientific writing, the する (and の) may sometimes be dropped.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ～になる・～くなる (N5, To become (Adjective)): 化する and ～になる・～くなる both express change. 化する attaches to nouns and means '~ify' or '~ize', e.g. データ化する 'to digitize' (literally, 'to turn into data'). ～になる and ～くなる are more general-purpose ways to express becoming something, e.g. 綺麗になる 'become clean' or 白くなる 'to become white'.

chapterTitle: Do it Like this, Did it Like that - Advanced

summary: A verb form which indicates either a direct order, or a strong challenge.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 命令形
text: In Japanese, there are numerous ways to express an order, command, or instruction. The most direct, abrasive, and therefore least used method is called the imperative form, which happens to be one of the basic conjugations of verbs.

Without particles following it, the imperative form is fairly uncommon in daily life, but will often be seen on traffic signs, posters, or banners. In addition, it can also be heard shouted at demonstrations, when cheering at sports events, or in urgent situations, such as an officer yelling at a suspect to stop.

Verbs are conjugated into the imperative form in the following way. For う-Verbs, simply replace the last kana of any verb with the equivalent え sound kana from the same row. For る-Verbs, replace る with either ろ or よ.

The imperative form may sometimes be softened with the particle よ. This is a pattern which is mostly used by men that are familiar with each other, in order to offer advice or encouragement. Women tend to use the more polite て-form of verbs instead.
Any verb except for ある and いる may be conjugated to the imperative form, due to their meanings being based on existence and nothing more.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: Originally, よ was used instead of ろ with る-Verbs. Despite this, with time it has been gradually losing popularity, and nowadays it is considered to be a more formal, written variant.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Avoid using this conjugation since it might sound rude and threatening.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: たらどう (N4, Why don't you...?, What if you did...?): The imperative or command form (命令形) is used for blunt orders, e.g. 止まれ ('Stop!'), which can be harsh. In contrast, たらどう is a soft suggestion, similar to 'Why don't you (A)?' in English, e.g. 行ってみたらどう？ ('Why don't you try going?'). It gives the listener more freedom and therefore sounds more gentle.

ことだ (N3, Should, Ought): The imperative or command form (命令形) gives direct, blunt commands, e.g. 止まれ ('Stop!'). It can sound harsh unless softened with particles like よ, e.g. 頑張れよ ('Try harder, okay?'). In contrast, ことだ offers soft advice, e.g. 早起きすることだ ('You should wake up early.'), and is often used when giving recommendations or suggestions.

Verb[て] (N4, Please do for me (Casual request)): The imperative or command form (命令形) gives blunt commands, e.g. 止まれ ('Stop!'), often sounding forceful. Verb[て] form is softer and used for casual requests, e.g. 見て 'Look!'. Adding よ or ね softens it further, e.g. 見てね ('Take a look, okay?'), which is commonly done in friendly, everyday speech.

なさい (N4, Command to do): The imperative or command form (命令形) gives strong, direct commands, e.g. 食べろ ('Eat!'). On its own, it sounds harsh, so it's often softened. なさい is a more polite alternative, often used by parents or teachers toward children, e.g. 野菜を食べなさい ('Eat your vegetables!'). Both forms command action but differ in tone.

chapterTitle: Do it Like this, Did it Like that - Advanced

meaning: So that, In order to, In such a way that
summary: A structure implying that (A) is done in a manner which will enable success.
formation: Verb［できる］(3) + ように + Phrase

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ように
text: When partnered with verbs in the potential form, or in the negative form, the auxiliary verb ようだ (in its adverbial form ように) implies that the speaker has a lack of direct control over an outcome, and therefore is 'trying to do (B) in the manner of (A)', but cannot guarantee the result. This grammar point is usually translated as 'to do (A) in such a way that will enable (B)', or 'in order to allow (B)'.
To use ように in this way, simply add it to the non-past form of any verb in its negative, potential, or standard conjugation.
As mentioned in our lesson about potential verbs, する does not actually have a potential form, and therefore できる will be used instead.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ようになる (N4, To reach the point that, To come to be that, To turn into): ように means 'in such a way' and expresses doing something to achieve a certain result, e.g. 忘れないようにメモした ('I took a memo so I wouldn't forget.'). ようになる, on the other hand, describes a situation changing to a certain state, without specifying the cause, e.g. 話せるようになった ('I became able to speak.').

ようにする (N4, To try to, To make sure to, To endeavor to): The core meaning of ように is 'in such a way'. It's used to show an action done to achieve a result, e.g. 勉強できるように新しい本を買った ('I bought a new book so I can study.'). ようにする builds on this to express making a habit or effort, like 毎日、日本語を勉強するようにしている ('I try to study / make a habit of studying Japanese every day.').

れる・られる + ままに (N1, Do as (one is told or ordered…), In accordance with, In compliance with, Just like): Both structures express doing something in a certain way. れる・られる + ままに is used when someone acts as they're told, e.g. 言われるがままに 'just as told'. ように can express acting of one's own accord, e.g. 間に合うように早めに出た ('I left early so I could make it on time.').

ようにいう (N4, To tell, request, or order to do (in such a way)): The core meaning of ように is 'in such a way.' It shows doing something to achieve a result, e.g. 間に合うように早めに出かけた ('I left early so I could be on time.'). ようにいう builds on this and means 'to instruct someone to do something', e.g. 間に合うように言っておいた ('I told them to be on time.').

ようにいのる (N4, Pray that/for, Hope that/for, Keep fingers crossed that): The core meaning of ように is 'in such a way'. In general usage, this conveys performing a certain action in order to achieve a stated result, e.g. 合格できるように毎日勉強した ('I studied every day so I could pass.'). ようにいのる (often written in kanji as 祈る 'pray') is one form of this and expresses a wish or hope, e.g. 合格できるように祈っているよ ('I'm hoping/praying you'll pass.').

如何 (N1, Depending on): 如何 (read as いかん) is a formal term meaning 'how' or 'in what way', used mainly in formal or academic writing. It appears after nouns, often in the pattern 如何によって ('depending on'). 状況の如何で決まる = 'It will be decided depending on the situation.' ように is a more common, casual form, e.g. 忘れないようにメモした ('I took a memo so I wouldn't forget.').

ように～てほしい (N4, Want ~ to ~ like ~, Want ~ to be able to ~, Want ~ to ~ in the way of ~): The core meaning of ように is 'so that' or 'in order to', and it is commonly used in patterns like ようにする 'make an effort to (A)' or ようにいう 'ask someone to (A)'. When used together with the ～てほしい form, it expresses wanting someone else to do the action. For example, 忘れないようにする ('I'll try not to forget.') vs. 忘れないようにしてほしい ('I want you to try not to forget.').

summary: A semi-polite way to express uncertainty, that is primarily used only by women.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About かしら
text: Originally, かしら was an abbreviation of か{知|し}らぬ, or かしらん, which are both ways of expressing 'whether it's (A), I don't know'. These days, かしら is a standalone sentence ending particle that works in a similar way to かも, by expressing the speaker's uncertainty about the previous statement.
かしら may be attached to the end of almost any phrase that the speaker wants to express doubt about.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Although the original forms of か{知|し}らぬ, or かしらん were useable by anybody, かしら is thought to be very feminine in modern Japanese, and therefore is not often used by men.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ～のだろうか (N4, I wonder...): Both express uncertainty or internal questioning, like 'I wonder'. ～のだろうか (or the polite ～のでしょうか) is neutral and used by all genders. かしら has a softer, feminine tone and is rarely used by men. The explanatory の adds a nuance of seeking an answer, which かしら does not.

かな (N4, I wonder): Both かな and かしら can express doubt, similar to the English 'I wonder if (A)'. Comparing the two, かな is the more common and casual expression, used by both genders in a wide variety of contexts and settings. In contrast, かしら has a softer tone that can come off as more polite and feminine.

meaning: typical of, -ish・like, appropriate for, becoming of, befitting
summary: A word showing that (A) is expressing typical features that would usually be expected of itself, or typical of itself.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About らしい ②
text: In our first らしい lesson, we discussed the auxiliary verb use of らしい. In this lesson we will focus on the {形容詞|けいようし}の{一部|いちぶ} (auxiliary adjective) usage. An auxiliary adjective is a type of adjective that must be attached to another word for it to have any meaning.

To use らしい in this way, it must be attached to the end of a noun, and will imply that something is 'typical of (A)', where (A) is the noun that comes before it. As this らしい behaves like an い-Adjective, it may also be conjugated to らしく, before a (B) phrase will explain more about 'what' is/was typical of (A).

The primary use of this らしい is to express that (A) has some feature or trait that is expected of itself. It can be used for people, 'studying all night is so typical of Tanaka', or it can be used for things like seasons 'this heat is so typical of the Japanese Summer'. Other common translations are 'to be befitting of (A)', or 'to be appropriate for (A)'.
However, it may also be used negatively, to show that something is (often surprisingly) 'uncharacteristic of (A)'.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: Noun＋型 (N3, Model, Type, Pattern, Kind, Shape, Size(d)): Both describe attributes, but with different focuses. 型 emphasizes form or category, e.g. 家族型の会社 ('A family-style company') らしい expresses what seems typical or characteristic of something, often based on impression, e.g. 家族らしい雰囲気 ('A family-like atmosphere', warm and loving, as one might expect from a family)

ならでは (N1, Unique to, Only, Impossible if not, Expected only of): These expressions can be used in similar cases to describe something that is characteristic of a certain person, place, situation, etc., but with slightly different nuances. ならでは implies uniqueness, e.g. 彼ならではの意見 'an opinion only he would have'. In contrast, らしい② suggests something is typical/representative of that thing, but not necessarily unique, e.g. 彼らしい意見 'an opinion you'd expect from him'.

らしい ① (N4, Seems like, Apparently, I heard): らしい has two related but distinct functions. らしい ① conveys information heard from a third-party source with a nuance that the speaker believes it to be true, e.g. 雨が降るらしい ('Apparently, it's going to rain.'). らしい ② serves as an adjective, describing a typical characteristic, e.g. 春らしい天気 'spring-like weather'.

風 (N4, -style, Way, Fashion): 風 and らしい② both express resemblance but differ in nuance. 風 means something has the 'air' or appearance of a type, e.g. 日本風建築 'Japanese-style architecture'. らしい② implies it embodies the ideal of that category, e.g. 日本らしい建築 implies 'quintessential Japanese architecture'.

的 (N3, ~ly・~like・~al, Typical): 的 and らしい both describe being 'like' something, but differ in usage and nuance. 的 is highly versatile, converting nouns into な-Adjectives, e.g. 感情的な 'emotional' or 定期的に 'regularly'. In contrast, らしい expresses embodying the ideal or typical qualities of something, e.g. 春らしい天気 'spring-like weather'.

めく・めいた (N1, Like, To show signs of, To have the appearance of, To come to a (state) similar to, Somewhat, An air of, Feels almost like): Both describe something becoming like something else, but the nuance is different. めく・めいた means ‘showing signs of’ and refers to a noticeable change in atmosphere or appearance, without judging whether it is typical, as in 秋めいてきた ('It has started to feel autumn-like.'). らしい②, especially in らしくなってきた, focuses on becoming more typical or expected for that thing, emphasizing how well it matches the usual image, as in 秋らしくなってきた ('It has started to feel properly autumn-like.').

っぽい (N3, -ish, -like, Characteristic of, Typical of, Tendency to): っぽい and らしい② both express resemblance. っぽい is casual, like '-ish' in English, e.g. 子どもっぽい 'childish' (usually with a negative nuance). らしい② implies that someone or something embodies expected traits, e.g. 男らしい 'manly' with a nuance of fulfilling cultural expectations of what a man should be.

～(の)姿 (N3, Figure, Shape, Appearance, Looks, Wearing, Dressed in, Presence): Both relate to appearance, but with quite different nuances. ～(の)姿 refers to someone's outward form, posture, or visual state, e.g. 彼女の頑張っている姿 ('The sight/figure of her working hard'). In contrast, ～らしい② is used to describe traits or appearances typical of a category or role, e.g. 男らしい ('Manly'). While 姿 describes the appearance or form itself, ～らしい② is about how that form embodies social or cultural norms.

なりに (N1, In one's own way, Of someone's own, Do one's best in one's own way, As much as one can): Both なりに and らしい② can connect to the idea of 'being appropriate to someone' but in different ways. なりに means “in one’s own way/to the extent of one’s ability or circumstances,” and it evaluates an action or result as the best (or at least reasonable) within those limits, as in 自分なりに考えた (‘I thought as best I could.'), and can be used in a self-deprecating sense. らしい② means 'typical' or 'true to (someone or something)', focusing on whether a behavior or style fits a person’s usual character, not on limits or 'doing one’s best', as in 彼らしくやった ('He did it how you'd expect from him.')

べくして (N1, As expected, Meant to, Supposed to, Destined to, Sure to): Both relate actions to what is natural or fitting, but with different nuance. らしく means 'in a way typical of' or 'true to,' judging whether behavior matches a person’s character or role, as in 彼は彼らしく行動した ('He acted in a way true to himself.'). べくして does not evaluate character but inevitability, stating that an outcome was the natural result of circumstances or causes, as in 事故は起こるべくして起こった ('The accident happened as was inevitable.').

みたいに・みたいな (N4, Like, Similar to, Resembling): みたいに・みたいな and らしい② both express likeness but differ in nuance. みたい suggests resemblance despite being different, e.g. 春みたいな天気 ('spring-like weather' in another season). らしい describes something that fits the typical image of what it actually is, e.g. 春らしい天気 ('weather that's just like you'd expect in spring', when it is actually spring.).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About って感じ
text: って{感|かん}じ is a casual phrase which is used to say that something 'feels like' or has the 'vibe' of something. It is made up of the casual quotation marker って and the noun {感|かん}じ, meaning 'feeling'. Similar to ending a sentence with '...kind of thing', って{感|かん}じ tends to soften a statement and make it sound more indirect.
As this phrase uses the quotation marker って, grammatically, it can follow any type of word or phrase.
って{感|かん}じ is frequently used to wrap up a loose train of thought. A speaker may explain a situation and then add って{感|かん}じ to summarize the general gist or atmosphere of what they just said.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About にみえる
text: にみえる (primarily written only in hiragana) is a phrase that combines the case marking particle に, with the る-Verb {見|み}える 'to appear', or 'to be visible'. This construction is regularly used with nouns, to show that something 'appears to be (A)', but it may also be partnered with the auxiliary verbs ようだ or そうだ (in their adverbial forms ように and そうに) to add a level of uncertainty. In these cases, it sounds closer to 'to seem to be (A)' in English.

As with many other ようだ structures, みたい may be used instead. This creates the expression みたいにみえる. While this may appear confusing at first, it just means 'to look like something that could be (A)'. In this way it reinforces the 'guess' that the speaker is making.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: In grammar constructions like this, kanji will very rarely be used. This is primarily because it will change the way a native speaker perceives the meaning. Many grammar structures are written purely in hiragana, specifically to express that they are a 'set' construction. Adding kanji can lead a reader to assume that the writer is highlighting the kanji's meaning, rather than the more common grammatical meaning.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ～(の)姿 (N3, Figure, Shape, Appearance, Looks, Wearing, Dressed in, Presence): Both expressions relate to appearance, but with different nuance and usage. ～(の)姿 refers to someone's outward form, posture, or visual state, e.g. 彼女の頑張っている姿 ('The sight/figure of her working hard'), while ～ように見える expresses how something visually seems or appears to the speaker, e.g. 彼は悲しそうに見える ('He looks sad') or 葉っぱに見える ('It looks like a leaf').

とみえる (N4, It seems that, It can be deduced, One can conclude that): にみえる describes appearance based on what's visually perceived, e.g. 暑そうにみえる ('It looks hot.'). とみえる is used for logical inference based on context, as in 暑いとみえる ('It must be hot', e.g. if everyone's taking off their coats). The latter is less about sight, and more about reasoning.

ようだ (N4, It seems that, It appears that, It looks like): Both ようだ and に見える express observations, but differ in nuance. ようだ means 'appears to be' based on various cues, e.g. 虫のようだ ('It seems to be an insect.', based on looks, behavior, or context). に見える focuses specifically on visual appearance, e.g. 虫に見える ('It looks like an insect.'), without implying that the speaker thinks it actually is one.

がする (N4, To give off, Smell, Sound, Taste, Sensation): がする and にみえる (often written in kanji as に見える) both describe sensations, but differ in usage. がする is used with sensory words, e.g. 音がする 'I hear', 匂いがする 'I smell', and 味がする 'I taste' (literally, 'It gives off a sound/smell/taste.'). に見える specifically describes visual sensations and means 'looks like', e.g. 石に見える ('It looks like a rock.'), without implying that it is the thing it visually resembles.

そうに・そうな (N4, Seem, Look like, Sound): Both そうに・そうな and にみえる express appearance, but with different nuances. そうに・そうな conveys a subjective impression of a state, e.g. 優しそうな目 'kind-seeming eyes', or an event about to happen, e.g. 雨が降りそうな天気 'weather that seems like it's about to rain'. にみえる, used with そう or alone, e.g. 優しそうにみえる ('He/she seems kind.') or 虫にみえる ('It looks like a bug.'), specifically emphasizes visual appearance.

らしい ① (N4, Seems like, Apparently, I heard): Both らしい ① and にみえる can convey observations, but with different nuances. らしい ① implies hearsay or information from a third-party source, e.g. 雨が降るらしい ('Apparently it's going to rain.'). In contrast, にみえる expresses a direct visual observation, e.g. 雨が降るようにみえる ('It looks like it's going to rain.', based on visual cues like the sky).

みたい (N4, Like, Similar to, Resembling): にみえる and みたい both express that something 'seems' a certain way, but with different nuance. にみえる specifically refers to visual appearance, e.g. 'looks like', and can be used with そうだ or ようだ. みたい means 'is like' or 'seems like' more in a more general sense, not necessarily related to appearance, and is more casual than にみえる.

そう (N4, Look like, Appear, Seem, Have a feeling that): にみえる and そう both express that something 'seems' a certain way, but with different nuance. にみえる specifically refers to visual appearance and can be combined with そう, e.g. 面白そうにみえる ('It looks interesting.'). そう alone expresses general impression and doesn't necessarily rely on visual cues, e.g. 面白そう ('It seems interesting.'), which could be based on hearing about it, etc.

のように・のような (N4, Like (Noun), Similar to (Noun)): Both のように・のような and にみえる express how something 'appears,' but with different nuances. のように・のような is used for comparisons and connects to nouns or the rest of the sentence, e.g. 春のような天気 'spring-like weather'. にみえる specifically refers to visual appearance and can be used alone, e.g. その虫は葉っぱに見える ('That bug looks like a leaf.').

ように・ような (N4, As・like, Just like): ように・ような and にみえる can both describe similarities in appearance, but differ in usage. ように・ような follows the plain form of a verb or adjective and expresses general similarity. にみえる follows a noun or な-adjective (note: よう functions as a な-adjective) and means 'looks like'. The two can be used together, for example, 台風が来たように見える ('It looks as if a typhoon had come.').

meaning: It seems that, It can be deduced, One can conclude that
summary: An expression that makes a conclusion about the way that something appears.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About とみえる
text: とみえる (primarily written only in hiragana) is a phrase that combines the case marking particle と, with the る-Verb{見|み}える 'to appear', or 'to be visible'.

This use of the と particle in Japanese is called a result, and marks when (A) is something that has come to a conclusion, or can be concluded. In this way とみえる literally means 'from the way it appears, one can conclude that it's (A)'. However, this translates a bit more smoothly as 'it can be deduced that (A)', or 'it seems that (A)'.
This expression is always used directly after the phrase that it is drawing as a conclusion. However, nouns and な-Adjectives will require だ before とみえる.

While this phrase is conjecture (making a guess about something), it usually implies that the speaker has done some sort of research, or has some reason that led them to 'draw (A) as a conclusion'. Due to this, it appears reasonably confident.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: らしい ① (N4, Seems like, Apparently, I heard): らしい ① and にみえる both express observations, but differ in nuance and formality. らしい ① suggests hearsay or information from a third-party source, e.g. 知っていたらしい ('Apparently he/she knew.'). In contrast, とみえる is more formal and expresses the speaker's deduction based on evidence, e.g. 知っていたと見える ('It appears he/she knew.', as if drawing a conclusion based on evidence).

ようだ (N4, It seems that, It appears that, It looks like): Both ようだ and と見える express observations, but differ in nuance and formality. ようだ is commonly used to say something appears a certain way, based on various cues. と見える is more formal or literary and implies a deduction based on specific evidence, which is usually mentioned, e.g. 慌てているところを見ると、何かあったと見える ('Judging by how flustered he looks, something must've happened.').

にみえる (N4, To look, To seem, To appear): にみえる describes appearance based on what's visually perceived, e.g. 暑そうにみえる ('It looks hot.'). とみえる is used for logical inference based on context, as in 暑いとみえる ('It must be hot', e.g. if everyone's taking off their coats). The latter is less about sight, and more about reasoning.

summary: A suffix highlighting that something is in the style or air of (A).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 風
text: {風|ふう} is a suffix that is used in Japanese to convey the meaning of 'in the style of (A)', or 'in the fashion of (A)'. Literally, this translates to 'in the wind of (A)', which is just the Japanese way of expressing the former statements.
To use {風|ふう}, attach it to the end of a noun that you want to label something as being in the 'style' of.
の may also be attached to the end of {風|ふう}, before connecting it to another noun. This will show that '(B) is in the style of (A)'.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: As a compound structure, this suffix is always pronounced ふう, never かぜ (the standard reading of {風|かぜ}).

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: 風 is read "ふう", not "かぜ"

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: Noun＋型 (N3, Model, Type, Pattern, Kind, Shape, Size(d)): Both describe style or appearance, but with different nuance. 型 refers to a concrete type, model, or category, e.g. 新型のスマホ ('A new model of smartphone') 風 suggests resemblance or outward style, often subjective or superficial, e.g. 昔風の家 ('A house in the old-fashioned style')

らしい ② (N4, typical of, -ish・like, appropriate for, becoming of, befitting): 風 and らしい② both express resemblance but differ in nuance. 風 means something has the 'air' or appearance of a type, e.g. 日本風建築 'Japanese-style architecture'. らしい② implies it embodies the ideal of that category, e.g. 日本らしい建築 implies 'quintessential Japanese architecture'.

的 (N3, ~ly・~like・~al, Typical): 風 (ふう) and 的 (てき) are suffixes that turn nouns into descriptors. 風 suggests a style or 'air,' and is more limited in use, e.g. 日本風 or 和風 'Japanese-style'. 的 is broader, used for both adjectives and adverbs, e.g. 感情的 'emotional' and 定期的に 'regularly'.

ように・ような (N4, As・like, Just like): 風 (ふう) and ように・ような both express resemblance. 風 attaches directly to nouns, e.g. アメリカ風料理 'American-style food', while ような requires の before nouns, e.g. ハンバーガーのような料理 'food like a hamburger'. 風 often has a more stylistic nuance, while ような is a more neutral comparison.

みたいに・みたいな (N4, Like, Similar to, Resembling): 風 (ふう) and みたいに・みたいな both express resemblance or appearance. 風 attaches directly to nouns, e.g. アメリカ風料理 'American-style food' and can sound more formal. みたいな also attaches to nouns, but is more casual and makes a more straightforward comparison, e.g. ハンバーガーみたいな料理 = 'food like a hamburger'.

meaning: Can see, Can be seen, Can observe, Can be observed, Be evident, Chance to see something
summary: A grammar point indicating that (A) can be observed, given the right opportunity or ability of the viewer.
formation: Noun + が(1) + 見（み）られる
Noun + が(1) + 見（み）られます (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About がみられる
text: Unlike {見|み}える 'to be visible', which focuses on whether something can be seen or not, {見|み}られる (the potential form of {見|み}る) focuses on the viewer's physical ability to see something. Due to this が{見|み}られる is used to highlight things that require some form of 'effort' to see, like 'changes', 'trends', etc.

As a result of the 'effort' that is required, が{見|み}られる is often translated as 'for (A) to be evident', 'it can be observed that (A)', 'it can be seen that (A)', and other similar structures. To use {見|み}られる, simply add it after the noun that you would like to show as being 'evident'.

As られる is both the potential and passive form of {見|み}る, it may be interpreted either way. However, in the case of ラ{抜|ぬ}き{言葉|ことば} (ら removed verbs), only {可能|かのう} (possibility) may be expressed, not {受|う}け{身|み} (passivity).

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: 見える (N4, To be visible, To seem, To be in sight): Both みられる and 見える mean 'can see' (potential form) but differ in nuance. 見える means something is visible, while 見られる refers to the ability to watch or view. For example, stars on a clear night would be 見える, but being able to watch a movie on a streaming service would be 見られる.

summary: A way to highlight that someone's attention has been drawn to (A).
formation: Verb + こと(1) + に気（き）がつく
Verb + こと(1) + に気（き）がつきます (polite)
Noun + に気（き）がつきます (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About にきがつく
text: に{気|き}が{付|つ}く is a common expression that highlights when someone 'notices that (A)', or 'realizes that (A)'. {付|つ}く 'to be attached' is the intransitive form of {付|つ}ける 'to attach', meaning that it is something that happens by itself. The case marking particle に marks the 'location' to where your {気|き} (sometimes interpreted as 'attention') becomes attached.
This structure may be used after nouns, or verbs that have been nominalized with either の, or こと.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: There are many different translations for {気|き} in English. These can range from 'spirit', to 'attention', to 'will', or even 'consciousness'. However, perhaps one of the most accurate ways to translate {気|き}, is 'presence of mind'. The 'location' to which your focus, attention, or perception is drawn, will always highlight your {気|き}.

formation: Noun (A) + でも + Noun (B) + でも

Noun (A) + でも + Noun (B) + でも + Phrase［ない］

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 〜でも 〜でも
text: When the adverbial particle でも is used more than once in a sequence, it is an extension of one of its regular meanings, analogical reasoning. However, several 'analogies' are being presented.
This use of でも is regularly translated as 'whether it is (A), or (B)', or 'neither (A) nor (B)', depending on whether the rest of the phrase is positive, or negative.
Literally, the translation of 〜でも〜でも is closer to the following:
Even if it's (A), even if it's (B), (C) is the result. (In a positive sentence)
Even if it's (A), even if it's (B), (C) is not the result. (In a negative sentence)

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: かどうか (N4, Whether or not, If...or not): かどうか expresses uncertainty, as in 来るかどうか分からない ('I don't know whether or not they'll come.'). 〜でも〜でも lists multiple alternatives and suggests the outcome is unchanged. For example, 雨でも晴れでも行く ('Whether it rains or shines, I'll go.').

にしろ～にしろ (N2, Whether… or): 〜でも〜でも and にしろ～にしろ both express 'whether it's (A) or (B)'. にしろ～にしろ sounds a bit more formal and hypothetical and works with a wider range of grammar, including verbs. Both forms show that the result or evaluation doesn't change regardless of the options given.

にしても～にしても (N2, Regardless of whether): 〜でも〜でも and にしても～にしても both show multiple options and that the result doesn't change. にしても～にしても has a slightly more hypothetical tone and works with verbs as well as nouns, e.g. 犬にしても猫にしても大変だ ('Whether it's a dog or cat, it's tough.').

～ても～なくても (N3, Whether ~ or not): 〜でも〜でも and ～ても～なくても both express 'whether or not'. 〜でも〜でも shows multiple possibilities, e.g. クッキーでもケーキでも甘いものは食べたい ('I want sweets, whether it's cookies or cake.'). ～ても～なくても shows opposition, e.g. 行っても行かなくても大丈夫 ('It's okay whether you go or not.').

summary: A phrase used for giving additional information, by stating on that which was said, or to that which was said.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About それに
text: The conjunction それに is regularly considered to be one word in Japanese, but is more correctly just a combination of the pronoun それ, and the case marking particle に.

The thing that それ is 'substituting' for is the entire clause/sentence that came before it, while に highlights that extra information is about to be added. In this way, it translates to 'and to that', or 'and on that', where 'that' is the previous information. Often, it is translated simply as 'moreover', 'in addition', or 'and'.

Because それに is 'adding' information with に, the (B) information itself must be something that would logically happen 'in addition to (A)', or 'as a result of (A)'. Therefore, それに will highlight something that has either all positive, or all negative connotations. Never both.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: しかも (N2, Moreover, Furthermore): それに and しかも both add information, but しかも is stronger. それに is neutral: it adds a point that logically follows. しかも emphasizes what comes next, like 'what's more' or 'on top of that', e.g. 安い。それに美味しい。しかも体にいい ('It's cheap. And tasty. And what's more, it's good for your body.').

その上 (N2, Besides, In addition, Furthermore): それに and その上 both add information. それに is neutral and casual. その上 has a slightly more formal tone and implies building upon the previous statement, e.g. 彼は優秀だ。その上、性格もいい ('He's capable, and what's more, he's kind too.').

おまけに (N2, In addition, On top of that, What is more, To make matters worse): それに and おまけに both add information. それに is neutral and just adds a point that logically follows. おまけに adds something extra or unexpected, often with a tone of surprise or bonus, e.g. おいしかったし、おまけに安かった ('It was delicious, and cheap too!').

なお② (N2, In addition, Incidentally, Furthermore, Moreover): なお② and それに both add information, but differ in tone. それに is neutral and used in everyday speech. なお② is formal and often written, with a tone of explanation or emphasis, e.g. 商品の仕様は変更される場合があります。なお、返品はできません ('The product specifications may be changed. Furthermore, returns are not accepted.').

すると (N3, Having done..., If...is done..., (And/just) then, Thereupon, If so): すると and それに are both sentence starters but differ in usage. すると shows result or reaction, e.g. 雨が降った。すると傘を差した ('It started raining. Then he opened an umbrella.'). それに is additive and neutral: 雨が降っていた。それに寒かった ('It was raining. And cold too.').

また (N4, Also, As well, Moreover, Again, Additionally): Both それに and また can be used to provide added information, like the English 'in addition' or 'moreover', but with slightly different nuances. また has a slightly formal tone, and adds information in a neutral sense. それに is more colloquial and has the nuance of adding information that supports or reinforces the previous statement.

meaning: Because of that, So?, And then?, Therefore, With that
summary: A casual sentence starter used either to explain the result of what was said previously, or ask what happened with that.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About それで
text: Like それに, それで is another conjunction that is regularly considered to be one word in Japanese, but is more correctly just a combination of the pronoun それ, and the case marking particle で.

The thing that それ is 'substituting' for is the entire clause/sentence that came before it, while で highlights that 'with that', or 'by means of that'. In this way, it translates to 'therefore', 'because of that', or 'with that' where 'that' is the previous information. それで is frequently used at the beginning of a second sentence, to highlight the information from the first.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: そのため(に) (N3, For that reason, Because of that, To that end): そのため(に) and それで both show cause and effect. それで is casual and used in everyday speech: 道が混んでた。それで遅れた ('The road was crowded, so I was late.'). そのため is more formal and can also express purpose, e.g. 健康のため、運動している 'I'm exercising for my health.').

summary: A particle used to highlight questions or statements of uncertainty within longer sentences.
formation: Question Word + か + わかる(1)
(1) 覚（おぼ）える、決（き）める、知（し）っている and so on

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About Question-phrase + か
text: Often, the adverbial particle か is used in the middle of a sentence, in the same way that it is as a sentence ending particle. The main differences are as follows:
Adverbial Particle: {副助詞|ふくじょし} - Highlights uncertain things '{不確|ふたし}かであること'. This is the same か as in どこか 'somewhere'.
Sentence Ending Particle: {終助詞|しゅうじょし} - Highlights doubts and questions '{疑問|ぎもん}や{質問|しつもん}'. This is a direct question.
In the case of the adverbial particle か and 'uncertain things', this will almost always be followed by a word that is seeking information about the uncertain thing.

As can be seen in these examples, sometimes the adverbial particle will appear by itself, and sometimes it will appear together with the sentence ending particle in the same sentence. However, due to the 'uncertainty' being displayed by the adverbial particle, the question marker at the end of the sentence is not required.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: This か should not be preceded by だ (or です), this is why words like どこか and {誰|だれ}か are not どこだか and {誰|だれ}だか.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Do not attach だ or です to nouns or な-adjectives preceding か

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: 誰か・どこか・誰も・どこも (N5, Someone, Somewhere, Not anyone, Not anywhere): The 誰か・どこか・誰も・どこも pattern combines question words like 誰 ('who') and どこ ('where') with particles to express ideas like 'someone' or 'somewhere.' These forms are also related to how the particle か is used with question phrases in embedded questions. For example, 誰が来るか分かりますか？ means 'Do you know who will come?'

か (N5, Or): Both uses of か are extensions of its basic function as a question particle. When following a Wh-question word (like who, what, where, why, how), it creates a phrase meaning 'some-(word)' (e.g., 誰か = 'someone,' どこか = 'somewhere,' いつか = 'sometime'). When following regular nouns, it means 'or' (e.g., 今日か明日休みます = 'I'll take off today or tomorrow').

か〜ないかのうちに (N2, Right after, As soon as, Just when, Barely): Question-phrase + か embeds a question, e.g. 来るか分からない ('I don't know if they're coming.'). か〜ないかのうちに expresses something happening immediately at a moment of uncertainty, e.g. 来るか来ないかのうちに 'just as they arrived'.

なにか・なにも (N5, Something, Nothing, Anything, Not anything, Some kind of, Not any kind of): The なにか・なにも pattern combines the question word なに with particles to express ideas like 'something' or 'nothing.' This structure is based on how the particle か is used with question words within a sentence. For example, 何が食べたいか分かりますか？ means 'Do you know what (they) want to eat?'

かどうか (N4, Whether or not, If...or not): Both are embedded question forms. A question phrase plus か makes an indirect question, like 何時に来るか分からない ('I don't know what time they'll come'). かどうか focuses specifically on yes/no questions, like 来るかどうか分からない ('I don't know whether or not they'll come.').
