meaning: But still, And yet, Even so, Nevertheless
summary: An expression that highlights that despite the previous statement, something still occurs.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About それでも
text: それでも is a combination of the pronoun それ, and the adverbial particle でも. It is often translated simply as 'even so', or 'nevertheless'. Literally, it is a bit closer to 'even with that'.
それでも is usually used between an (A) and a (B) phrase, to show that there is more information (usually surprising) to be considered.
This grammar point primarily expresses that 'even with' what has been said previously, it is not all there is to think about.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: のに (N4, Despite, Although, Even though): のに expresses contrast, similar to 'although,' and follows verbs, adjectives, or nouns (with な for nouns and な-adjectives). It's typically used at the end of a clause or sentence. それでも also shows contrast, but appears at the beginning of a sentence. The それ refers to the previous statement, giving it the meaning of 'Even so' or 'But still.'

ところが (N3, Even so, However, Even though, But): それでも and ところが both show contrast, like 'even so' or 'and yet'. それでも has a neutral tone and simply adds something that goes against the previous statement. ところが implies something unexpected or surprising happened, especially outside the speaker's control.

だって (N3, I heard/was said, Because, But, Even or also, Even if or even though): だって and それでも both express contradiction. だって is casual and often used at the start of a sentence to offer an objection, e.g., だって疲れたもん ('But I'm tired!'). それでも is less casual and shows contrast with a neutral tone, e.g., 雨だった。それでも行った ('It was rainy, but I still went.').

それにしても (N2, Nevertheless, Even so): それでも and それにしても both express contrast. それでも adds a contradictory point neutrally. それにしても accepts the previous idea, but adds what the speaker really thinks, often a more critical or stronger opinion, e.g., 暑いね。それにしてもよく歩くね ('It's hot. Still, you sure walk a lot.').

くせに (N3, Even though, And yet, Despite): それでも and くせに both express contrast, but differ in tone. それでも is neutral, like the English 'even so'. くせに adds a critical nuance, often pointing out something negative or unjustified, e.g. 若いくせにやる気がない ('Even though he's young, he has no motivation.'), which implies disapproval.

それなのに (N2, And yet, Despite this): それでも and それなのに both show contrast. それでも means 'even so' and sounds neutral, e.g. 雨だった。それでも行った ('It was rainy, but I went anyway.'). それなのに has a stronger emotional tone, often of disbelief or disapproval, e.g. 優しくした。それなのに怒られた ('I was nice and still got yelled at!').

だが・ですが (N4, But, Still, However, Nevertheless): Both それでも and だが・ですが express contrast, similar to 'but' or 'however' in English, but with different nuances. それでも highlights a result or situation that goes against expectations. だが・ですが is more neutral and often used to transition to a contrasting point. Structurally, だが・ですが can appear mid-sentence or at the end of a clause, while それでも typically begins a sentence.

しかしながら (N2, However, Nevertheless, But): しかしながら and それでも both mean 'however' or 'nevertheless'. but differ in formality. しかしながら is very formal, often seen in academic or business writing. それでも is used in conversation and everyday writing. Both acknowledge one fact, then present a contrasting one.

meaning: Why don't you...?, What if you did...?
summary: A casual, sometimes sarcastic way to suggest that someone do (A). When doing (A), how 'bout that?
formation: Verb［たら］+ どう + です + か。 (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About たらどう
text: When the conjunction particle たら is used before the adverb どう, it primarily presents a situation, then asks a question about it potentially happening. This construction can be translated as 'why don't you (A)?', or 'what if you did (A)?'. Realistically, it just means 'when (A), how about that?'. It is often used for giving advice.
To use this expression, convert the verb that you want to use into its たら form, and then add どう.
Sometimes たら is used by itself, with a tone that implies that it is a question (or simply by adding a question mark in written language). This is an abbreviation of たらどう, and carries the same nuance.
だ or か may be added to the end of たらどう, to emphasize the 'question' even further. However, they are not required.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: It can be further contracted to たら by itself in very casual conversations.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: 命令形 (N4, (Verb)!, Do (something)!): The imperative or command form (命令形) is used for blunt orders, e.g. 止まれ ('Stop!'), which can be harsh. In contrast, たらどう is a soft suggestion, similar to 'Why don't you (A)?' in English, e.g. 行ってみたらどう？ ('Why don't you try going?'). It gives the listener more freedom and therefore sounds more gentle.

ませんか (N5, Won't you, Would you not, Why don't we): ませんか is a polite way to extend an invitation, similar to 'Won't you…?' or 'Wouldn't you like to...?' in English. In contrast, たらどう has a stronger tone and is used to suggest or advise a course of action. For example, 何か食べませんか？ is a polite offer (e.g. to a guest), while 何か食べたらどう？ implies the speaker thinks the listener should eat something.

たらいい・といい (N3, It would be nice if, It would be good if, Should, I hope): たらどう is a gentle, open-ended suggestion, e.g. 休んだらどう？('Why don't you take a break?'). たらいい・といい can also suggest, but sounds more like advice, e.g. 休んだらいいよ ('You should take a break.'). It can also express hope, like 雨が止むといいね = 'I hope the rain stops.'.

たほうがいい (N5, It'd be better to, Should do): Both たらどう and たほうがいい can be used to give advice or suggestions. The key difference is that たほうがいい has a strong nuance that the speaker is advising the listener on what to do or what would be the best course of action ('You should...'), while たらどう is more gentle, as if suggesting a potential option but not strongly insisting on it ('How about if you...?')

たら (N4, When, From when, Just when, If): たら expresses a condition or hypothetical, and when combined with どう, forms a casual suggestion. For example, 散歩に行ったらどう？ means 'How about going for a walk?'. Similar to the English phrase 'Why don't you (A)?' or 'How about (A)?', it isis common in informal conversation.

slug: とかんがえられている
pattern: とかんがえられている
reading: と{考|かんが}えられている
meaning: Is considered, Is thought of as
summary: A way of expressing that something is often thought of as (A), or considered as (A).
formation: Phrase + と考（かんが）えられている
Phrase + と思（おも）われている
Phrase + と考（かんが）えられています (polite)
Phrase + と思（おも）われています (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About とかんがえられている
text: In its citation usage, the case marking particleと is often used with verbs in the passive form. Two of these regularly occurring verbs are {考|かんが}えられている 'to be considered', and {思|おも}われている 'to be thought'.

This grammar point is used after a phrase, and translates as 'it is considered that (A)', or 'it is thought that (A)'. It is generally used to highlight a commonly held opinion that most people agree on (not your personal opinion).
The primary reason that these constructions are used in their displacement (passive) form, is to show that the thought itself is not something that is related to the speaker's own opinions.
However, people will often use this form as a way to strengthen their own opinions, in a similar way to how English speakers would say 'everyone knows that (A)'.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: と考えられる (N2, Can be considered as, Is thought to be, One can think that, It is conceivable that): と考えられる and と考えられている are similar but differ slightly in nuance. と考えられる means 'it can be considered (A)' and implies a basis in evidence or reasoning. On the other hand と考えられている suggests something is a commonly held belief or consensus, like the English 'it is (generally) thought that (A)'.

といわれている (N4, It is said that, Is known as): といわれている 'it is said' and とかんがえられている 'it is thought' both soften a statement and make it feel more objective or widely accepted. This can make an idea sound more trustworthy or backed by others. Both are formal and common in writing.

～は～となっている (N3, It is (has been), Have/has become, Happen to be, Has been established): ～は～となっている and と考えられている both express current states or views, but differ in tone. ～は～となっている describes some sort of established fact that is now 'the way things are', e.g. 店は日曜休業となっている ('The store is closed on Sundays'). と考えられている expresses a generally held belief or reasoning and is often used to make a statement sound less direct, e.g. 彼は天才だと考えられている ('He is thought to be a genius').

とされている (N4, To be considered, To be deemed, Be regarded as, Be accepted as, To be said, To be accredited with): とされている and とかんがえられている both mean 'It is believed/considered (A)' and are used to present ideas objectively. Both make statements sound more neutral or widely accepted, often in formal writing, academic papers, or news reports.

考えられない (N3, Unthinkable, Inconceivable, Unimaginable, Cannot think): These two forms of the verb 考える express opposite sentiments. 考えられない (lit. 'one cannot think') expresses strong disbelief or the idea that something is inconceivable, e.g. 'そんなことは考えられない' ('I can't imagine such a thing'). In contrast, と考えられている indicates a commonly accepted or reasoned belief, often used in formal writing to make statements less direct, e.g. 'これは効果的だと考えられている' ('This is considered effective').

meaning: To be considered, To be deemed, Be regarded as, Be accepted as, To be said, To be accredited with
summary: An expression highlighting that something is considered or accepted as (A). It presupposes that (A) is true.
formation: Noun + （だ） + とされています (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About とされている
text: とされている is an expression that is commonly translated as 'to be considered as (A)', or 'to be regarded as (A)'. Conceptually, it is similar to にする, which means 'to decide on (A)'. However, due to する being in the passive form in this construction, it is closer to 'to be decided on', and expresses the general opinions/thoughts of large groups of people.
The と in this expression is a case marking particle, and expresses the result nuance of this particle.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ということだ (N3, I heard that, Rumor has it that, It is said that, It means that): とされている and ということだ both report other people's opinions. ということだ has a nuance of direct hearsay: 'They say that (A)'. On the other hand, とされている presents something as generally believed or accepted. It's less about quoting someone and more about shared public perception.

とかんがえられている (N4, Is considered, Is thought of as): とされている and とかんがえられている both mean 'It is believed/considered (A)' and are used to present ideas objectively. Both make statements sound more neutral or widely accepted, often in formal writing, academic papers, or news reports.

～は～となっている (N3, It is (has been), Have/has become, Happen to be, Has been established): Both present an accepted state or fact, but differ in nuance. ～は～となっている describes that something has been established and is now 'the way things are', e.g. 朝礼は毎朝１０時開始となっている ('The morning meeting is set to start every day at 10 a.m'). とされている conveys that it is generally regarded in a certain way or as something, e.g. この神社は最古のものとされている ('This shrine is considered the oldest one').

meaning: It is said that, Is known as
summary: A grammar point that highlights a whole phrase as often being said, or as a common opinion.
formation: Phrase + といわれています (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About といわれている
text: といわれている is often translated as 'to be said that (A)', or 'it is known that (A)'. Like とされている, it is another construction that links the case marking particleと, with the passive form of another verb, to mark a commonly held/public opinion. The verb in this case being {言|い}う.

However, unlike とされている which expresses a 'result', といわれている expresses {引用|いんよう} a 'quotation'. To use といわれている, add it to the end of a phrase that you would like to express as being a common thing that is said.
This particular grammar point is regularly seen both with, and without the kanji for {言|い}う, as the meaning will not change depending on its usage.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: とかんがえられている (N4, Is considered, Is thought of as): といわれている 'it is said' and とかんがえられている 'it is thought' both soften a statement and make it feel more objective or widely accepted. This can make an idea sound more trustworthy or backed by others. Both are formal and common in writing.

という (N3, Called, Named, Known as, As much as): という is versatile: AというB = 'a (B) called (A)' or to show hearsay, e.g. 面白いという本 'a book said to be interesting'. といわれている is more formal and emphasizes that something is generally said or believed by many people, especially in written or academic contexts.

そうだ (N3, I heard that, It is said that): といわれている and そうだ both report something heard, but differ in nuance. といわれている is more general and formal, e.g. 'It is said that (A)'. On the other hand, そうだ often implies someone specific said it and is more casual, e.g., 雨が降るそうだ ('I heard it's going to rain.').

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ばよかった
text: ばよかった is a common expression used when someone regrets that something has not been/was not done. It is a pairing of the conjunction particle ば, and the past form of the い-Adjective, {良|い}い (remembering that conjugations of いい use よ, and not い). This construction is often translated to 'I wish I did (A)', or 'I should have done (A)'.
ばよかった is used after verbs, so requires the standard ば conjugation, before adding よかった.
As ば highlights hypothetical situations, ばよかった literally means that 'it would have been good if (A)', where (A) is the thing that the speaker wishes had happened.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: たらいい・といい (N3, It would be nice if, It would be good if, Should, I hope): ばよかった and たらいい・といい are similar in that both express the speaker's wish or hope. ばよかった is used when expressing regret over something that happened (or didn't happen) in the past, e.g. 行けばよかった ('I wish I had gone.') which implies 'but I didn't'. In contrast, たらいい・といい typically expresses something the speaker hopes will happen in the future, e.g. 明日晴れるといいけど ('I hope it's sunny tomorrow.').

てよかった (N4, I'm glad that): Though they may look similar, てよかった and ばよかった express opposite feelings. てよかった conveys relief or happiness about something that happened, e.g. 行ってよかった ('I'm glad I went.' or literally 'It was good that I went.'). In contrast, ばよかった expresses regret about something that didn't happen, e.g., 行けばよかった ('I wish I had gone.' or literally, 'It would have been nice if I went.').

questions.ja: この{漢字|かんじ}の{意味|いみ}があまり{分|わ}からないので、{先生|せんせい}に（　　）。
questions.en: I do not really understand the meaning of this kanji. I should have asked the teacher about it.
questions.audio: https://dk3kgylsgq3k1.cloudfront.net/audio/grammar/n4/この漢字の意味があまり分からないので、先生に聞けば良かった。.mp3

questions.ja: クリスマスにＮｉｎｔｅｎｄｏ（ニンテンドー）スイッチが{欲|ほ}しかったら、そう（　　）。
questions.en: If you wanted a Nintendo Switch for Christmas, you should have said so.
